## Property: `packaging`

- Required: yes
- Type: `js-bundle | prebuilt-image | dockerfile | buildpack`

Configures the container image for the service.

Choices:
- `js-bundle` (`JsBundleCwImagePackaging`) — Builds a container image from a bundled JavaScript or TypeScript entry file.. Properties: `requiresGlibcBinaries?: boolean`, `customDockerBuildCommands?: Array<string>`, `runtime?: string: "bun" | "deno" | "node"`, `entryfilePath: string`, `includeFiles?: Array<string>`, `excludeFiles?: Array<string>`, `excludeDependencies?: Array<string>`, `tsConfigPath?: string`, `emitTsDecoratorMetadata?: boolean`, `dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle?: Array<string>`, `dependenciesToExcludeFromDeploymentPackage?: Array<string>`, `outputModuleFormat?: string: "cjs" | "esm"`, `nodeVersion?: number: 16 | 17 | 18 | 19 | 20 | 21 | 22 | 23 | 24`, `disableSourceMaps?: boolean`, `outputSourceMapsTo?: string`, `minify?: boolean`, `minifyIdentifiers?: boolean`, `bundleAwsSdk?: boolean`.
- `prebuilt-image` (`PrebuiltCwImagePackaging`) — Uses a pre-built container image.. Properties: `repositoryCredentialsSecretArn?: string`, `entryPoint?: Array<string>`, `image: string`, `command?: Array<string>`.
- `dockerfile` (`DockerfileCwImagePackaging`) — Builds a container image from your own Dockerfile.. Properties: `entryPoint?: Array<string>`, `dockerfilePath?: string`, `buildContextPath: string`, `buildArgs?: Array<DockerBuildArg>`, `command?: Array<string>`.
- `buildpack` (`BuildpackCwImagePackaging`) — Builds a container image from a project directory without a Dockerfile.. Properties: `sourceDirectoryPath?: string`, `startCommand?: string`, `buildCommand?: string`, `installCommand?: string`, `packages?: unknown`, `aptPackages?: Array<string>`, `buildEnvironment?: Array<EnvironmentVar>`, `railpackConfig?: unknown`.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `resources`

- Required: yes
- Type: `ContainerWorkloadResourcesConfig`

CPU, memory, and compute engine for the container.

Two compute engines:

**Fargate** (default): Serverless — just specify `cpu` and `memory`.
**EC2**: Specify `instanceTypes` for more control and potentially lower cost.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 2048
        architecture: arm64
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `connectTo`

- Required: no
- Type: `Array<string>`

Give this resource access to other resources in your stack.

List the names of resources this workload needs to communicate with. Stacktape automatically:

**Grants IAM permissions** (e.g., S3 read/write, SQS send/receive)
**Opens network access** (security group rules for databases, Redis)
**Injects environment variables** with connection details: `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]`

Example: `connectTo: ["myDatabase", "myBucket"]` gives this workload full access to both
resources and injects `STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`, `STP_MY_BUCKET_NAME`, etc.

 What each resource type provides:

**`Bucket`** — read/write/delete objects → `NAME`, `ARN`

**`DynamoDbTable`** — CRUD + scan/query → `NAME`, `ARN`, `STREAM_ARN`

**`RelationalDatabase`** — network access + connection details → `CONNECTION_STRING`, `HOST`, `PORT`.
Aurora also gets `READER_CONNECTION_STRING`, `READER_HOST`.

**`MongoDbAtlasCluster`** — temporary credential-less access → `CONNECTION_STRING`

**`Redis`** — network access → `HOST`, `READER_HOST`, `PORT`

**`Function`** — invoke permission → `ARN`

**`BatchJob`** — submit/list/terminate → `JOB_DEFINITION_ARN`, `STATE_MACHINE_ARN`

**`EventBus`** — publish events → `ARN`

**`UserAuthPool`** — full control → `ID`, `CLIENT_ID`, `ARN`

**`SqsQueue`** — send/receive/delete → `ARN`, `NAME`, `URL`

**`SnsTopic`** — publish/subscribe → `ARN`, `NAME`

**`UpstashRedis`** → `HOST`, `PORT`, `PASSWORD`, `REST_TOKEN`, `REST_URL`, `REDIS_URL`

**`PrivateService`** → `ADDRESS`

**`EmailSender`** — scoped SES sending permission → `IDENTITY`, `IDENTITY_ARN`, `REGION`, `CONFIGURATION_SET_NAME`

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
      connectTo:
        - mainDb
        - uploads
  mainDb:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      credentials:
        masterUserPassword: $Secret('db-password')
      engine:
        type: postgres
        properties:
          version: '16'
          primaryInstance:
            instanceSize: db.t4g.micro
  uploads:
    type: bucket
    properties: {}
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `enableRemoteSessions`

- Required: no
- Type: `boolean`
- Default: `false`

Allow SSH-like access to running containers for debugging.

Enables `stacktape container shell` to open an interactive shell inside the container.
Adds a small SSM agent that uses minimal CPU/memory.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      enableRemoteSessions: true
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `environment`

- Required: no
- Type: `Array<EnvironmentVar>`

Environment variables injected into the container at runtime.

Use for configuration like API keys, feature flags, or secrets.
Variables from `connectTo` (e.g., `STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`) are added automatically.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      environment:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          value: info
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: $ResourceParam('mainDb', 'connectionString')
      connectTo:
        - mainDb
  mainDb:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      credentials:
        masterUserPassword: $Secret('db-password')
      engine:
        type: postgres
        properties:
          version: '16'
          primaryInstance:
            instanceSize: db.t4g.micro
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `iamRoleStatements`

- Required: no
- Type: `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>`

Raw IAM policy statements for permissions not covered by `connectTo`.

Added as a separate policy alongside auto-generated permissions. Use this for
accessing AWS services directly (e.g., Rekognition, Textract, Bedrock).

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  processor:
    type: batch-job
    properties:
      container:
        packaging:
          type: js-bundle
          properties:
            entryfilePath: src/job.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 2048
      iamRoleStatements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action:
            - textract:AnalyzeDocument
          Resource:
            - '*'
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `internalHealthCheck`

- Required: no
- Type: `ContainerHealthCheck`

Health check that auto-replaces unhealthy containers.

If a container fails the health check, it's terminated and replaced automatically.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      internalHealthCheck:
        healthCheckCommand:
          - CMD-SHELL
          - curl -f http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
        intervalSeconds: 30
        retries: 3
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `logging`

- Required: no
- Type: `ContainerWorkloadContainerLogging`

Logging configuration.

Container output (`stdout`/`stderr`) is automatically sent to CloudWatch and retained for 90 days.
View logs with `stacktape logs` or in the Stacktape Console.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      logging:
        retentionDays: 30
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `releaseCommand`

- Required: no
- Type: `ReleaseCommand | option-2`

Run a command once on each deploy, in the deployed image, before any workload gets the new code.

Use it for database migrations. Stacktape runs the command in a one-off ECS task with the same image, environment
variables, secrets, IAM role and network access as this service. The deploy waits for the task, prints its logs, and
stops if the command fails, so the running version keeps serving.

The old code keeps running against the new schema until the rollout finishes, so migrations must stay compatible
with it. A retry runs the command again, so it must be idempotent. Neither a failed deploy nor `stacktape rollback`
reverses what the command changed.

Choices:
- `ReleaseCommand` (`ReleaseCommand`) — A command that runs once on each deploy, before any workload gets the new code.. Properties: `command: string`, `runWhenChanged?: Array<string>`, `timeout?: number`, `container?: string`.
- `option-2`

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
releaseCommand: npx prisma migrate deploy
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 2 (typescript)

```typescript
releaseCommand: {
  command: 'npx prisma migrate deploy',
  runWhenChanged: ['prisma/migrations']
}
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `scaling`

- Required: no
- Type: `ContainerWorkloadScaling`

Auto-scaling: add/remove container instances based on demand.

Traffic is automatically distributed across all running containers.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
      scaling:
        minInstances: 2
        maxInstances: 10
        scalingPolicy:
          keepAvgCpuUtilizationUnder: 70
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `sideContainers`

- Required: no
- Type: `Array<ServiceHelperContainer>`

Helper containers that run alongside the main container.

**`run-on-init`**: Runs to completion before the main container starts (e.g., database migrations).
**`always-running`**: Runs for the entire lifecycle (e.g., log forwarders, monitoring agents).
Can reach the main container via `localhost`.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `stopTimeout`

- Required: no
- Type: `number`
- Default: `30`

Seconds to wait for graceful shutdown before force-killing the container.

The container receives `SIGTERM` first, then `SIGKILL` after this timeout. Must be 2-120.

A full deploy waits until the old containers have stopped, so an app that ignores `SIGTERM` makes every deploy
up to this much slower. Exit once in-flight work is done. A hot-swap deploy lets old containers stop in the
background. Services with a gradual `deployment` (blue/green) default to 2 seconds.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      stopTimeout: 60
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `tracing`

- Required: no
- Type: `TracingOptions | option-2`

Distributed tracing for this service.

Overrides the stack-wide `stackConfig.tracing` setting: `false` opts this service out, `true`
opts it in with the stack-wide sampling, an object opts it in with its own settings.

When enabled, Stacktape runs an OpenTelemetry collector as a sidecar container and points the
service's OpenTelemetry SDK at it (`http://localhost:4318`) through standard `OTEL_*`
environment variables. The service needs the OpenTelemetry SDK in the application (any
language) — spans it emits are picked up without further configuration.

Traces are stored in your AWS account via X-Ray Transaction Search; see `stackConfig.tracing`
for the account-level effects.

Choices:
- `TracingOptions` (`TracingOptions`). Properties: `enabled?: boolean`, `samplingRate?: number`.
- `option-2`

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
stackConfig:
  tracing:
    enabled: true
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
      tracing:
        samplingRate: 0.5
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `usePrivateSubnetsWithNAT`

- Required: no
- Type: `boolean`
- Default: `false`

Run the workload in the private subnets, without a public IP, with outbound traffic through the stack's NAT.

What you get: the container has no public IP, and all of its outbound internet traffic leaves through the stack's
NAT with one static Elastic IP per availability zone (useful when a third party allowlists your IPs).

Requires `stackConfig.nat` (`ec2`, `ha-ec2` or `gateway`); the cost depends on that choice, and `gateway` adds a
per-GB processing fee on top. Workloads that only talk to AWS services and other stack resources do not need it.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
stackConfig:
  nat: ha-ec2
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      usePrivateSubnetsWithNAT: true
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
## Property: `volumeMounts`

- Required: no
- Type: `Array<ContainerEfsMount>`

Persistent EFS volumes shared across containers and restarts.

Data stored in EFS volumes persists even when containers are replaced.
Multiple containers can mount the same volume. All data is encrypted in transit.

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
docs.content:
### Example 1 (yaml)

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
      volumeMounts:
        - type: efs
          properties:
            efsFilesystemName: sharedData
            mountPath: /data
  sharedData:
    type: efs-filesystem
    properties: {}
```

docs.title: WorkerServiceProps API Reference
Build runners
docs.content:
# Build runners

A runner is an EC2 instance in your AWS account that builds and deploys a project for the Stacktape Console. Each
project gets one runner per AWS account and region it deploys to from Git. It keeps a build cache between deploys and
stops when it has nothing to do.

A runner runs:

- [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console): pushes, pull request previews and their deletion;
- `stacktape deploy --runner ec2`, when you want the build to run in AWS instead of on your machine;
- [GitHub Actions jobs](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners), when you turn them on for the project;
- AI runs you start from an incident.

Deploys from your terminal and from [your own pipeline](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd) build on that machine and
don't need a runner.

docs.title: Build runners
docs.content:
## When it starts and stops

Stacktape creates a project's runner the first time it needs one, usually when you create the project's first Git
deployment. A job starts the stopped instance and reuses its cache. After the runner has been idle for 15 minutes,
Stacktape stops it. Instances that support EC2 hibernation hibernate instead, so they resume faster.

The idle time is a setting: from 5 minutes to 24 hours, or **Keep running**. A runner that keeps running has no start
delay and bills compute all the time.

A runner runs up to two deployments at once, plus up to two background jobs (GitHub Actions jobs and AI runs). More
work waits for a free slot.

docs.title: Build runners
docs.content:
## What it costs

AWS bills your account for:

- EC2 compute while the instance runs, including the idle time before it stops;
- its two EBS disks all the time, also while it is stopped;
- ordinary data transfer and CloudWatch charges from its work.

The default disks are a 50 GiB system disk and a 50 GiB build cache disk, about $8.80 a month in Ireland at gp3 rates.
Larger instance sizes get a larger system disk for hibernation. The cache disk grows as the cache fills, up to the
**Build cache limit** (200 GiB by default). The **Runners** page shows each runner's estimated cost from AWS list
prices in its region.

The runner, its disks and its IAM role are deleted when you delete the project or its last Git deployment in that AWS
account and region, unless GitHub Actions jobs still use it.

docs.title: Build runners
docs.content:
## Settings

Open **Configuration → Runners** in the Console, select the project's runner and open its **Settings** tab.

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Instance size** | CPU and memory for builds. Bigger builds faster and costs more per hour. |
| **When idle** | How long the runner waits before it stops, or **Keep running**. |
| **Build cache limit** | The largest the cache disk grows, from 50 to 2,000 GiB. |
| **GitHub Actions** | Runs the repository's GitHub Actions jobs on this runner. See [Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners). |
| **Setup commands** | Shell commands each deployment runs before it builds. See below. |

Changes apply when the runner next prepares for work. A new size replaces the instance after its current work and
keeps the build cache.

docs.title: Build runners
docs.content:
### Instance sizes

| Instance size | vCPU | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| `m6a.large` | 2 | 8 GiB |
| `m6a.xlarge` | 4 | 16 GiB |
| `c7a.xlarge` | 4 | 8 GiB |
| `c7a.2xlarge` | 8 | 16 GiB |
| `c7a.4xlarge` | 16 | 32 GiB |
| `c7a.8xlarge` | 32 | 64 GiB |

**Automatic**, the default, is `c7a.2xlarge`. In regions without C7a instances it is `c6i.2xlarge`, which has the
same size. `c7a` suits CPU-heavy work such as compiling and building images; `m6a` has more memory per vCPU. Start with
the default and change it when build times or memory use say so.

docs.title: Build runners
docs.content:
### Setup commands

Setup commands run before `stacktape deploy`, in a fresh checkout of your code. Use them to install a tool the build
needs, point a package manager at a private registry, or export variables for the build (`export NAME=value`).

- **Every project:** Owners and Admins edit them with **Setup commands** at the top of the **Runners** page. They run
  first.
- **One project:** edit them on the runner's **Settings** tab. They run after the commands for every project.

The commands run in order in Bash as a user without root, so install tools into the home directory (for example
`pip install --user` or `npm install -g`). If a command fails, the deployment stops and its log shows the output.
Deletes, rollbacks and GitHub Actions jobs don't run setup commands. A line starting with `#` names the commands under
it, and a blank line starts a new group. Pin tool versions and don't print secrets.

docs.title: Build runners
docs.content:
## Build cache

The cache disk keeps package manager caches, Docker layers and build output between jobs, so unchanged dependencies
and images aren't downloaded or rebuilt. Deployments and GitHub Actions jobs keep separate caches.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
# Custom CI/CD

This page sets up a pipeline that runs [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) after your own steps, such as tests or a
manual approval. Any CI that runs shell commands works. If a push should simply deploy, with no steps before it,
[Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) need no pipeline file.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content: ## Authenticate the pipeline

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
### Without a Stacktape account

Give the job AWS credentials and don't set `STACKTAPE_API_KEY`. The CLI deploys to the AWS account the credentials
belong to. On GitHub Actions, use an IAM role that trusts GitHub's OIDC provider, so no AWS key is stored. See
[CI/CD without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli#cicd-without-an-account) for a complete workflow.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
### With the Console

Set `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` in the job. Deploys are then recorded in the Console, and Console features in your config work.

Use an organization key, not a personal one. A personal key acts as the person who created it and stops working when
they leave the organization. Owners and Admins create an organization key in the Console under **API keys** →
**Organization keys** → **New organization key**, with the Developer role limited to the projects and AWS accounts the
pipeline deploys. See [Organization keys for CI](/stacktape-console/api-keys#create-an-organization-key).

The CLI deploys into an AWS account connected to your organization:

- With one connected account, it uses that one.
- With several, pass `--aws-account <name>`.
- If the job also has AWS credentials, the CLI uses the connected account they belong to.

See [Choosing the account for a CLI command](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account#choosing-the-account-for-a-cli-command).

Store the key, or the AWS credentials, in your CI's secret store:

| CI | Where |
|---|---|
| GitHub Actions | Repository **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions** |
| GitLab CI | **Settings → CI/CD → Variables**, masked |
| Bitbucket Pipelines | **Repository settings → Repository variables**, secured |
| CircleCI | **Project Settings → Environment Variables** |

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
## The deploy command

```bash
npx stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

- **`--stage` and `--region`** pick the target. Pass both, so the target never depends on the worker's defaults. If
  the pipeline deploys more than one project, also pass `--project` or set the project name in each config.
- **`--yes`** approves what the CLI would otherwise ask about: an update that deletes or replaces a database or another
  stateful resource, a Console project that doesn't exist yet, and every `delete`. A CI job can't answer, so without
  `--yes` such a run stops with an error and changes nothing. A routine deploy never asks.
- **`--auto-rollback`** returns the stack to its last successful deployment when the deploy fails. By default a failed
  deploy keeps what it changed, and the next run continues from there. See [Rollbacks](/deployment-and-lifecycle/rollbacks).

The deploy installs your JavaScript dependencies from the lockfile itself (`npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`
and so on), so it needs no install step of its own. npm comes with Node.js. For pnpm, Yarn or Bun, install the package
manager in the job first.

To deploy to several regions, run the command once per region. Each region gets its own stack.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
### Docker in the job

Building a container image needs the Docker CLI with Buildx and a running Docker daemon. Every container workload needs
one (`js-bundle`, `buildpack` and `dockerfile` packaging), and so do Lambda functions with `buildpack` packaging and
some native dependencies of `js-bundle` functions. GitHub's hosted Ubuntu runners have Docker. The GitLab, Bitbucket
and CircleCI examples below run in a plain Node.js container without it, so as written they deploy only stacks that
need no Docker build. For anything else, give the job Docker the way your CI documents it:
[GitLab Docker-in-Docker](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/docker/using_docker_build/),
[the Bitbucket Docker service](https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/run-docker-commands-in-bitbucket-pipelines/)
or [CircleCI's machine executor or remote Docker](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/execute/building-docker-images/).

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
## GitHub Actions

Create `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`. The deploy job runs only after the tests pass:

```yaml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
headingPath: Deploys of production run one at a time.
docs.content:
# Deploys of production run one at a time.
concurrency:
  group: deploy-production

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - name: Deploy
        env:
          STACKTAPE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.STACKTAPE_API_KEY }}
        run: npx stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

With the `concurrency` group, a new run waits while another one deploys. GitHub keeps only the newest waiting run and
cancels older waiting ones, so after three quick pushes the middle one never deploys. That is usually what you want,
because the newest commit includes the others. To deploy every commit in order, add `queue: max` to the group.

To pin the CLI version the pipeline uses, replace `npx stacktape` with `npx stacktape@4.0.0`, or the version you
tested. Then a Stacktape release never changes what the pipeline does.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
headingPath: Deploys of production run one at a time.
docs.content:
### Pull request previews

One workflow deploys a stage for every pull request and deletes it when the pull request closes:

```yaml
name: Preview
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, closed]

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
headingPath: One group per pull request keeps its deploys and the delete in order.
docs.content:
# One group per pull request keeps its deploys and the delete in order.
concurrency:
  group: preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}

jobs:
  deploy:
    if: github.event.action != 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - name: Deploy preview
        env:
          STACKTAPE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.STACKTAPE_API_KEY }}
        run: npx stacktape deploy --stage pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --region eu-west-1 --yes

  delete:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - name: Delete preview
        env:
          STACKTAPE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.STACKTAPE_API_KEY }}
        run: npx stacktape delete --stage pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

The shared group matters. Without it, a delete that runs before a queued deploy leaves that deploy to create the
preview again after the pull request closed. With it, closing the pull request replaces any deploy that hasn't started
yet, and the delete runs after the one that is running.

The `if` conditions skip pull requests from forks. GitHub doesn't give fork pull requests your repository's secrets,
and code from outside your repository shouldn't deploy into your AWS account.

[Stacks per Git branch](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) covers naming and the cost of previews.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
## GitLab CI

Add `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Staging deploys on every push to `develop`, and production waits for someone to click **Run** on
`main`:

```yaml
stages:
  - test
  - deploy

test:
  image: node:24
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test

deploy-staging:
  image: node:24
  stage: deploy
  resource_group: deploy-staging
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "develop"
  script:
    - npx stacktape deploy --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --yes

deploy-production:
  image: node:24
  stage: deploy
  resource_group: deploy-production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
      when: manual
  script:
    - npx stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

`STACKTAPE_API_KEY` or the AWS credentials come from the project's CI/CD variables. A `resource_group` runs one job at
a time per group. To build container images, add Docker to the job; see [Docker in the job](#docker-in-the-job).

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
## Bitbucket Pipelines

Add `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`:

```yaml
image: node:24

pipelines:
  branches:
    main:
      - step:
          name: Deploy to production
          script:
            - npx stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

Store `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` or the AWS credentials as secured repository variables. To build container images, add Docker to the job; see [Docker in the job](#docker-in-the-job).

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
## CircleCI

Add `.circleci/config.yml`:

```yaml
version: 2.1
jobs:
  deploy:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/node:lts
    steps:
      - checkout
      - run:
          name: Deploy to production
          command: npx stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
workflows:
  deploy-on-push:
    jobs:
      - deploy:
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main
```

Store `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` or the AWS credentials as project environment variables. To build container images, add Docker to the job; see [Docker in the job](#docker-in-the-job).

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
## Review changes before an approval

In a pipeline with a manual approval, run [`stacktape diff`](/cli/diff) before the approval step, so the reviewer sees
which resources the deploy adds, changes or replaces:

```bash
npx stacktape diff --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

`diff` needs the same credentials as the deploy, and it isn't free of side effects. It packages your code, and before
it compares, it creates the missing secrets and SSM parameters a deploy would create, such as generated database
passwords.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
headingPath: When two deploys of a stage run at once
docs.content:
## When two deploys of a stage run at once

A stack runs one deploy, rollback or delete at a time, including fast code-only deploys. A second deploy waits for the
first, prints who holds the stage while it waits, and then deploys on top of what the first one left. If a CI job is
killed mid-deploy, its hold on the stage expires within two minutes and the waiting deploy continues.

Waiting deploys don't keep the order of their commits, so an older commit can finish last. A GitHub Actions
`concurrency` group fixes that: it keeps only the newest waiting run, so the stage ends on the newest commit, and no
runner time is spent waiting. A GitLab `resource_group` runs one job at a time; set its process mode to `newest_first`
to get the same result.

The first deploy of a new stage is the exception. If two first deploys of the same stage run at once, the second stops
without changing anything. Run it again.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
headingPath: "needs confirmation, and this run cannot ask for it"
docs.content:
### "needs confirmation, and this run cannot ask for it"

The deploy would delete or replace a stateful resource, or the command is a `delete`. The error lists the resources.
If the change is intended, run it again with `--yes`.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
### "Missing 2 secret(s)"

The config references secrets that don't exist in the target region, and a CI job can't prompt for their values.
Create them once with [`stacktape secret set`](/cli/secret-set) and run the pipeline again.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
docs.content:
### Authentication fails

Without an account, check that the step that sets AWS credentials runs before the deploy and that the role or keys are
valid. With the Console, check that `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` is set in the deploy step (the name is case-sensitive) and that
the key isn't revoked or expired under **API keys** in the Console.

docs.title: Custom CI/CD
headingPath: The stack name is too long
docs.content:
### The stack name is too long

The stack name is the project name, a dash and the stage, and CloudFormation allows 128 characters. The error says how
long the stage can be for your project. Shorten generated stage names: `pr-42`, not the full branch name.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
# Git deployments

A Git deployment makes the Stacktape Console deploy a stage when someone pushes to a branch, or deploy a preview stage
for every pull request. It works with GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket, and there is no pipeline file to maintain.
Deployments build and run on a [runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) in your AWS account.

There are two kinds:

- **Push to a branch** deploys a fixed stage, such as `production`, on every push to one branch.
- **Pull request opened** deploys the stage `pr-<number>` for every pull request (merge request on GitLab) into one
  branch, redeploys it on new commits and deletes it when the pull request closes.

A Git deployment deploys on every matching event. If tests or an approval must pass first, require them in your Git
provider before merge, or deploy from [your own pipeline](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd).

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
## Before you start

1. **An AWS account connected** to your Stacktape organization. See
   [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account).
2. **A Git connection** for the provider that hosts the repository. An Owner or Admin creates it once for the
   organization; the steps are below.
3. **The project linked to its repository.** Owners, Admins and Developers can link a repository and manage Git
   deployments.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
## Connect your Git provider

In the Console sidebar, open **Configuration → Git connections**, click **Connect Git provider** and pick the
provider.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
### GitHub

1. Choose **GitHub**. GitHub opens the installation page of the Stacktape GitHub App.
2. Choose the GitHub account or organization, and select the repositories Stacktape can access.
3. GitHub asks you to authorize Stacktape. This confirms that you installed the app; Stacktape removes the temporary
   authorization afterwards.

You are returned to the Console, and the connection appears in the list. One GitHub App installation can be connected
to only one Stacktape organization. Disconnecting GitHub in the Console also uninstalls the app from that GitHub
account.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
### GitLab

GitLab connections work with groups on gitlab.com.

1. Choose **GitLab** and sign in to GitLab. Approve the access Stacktape requests (the `api` scope).
2. In **Choose a GitLab group**, select the group and click **Connect group**. Only groups you own are listed.
   Repositories in its subgroups are included.

Runners clone repositories with a read-only group deploy token named `Stacktape read-only …`, which Stacktape replaces
before it expires.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
### Bitbucket

Bitbucket connects through the Stacktape app for Bitbucket Cloud. A workspace admin installs it.

1. Choose **Bitbucket**. Atlassian opens the installation page of the app. Install it in your workspace and approve
   the permissions it requests.
2. In Bitbucket, open **Workspace settings**. Under **Forge Apps**, select **Stacktape deployments** and click
   **Continue to Stacktape**.
3. In the Console, choose the Stacktape organization and click **Connect workspace**. A Stacktape Owner or Admin must
   finish this step.

If the Console says the connection link has expired, repeat step 2. A Bitbucket workspace can be connected to only one
Stacktape organization. Disconnecting Bitbucket in the Console doesn't remove the app from Bitbucket; uninstall it in
your workspace settings.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
### Connection status

| Status | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Connected** | Pushes deploy. |
| **Needs approval** (GitHub) | Stacktape asked for write access, which it uses only to open security fix pull requests. Pushes still deploy. An owner of the GitHub account approves it in GitHub. |
| **Not deploying** (GitLab, Bitbucket) | The provider no longer accepts Stacktape's access, for example because the group owner revoked it. Pushes don't deploy until an Owner or Admin clicks **Reconnect**. |

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
### Connections from Stacktape v3

GitLab connections made with a personal or group access token, and Bitbucket connections made with the older OAuth
flow, are removed in v4. Projects that used them no longer deploy on push. Connect GitLab or Bitbucket again with the
steps above. If a project still doesn't deploy after that, email [support@stacktape.com](mailto:support@stacktape.com).
GitHub App connections keep working.

docs.title: Git deployments
headingPath: Link a project to its repository
docs.content:
## Link a project to its repository

A project created by `stacktape deploy` from your machine has no repository yet. Open the project and click
**Connect** next to "No Git repository". Choose the repository from your Git connections and click **Connect**.
Deployments use the Stacktape config committed in the repository.

After the first successful deploy of a new stage, a CLI signed in to the Console offers to set this up. It asks
whether pushes to your current branch should deploy that stage, opens the browser to connect the provider if needed,
and creates the Git deployment.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
## Create a Git deployment

1. Open the project, click the gear icon next to its name and choose **Configure Git deployments**.
2. With no Git deployments yet, the page offers two starting points: **Deploy production on every push to main** and
   **Preview every pull request into main** (with your stage and default branch). Click **Set up** on one, or click
   **New Git deployment**.
3. Choose **Push to a branch** or **Pull request opened**, and fill in the form:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Branch** / **Pull requests into** | The branch that is pushed to, or that pull requests merge into. The name must match exactly; patterns are not supported. |
| **Deploys stage** | The stage to deploy, such as `production`. Only for pushes. Previews always use `pr-<number>`. |
| **Delete the preview when the pull request closes** | Only for pull requests, on by default. |
| **Stacktape config** | Shown only when the repository has more than one Stacktape config. |
| **Deploys to** | The AWS account and region, preset to where the project's newest stage runs. Click **Change** to pick others. |

4. Check the sentence at the bottom of the form, for example "Every push to main deploys production in eu-west-1",
   and click **Create Git deployment**.


> Screenshot: The New Git deployment dialog: Push to a branch, branch main, stage staging, the target AWS account and region, the sentence Every push to main deploys staging in eu-west-1, and the Create Git deployment button Caption: The sentence above the buttons says what every matching push will deploy, and where.


The form also says what the build costs. The first Git deployment in an AWS account and region starts a runner there:
AWS bills it by the hour while it builds and bills its disks while it is stopped, about $8.80 a month in Ireland. A
second Git deployment in the same place shares that runner. See [Runner cost](#runner-cost).

To change a Git deployment, open the row's menu and choose **Edit**. You can change the trigger, branch, stage, config
and preview deletion; for another AWS account or region, create a new one. **Delete** stops future deploys. Stages it
already deployed keep running; remove them with [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) or in the Console.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
## What triggers a deployment

| Event | Result |
|---|---|
| Push to a branch with a **Push to a branch** rule | Deploys the rule's stage with the pushed commit. Creates the stage if it doesn't exist. |
| Pull request opened (or reopened) into a branch with a **Pull request opened** rule | Deploys `pr-<number>`. |
| New commits pushed to that pull request | Redeploys `pr-<number>` with the latest commit. |
| Pull request merged or closed | Deletes `pr-<number>` if the rule deletes previews. Otherwise the stage keeps running. |

These events don't deploy anything:

- pushes of tags, and branch deletions;
- pull requests from forks, so code from outside the repository never runs with your project's credentials;
- on GitLab, merge request changes that add no commits, such as a new title or reviewer;
- on GitHub, pull requests that Stacktape opens from `stacktape/fix-` branches.

On Bitbucket, any update to an open pull request, including a title change, redeploys its preview.

One event can match several rules. For example, two **Push to a branch** rules for `main` can deploy to two regions
or two AWS accounts, and each starts its own deployment.

A runner runs up to two deployments at once; more wait for a free slot. Deploys of one stage never overlap: if you push
again while a stage deploys, the new deployment waits for the current one.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
## Following a deployment

Git deployments appear in the Console with their logs, like any other deployment.

- **Pull request previews:** Stacktape comments on the pull request when the preview deploy starts and updates the
  comment with the result. It comments the same way when it deletes a preview. If a preview can't start, for example
  because the AWS account is no longer connected, the comment says so.
- **GitHub:** each deployment also appears in the repository's **Deployments**, marked successful or failed.
- **Alerts:** to get a message in Slack, email or another channel, create a
  [notification rule](/observability/notifications) for the **Git deployments** events.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
## Runner cost

Creating the first Git deployment for an AWS account and region prepares a runner in the background. It installs its
tools and stops until the first push arrives. It doesn't clone your repository during this preparation.

A stopped runner has no EC2 compute charge, but its disks are billed. The default 50 GiB system disk and 50 GiB build
cache disk cost about **$8.80 a month in Ireland** at gp3 rates. The cache disk grows with the build cache, up to the
limit set on the runner. The Console's **Runners** page shows the estimate for each runner. See
[AWS EBS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/).

Stacktape removes the runner, with its disks, build cache and IAM role, when you delete the project or the last Git
deployment that uses its AWS account and region. A deployment that is already running finishes first. If the project's
[GitHub Actions runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners) uses the same account and region, the
runner stays.

Previews also cost whatever their AWS resources cost, until they are deleted. Keep **Delete the preview when the pull
request closes** on unless you need previews after merge, for example for QA.

docs.title: Git deployments
headingPath: Provider permissions for security fix pull requests
docs.content:
## Provider permissions for security fix pull requests

When you ask Stacktape to prepare a security fix, it creates a `stacktape/*` branch, commits the selected file changes
and opens a pull request. It never force-pushes, writes to the default branch, closes pull requests or sets commit
statuses. Starting a fix needs `security:manage` access to the project.

The connection must allow these writes:

- **GitHub:** read and write access to repository Contents, Pull requests and Commit statuses. When Stacktape asks for
  new permissions, an owner of the GitHub account approves them on the existing installation. Until then the
  connection shows **Needs approval**.
- **GitLab:** the group connection's `api` scope covers the branch, commit and merge request. The read-only deploy
  token is used only for cloning.
- **Bitbucket:** read and write access to repositories and pull requests. When the app's permissions change, a
  workspace admin approves the app upgrade in Bitbucket.

Deployments keep working while new permissions wait for approval. Only security fix pull requests wait.

docs.title: Git deployments
docs.content:
## A push did not deploy

Check, in this order:

1. **Configuration → Git connections**: the provider's connection. **Not deploying** on GitLab or Bitbucket stops all
   pushes; reconnect it. **Needs approval** on GitHub does not stop pushes, so look further.
2. The project page shows the repository, not "No Git repository".
3. A Git deployment of the project watches exactly the branch you pushed to, or, for previews, the branch the pull
   request merges into.
4. The event is one that deploys: not a tag, a branch deletion or a pull request from a fork.
5. On GitHub, the Stacktape GitHub App can access the repository. Check the app's repository access in your GitHub
   account or organization settings.

If the deployment started and failed, its log in the Console shows why.

docs.title: CI/CD overview
docs.content:
# CI/CD overview

Stacktape can deploy automatically in two ways. You choose per stage, and both can run in the same project.

- **Git deployments.** In the Stacktape Console, connect GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket and choose which branch deploys
  which stage. Every pull request can get its own preview stage. Stacktape builds and deploys on a runner in your AWS
  account, and you write no pipeline file.
- **Your own pipeline.** Run `stacktape deploy` as a step in GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or any CI that runs shell
  commands. Tests, approvals and other steps run around it. This works with or without a Stacktape account.

Use Git deployments when a push should simply deploy. Use your own pipeline when something must pass first, such as
tests or a manual approval.

docs.title: CI/CD overview
docs.content: ## Compare the options

docs.title: CI/CD overview
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Git deployments | Your own pipeline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stacktape account | Needed (Free plan works) | Optional |
| Setup | A form in the Console | A workflow file you maintain |
| Where the build runs | A runner in your AWS account | Your CI's worker |
| Tests and approvals | In your Git provider, before merge | Steps before the deploy |
| Pull request previews | Built in, deleted on close | Deploy and delete jobs you write |
| Cost | Runner time and disks in AWS | Your CI minutes |


A common setup uses both:

| Stage | Deployed by | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `staging` | A Git deployment | Every push to `develop` deploys, with nothing to maintain |
| `pr-<number>` | A Git deployment | Every pull request gets its own stage |
| `production` | Your own pipeline | Tests and an approval run before `main` deploys |

Deploys of one stage never overlap, whichever way they start. A second deploy waits until the first finishes.

docs.title: CI/CD overview
docs.content:
## Git deployments

You connect your Git provider once, link the project to its repository and create a Git deployment for each branch
that should deploy. A Git deployment either deploys a fixed stage on every push to a branch, or deploys a preview stage
`pr-<number>` for every pull request into a branch.

A project's first Git deployment in an AWS account and region creates a [build runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners)
for that project there. More Git deployments of the same project, account and region share it. AWS bills each runner's
compute while it builds and its disks while it is stopped: the default disks cost about $8.80 a month per runner in
Ireland, so ten projects deploying to one account and region cost about $88 a month in disks. A runner and its disks
are removed with the last Git deployment that uses them.

After the first successful deploy of a new stage, a CLI signed in to the Console offers to set this up: it asks whether
pushes to your current branch should deploy that stage.

[Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) walks through connecting each provider and creating the
rules.

docs.title: CI/CD overview
docs.content:
## Your own pipeline

The pipeline authenticates in one of two ways:

| Credentials | When |
|---|---|
| AWS credentials only | Without a Stacktape account. The CLI deploys to the AWS account the credentials belong to. On GitHub Actions, use an IAM role that GitHub assumes through OIDC, so no AWS key is stored. |
| `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` | With the Console, so deploys are recorded and Console features work. Use an [organization key](/stacktape-console/api-keys#create-an-organization-key), which keeps working when people leave. |

If you deployed with `stacktape init`, the wizard's **Deploy on every push** card writes the pipeline for you: a
GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD or Bitbucket Pipelines file, and the list of secrets to add. The GitHub workflow assumes
an IAM role through OIDC.

[Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd) has workflows for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Bitbucket Pipelines and
CircleCI, with tests, approvals, previews and concurrency, and what a job needs to build container images.

If your jobs run on GitHub Actions and hosted runners are too slow or can't reach your VPC,
[self-hosted GitHub Actions runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners) run them on a Stacktape
runner in your AWS account.

docs.title: CI/CD overview
docs.content:
## Pull request previews

A preview is a separate stage for one pull request, with its own functions, containers, databases and URLs. Previews
are non-production stages, so they share the AWS account's non-production VPC instead of creating one each.

Each preview costs what its resources cost, for as long as it exists. A database or container keeps billing when no
one opens the preview. Delete previews when their pull request closes: Git deployments do it with one checkbox, and
your own pipeline does it with a `stacktape delete` job.

[Stacks per Git branch](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) covers stage naming, cost and cleanup.

docs.title: CI/CD overview
docs.content:
## When an automated deploy fails

By default, a failed deploy keeps what it changed, and the next run continues from there. Fix the problem and push
again. If the deploy finished but the new code is broken, push a revert commit, or return to the previous version with
[`stacktape rollback`](/cli/rollback). If CloudFormation left the stack in a failed state, recover it with
[`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover). [Rollbacks](/deployment-and-lifecycle/rollbacks) explains which to use
when.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
docs.content:
# Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners

Stacktape can run your GitHub Actions jobs on the project's [build runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners), an EC2
instance in your AWS account. You keep your workflow files; a job opts in with one label. Use it when GitHub's hosted
runners are too slow for your builds, or when jobs need more CPU and memory than they offer.

If you only need push-to-deploy without tests in the workflow, [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console)
need no workflow file.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
docs.content:
## Requirements

Stacktape runs a job only when all of these hold. Otherwise it cancels the job's workflow run.

- The repository is **private** and not archived. Public repositories are refused.
- The run doesn't come from a **fork**, and its event isn't `pull_request_target`.
- The repository is connected through the Stacktape GitHub App (see
  [Connect your Git provider](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console#connect-your-git-provider)) and linked to a
  Stacktape project.
- Exactly **one** project linked to that repository has GitHub Actions turned on.
- The runner's AWS account is still connected and active.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
docs.content:
## Turn it on

1. In the Console, open **Configuration → Runners** and select the project's runner. A project that doesn't have a
   runner yet is listed under "projects have no runner yet"; open it from there.
2. On the **Settings** tab, under **GitHub Actions**, turn on **Run jobs on this runner**.
3. Add the label it shows to the jobs that should run there:

```yaml
name: Test and deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, stacktape]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npx stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

Jobs run in the runner's AWS account and region, with its instance size. Jobs without the `stacktape` label run on
whatever their `runs-on` says, so one workflow can mix them: lint on `ubuntu-latest`, build and deploy on the Stacktape
runner.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
docs.content:
## Credentials in the job

Stacktape commands in the job authenticate on their own. You don't store `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` or AWS keys in GitHub.
For each job, Stacktape issues a key limited to this project and the runner's AWS account, valid only while the job
runs and for at most two hours. Deploys from the job appear in the Console like any other.

Other tools in the job that need credentials, such as a package registry, get them the usual way, from GitHub secrets.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
docs.content:
## What is installed

The runner runs Amazon Linux with Node.js (npm, pnpm and Yarn), Bun, Python 3, Go, Java (Corretto 11, 17 and 21),
Ruby, Docker, the AWS CLI, Git and common build tools such as `make` and `gcc`. Install anything else as a workflow
step. Each job runs as an unprivileged user in its own directory, with Docker in rootless mode. Package manager and
Docker caches stay on the runner's cache disk between jobs.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
docs.content:
## Start time and cost

A stopped runner starts when a job arrives, so the first job after a quiet period waits for the instance to boot or
resume from hibernation. Later jobs start right away while the runner is still running. Each job also waits a few
seconds while Stacktape registers it with GitHub.

The runner stops after its idle time, 15 minutes by default. AWS bills compute while it runs and its disks all the
time; see [Build runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners#what-it-costs). The runner runs up to two background jobs at
once (GitHub Actions jobs and AI runs) next to up to two deployments. Further jobs wait.

Compared with GitHub's hosted runners, you pay EC2 rates for the time the instance runs instead of per-minute runner
prices. That is usually cheaper for long or frequent builds and more expensive for a few short ones.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
docs.content:
## Turn it off

Turn off **Run jobs on this runner** on the runner's **Settings** tab. First change the jobs' `runs-on` to a hosted
label such as `ubuntu-latest`: once no project runs them, Stacktape cancels workflow runs that still ask for the
`stacktape` label.

docs.title: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners
headingPath: A job was cancelled or never started
docs.content:
## A job was cancelled or never started

Check the [requirements](#requirements) first. The common causes are a public repository, a pull request from a fork,
a second project linked to the same repository with GitHub Actions on, and a disconnected AWS account. Jobs that did
run are listed on the runner's page in the Console with their status, and their output is in the GitHub job log.

docs.title: Stacks per Git branch
docs.content:
# Stacks per Git branch

A stage is one complete, separate deployment of your project: its own stack, functions, containers, databases and
URLs. Deriving the stage from the Git branch or pull request gives each line of development its own environment. This
page covers the three common shapes, how to name the stages and how to keep their cost down.

| Shape | Git event | Stage | Lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long-lived branch | Push to `main`, `develop` | A fixed name: `production`, `staging` | Permanently, updated on every push |
| Pull request preview | Pull request into `main` | `pr-<number>`, such as `pr-42` | Until the pull request closes |
| Feature branch | Push to `feat/payments` | A short name: `feature-payments` | Until the feature ships |

A deployment is identified by project, stage, AWS account and region. Two stages of a project in the same account and
region never share resources, except the non-production network described under [Cost](#cost).

docs.title: Stacks per Git branch
docs.content:
## Long-lived branch stages

Map each permanent branch to a stage. The stage name doesn't have to match the branch:

| Branch | Stage |
|---|---|
| `main` | `production` |
| `develop` | `staging` |

- **With Git deployments**, create one **Push to a branch** Git deployment per branch. It watches one exact branch
  name. See [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console#create-a-git-deployment).
- **In your own pipeline**, deploy with a fixed stage in the job for that branch:
  `npx stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes`. A pipeline can also route by pattern, such as
  every `release-*` branch, which Git deployments can't. See [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd).

docs.title: Stacks per Git branch
docs.content:
## Pull request previews

Every pull request gets the stage `pr-<number>`. Reviewers try the change on real AWS resources before merge, and one
pull request never overwrites another's state.

- **With Git deployments**, create a **Pull request opened** Git deployment for the branch pull requests merge into.
  Stacktape deploys `pr-42` when pull request #42 opens, redeploys it on new commits, comments on the pull request with
  each result, and deletes the stage when the pull request closes if **Delete the preview when the pull request
  closes** is on. Pull requests from forks never get a preview.
- **In your own pipeline**, deploy on open and on new commits, and delete on close. On GitHub Actions, use the
  [preview workflow](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd#pull-request-previews), which keeps deploys and the delete in
  order and skips forks. On GitLab CI, the merge request number is `$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID`:

```bash
npx stacktape deploy --stage "pr-${CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID}" --region eu-west-1 --yes
npx stacktape delete --stage "pr-${CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID}" --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

| CI | Pull request number | Branch name |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions | `${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}` | `${{ github.ref_name }}` |
| GitLab CI | `$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID` | `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` |
| Bitbucket Pipelines | `$BITBUCKET_PR_ID` | `$BITBUCKET_BRANCH` |

To fill a preview's database with test data on each deploy, use a [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts)
or a [hook](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts). Treat preview data as disposable: deleting the stage deletes it.

docs.title: Stacks per Git branch
docs.content:
## Feature branch stages

A feature that takes weeks, or that several people work on, can get its own stage for as long as it lives:

```bash
npx stacktape deploy --stage feature-payments --region eu-west-1
```

Delete it when the feature ships:

```bash
npx stacktape delete --stage feature-payments --region eu-west-1
```

A **Push to a branch** Git deployment for `feat/payments` can deploy it automatically. For a change that takes a day
or two, a pull request preview is simpler, because its cleanup is automatic.

docs.title: Stacks per Git branch
docs.content:
## Naming stages

A stage name has at least 2 characters: lowercase letters, numbers and dashes. The stack name is the project name, a
dash and the stage, and CloudFormation allows 128 characters. Branch names often break these rules (`feat/Payments_v2`),
so derive a short name from your CI's branch variable instead of using the branch as it is:

```bash
STAGE="feature-$(echo "$BRANCH" | sed 's|.*/||' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/[^a-z0-9-]/-/g' | cut -c1-20)"
```

When neither `stackConfig.stageType` in your config nor the Console sets the stage type, the name decides it. Names with
`dev`, `staging`, `test`, `preview`, `pr` or `feature` are non-production; names with `prod`, `production` or `live` are
production. A name that says neither, such as `payments` or `mc`, gets a network of its own. Prefer `pr-42`,
`feature-payments` and `dev-mc`.

docs.title: Stacks per Git branch
docs.content:
## Cost

Each stage costs what its resources cost, for as long as it exists. A preview with a database or a container keeps
billing when no one opens it. Functions, DynamoDB tables and other pay-per-request resources cost almost nothing while
idle.

Non-production stages in an AWS account and region share one VPC and, when they need outbound internet, one small NAT
instance (about $7.70 a month for all of them). Each stage keeps its own security groups, so a preview's database
admits only that preview's workloads. A new preview therefore doesn't create a VPC.

To keep previews cheap:

- **Delete them when the pull request closes.** Keep the checkbox on in the Git deployment, or run `stacktape delete`
  on close in your pipeline. Forgotten previews with a database are the usual cause of a surprise bill.
- **Make them smaller.** Use [stage-specific configuration](/configuration/stages-and-environments) to give previews a
  smaller database instance or fewer containers than production.
- **Set a budget.** A [budget](/managing-costs/budgets) alerts you when the account's spend passes a threshold.
- **List what runs.** [`stacktape stack list`](/cli/stack-list) shows every deployed stage, so you can delete the
  stale ones.

Previews can be the wrong choice when one stage costs a lot per hour (large databases, many containers, GPU jobs) or
takes a long time to create. A shared staging stage with feature flags is then cheaper.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
# Command index

Every command runs as `stacktape <command>`, or `stp <command>` for short, and `stacktape help <command>` prints its flags. Commands that act on a stack use your local AWS credentials. The ones marked Console also need a Stacktape sign-in: [`stacktape login`](/cli/login), or a `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` in CI.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Set up

- [`init`](/cli/init): Creates the Stacktape configuration for your project, or a new project from a starter, and guides you through the first deploy.
- [`aws-profile create`](/cli/aws-profile-create): Creates an AWS profile on your machine.
- [`aws-profile list`](/cli/aws-profile-list): Lists the AWS profiles on your machine.
- [`aws-profile update`](/cli/aws-profile-update): Updates an AWS profile.
- [`aws-profile delete`](/cli/aws-profile-delete): Deletes an AWS profile.
- [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set): Sets default values for flags such as the region, stage and AWS profile.
- [`defaults list`](/cli/defaults-list): Prints the defaults you set.
- [`domain add`](/cli/domain-add): Adds a registered domain to your AWS account, so Stacktape can manage its DNS records and certificates.
- [`upgrade`](/cli/upgrade): Upgrades the CLI to the latest version.
- [`version`](/cli/version): Prints the installed CLI version.
- [`help`](/cli/help): Prints the commands, or the flags of one command.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Deploy and manage stacks

- [`validate`](/cli/validate): Checks your configuration without deploying anything.
- [`diff`](/cli/diff): Shows what a deploy would change in the stack.
- [`synth`](/cli/synth): Writes the CloudFormation template your configuration produces to a file.
- [`package`](/cli/package): Builds the deployment packages of your functions and containers.
- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy): Creates or updates a stage in your AWS account.
- [`status`](/cli/status) (Console): Shows a deployed stack's URLs, outputs and resources.
- [`stack list`](/cli/stack-list): Lists the stacks deployed in a region.
- [`stack history`](/cli/stack-history) (Console): Lists recent deploys and other operations with their result.
- [`rollback`](/cli/rollback): Returns the stack to a previous deployment version.
- [`stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover): Recovers a stack stuck in `UPDATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`.
- [`stack update-modules`](/cli/stack-update-modules): Updates the CloudFormation modules the stack uses.
- [`deployment-script run`](/cli/deployment-script-run): Runs a deployment script of the stack in AWS.
- [`bucket sync`](/cli/bucket-sync): Mirrors a local directory into a bucket, removing files that no longer exist locally.
- [`delete`](/cli/delete): Deletes a stage and its resources.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Develop locally

- [`dev`](/cli/dev): Runs your app on your machine, connected to its resources.
- [`dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop): Stops a dev session started with `dev --agent`, and cleans up containers left by crashed sessions.
- [`dev network`](/cli/dev-network): Shows the dev network of an AWS account and region.
- [`dev network delete`](/cli/dev-network-delete): Deletes the dev network of an AWS account and region.
- [`script run`](/cli/script-run): Runs a script from your configuration.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Secrets and parameters

- [`secret set`](/cli/secret-set): Creates or updates a secret in AWS Secrets Manager.
- [`secret get`](/cli/secret-get): Prints a secret's details, and its value only when you ask.
- [`secret delete`](/cli/secret-delete): Deletes a secret.
- [`param get`](/cli/param-get): Prints one parameter of a deployed resource, such as a URL or ARN.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Inspect and debug

- [`logs`](/cli/logs): Prints and filters the logs of a deployed resource.
- [`metrics`](/cli/metrics): Prints CloudWatch metrics of a deployed resource.
- [`alarm list`](/cli/alarm-list): Lists the alarms of the stack and their state.
- [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call): Runs a read-only AWS SDK call against the stack's resources.
- [`container shell`](/cli/container-shell): Opens a shell inside a running container.
- [`container exec`](/cli/container-exec): Runs one command in a running container and prints the output.
- [`bastion shell`](/cli/bastion-shell): Opens a shell on the stack's bastion host.
- [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel): Opens a tunnel from your machine to a private database or cache.
- [`query sql`](/cli/query-sql): Runs a read-only SQL query against a relational database.
- [`query dynamodb`](/cli/query-dynamodb): Reads items and the schema of a DynamoDB table.
- [`query redis`](/cli/query-redis): Reads keys, values and server info from a Redis cache.
- [`query opensearch`](/cli/query-opensearch): Searches an OpenSearch domain.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Incidents and errors

- [`incident list`](/cli/incident-list) (Console): Lists incidents: downtime, failing checks, firing alarms and production errors.
- [`incident show`](/cli/incident-show) (Console): Prints everything known about one incident.
- [`incident ack`](/cli/incident-ack) (Console): Marks an incident as being handled.
- [`incident watch`](/cli/incident-watch) (Console): Waits until an incident recovers and stays recovered.
- [`incident resolve`](/cli/incident-resolve) (Console): Resolves an incident after you deployed and verified a fix.
- [`error list`](/cli/error-list) (Console): Lists runtime errors from your functions and containers.
- [`error resolve`](/cli/error-resolve) (Console): Marks an error as resolved. It reopens if the error comes back.
- [`error ignore`](/cli/error-ignore) (Console): Ignores an error, so it does not reopen or alert.
- [`error reopen`](/cli/error-reopen) (Console): Reopens a resolved or ignored error.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Console and account

- [`login`](/cli/login): Signs this machine in to Stacktape.
- [`logout`](/cli/logout): Signs this machine out of Stacktape.
- [`connect`](/cli/connect): Connects the AWS account of your local credentials to the Console, without redeploying anything.
- [`whoami`](/cli/whoami) (Console): Shows your user, organization, connected AWS accounts and projects.
- [`org list`](/cli/org-list) (Console): Lists the organizations you can access.
- [`org create`](/cli/org-create) (Console): Creates an organization.
- [`org delete`](/cli/org-delete) (Console): Deletes the organization of your API key.
- [`project list`](/cli/project-list) (Console): Lists projects with their stages, status and costs.
- [`project create`](/cli/project-create) (Console): Creates a project.
- [`project delete`](/cli/project-delete) (Console): Deletes a project.
- [`alarm export`](/cli/alarm-export) (Console): Prints alarm rules created in the Console as configuration you can paste.

docs.title: Command index
docs.content:
## Coding agents

- [`mcp`](/cli/mcp): Starts the Stacktape MCP server for coding agents.
- [`mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add): Registers the MCP server with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code and other agents.
- [`mcp remove`](/cli/mcp-remove): Removes the MCP server registration.
- [`ai connect`](/cli/ai-connect) (Console): Connects your own AI subscription for the AI incident runs in the Console.
- [`ai disconnect`](/cli/ai-disconnect) (Console): Removes an AI subscription you connected.

docs.title: ai connect
docs.content:
# ai connect

`stacktape ai connect` connects your own AI subscription to Stacktape for the hosted AI incident runs you request ([Investigate with AI and Fix with AI](/observability/incident-ai)). It first asks which provider to connect (unless you pass `--ai-provider`) and explains what will happen, then, in a terminal, waits for your confirmation. It stores the sign-in with Stacktape under your user and the organization of your API key, and never prints it. Only runs you request use it, and they run the provider's coding agent.

docs.title: ai connect
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape ai connect
stacktape ai connect codex
```

In a terminal you can leave out the provider and the command asks; a non-interactive run must pass it. The command needs a valid API key for your own user (run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) first) and the provider's own CLI on your `PATH`. Without it, the command stops and tells you how to install it.

docs.title: ai connect
docs.content:
## Providers

| `<ai-provider>` | Connects | For | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claude` | Your Claude subscription (Anthropic) | Claude Code | Runs `claude setup-token`, which signs you in to Claude in your browser and prints a long-lived token, and stores that token. |
| `codex` | Your ChatGPT plan (OpenAI) | Codex | Uses the ChatGPT sign-in of your Codex CLI: runs `codex login` first when Codex is not signed in with ChatGPT, then stores the tokens Codex keeps in `~/.codex/auth.json`. |
| `grok` | Your Grok sign-in (xAI) | Grok | Uses the sign-in of your Grok CLI: runs `grok login` first when there is none it can use (with a device code when the terminal cannot open a browser), then stores the sign-in Grok keeps in `~/.grok/auth.json`, without your name, email and picture. |
| `opencode` | What your OpenCode CLI is signed in to | OpenCode | Uses what `opencode auth login` connected: plans such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot or OpenCode Go, and provider API keys you gave OpenCode. Runs `opencode auth login` first when there is none, then stores `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`. |

For Claude, the sign-in always needs an interactive terminal. On Linux and macOS it runs inside a recorded pseudo-terminal, so the token is captured for you; on Windows it runs on your terminal and you paste the token it printed when asked.

For Codex, Grok and OpenCode, a sign-in the CLI already keeps connects without a terminal, for example in a script. Signing in needs a terminal. If your Codex keeps its sign-in in the system keyring instead of `~/.codex/auth.json`, the command says how to switch it to the file.

A Codex signed in with an OpenAI API key is refused: an API key is not a subscription. An Admin or Owner connects an OpenAI API key once for the whole organization, on an incident page in the Stacktape Console. The same holds for Anthropic and xAI API keys.

docs.title: ai connect
docs.content:
## What it connects

- **Your subscription, for your runs.** A run you fund with your own sign-in on an incident page uses it. One member's sign-in never funds another member's run, and Stacktape never switches a run to one of the organization's API keys.
- **Your organization only.** The sign-in is stored for the organization of the API key you are logged in with. Run the command again after switching organizations to connect it there too.
- **Replaceable.** Running the command again replaces it. Remove it with [`stacktape ai disconnect`](/cli/ai-disconnect).

The subscription is your own arrangement with the provider, under the provider's terms. Stacktape does not check the plan or promise that its limits cover a run; a run whose sign-in is expired, rejected or out of quota fails and says so.

docs.title: ai connect
docs.content:
## Sign-ins that refresh

A Codex, Grok or OpenCode sign-in holds a refresh token, and Stacktape stores a copy. A run can refresh its copy, and your own CLI refreshes its copy. When either refreshes, the provider may replace the refresh token, and the other copy then stops working: your CLI asks you to sign in again, or a run fails saying the provider did not accept the sign-in. Run `stacktape ai connect` again to connect a fresh one. Stacktape never writes a refreshed sign-in back.

To keep the runs' sign-in apart from your own CLI's, sign in once more in a separate home for the agent, for example:

```bash
CODEX_HOME=~/.codex-stacktape stacktape ai connect codex
GROK_HOME=~/.grok-stacktape stacktape ai connect grok
XDG_DATA_HOME=~/.local/share/opencode-stacktape stacktape ai connect opencode
```

A Claude token from `claude setup-token` does not refresh, so this does not apply to it.

docs.title: ai connect
docs.content: ## Options

docs.title: ai connect
docs.content:
## CLI Options: `stacktape ai connect`

| Option | Required | Type | Description | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--ai-provider (positional 1)` | no | `string` | AI Provider — The AI provider whose subscription to connect for hosted incident runs, and so the coding agent those runs use: `claude` (a Claude subscription for Claude Code, through `claude setup-token`), `codex` (a ChatGPT plan for Codex, from `codex login`), `grok` (a Grok sign-in, from `grok login`) or `opencode` (what OpenCode is signed in to, from `opencode auth login`). When omitted in a terminal, the command asks which provider to use; a non-interactive run must pass it. | `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `opencode` |
| `-h, --help` | no | `string` | Show Help — If provided, the command will not execute and will instead print help information. | - |
| `--log-level` | no | `string` | Log Level — The level of logs to print to the console. • `info`: Basic information about the operation. • `error`: Only errors. • `debug`: Detailed information for debugging. | `info`, `debug`, `error` |
| `--quiet` | no | `boolean` | Quiet — Hide progress, banners, success messages and hints. Command output, warnings and errors are still printed. | - |

docs.title: ai disconnect
docs.content:
# ai disconnect

`stacktape ai disconnect` removes your own sign-in with one AI provider from Stacktape, in the organization of your API key. It asks which provider to disconnect unless you pass it as an argument (`ai disconnect <ai-provider>`). Hosted AI incident runs you request can no longer be funded by that sign-in until you connect it again with [`stacktape ai connect`](/cli/ai-connect). A run already running is not affected; a queued run funded by it fails without starting.

Your own CLI's sign-in on your machine stays as it is.

docs.title: ai disconnect
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape ai disconnect
stacktape ai disconnect grok
```

A non-interactive run must pass the provider. The command needs a valid API key for your own user. Removing a sign-in that is not connected succeeds and changes nothing.
