docs.title: alarm export
docs.content:
# alarm export

`stacktape alarm export` prints the alarm rules created in the Stacktape Console as entries for the `alarms` list of a resource in your configuration. The Console no longer creates or edits alarm rules. The old ones are listed under **Legacy alarm rules** on the Console's Alarms page and keep applying to every matching resource until you exclude or delete them.

The command needs a Console sign-in ([`stacktape login`](/cli/login)) and changes nothing. It only prints.

docs.title: alarm export
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape alarm export
```

The output starts with how many rules it found. Each rule follows as a YAML list entry, with a comment that names the rule and the projects and stages it applies to:

```yaml configExample="fragment"

docs.title: alarm export
docs.content: # alarm "api-error-rate"

docs.title: alarm export
headingPath: applies to projects: all · stages: production
docs.content:
# applies to projects: all · stages: production
- trigger:
    type: lambda-error-rate
    properties:
      thresholdPercent: 5
  notificationChannels:
    - type: console-channel
      properties:
        channelName: production-alerts
```

The Console channels a rule sent to become `console-channel` entries. When the organization has no Console rules, the command prints `This organization has no Console-defined alarms. Nothing to export.`

docs.title: alarm export
headingPath: Moving the rules into your configuration
docs.content:
## Moving the rules into your configuration

1. Run `stacktape alarm export`.
2. Add each entry to the `alarms` list of every resource it should watch. Where a rule applies only to some stages, use [stage-based configuration](/configuration/stages-and-environments).
3. On the same resources, add the rule's name to `disabledGlobalAlarms`. Without it the Console rule keeps applying next to your new alarm, and the resource gets two alarms that notify twice.
4. Deploy each affected stage.
5. Check the alarms on the Console's Alarms page or with [`stacktape alarm list`](/cli/alarm-list). Once every stack the rule applies to has deployed, delete the legacy rule in the Console.

For the `api-error-rate` rule above, the function's configuration looks like this:

```yaml configExample="fragment"
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      # ...
      alarms:
        - trigger:
            type: lambda-error-rate
            properties:
              thresholdPercent: 5
          notificationChannels:
            - type: console-channel
              properties:
                channelName: production-alerts
      disabledGlobalAlarms:
        - api-error-rate
```

[Alarms](/observability/alarms#migrating-legacy-console-alarm-rules) explains the alarm settings.

docs.title: alarm export
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`alarm list`](/cli/alarm-list) shows the state of the alarms of a deployed stack.
- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) creates the alarms you added to the configuration.

docs.title: alarm list
docs.content:
# alarm list

`stacktape alarm list` shows the CloudWatch alarms of a deployed stage and their current state, so you can see what is firing without opening the AWS console. It lists the alarms whose names start with the stack name, such as the [alarms](/observability/alarms) your config defines. It needs AWS credentials and works without a Stacktape account.

docs.title: alarm list
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape alarm list --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

For each alarm you get its name, the Stacktape resource it belongs to, its state, the metric, threshold and comparison, and when the state last changed. A firing alarm also shows why.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OK` | The metric is within the threshold. |
| `ALARM` | The metric crossed the threshold for the required number of periods. |
| `INSUFFICIENT_DATA` | Not enough data yet, common for a new alarm or a resource without traffic. |

docs.title: alarm list
docs.content:
## Filter by resource or state

Firing alarms of one resource:

```bash
stacktape alarm list --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --resource-name myApi --state ALARM
```

`--resource-name` takes the resource name from your config. `--state` takes `OK`, `ALARM` or `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`.

docs.title: alarm list
docs.content:
## Check from a script

With `--agent`, the command prints NDJSON: one JSON object per line. The list arrives as JSON text in the `message` of a `log` line, as `{ "alarms": [...] }`, and each alarm has `name`, `resource`, `state`, `metric`, `threshold`, `comparison`, `lastUpdated` and, when firing, `reason`. This prints how many alarms are firing:

```bash
stacktape alarm list --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --state ALARM --agent \
  | jq 'select(.type == "log") | .message | fromjson? | .alarms | length'
```

Legacy alarm rules that were created in the Console, not in your config, move into the config with [`alarm export`](/cli/alarm-export).

docs.title: alarm list
docs.content: ## Options

docs.title: alarm list
docs.content:
## CLI Options: `stacktape alarm list`

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
# aws call

`stacktape aws call` sends a reviewed read-only AWS SDK v3 operation against resources in a deployed Stacktape
stack. Use it when Stacktape's purpose-built inspection commands do not expose the AWS data you need.

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
## Safety model

Stacktape uses an explicit allowlist for every supported AWS service. A command is accepted only when its exact
service and operation pair has been reviewed and appears in that service's list.

This is not a prefix check. An operation is not accepted merely because its name begins with `Get`, `List`,
`Describe`, `Head`, or `Batch`. For example, Stacktape rejects:

- DynamoDB `BatchWriteItem`, because it writes data.
- SQS `ReceiveMessage`, because it hides messages from their consumers for the visibility timeout.
- Step Functions `GetActivityTask`, because it claims work and starts the task timeout.

Unknown services and unlisted operations are rejected. The error includes the operations that `aws call` accepts for
the selected service. Coverage is deliberately incomplete: a genuinely read-only operation remains unavailable until
it has been reviewed and added to the service's allowlist.

The explicit secret-value reads are not on the list either, because the caller is often a coding agent whose context
and transcript would keep the value: Secrets Manager `GetSecretValue` and the SSM Parameter Store reads `GetParameter`,
`GetParameters`, `GetParametersByPath` and `GetParameterHistory`. Their metadata operations, such as `DescribeSecret`,
`ListSecrets` and `DescribeParameters`, remain. To see a secret's value, run [`secret get --show-secrets`](/cli/secret-get) in your
own terminal.

Lambda function configurations, ECS task definitions and Batch job definitions come back with environment variable
values replaced by `[redacted]`; variable names and the other settings stay. Cognito `DescribeUserPoolClient` redacts
the client secret. CloudFormation `GetTemplate` returns the template's structure without any value, as JSON whether
the stack was deployed from JSON or YAML: logical IDs, resource types, conditions, dependencies, property names and
what `Ref`, `Fn::GetAtt`, `Fn::Sub` and `Fn::If` reference stay, and every literal value reads `[value]`. Parameters,
mappings and outputs keep their names only. Other accepted reads return application data as it is: log
events, S3 objects and DynamoDB items contain whatever the application wrote. Read them when a diagnosis needs that
data.

One accepted operation starts a job rather than only reading: CloudWatch Logs `StartQuery` runs a Logs Insights query,
which AWS charges for by the data it scans. `StopQuery` is not accepted.

Stacktape enforces the allowlist where the AWS request is sent, so the dev mode agent's
[`/aws/sdk` endpoint](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev#aws-sdk-access) applies the same list. It is a read-only guard,
not an IAM permission boundary. The call runs with the deployed stack's read-only debug role, assumed with the
caller's selected AWS credentials. The role reads only the stack's own resources in the stack's region: it identifies
them by the stack-name tag CloudFormation puts on every resource, or by their identifiers in the template. CloudWatch
metric and alarm reads cover the whole region, because metrics belong to no stack. A read of another stack, another
region, the account-wide `aws/spans` trace log group or a Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store value returns
AccessDenied. If the stack has no debug role or it cannot be assumed, the command fails with
`CLI_DEBUG_AGENT_ROLE_MISSING` or `CLI_DEBUG_AGENT_ROLE_ASSUME_FAILED` instead of using your own, broader credentials;
redeploy the stack to create or repair the role. A stack whose first deployment failed before it had outputs has no
role yet: there, only CloudFormation reads of that stack are accepted, and they run with your selected credentials.

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
## Target stack and credentials

`aws call` always initializes services for an existing deployed Stacktape stack. It does not require a local
`stacktape.ts` file, but it does require enough information to identify a deployed stack:

- `--region` is required.
- `--project` and `--stage` may be omitted only when your configured Stacktape defaults already identify the
  target stack.
- Otherwise, provide the missing `--project` and `--stage` values explicitly.

Use `--profile` to select a local AWS profile or `--aws-account` to select a connected Stacktape AWS account. These
credentials assume the deployed stack's debug role; the AWS request itself runs with the role.

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
## Basic usage

Read the configuration of one of the stack's Lambda functions:

```bash
stacktape aws call lambda GetFunctionConfiguration \
  --project my-project \
  --stage production \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --input '{"FunctionName":"my-project-production-api"}'
```

Pass command input as JSON:

```bash
stacktape aws call dynamodb Scan \
  --project my-project \
  --stage production \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --input '{"TableName":"my-table","Limit":10}'
```

If project and stage defaults are configured, you can omit those two flags:

```bash
stacktape aws call logs FilterLogEvents \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --input '{"logGroupName":"/aws/lambda/my-function","limit":20}'
```

The command prints the AWS response as JSON. In agent mode, the response is wrapped in a structured object containing
`ok`, `service`, `command`, and `data`.

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
## Choosing the right command

Prefer Stacktape's resource-aware commands when one exists. They resolve Stacktape resource names, apply
resource-specific validation, and usually provide more useful output.

| Task                                    | Preferred command                           |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Read function or service logs           | [`logs`](/cli/logs)                         |
| Inspect CloudWatch metrics              | [`metrics`](/cli/metrics)                   |
| Inspect a Stacktape DynamoDB table      | [`query dynamodb`](/cli/query-dynamodb)     |
| Inspect a Stacktape relational database | [`query sql`](/cli/query-sql)               |
| Inspect a Stacktape Redis cache       | [`query redis`](/cli/query-redis)           |
| Inspect a Stacktape OpenSearch domain   | [`query opensearch`](/cli/query-opensearch) |
| Call another reviewed read-only AWS API | `aws call`                                  |

docs.title: aws call
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
### The service is not supported

The service has no reviewed operations in the `aws call` allowlist. Use a Stacktape purpose-built command, use the AWS
CLI directly when appropriate, or request review of the specific read-only operation you need.

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
### The operation is rejected

The exact service and operation pair is not allowlisted. The error lists the operations accepted for that service.
Do not infer support from the operation's verb prefix.

docs.title: aws call
headingPath: The target stack cannot be found
docs.content:
### The target stack cannot be found

Confirm that the stack is already deployed in the selected region. Then provide `--project` and `--stage`, or
configure defaults that identify that same stack.

docs.title: aws call
docs.content:
### The call returns AccessDenied

The debug role does not allow the operation for the requested resource. It reads only the target stack's resources in
the stack's region, and it cannot list resources account-wide, as `ListFunctions` or `ListTables` would. Verify the
selected AWS account/profile and target stack. The allowlist prevents known state-changing operations; it does not
grant IAM permissions.

docs.title: aws call
headingPath: Can I use `aws call` without a Stacktape project?
docs.content:
### Can I use `aws call` without a Stacktape project?

No. A local configuration file is optional, but a deployed target stack is not. Use the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK directly
for resources that are not associated with a deployed Stacktape stack.

docs.title: aws-profile create
docs.content:
# aws-profile create

`stacktape aws-profile create` creates a new AWS profile on your local machine. It prompts you for a profile name, AWS Access Key ID, and AWS Secret Access Key, then stores them in the default AWS credentials location in your home directory. Other AWS tools — including the AWS CLI — can use these profiles.

docs.title: aws-profile create
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape aws-profile create
```

The command is fully interactive. It walks you through three prompts:

1. **Profile name** — an arbitrary name for the profile. Leave blank to use `default`. A profile named `default` is used automatically when no `--profile` flag is passed to other Stacktape commands.
2. **AWS Access Key ID** — the access key from your IAM user's security credentials.
3. **AWS Secret Access Key** — the corresponding secret key (input is masked).

If a profile with the chosen name already exists in your credentials or config file, the command fails with an error. Use [`aws-profile update`](/cli/aws-profile-update) to change credentials for an existing profile. All prompts are handled interactively — there are no required flags.

docs.title: aws-profile create
docs.content:
## Examples

Create a profile named `default` (used automatically when no profile is specified):

```bash
stacktape aws-profile create
```

When prompted for a profile name, press Enter without typing anything. The profile is saved as `default`.

Create a named profile for a specific AWS account or purpose:

```bash
stacktape aws-profile create
```

When prompted, enter a name like `staging` or `production`. You can then pass `--profile staging` to commands like [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) to use that profile's credentials.

Reduce log output to errors only:

```bash
stacktape aws-profile create --log-level error
```

docs.title: aws-profile create
docs.content:
## Where credentials are stored

Credentials are stored in the default AWS credentials location in your home directory. This is the same location used by the AWS CLI and AWS SDKs, so profiles created with Stacktape work with any AWS tooling on the same machine.

To let the Stacktape Console manage AWS access instead of keeping keys on your machine, see [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account).

# aws-profile delete

`stacktape aws-profile delete` removes an AWS profile from your system. It reads profiles from both the AWS credentials file (`~/.aws/credentials`) and the AWS config file (`~/.aws/config`), deduplicates them, presents them in an interactive selector, and deletes the chosen profile. Use this when you need to clean up stale or unused AWS profiles from your local machine. If no profiles exist, the command exits with an error.

docs.title: aws-profile delete
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape aws-profile delete
```

The command is fully interactive — it reads all profiles configured in your AWS credentials and config files, then prompts you to select which one to delete. No flags are required.


> **Warning:** This command modifies your local AWS profile configuration by deleting the selected profile. The deleted profile will no longer be available to Stacktape or any other AWS tooling on your system.

docs.title: aws-profile delete
docs.content:
## Examples

Delete a profile with debug logging enabled:

```bash
stacktape aws-profile delete --debug
```

docs.content:
# aws-profile list

`stacktape aws-profile list` prints the AWS profiles in your AWS credentials file (`~/.aws/credentials`) that hold a static access key pair. For each one it shows the name, the access key ID and a masked secret access key. Use it to check which static keys are on this machine, for example before you [update](/cli/aws-profile-update) or [delete](/cli/aws-profile-delete) one.

SSO and role profiles live in `~/.aws/config` without static keys, so they are not listed even when they work. To check that a profile works, run `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile <name>`, or pass `--profile <name>` to any Stacktape command.

docs.title: aws-profile list
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape aws-profile list
```

```text
Profile      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID        AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
default      <access key ID>          ************************************abcd
production   <access key ID>          ************************************wxyz
```

Only the last 4 characters of each secret access key are shown, in the terminal and in the `--agent` result. Add `--show-secrets` to print the whole keys. When the file has no static key pair, the command says so and suggests [`aws-profile create`](/cli/aws-profile-create).

docs.content:
# aws-profile update

`stacktape aws-profile update` replaces the AWS access key credentials for an existing AWS profile stored on your machine. Use it when you rotate IAM user keys or need to correct a misconfigured profile without deleting and recreating it.

docs.title: aws-profile update
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape aws-profile update
```

The command is fully interactive. It reads the profiles already configured in your AWS credentials file (`~/.aws/credentials`) and walks you through three prompts:

1. **Choose a profile** — a selectable list of every profile in your credentials file.
2. **AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID** — the new access key ID from your IAM user's security credentials.
3. **AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY** — the corresponding secret key (input is masked).

After the prompts complete, Stacktape updates the selected profile's credentials and prints `Updated credentials for AWS profile <profile>.`


> **Warning:** If no AWS profiles exist on your system, the command exits with an error. Use [`aws-profile create`](/cli/aws-profile-create) to set up your first profile.

docs.title: aws-profile update
docs.content:
## Examples

Update credentials for an existing profile with debug-level logging:

```bash
stacktape aws-profile update --debug
```

docs.title: bastion shell
docs.content:
# bastion shell

`stacktape bastion shell` starts an interactive shell on a deployed [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host). The session is established over SSM, so no SSH keys or open inbound ports are required.

docs.title: bastion shell
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape bastion shell --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

Your stack must contain at least one `bastion` resource. The `--bastion-resource` flag is optional — use it when the deployed stack has multiple bastions and you need to choose which one to connect to.

```bash
stacktape bastion shell --stage production --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion
```

The command does not modify your stack and does not require a Stacktape configuration file.

docs.title: bastion shell
docs.content:
## How it works

When you run `bastion shell`, Stacktape initializes stack services, resolves the bastion EC2 instance ID from the deployed stack overview, and starts an SSM shell session in the selected region. Your terminal becomes an interactive shell on the bastion host.


> **Info:** The `bastion shell` command resolves the bastion EC2 instance ID from the deployed stack overview and starts an SSM shell session in the target region. If Stacktape cannot resolve the instance ID, verify that the target stack includes the selected bastion resource.

docs.title: bastion shell
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: bastion shell
headingPath: Connect to the only bastion in a stack
docs.content:
### Connect to the only bastion in a stack

When your stack has a single bastion resource, you can omit `--bastion-resource`.

```bash
stacktape bastion shell --stage dev --region us-east-1
```

docs.title: bastion shell
headingPath: Connect to a specific bastion by name
docs.content:
### Connect to a specific bastion by name

When your configuration defines more than one bastion, specify which one to connect to.

```bash
stacktape bastion shell --stage production --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource vpnBastion
```

docs.title: bastion shell
docs.content:
### Use a specific AWS profile

```bash
stacktape bastion shell --stage staging --region eu-central-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

docs.title: bastion shell
docs.content:
## Troubleshooting

The command requires a deployed `bastion` resource in the target stack. If Stacktape cannot resolve a bastion resource from the deployed stack, the command fails. Ensure you have deployed a stack that includes at least one bastion before running this command.

When using `--bastion-resource`, the value must match the name of a bastion resource in your configuration. If the name does not match any bastion in the deployed stack, the command reports an error.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
# bastion tunnel

`stacktape bastion tunnel` creates a secure tunnel through a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) to reach resources inside a private VPC. Use it to connect local tools — database GUIs, Redis CLIs, or HTTP clients — to resources that have no public endpoint. The command establishes the tunnel through AWS SSM Session Manager.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape bastion tunnel myDatabase --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

The command opens one or more local ports, prints the local-to-remote mapping, and keeps running until you press `Ctrl+C`. Your stack must contain a [bastion](/resources/security/bastion-host) resource.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
## Important flags

**`<resource-name>`** (required, positional argument) — the name of the target resource you want to reach through the tunnel, as defined in your Stacktape configuration.

**`--bastion-resource`** — selects which bastion resource to tunnel through. Use this when your stack has multiple bastion hosts.

**`--local-tunneling-port`** — sets the local port passed to the tunneling helper. If not specified, Stacktape automatically selects an available port. If the target resolves to multiple tunnel targets, Stacktape opens one port-forwarding session per target and prints the actual local ports.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
## Supported resource types

Bastion tunneling works with four resource types. Stacktape resolves the tunnel targets for the resource and opens one or more port-forwarding sessions accordingly.

| Resource type | Notes |
|---|---|
| [relational-database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | Tunnels to the database endpoints resolved for the resource. |
| [redis](/resources/databases/redis) | Tunnels to the Redis endpoints resolved for the resource. |
| [application-load-balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) | Tunnels to the load balancer's listener ports. |
| [private-service](/resources/compute/private-service) | Tunnels through the private service's nested load balancer. Requires the deployed private service to have a nested load balancer. |

If you target a resource type not listed above, Stacktape fails the command with an unsupported-tunnel-target error.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
### Tunnel to a relational database

Connect a local database GUI (pgAdmin, DataGrip, DBeaver) to a VPC-only PostgreSQL or MySQL database.

```bash
stacktape bastion tunnel myDatabase --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

The output prints each local-to-remote mapping. When tunnel metadata includes an additional string, Stacktape prints it with the remote host and port replaced by the local tunnel address.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
headingPath: Tunnel on a specific local port
docs.content:
### Tunnel on a specific local port

Pin the local port so bookmarked database connections stay stable across sessions.

```bash
stacktape bastion tunnel myDatabase --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --local-tunneling-port 5433
```

Stacktape starts one port-forwarding session for each resolved target and prints the local port for each tunnel.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
### Tunnel to a Redis cache

Access a VPC-only [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) from a local `redis-cli` or Redis GUI.

```bash
stacktape bastion tunnel myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
### Tunnel to a private service

Reach a [private service](/resources/compute/private-service) through its load balancer.

```bash
stacktape bastion tunnel myPrivateApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
### Specify which bastion to use

When a stack has multiple bastion hosts, pass the bastion name explicitly with `--bastion-resource`.

```bash
stacktape bastion tunnel myDatabase --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource devBastion
```

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content:
## How tunneling works

When you run `bastion tunnel`, Stacktape performs the following steps:

1. Initializes services for working with the deployed stack.
2. Looks up the target resource by name in the deployed stack. If the resource does not exist, the command fails with an error.
3. Validates that the target is a supported resource type. For `private-service`, it also checks that the resource has a nested load balancer.
4. Resolves the tunnel targets for the resource (hosts, ports, and optional connection string metadata) using the target resource name and the bastion resource name.
5. Passes `--local-tunneling-port` as the starting port to the port-forwarding session helper, which opens one SSM session per resolved target.
6. Prints the local-to-remote mappings, including substituted connection strings when available.
7. Registers cleanup hooks to close all tunnel sessions on exit.
8. Keeps the process alive until you press `Ctrl+C`.


> **Info:** The tunnel uses AWS SSM Session Manager under the hood, through AWS's [Session Manager plugin](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager-working-with-install-plugin.html). You do not install it yourself. The Windows installer includes it; on Linux and macOS, the first command that needs it downloads the version Stacktape pins from AWS, checks its SHA-256 against the checksum that Stacktape release pins, and keeps it under `~/.stacktape/tools` for later commands. On a machine without internet access, place the plugin there beforehand: when the download fails, the error names the URL, the expected checksum and the exact path.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: bastion tunnel
headingPath: Do I need SSH keys to use bastion tunnel?
docs.content:
### Do I need SSH keys to use bastion tunnel?

No. The `bastion tunnel` command uses AWS SSM Session Manager for port forwarding, not SSH, so there are no SSH keys to manage. Stacktape supplies the Session Manager plugin the tunnel needs (see [How tunneling works](#how-tunneling-works)), and your stack must include a [bastion](/resources/security/bastion-host) resource.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
headingPath: How do I connect a database GUI through the tunnel?
docs.content:
### How do I connect a database GUI through the tunnel?

Run `bastion tunnel` and note the local address printed in the output (e.g. `127.0.0.1:5433`). In your database GUI, set the host to `127.0.0.1` and the port to the printed local port. Use the same database credentials you normally use for the deployed resource; `bastion tunnel` only changes the host and port to the printed local address.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
headingPath: Why does my private service tunnel fail?
docs.content:
### Why does my private service tunnel fail?

Tunneling to a [private service](/resources/compute/private-service) requires the deployed service to have a nested load balancer. If your private service does not have one, the command fails with an error. The other supported targets are `relational-database`, `redis`, and `application-load-balancer`; any other resource type fails with an unsupported-tunnel-target error.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
headingPath: Can I run multiple tunnels at the same time?
docs.content:
### Can I run multiple tunnels at the same time?

Yes. Each `bastion tunnel` invocation keeps running while its port-forwarding sessions are open, so run another invocation in a separate terminal for a second tunnel. Pass a different `--local-tunneling-port` to each one to avoid local port collisions.

docs.title: bastion tunnel
headingPath: Can I tunnel to a publicly accessible database?
docs.content:
### Can I tunnel to a publicly accessible database?

You can, but there is no reason to. If a database has a public endpoint, connect to it directly. Bastion tunneling is designed for resources deployed in a private VPC with no public endpoint.

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
# bucket sync

`stacktape bucket sync` synchronizes the contents of a local directory with an S3 bucket. It mirrors the source directory into the bucket, removing any files from the bucket that no longer exist locally. Use it when you need a local build directory mirrored into an S3 bucket, either by resolving a bucket resource from a deployed Stacktape stack or by passing a bucket ID directly.

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
## Usage

There are two ways to specify which bucket to sync to.

**Using your Stacktape configuration** — provide `--stage` and the resource name (`bucket sync <resource-name>`). Stacktape resolves the bucket from your deployed stack and uses the `directoryUpload.directoryPath` defined in your config. Additional `directoryUpload` settings — `excludeFilesPatterns`, `fileOptions`, and `headersPreset` — are also applied automatically from the resource's configuration:

```bash
stacktape bucket sync myHostingBucket --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

**Using a bucket ID directly** — provide `--bucket-id` (the AWS bucket name or physical resource ID) and `--source-path`:

```bash
stacktape bucket sync --bucket-id my-app-assets-bucket --source-path ./dist --region eu-west-1
```


> **Warning:** Files in the destination bucket that are not present in the source directory are deleted. This is a one-way mirror sync, not an additive upload.

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
## Important flags

The `bucket sync` command accepts several optional flags that control caching headers, CDN invalidation, and source-path resolution. The flags below cover the most commonly used options beyond the resource name, `--stage`, `--bucket-id`, and `--region`.

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
### `--invalidate-cdn-cache`

When set to `true`, Stacktape finds any CloudFront distributions connected to the synced bucket and creates an invalidation for all paths (`/*`). Use this after updating a static site or SPA so users see the new content immediately instead of waiting for the CDN cache TTL to expire.

```bash
stacktape bucket sync website --stage production --region eu-west-1 --invalidate-cdn-cache
```

CDN invalidation starts immediately but may take a few seconds to propagate to all edge locations.

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
### `--headers-preset`

Configures HTTP headers on uploaded files based on a selected preset. The presets mainly control caching behavior for static websites and common frontend framework output directories. If you are syncing via config mode (`--stage` + `--resource-name`), this can also be set in your Stacktape configuration's `directoryUpload.headersPreset` property — the CLI flag overrides it.

Available presets:

| Preset | Behavior |
|--------|----------|
| `static-website` | Caches all content on CDN, never in browser |
| `single-page-app` | `index.html` is never cached; all other assets cached indefinitely |
| `gatsby-static-website` | Optimized for Gatsby output structure |
| `astro-static-website` | `_astro/**` assets marked immutable |
| `sveltekit-static-website` | `_app/**` assets marked immutable |
| `nuxt-static-website` | `_nuxt/**` assets marked immutable |

```bash
stacktape bucket sync --bucket-id my-spa-bucket --source-path ./build --region us-east-1 --headers-preset single-page-app
```

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
### `--source-path`

Path to the local directory to sync. Can be absolute or relative to the current working directory. `--source-path` is only valid with `--bucket-id`; providing `--source-path` without `--bucket-id` causes a validation error. In config mode (`--stage` + `--resource-name`), the source directory is always read from `directoryUpload.directoryPath` in your Stacktape configuration.

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
### `<resource-name>`

The name of the bucket resource as defined in your Stacktape configuration. Used together with `--stage` to identify the target bucket from your deployed stack. The source directory and headers preset are read from the resource's `directoryUpload` config.

docs.title: bucket sync
docs.content:
## Examples

Sync a React SPA build folder to a hosting bucket and invalidate CDN cache:

```bash
stacktape bucket sync frontend --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --invalidate-cdn-cache
```

Sync to an arbitrary S3 bucket with a preset for Astro. In `--bucket-id` mode, Stacktape uses the explicit `--source-path` and `--headers-preset` CLI inputs; config-only `directoryUpload` options such as `excludeFilesPatterns` and `fileOptions` are read only when syncing by `--stage` and `--resource-name`.

```bash
stacktape bucket sync --bucket-id my-astro-site-bucket --source-path ./dist --region us-east-1 --headers-preset astro-static-website
```

Sync with a specific AWS profile:

```bash
stacktape bucket sync assets --stage staging --region eu-central-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

docs.title: connect
docs.content:
# connect

`stacktape connect` adds the AWS account you deploy to with the CLI to the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview). It signs you in if needed, connects the account of your current AWS credentials to your organization, and finds the Stacktape stacks already in that account. Nothing is redeployed: your stacks keep their names, resources and URLs.

Use it after you deployed [without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli) and want the Console: logs, alarms, costs, Git deployments and team access. The Console is free up to $200 a month of AWS spend it manages. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).

docs.title: connect
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape connect
```

To connect a different account, pick its AWS profile:

```bash
stacktape connect --profile production
```

docs.title: connect
docs.content:
## What happens

1. **Sign-in.** When this machine is not signed in, the CLI opens the same browser sign-in as [`stacktape login`](/cli/login). Pass `--no-browser` to only print the address, for example over SSH.
2. **The AWS account.** The CLI reads the account of your local AWS credentials: `--profile`, `AWS_PROFILE` or the standard AWS credential chain.
3. **The connection.** When the account is not connected yet, the CLI creates the connection stack in it with your credentials. The stack creates an IAM role that the Console uses to read and deploy your stacks. It is a CloudFormation stack in `eu-west-1`, whatever region you deploy to. When the account is already connected, the CLI says so and skips this step.
4. **Your stacks.** The Console looks for the Stacktape stacks in the account. They appear as projects and stages, and the CLI prints how many it found.
5. **The Console address.** The CLI prints `Nothing was redeployed or changed.` and the address of your projects in the Console.

If creating the connection stack with your credentials fails, for example because they lack IAM permissions, the CLI opens the AWS CloudFormation console instead. Create the stack there and return to the terminal. [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) describes the Console side, including the `PENDING` and `BLOCKED` states.

docs.title: connect
docs.content:
## Who can connect an account

Owners and Admins can connect accounts. A Developer or Viewer reaches only the AWS accounts chosen for them, so the command stops with `Your role in <organization> cannot connect AWS accounts.` Ask an Owner or Admin to run `stacktape connect` with credentials for the account. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: connect
docs.content:
## In scripts and coding agents

With `--agent` the command never prompts and never opens a browser. It needs a sign-in first: run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) or set `STACKTAPE_API_KEY`. When creating the connection stack fails, the command stops with an error instead of opening the browser.

docs.title: connect
docs.content:
## When some stacks are missing

When the CLI cannot read stacks in a region, it names the region, and stacks there are not listed yet. When the search fails, the account stays connected. In both cases an Owner or Admin can run **Find existing stacks** on the AWS accounts page of the Console.

docs.title: connect
docs.content:
## Undo it

To make the CLI work without the Console again, run [`stacktape logout`](/cli/logout). Nothing deployed changes. To also remove the Console's access to the account, delete the connection on the AWS accounts page of the Console and delete the connection stack in the AWS CloudFormation console. See [Revoking access](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account#revoking-access).

docs.title: container exec
docs.content:
# container exec

`stacktape container exec` runs one command inside a running container of a deployed [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), [private service](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) or [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload), and prints its output as JSON. Use it to check a file, an environment variable or a process without opening a shell. It needs AWS credentials, connects through AWS ECS Exec and Session Manager (no SSH keys or open ports), and doesn't need a config file.

For an interactive shell, use [`container shell`](/cli/container-shell).

docs.title: container exec
docs.content:
## Usage

The resource name comes first, then the command in quotes:

```bash
stacktape container exec myService "ls -la /app" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

```json
{
  "resourceName": "myService",
  "containerName": "myService",
  "taskArn": "arn:aws:ecs:eu-west-1:123456789012:task/cluster/abc123",
  "command": "ls -la /app",
  "output": "total 24\ndrwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 ...",
  "exitCode": 0
}
```

`output` is what the command printed: its standard output, or its error output when it printed nothing else. `exitCode` is the exit code of the Session Manager session, not of your command. `0` means the session ran, so read `output` to see whether the command worked. A non-zero `exitCode` fails the CLI with `CONTAINER_EXEC_FAILED`. A command that runs longer than 60 seconds is stopped.

Outside a project directory, add `--project` or set a default project with [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set).

Changes the command makes in the container, such as written files, are lost when the task is replaced, for example on the next deploy.

docs.title: container exec
headingPath: Pick the task and the container
docs.content:
## Pick the task and the container

A service scaled to several tasks runs the command in the first running task of the service. One-off tasks, such as a running [release command](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands), are never picked. Pick another task with `--task-arn`, the full ARN or only the task ID:

```bash
stacktape container exec apiService "ps aux" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --task-arn abc123def
```

A workload with more than one container, such as a [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) with a sidecar, needs `--container`:

```bash
stacktape container exec myWorkload "cat /var/log/sidecar.log" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --container sidecar
```

docs.title: container exec
docs.content:
## Use it in a script

With `--agent`, the command prints NDJSON: one JSON object per line. The JSON above arrives as text in the `message` of a `log` line, and the last line is the command's `result`. To read `output`, select the log line and parse its message:

```bash
stacktape container exec apiService "cat /app/version.txt" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --agent \
  | jq -r 'select(.type == "log") | .message | fromjson? | .output'
```

docs.title: container exec
headingPath: Resource is not a deployed container workload
docs.content:
### Resource is not a deployed container workload

The name doesn't match a deployed web service, private service, worker service or multi-container workload in the stage. Check the name in your config and that the stage is deployed.

docs.title: container exec
docs.content:
### Resource contains multiple containers

The task has more than one container, or none with the name you passed. The error lists their names; run again with `--container <name>`.

docs.title: container exec
docs.content:
### No running task was found

The service has no running task, for example while a deployment is still starting it. Wait for a task to start, or check the service in the Console or the AWS ECS console.

docs.title: container exec
headingPath: Resource does not have a deployed ECS service
docs.content:
### Resource does not have a deployed ECS service

The stage is a dev stack. Dev mode runs containers on your machine, so there is nothing to connect to in AWS. Run the command against a deployed stage.

docs.title: container exec
docs.content:
### Task was not found

The `--task-arn` value doesn't match a running task. The error lists the task IDs you can use.

docs.content:
# container shell

`stacktape container shell` starts an interactive session inside a running container in your deployed stack. The session is established using ECS Exec and an SSM (Systems Manager) connection, giving you direct terminal access to debug, inspect files, or troubleshoot issues in a running container.

docs.title: container shell
docs.content:
## Usage

Open a session by specifying the target stage, region, and resource name.

```bash
stacktape container shell myService --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

This opens an interactive session inside the container running in the specified resource. The target workload must be a deployed workload with an ECS task definition. Stacktape looks for running ECS tasks before opening the session. When multiple tasks are running, Stacktape prompts you to choose one. Only the service's own tasks count; one-off tasks, such as a running [release command](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands), are left out.


> **Info:** This command does not require a Stacktape configuration file. It connects directly to the deployed stack using the resource name argument (`container shell <resource-name>`) and the `--stage` and `--region` flags. Use optional stack arguments such as `--project`, `--aws-account`, or `--profile` when your local defaults are not enough to identify the target stack or AWS credentials.

docs.title: container shell
docs.content:
## Important flags

The two most commonly used optional flags are `--command` and `--container`. Both affect which process and which container you connect to.

**`--command`** specifies the command that starts the interactive session inside the container. Use it to select a specific shell (like `bash`). To run a one-shot command and capture its output non-interactively, use [`container exec`](/cli/container-exec) instead.

Start a bash session:

```bash
stacktape container shell myService --stage production --region eu-west-1 --command /bin/bash
```

**`--container`** selects a specific container in multi-container workloads. If the target workload has more than one container definition, specify the container name with `--container`. Stacktape raises an error and includes the available container names when multiple containers exist and `--container` is omitted, or when the specified name does not match any container in the workload.

```bash
stacktape container shell myWorkload --stage production --region eu-west-1 --container nginx
```

docs.title: container shell
docs.content:
## Multiple running instances

When the target resource has multiple running tasks (for example, a scaled-out web service), the CLI prompts you to choose which instance to connect to. Each option shows the task ID and its start time so you can identify the right one.

docs.title: container shell
docs.content:
## Common errors

- **Resource cannot be resolved** — Stacktape throws an error when the resource name does not match a deployed workload with an ECS task definition. Check that the resource name matches a deployed workload in the target stage and AWS region.
- **Multiple containers without `--container` flag** — The target workload has more than one container. The error message lists the available container names. Re-run the command with `--container` set to one of those names.

docs.title: container shell
docs.content:
## Examples

The following examples show common `container shell` usage patterns across different workload types and configurations.

Inspect the filesystem of a running web service:

```bash
stacktape container shell apiServer --stage dev --region us-east-1
```

Connect to a specific container in a multi-container workload:

```bash
stacktape container shell myWorkload --stage production --region eu-west-1 --container sidecar
```

Open a bash session:

```bash
stacktape container shell backend --stage staging --region us-west-2 --command /bin/bash
```

# defaults list

`stacktape defaults list` prints all system-wide Stacktape defaults configured on your machine. Stacktape uses these defaults as fallback values for commands that accept the corresponding arguments, so you don't need to pass common flags like `--region` or `--stage` each time.

docs.title: defaults list
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape defaults list
```

This command takes no arguments. It reads stored defaults and prints each configured key-value pair. If no defaults are set, it suggests running [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set).

docs.title: defaults list
docs.content:
## What gets displayed

The output shows all defaults you've previously set with [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set). Configurable defaults include:

- `region` — AWS region used for deployments
- `stage` — default stage name
- `awsProfile` — AWS credentials profile
- `projectName` — default project name
- `awsAccount` — AWS account identifier

`defaults list` also prints other stored defaults, such as default executables for resolving Node.js directives, when configured.

Each default appears as a `key: value` pair. Stacktape uses these values as fallback arguments for commands that accept the corresponding options.


> **Info:** This command does not require a Stacktape API key. You can run it without being logged in.

docs.content:
# defaults set

`stacktape defaults set` saves default values for flags you would otherwise type on every command, such as the region, stage, project and AWS profile. A flag you pass still wins for that one command. Defaults apply to every project on this machine. The command needs no Stacktape account and no AWS credentials.

docs.title: defaults set
docs.content:
## Usage

Set one default:

```bash
stacktape defaults set region eu-west-1
```

```bash
stacktape defaults set stage dev-alice
```

After that, `stacktape deploy` with no `--region` deploys to `eu-west-1`, and `--region us-east-1` overrides it for one command. A stage you deploy every day, such as your own dev stage, is the usual default. A default stage still means `stacktape delete` with no `--stage` targets it, so pass `--stage` on destructive commands anyway.

Without arguments, the command asks for every default in turn and shows the current value. Press Enter to keep a value, type a new one to change it, or type a single space to reset it.

```bash
stacktape defaults set
```

The CLI prints the file it saved the defaults to. It is a file in your home directory, local to this machine. [`defaults list`](/cli/defaults-list) shows what is set.

docs.title: defaults set
docs.content:
## What you can set

| Key | Used as |
|---|---|
| `region` | `--region` |
| `stage` | `--stage` |
| `project` | `--project` |
| `profile` | `--profile`, the AWS profile (default `default`) |
| `aws-account` | `--aws-account`, a connected AWS account name in the Console |
| `api-key` | The Stacktape API key. [`login`](/cli/login) sets it for you. |
| `executable-python`, `executable-javascript` | The Python and Node.js executables Stacktape runs (default `python` and `node`). Change them only when they are not on your `PATH` under those names. |

An unknown key or an invalid value, such as a stage with capital letters, fails with the list of keys.

docs.title: delete
docs.content:
# delete

`stacktape delete` removes a deployed stage: the CloudFormation stack with all its resources, then the stage's deployment bucket and container image repository. Data in the stack's databases, buckets and tables is deleted with it, and there is no undo. Back up what you need first. The command asks for confirmation before it deletes anything.

docs.title: delete
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape delete --stage staging --region eu-west-1
```

The CLI shows the stack it found and asks you to confirm. Pass the flags you deploy with, such as `--stage`, `--project` and `--aws-account`, so it finds the right stack.

In CI or another run that can't ask, add `--yes`. Without it, the command fails with `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` and deletes nothing. `--agent` changes only the output; it doesn't confirm.

```bash
stacktape delete --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

docs.title: delete
docs.content:
## beforeDelete hooks

When the CLI loads a config, it runs the config's `beforeDelete` [hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) before it deletes anything, for example to export data or clean up something outside the stack. It loads a config when you pass `--config`, and also when it finds one in the working directory. To delete without running the hooks, run the command from a directory without a config.

docs.title: delete
docs.content:
## Protected stacks and resources

**Termination protection.** A stack with `terminationProtection: true` can't be deleted. [Deploy](/cli/deploy) with `terminationProtection: false`, then delete.

**Deletion protection.** When a resource has deletion protection on, such as a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) or an [Aurora DSQL database](/resources/databases/dsql) with `deletionProtection: true`, the command stops before it deletes anything and lists the protected resources. Deploy with `deletionProtection: false`, then delete. `stacktape init` turns deletion protection on for every database it adds.

When an earlier delete ended in `DELETE_FAILED`, the stack can't be deployed anymore. Turn the protection off in the AWS console for that resource, then delete again.

docs.title: delete
docs.content:
## Examples

Delete from the AWS account of a specific profile. When the CLI is signed in to the Console, that account must be connected to your organization.

```bash
stacktape delete --stage dev-john --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

Print debug logs while you troubleshoot a failed delete:

```bash
stacktape delete --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --log-level debug
```

docs.title: delete
docs.content: ## Options

| Option | Required | Type | Description | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

## Related commands

- [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) returns a stage to an earlier release and keeps it running.
- [`stack list`](/cli/stack-list) lists the stacks in a region.
- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) creates or updates a stage.

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
# deploy

`stacktape deploy` deploys your stack to AWS. It creates the stack when the stage doesn't exist yet and updates it when it does. It needs AWS credentials; a Stacktape account is optional.

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage <stage> --region <region>
```

The command reads the Stacktape configuration file in the current directory: `stacktape.yml`, `stacktape.yaml`, `stacktape.ts` or `stacktape.js`. If there is more than one, or the file is elsewhere, pass `--config`. The stage and region are required. When the config declares `projectName` and `region`, as the one [`init`](/cli/init) writes does, `--stage` is enough:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev
```

Flags override the config. The region can also come from `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` (not `AWS_REGION`), [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set) or your AWS profile.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
## What happens during deploy

Before it changes anything, the CLI prints the AWS account it loaded credentials for. Check it, especially with several profiles.

1. **Validate** — Reads your config, validates guardrails, and ensures referenced secrets exist.
2. **Build & package** — Packages workloads for deployment. Cached artifacts are reused when possible.
3. **Upload** — Uploads deployment artifacts for the stack.
4. **Deploy** — Creates or updates a CloudFormation stack. When only code changed, updates the changed functions and container services directly instead (see [Fast deployments](#fast-deployments)).
5. **Post-deploy** — Syncs hosting buckets, invalidates CDN caches, and prints resource URLs.

After a successful deploy, Stacktape prints short stack information and the URLs of your resources. When the CLI is signed in to the Stacktape Console, it also prints the Console link of the stage. Without an account, the first successful deploy of a project in an interactive terminal can print a one-line hint about the Console; see [Add the Console](/getting-started/add-the-console).

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
## Fast deployments

When only the code of functions or container services changed, `stacktape deploy` updates them directly instead of through CloudFormation. A function update takes seconds; a container service runs a normal rolling deployment. Stacktape decides this on its own for every deployment, using CloudFormation whenever anything else changed. It prints the reason when it does.

Code that several functions share is packaged into a Lambda layer. A change to it is a code change too: Stacktape publishes the new layer version itself and gives every function that uses it the new version together with its own code, so a change to shared code deploys as fast as a change to one function.

When both a handler and its shared code change, Stacktape attaches the new layer before switching the handler if the old handler can use it. This includes adding a helper and using it in the new handler. When compatibility cannot be proved, Stacktape temporarily keeps both generations available. A failed code update can leave the old handler on the new layer; deploying again completes the update.

The compatibility check protects the forward deployment. CloudFormation updates code and layers separately during a rollback, so rolling back across an edit that added a used export can briefly fail invocations if the old layer is restored before the new handler is replaced. Stacktape prints a note during the fast deployment when it detects this risk. See [rollback safety](/cli/rollback#safety-warnings).

A deployment uses CloudFormation when:

- the stack is new, or the template changes anything other than function code or container images built by Stacktape (configuration, environment variables, permissions, resources, external images),
- stack settings changed, such as tags or termination protection,
- a changed function uses an alias (`deployment` or provisioned concurrency) or a changed container service uses blue/green deployment,
- the stack has an `after:deploy` [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts), which runs through CloudFormation on every deployment,
- you pass `--full`.

For eligible Node.js Fargate web services, `properties.codeSwap: true` enables [in-place code swaps](/deployment-and-lifecycle/code-swap) with the same deploy command. The opt-in applies in every stage, including production, within the task cap. Failed memory screening or an unsupported change uses an image deploy, with the reason in CLI output. Old and new processes share memory during a swap; a sudden memory increase can fail in-flight requests.

A fast deployment is a release like any other: it gets the next version number, and [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) can return to it or from it. A deployment that changes nothing creates no release, even with `--full`. If some updates fail, Stacktape still finishes the others and lists which workloads run the new code. Deploying again updates the rest. The CloudFormation template is updated by the next full deployment.

docs.title: deploy
docs.content: ## Common flags

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
### `--full`

Deploys every change through CloudFormation, even when only code changed.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --full
```

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
### `--yes`

Confirms the deploy when it needs confirmation: an update that may delete stateful resources, or a project that does not exist yet and would be created. Use `--yes` in CI/CD pipelines and other non-interactive runs. Without it, such a deploy fails with `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` before it changes anything. `--agent` only switches the output to JSONL; it does not confirm.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
### `--auto-rollback`

By default, a failed deployment keeps what it created or updated. The stack stays in `CREATE_FAILED` (first deployment) or `UPDATE_FAILED` (update), and running `deploy` again after fixing the error continues from the failure instead of creating everything again. With `--auto-rollback`, CloudFormation undoes this deployment if it fails: an update returns to the last successful deployment, and a first deployment deletes the new stack. The flag overrides `deploymentConfig.autoRollback` for one deployment. When the config sets `deploymentConfig.triggerRollbackOnAlarms` or `monitoringTimeAfterDeploymentInMinutes`, rollback is on by default, and turning it off is an error.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --auto-rollback
```

To undo a failed update later, use [`stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover). To remove a failed first deployment, use [`delete`](/cli/delete). To return to an earlier successful version, use [`rollback`](/cli/rollback). See [when a deployment fails](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#when-a-deployment-fails).

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
### `--no-cache`

Forces a fresh build of all compute resources, ignoring cached artifacts from previous deploys. Use this when you suspect a stale cache is causing issues.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --no-cache
```

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
### `--no-layer-optimization`

By default, Stacktape extracts shared code into Lambda layers to reduce per-function deployment size. Disable this to bundle all code directly into each Lambda function — useful if you need to inspect the full function package or if layer extraction causes issues.

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
### `--show-secrets`

Includes secret values, such as database passwords and connection strings with credentials, in the `--agent` result (`data.result.stackInfo`) and in the stack-info file. Without it, each of them is `<<OMITTED>>`. Use it only where the output stays private, never in shared CI logs. The terminal summary never prints secret values.

### Deploy a new production stage

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region us-east-1
```

headingPath: Deploy to the account of an AWS profile
docs.content:
### Deploy to the account of an AWS profile

The deploy goes to the AWS account that `my-aws-profile` belongs to. When the CLI is signed in to the Console, that account must be connected to your organization, or the deploy fails.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --profile my-aws-profile --project my-app
```

docs.title: deploy
headingPath: Deploy to a named connected account
docs.content:
### Deploy to a named connected account

With the Console, choose one of the organization's connected AWS accounts by name.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 --aws-account production
```

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
### Preview changes before deploying

Use [`diff`](/cli/diff) to see what a deploy would modify without actually applying changes:

```bash
stacktape diff --stage production --region us-east-1
```

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
## Free plan cost limit

This applies only to organizations on the Console's Free plan. Without a Stacktape account there is no limit.

The Free plan covers up to $200 of managed AWS costs per calendar month (UTC). From $150, a successful deploy prints how
close the organization is and what the Flexible plan would cost:

```text
This organization is at $162.40 of the $200 Free limit for November 2026; on Flexible, this spend would cost about $41 (https://console.stacktape.com/subscription-plans).
```

The first time the organization goes over $200, a 7-day grace period starts and Owners and Admins get an email.
Deploys keep working during it, and each one prints the countdown. The grace period ends early when the calendar month
(UTC) ends: one that starts on November 29 doesn't cover December. After the grace period, and in any later month as
soon as the organization is over the limit, the deploy stops with a `Free Plan Limit Reached` error. The CLI has
loaded your AWS credentials by then, but nothing in your stack has changed:

```text
[x] Free Plan Limit Reached

Deploys are paused for this organization. The AWS costs Stacktape manages for it are $214.17 in November 2026, above
the Free plan's $200 a month. The 7-day grace ended on 24 Nov at 14:05 UTC. Deploys resume on December 1, or right
away when an Owner or Admin upgrades to the Flexible plan at https://console.stacktape.com/subscription-plans. Your
running infrastructure is not affected, and deleting or rolling back stages still works.
```

[`delete`](/cli/delete) and [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) keep working. When the month's costs aren't known yet, the
deploy goes ahead. See [Free plan cost limit](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription#free-plan-cost-limit) for
what counts.

docs.title: deploy
docs.content:
## Dev stacks cannot be deployed

Stages created by [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) (dev stacks) cannot be updated with `deploy`. If you attempt this, Stacktape rejects the deploy with an error. To deploy a production stack, use a different stage name (e.g., `--stage production`). To remove a dev stack, use [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete).

Stacktape does not currently check CloudFormation resource drift before deploying. Manual changes to stack resources can affect an update; review the proposed changes with [`diff`](/cli/diff).

docs.title: deployment-script run
docs.content:
# deployment-script run

`stacktape deployment-script run` re-packages and invokes a single [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts) without running a full [deploy](/cli/deploy). Use it to iterate on script logic — fix a migration, adjust a seed routine, or re-run a post-deploy step — without waiting for a complete stack update. The command rebuilds the script's Lambda function code from your local source, updates the existing Lambda with it, resolves the script's `parameters` from your current local configuration, invokes the function, and prints the response payload or error to your terminal.


> **Warning:** This command updates the script's **source code** and resolves `parameters` from your local configuration. Changes to environment variables, memory, timeout, VPC settings, or other Lambda configuration require a full [`deploy`](/cli/deploy).

docs.title: deployment-script run
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape deployment-script run runMigrations --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

The three required flags identify which deployed script to target:

- **`--stage`** — the stage where the script is deployed (e.g. `production`, `staging`, `dev`).
- **`--region`** — the AWS region of the stack.
- **`<resource-name>`** (positional argument) — the name of the deployment script resource in your Stacktape configuration.

The deployment script must already exist in your configuration **and** be deployed to the target stack. If the resource is not defined in your configuration file or not present in the deployed stack, the command fails. Add the resource and run [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) first.

docs.title: deployment-script run
docs.content:
## Examples

Re-run a database migration script against a staging stack:

```bash
stacktape deployment-script run runMigrations --stage staging --region us-east-1
```

Re-run a seed script with debug-level logging for more detailed CLI logs:

```bash
stacktape deployment-script run seedData --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --debug
```

Point to a non-default config file location:

```bash
stacktape deployment-script run postDeployHook --stage production --region us-west-2 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: deployment-script run
headingPath: When to use this vs deploy
docs.content:
## When to use this vs deploy

Use `deployment-script run` when you are iterating on the script's handler code and want fast feedback. The command rebuilds and updates only the script's function code, then invokes the Lambda — skipping a full stack update. The script's `parameters` are resolved from your current local configuration and sent as the invocation payload, so parameter changes take effect immediately without redeploying. Switch to a full [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) when you change Lambda configuration such as environment variables, memory, timeout, packaging settings, or VPC settings.

## Related commands

- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) — full stack deployment. Required to provision a new deployment script or update its configuration (environment, memory, timeout).
- [`script run`](/cli/script-run) — runs a local script defined in your configuration. Unlike `deployment-script run`, local scripts execute on your machine rather than as a Lambda function in AWS.
- [`delete`](/cli/delete) — tears down the entire stack, including any deployment scripts.

docs.title: dev network delete
docs.content:
# dev network delete

`stacktape dev network delete` deletes the [dev network](/cli/dev-network) of an AWS account and region: the VPC and the small EC2 instance, the dev box, that connect deployed dev functions to the databases on your machine. Delete it when nobody in the account uses [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) in that region anymore, or when a failed network blocks dev mode.

docs.title: dev network delete
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape dev network delete --region eu-west-1
```

Delete the dev stages that use the network first, with [`stacktape delete --stage <stage>`](/cli/delete). While dev functions still run in the network, the command refuses and lists them, because their network interfaces keep the subnets in use. The deletion takes about 2 minutes and also removes the relay port leases. When dev functions were deleted shortly before, it can take up to about 20 minutes: AWS releases their network interfaces with a delay, and CloudFormation waits for that before it deletes the subnets. The command reports its progress once a minute meanwhile. The next `stacktape dev` that needs a dev network creates it again.

The command asks for confirmation first. With `--json`, or outside a terminal, it cannot ask: pass `--yes`.

The command also refuses while someone else depends on the network:

- While a `stacktape dev` session uses it. The command asks the running dev box for its sessions and lists them. A box that has just started may not answer for about a minute; the command then refuses too. `--force` deletes the network anyway, and those sessions lose their connection.
- While a `stacktape dev` session creates or updates the network. Run the command again when CloudFormation has finished.

A `stacktape dev` that starts while the network is being deleted waits for the deletion to finish and then creates a new network.

docs.title: dev network delete
docs.content:
## When creating the network failed

The first `stacktape dev` deploys its dev stage into the network while CloudFormation still creates the network's last parts. When one of them fails, CloudFormation cannot delete the network again while the stage's functions use its subnets, and the network stays behind in `DELETE_FAILED`. `stacktape dev` and `stacktape dev network` then report the failure and the steps that remove it:

1. Delete the dev stages that use the network, with [`stacktape delete --stage <stage>`](/cli/delete).
2. Wait a few minutes: Lambda releases the network interfaces of deleted functions only after a while.
3. Run `stacktape dev network delete`. It deletes the failed network by its stack name and refuses while dev functions still use it.
4. Run `stacktape dev` again; it creates a new network.

docs.title: dev network
docs.content:
# dev network

The first [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) that needs it creates one dev network per AWS account and region: a VPC with a small EC2 instance, the **dev box**. Deployed dev Lambda functions reach the databases on your machine through the box, and VPC functions get internet access through it. [Connecting to local databases](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#connecting-to-local-databases) explains how it works and what it costs.

`stacktape dev network` shows the network of a region. [`stacktape dev network delete`](/cli/dev-network-delete) deletes it.

docs.title: dev network
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape dev network --region eu-west-1
```

The output names the dev box and whether it runs, the `stacktape dev` session that runs each stage, the dev functions that run in the network, and the stages that hold relay ports:

```
Dev network stacktape-dev-network in eu-west-1 (VPC vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718)
  Dev box: i-0123456789abcdef0, running (about $0.01 per hour; it stops itself 30 minutes after the last session)
  Dev sessions (stage: who runs it, since when):
    shop-dev-jane: Jane Doe (jane-laptop, ~/projects/shop), since 10/24/2026, 9:12:40 AM (1 h 5 min)
  Dev functions in the network: shop-dev-jane-api, shop-dev-jane-worker
  Stacks with relay ports: shop-dev-jane
```

The sessions come from the running dev box, which knows every session connected to it: the user, the host and the project directory of each, and when it started. A session keeps the box running, so a stopped box has none and is not started to ask. A box that has just started may not answer for about a minute; the sessions are then shown as unknown, with the reason.

With `--agent`, the command prints the same as JSON. `sessions` lists `{ stack, holder, since }` entries, `since` as an ISO timestamp, and is `null` with a `sessionsUnknownReason` when the box did not answer.

docs.title: dev network
docs.content:
## Who can reach the tunnels

The dev network is shared by the whole AWS account and region. Every dev function in it can connect to every developer's tunnel ports, not only the functions of that developer's stage. The AWS account is the trust boundary: anyone who can deploy a function into the dev network can reach the databases on the machines of other developers while their `stacktape dev` runs. Local DynamoDB and OpenSearch have no password, and local Redis has one only when its `defaultUserPassword` is set. Use a separate AWS account for people who must not reach each other's local databases.

docs.title: dev network
docs.content:
## Deleting the dev network

[`stacktape dev network delete`](/cli/dev-network-delete) deletes the network of a region, for example to stop paying for the dev box. Delete the dev stages that use it first. The next `stacktape dev` that needs a dev network creates it again.

docs.title: dev stop
docs.content:
# dev stop

`stacktape dev stop` gracefully stops a running dev agent that was started with [`stacktape dev --agent`](/cli/dev). Dev agents expose a local HTTP status endpoint, and `dev stop` uses the selected port to stop the matching agent. It can also clean up orphaned Docker containers left behind by crashed dev sessions.

docs.title: dev stop
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape dev stop
```

Running `stacktape dev stop` without flags stops the dev agent of the project in the current directory. It finds the agent through the lock files in the project directory, or, when they are gone, by asking each of your running agents for its project directory. It never stops an agent of another directory: when no agent of this project runs, it stops nothing and lists the agents of other directories.

When several stages of the project run, `dev stop` stops none of them and fails (`ok: false`, code `CLI_DEV_STOP_AMBIGUOUS`) with the list. Choose one with `--stage`.

The agent accepts only requests that carry its session token. `dev stop` reads it from `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token`, so `--agent-port` works from any directory.

docs.title: dev stop
docs.content:
## Important flags

The `dev stop` command accepts flags that control which agent to stop and whether to clean up leftover containers.

docs.title: dev stop
docs.content:
### --stage and --cwd

`--stage` stops the agent of that stage. `--cwd` stops the agent of another project directory, for example a second Git worktree.

```bash
stacktape dev stop --cwd ../my-app-worktree --stage dev
```

docs.title: dev stop
docs.content:
### --agent-port

Pass `--agent-port` with the port number to stop the agent on that port, wherever it was started.

```bash
stacktape dev stop --agent-port 7332
```

docs.title: dev stop
docs.content:
### --cleanup-containers

A dev session removes its database containers when it stops; their data stays in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/`. A session that crashed or was killed leaves its containers behind. The `--cleanup-containers` flag removes the containers that dev sessions of this project directory left behind: stopped ones, and running ones whose session has ended. With `--stage`, it removes only that stage's. Containers of other projects and Git worktrees stay; add `--all` to remove those of every project on the machine. The result lists the removed containers in `removedContainers`. After cleanup, the command checks for running agents via lock files — if none are found, it exits; if agents are found, normal agent-stop behavior continues (stopping the project's agent, or failing with the list when several stages run).

```bash
stacktape dev stop --cleanup-containers
stacktape dev stop --cleanup-containers --all
```

You can combine `--cleanup-containers` with `--agent-port` to both clean up containers and stop a specific agent in one command.

```bash
stacktape dev stop --cleanup-containers --agent-port 7332
```
