docs.title: package
docs.content:
# package

`stacktape package` builds your Lambda packages and container images without deploying. It runs the same packaging step as [`deploy`](/cli/deploy), so build errors show up before you deploy.

docs.title: package
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape package --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The command packages every compute resource of the stack. It never uses the packaging cache, so each run builds from the current source. It reads the Stacktape config in the current directory; for one elsewhere, pass `--config`:

```bash
stacktape package --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: package
docs.content:
## Examples

Package all compute resources for a staging stage in `us-east-1`:

```bash
stacktape package --stage staging --region us-east-1
```

Package with debug logging to see detailed build output:

```bash
stacktape package --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --debug
```

Package using a specific AWS profile:

```bash
stacktape package --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

docs.title: package
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: package
docs.content:
### How is `package` different from `validate --with-package`?

[`validate`](/cli/validate) validates your configuration, resolves resources, and synthesizes the CloudFormation template in memory. Adding `--with-package` also validates workload packaging. Use `validate --with-package` when you want configuration validation combined with packaging checks. Use `package` when you specifically want to run the packaging step on its own.

docs.title: package
docs.content:
### Does `package` require AWS credentials?

Only when your configuration reads something from AWS. `package` builds on your machine, so a typical project packages without AWS credentials and without any request to AWS. Credentials are loaded when packaging needs them: for a directive such as [`$Secret`](/configuration/directives), `$StackOutput` or `$AwsAccountId`, or for a web framework build whose environment references deployed resources. Stacktape then uses the profile selected with `--profile` or `AWS_PROFILE`, or the standard AWS credential chain.

docs.title: package
headingPath: Can I package only specific workloads?
docs.content:
### Can I package only specific workloads?

By default, the `package` command packages all compute resources in your configuration. To target a subset, pass `--only-workloads` with a comma-separated list of workload names (for example, `--only-workloads myFunction,myContainer`). Other workloads are skipped.

docs.title: package
headingPath: What is the difference between `package` and `synth`?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between `package` and `synth`?

[`synth`](/cli/synth) writes the CloudFormation template and builds no application code. `package` builds your code, according to each resource's [packaging mode](/packaging/overview), and writes no template. [`validate --with-package`](/cli/validate#validation-levels) does both checks in one run.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
# param get

Retrieve the runtime value of a [referenceable parameter](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) from a resource in a deployed stack. Use `param get` to fetch URLs, connection strings, ARNs, and other outputs directly from the CLI — without opening the AWS Console or parsing CloudFormation outputs. The three required arguments are `--region`, `--resource-name`, and `--param-name`.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape param get myApi url --region eu-west-1
```

The command does not require a local Stacktape configuration file. The command takes the resource name and the parameter name as positional arguments (`param get <resource-name> <param-name>`) and requires `--region`; optional stack-selection arguments such as `--stage` or `--project` can still be used when needed to identify the target stack. `--stage` is optional; pass it when you need to target a specific stage explicitly.

Common scenarios for `param get`:

- Feed an endpoint URL into a local script or test harness.
- Retrieve a database connection string for a one-off migration tool.
- Read a resource ARN to pass into another CLI command or CI step.
- Verify the actual deployed value of a parameter after a deploy completes.

If you need a broader overview of all stack outputs and resources at once, use [`status`](/cli/status) instead.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
## Examples

Retrieve a parameter from a deployed resource.

```bash
stacktape param get api url --region us-east-1
```

Pass `--stage` when you want to target a specific stage explicitly. Include it unless you have set a default stage via [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set).

```bash
stacktape param get mainDatabase connectionString --region eu-west-1 --stage production
```

A parameter that holds a credential, such as a database `password` or a `connectionString` that contains one, comes back as `<<OMITTED>>` unless you pass `--show-secrets`. Use the flag only where the output stays private:

```bash
stacktape param get mainDatabase connectionString --region eu-west-1 --stage production --show-secrets
```

For programmatic consumption in scripts or CI steps, use `--agent` or `--json` to get machine-readable JSONL output. The default interactive output includes formatting that is not suitable for shell variable capture.

```bash
stacktape param get api url --region eu-west-1 --agent
```


> **Info:** The available parameter names depend on the resource type. See [referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) for the full list grouped by resource type.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
## Error handling

If the resource name does not exist in the deployed stack overview, the command throws the missing-resource error (`e77`) for that stack and resource lookup. Double-check that the resource name matches the key used in your Stacktape configuration.

If the parameter name is not found for the given resource, the command throws the invalid-parameter error (`e78`) and passes the resource type plus the available referenceable parameter names to the error handler. This makes it straightforward to discover the correct parameter name without leaving the terminal.

docs.title: param get
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: param get
headingPath: How do I find the available parameter names for a resource?
docs.content:
### How do I find the available parameter names for a resource?

Each Stacktape resource type exposes a specific set of referenceable parameters. The full list is documented at [referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters). You can also trigger the `e78` error intentionally by passing an invalid `--param-name` — the error output includes the valid parameter names for that resource type.

docs.title: param get
headingPath: Does param get require a deployed stack?
docs.content:
### Does param get require a deployed stack?

Yes. The command queries a deployed stack to read the parameter's runtime value. If the stack has not been deployed yet, there is nothing to retrieve. Deploy first with [`deploy`](/cli/deploy), then use `param get` to read outputs.

docs.title: param get
headingPath: How do I capture the value in a shell script or CI step?
docs.content:
### How do I capture the value in a shell script or CI step?

Pass `--agent` or `--json` to get machine-readable JSONL output (one JSON object per line). The default interactive output includes colors and formatting that are not suitable for capturing into a shell variable or parsing in a pipeline step.

docs.title: param get
headingPath: What is the difference between param get and status?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between param get and status?

[`param get`](/cli/param-get) retrieves a single parameter value from a single resource — ideal for scripting and automation. [`status`](/cli/status) returns a broader overview of all outputs and AWS resources in the stack — better for exploration and discovery after a deployment.

# project create

`stacktape project create` creates a project in your organization in the Stacktape Console. You rarely need it: a signed-in deploy creates a missing project itself, and asks first when the name comes from `--project` rather than the config. Use it to set up a project before its first deploy, for example from a script. It needs a Console sign-in ([`stacktape login`](/cli/login) or `STACKTAPE_API_KEY`).

docs.title: project create
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape project create payments-service
```

Names use lowercase letters, numbers and dashes. In a terminal you can leave the name out and the CLI asks for it. With `--agent` there is no prompt, so the name is required.

```bash
stacktape project create payments-service --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

docs.content:
# project delete

`stacktape project delete` deletes a project from the current Stacktape organization. The Console removes the
project with its deploy history, stage settings and build runner. Use it to clean up projects you no longer need, such
as test projects created by automation.

The command never deletes AWS stacks. If the project still has deployed stages in a connected AWS account, it refuses,
lists the stages and prints the [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) command for each of them. Delete those stages first,
then run `project delete` again.

You need the `projects:delete` permission on the project. Owners and Admins have it.

docs.title: project delete
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape project delete my-api
```

In a terminal, you confirm by typing the project name. Without a terminal, for example in CI or with `--agent`, add
`--yes`; otherwise the command fails with `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED`. The Stacktape MCP server passes `--yes` only after
you confirm the deletion.

docs.title: project delete
docs.content:
## Examples

Delete a project and confirm by typing its name:

```bash
stacktape project delete payments-service
```

Delete a test project in a script or CI job:

```bash
stacktape project delete e2e-run-42 --yes
```

A project with a deployed stage is kept, and the output tells you what to delete first:

```text
Project payments-service still has 1 deployed stage: staging (eu-west-1, AWS account main). Deleting the
project never deletes stacks, so it was kept.

Hints:
  → Delete the stage first:
  → stacktape delete --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --project payments-service --aws-account main
  → Then run stacktape project delete --project payments-service again.
```

With `--agent`, the result's `data.deployedStages` lists the same stages.

# project list

`stacktape project list` lists all projects in your current organization along with their deployed stages, deployment status, and monthly costs. Use it to review projects in your organization, see deployed and undeployed stage counts, spot in-progress or errored stages, and compare current and previous month costs. It needs a Console sign-in: [`stacktape login`](/cli/login), or `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` in CI.

docs.title: project list
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape project list
```

The command requires no arguments. You must be [logged in](/cli/login) to Stacktape, and the output reflects the organization your CLI session is scoped to. Run [`whoami`](/cli/whoami) to verify which organization you're authenticated against.

docs.title: project list
docs.content:
## Output

The `project list` command prints a summary table followed by per-project detail. The summary table includes these columns:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| **Project** | The project name. |
| **Stages** | Total stage count with deployed count in parentheses — e.g. `3 (2 deployed)`. |
| **In Progress** | Number of stages with a deployment currently running. |
| **Errored** | Number of stages in an error state. |
| **This Month** | Aggregated cost across all stages for the current month. |
| **Prev Month** | Aggregated cost across all stages for the previous month. |

Projects are sorted by most recent stage activity first, then alphabetically by name. Costs use the currency code returned with stage cost data; when no current-month currency code is present, the command falls back to USD.

docs.title: project list
docs.content:
## CI and agent usage

In CI pipelines or when consumed by AI coding agents, pass `--agent` to get machine-readable JSONL output instead of the interactive table. The `--output-format` flag provides finer control over formatting.

List projects as JSONL for scripting:

```bash
stacktape project list --agent
```

Use plain text output (no colors or animations):

```bash
stacktape project list --output-format plain
```

docs.title: project list
docs.content:
## Examples

Check all projects and their cost at a glance:

```bash
stacktape project list
```

Pipe JSONL output into `jq` for scripting:

```bash
stacktape project list --agent | jq .
```

Suppress info-level CLI log messages, showing only errors from the CLI framework itself:

```bash
stacktape project list --log-level error
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
# query dynamodb

`stacktape query dynamodb` lets you inspect data in a deployed [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) directly from the command line. It supports five read-only operations — `sample`, `scan`, `query`, `get`, and `schema` — so you can check table structure, look up items by key, or browse data without leaving the terminal.

Use this command as your first tool when you need to verify data in a deployed DynamoDB table. The command resolves your Stacktape `DynamoDbTable` resource by name and runs read-only operations against the deployed table, so there's no risk of accidental writes.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb <tableName> --stage <stage> --region <region> --operation <operation>
```

The resource name argument must match the name of a `DynamoDbTable` resource in your Stacktape configuration. If you omit `--operation`, the command defaults to `sample`. When `--limit` is omitted, the command uses a default limit of 100.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Operations

The `query dynamodb` command supports five operations. All are read-only.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### sample

The `sample` operation returns items from the table — useful for a quick sanity check that data exists and looks right. This is the default operation when `--operation` is omitted. Use `--limit` to control how many items are returned.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation sample
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### schema

The `schema` operation returns schema information for the table. Run this first when you're unfamiliar with a table — use the returned metadata to choose values for `--pk`, `--sk`, or `--index`.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation schema
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### scan

The `scan` operation reads items from the table without filtering by key. Use `--limit` to control how many items are returned (defaults to 100 when omitted). Scans read the table sequentially, so they consume read capacity proportional to the data scanned — keep `--limit` reasonable on large tables.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation scan --limit 20
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### query

The `query` operation fetches items matching a specific partition key, optionally filtered by sort key. Requires `--pk` with a JSON object mapping the partition key name to its value. Use `--sk` to narrow results by sort key, and `--index` to query a global secondary index instead of the primary table.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation query --pk '{"userId": "u-42"}'
```

Query a GSI with a sort key filter:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation query --pk '{"status": "shipped"}' --sk '{"createdAt": "2025-01-01"}' --index statusIndex
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### get

The `get` operation retrieves a single item by its full primary key (partition key + sort key if the table has one). Requires `--pk`; use `--sk` when the table has a composite key. If no item matches, the command prints the result returned by DynamoDB.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --pk '{"userId": "u-42"}' --sk '{"orderId": "ord-99"}'
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Programmatic output

The `--agent` flag switches to programmatic output mode. With `--agent`, `query dynamodb` prints the operation result as a JSON object (with `ok`, `resource`, `operation`, and the operation-specific data) for programmatic consumption by scripts or AI coding agents.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation sample --agent
```


> **Tip:** Run `--operation schema` first on unfamiliar tables. It returns table metadata you need to choose values for `--pk` and `--sk`.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Examples

Quickly check if a table has data after a fresh deployment:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage dev --region us-east-1
```

Inspect the key schema and indexes before writing a query:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation schema
```

Fetch all items for a specific user:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation query --pk '{"userId": "abc-123"}' --limit 50
```

Get a single item by composite key:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --pk '{"userId": "abc-123"}' --sk '{"createdAt": "2025-03-15T10:00:00Z"}'
```

Scan for recent items (up to 10):

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb eventsTable --stage staging --region us-east-1 --operation scan --limit 10
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: Can I query a global secondary index?
docs.content:
### Can I query a global secondary index?

Yes. Pass `--index <indexName>` with the `query` operation. The `--pk` value must match the GSI's partition key, not the table's primary partition key. Run `--operation schema` first to inspect the table metadata before querying.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### What format does --pk expect?

The `--pk` flag takes a JSON object mapping the key attribute name to its value — for example, `'{"userId": "abc-123"}'`. The attribute name must match the partition key name in the table's schema. The same format applies to `--sk`. If the JSON is malformed, the command returns an error asking for valid JSON objects.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: What is the default limit for sample and scan?
docs.content:
### What is the default limit for sample and scan?

When `--limit` is omitted, the command uses a default limit of 100 items, for both `sample` and `scan`. Use `--limit` to request fewer or more items.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: Is this command safe to run against production tables?
docs.content:
### Is this command safe to run against production tables?

Yes. All five operations are strictly read-only — the command never writes, updates, or deletes items. Be mindful of `scan` on large tables: it consumes DynamoDB read capacity units proportional to the data scanned, which could affect performance if your table's provisioned capacity is low. Use `--limit` to keep scans bounded.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: How is this different from aws call, and can I use it on tables not managed by Stacktape?
docs.content:
### How is this different from aws call, and can I use it on tables not managed by Stacktape?

The [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call) command gives raw AWS SDK access and requires you to construct the full DynamoDB API input (including the physical table name and marshalled attribute values). `query dynamodb` instead resolves your Stacktape resource name to the underlying table and provides higher-level operations like `schema` and `sample`, so you can inspect data without knowing the physical table name or DynamoDB API shape. The trade-off: it only accepts a deployed Stacktape resource whose type is `dynamo-db-table`. For tables outside Stacktape, use [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call) with the DynamoDB SDK commands directly.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: Does this command need a bastion tunnel or VPC access?
docs.content:
### Does this command need a bastion tunnel or VPC access?

No. DynamoDB is a regional AWS service accessible over the public internet — it does not run inside a VPC. No bastion tunnel is needed, unlike VPC-only resources such as [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) or [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis).

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
# query opensearch

`stacktape query opensearch` runs read-only queries against a deployed [OpenSearch domain](/resources/databases/opensearch) directly from your terminal. Use it to list indices, check document counts, inspect field mappings, retrieve individual documents, or search with Query DSL — without setting up a separate OpenSearch client or dashboard.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation indices
```

The command takes the domain's resource name as a positional argument (`query opensearch <resource-name>`) and always requires `--stage` and `--region`. The resource name must match an OpenSearch domain resource defined in your Stacktape configuration. Additional flags depend on the operation.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
## Operations

The `--operation` flag selects what kind of query to run. Five operations are available: `indices`, `mapping`, `count`, `get`, and `search`. If omitted, the command defaults to `indices`.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### indices

Lists all indices in the OpenSearch domain. This is the default operation and the best starting point when exploring an unfamiliar domain. No additional flags are needed.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation indices
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### mapping

Returns the field mapping for a specific index — useful for understanding the index schema before writing search queries. Requires `--index`.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation mapping --index users
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### count

Returns the document count. You can pass `--index` to count documents in a specific index; omit it to count across all indices.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation count --index orders
```

Count across the entire domain (no `--index`):

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation count
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### get

Retrieves a single document by ID. Requires both `--index` and `--id`.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --index users --id doc123
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### search

Runs an OpenSearch Query DSL search. Requires `--query` with a valid JSON string. You can optionally scope the search to a specific index with `--index` and control result count with `--limit` (defaults to 10).

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation search --query "{\"match_all\": {}}"
```

Search within a specific index with a limited result set:

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation search --index users --query "{\"match\": {\"name\": \"alice\"}}" --limit 5
```


> **Info:** The `--query` flag accepts [OpenSearch Query DSL](https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/query-dsl/) as a JSON string. The command parses the JSON before sending it — malformed JSON is rejected with `Invalid JSON in --query` and the hint `Provide valid OpenSearch query DSL JSON`. On Windows, escape inner double quotes with backslashes. On Linux/macOS, wrap the entire value in single quotes.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
## Agent mode

When running with `--agent`, the command prints a structured JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `operation`, and the operation result. This makes it suitable for programmatic consumption by AI coding assistants and automation scripts.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --agent --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation indices
```

For automation, prefer `--agent`. The global `--output-format` flag is documented in the flags reference below.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### Check what indices exist

Start here when exploring an unfamiliar OpenSearch domain. The `indices` operation is the default, so `--operation` can be omitted.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query opensearch

docs.content:
### Inspect field mappings for an index


docs.content:



### Retrieve a specific document by ID

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --index users --id user-42
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### Run a full-text search

The `--query` flag takes OpenSearch Query DSL as a JSON string. This example searches for error-level log entries across the `logs` index.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation search --index logs --query "{\"match\": {\"level\": \"error\"}}" --limit 20
```

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: Match all documents in an index
docs.content:
### Match all documents in an index

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation search --index products --query "{\"match_all\": {}}" --limit 50
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### Use agent mode for automation

Parse the JSON result programmatically in a CI pipeline or AI coding assistant.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --agent --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation count --index users
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: Which flags does each operation require?
docs.content:
### Which flags does each operation require?

The `mapping` operation requires `--index`. The `get` operation requires both `--index` and `--id`. The `search` operation requires `--query`. For `indices`, no additional flags are needed. For `count`, `--index` is optional — omit it to count across all indices.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: Do I need a bastion host to query OpenSearch?
docs.content:
### Do I need a bastion host to query OpenSearch?

No. The command reads the deployed domain endpoint from the stack, connects over HTTPS, and authenticates with the stack's read-only debug role. The role can send only GET and HEAD requests to the stack's own domains, so the command sends searches as GET with the query in the request body. OpenSearch refuses the role any other request, such as indexing, updating or deleting documents. The command also refuses an `--index` that contains `/` or starts with `_`, since that would reach another endpoint rather than an index. When the stack has no such role or it cannot be assumed, the command fails instead of using your configured AWS credentials. Unlike [`query sql`](/cli/query-sql) or [`query redis`](/cli/query-redis), `query opensearch` does not accept a `--bastion-resource` flag.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: What format does the --query flag expect?
docs.content:
### What format does the --query flag expect?

The `--query` flag accepts a JSON string containing an [OpenSearch Query DSL](https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/query-dsl/) query body. The command parses the JSON before sending it. If the JSON is malformed, the command rejects it with `Invalid JSON in --query` and the hint `Provide valid OpenSearch query DSL JSON`. On Windows, escape inner double quotes with backslashes; on Linux/macOS, wrap the entire value in single quotes.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: How is query opensearch different from OpenSearch Dashboards?
docs.content:
### How is query opensearch different from OpenSearch Dashboards?

`query opensearch` is a CLI tool for quick, ad-hoc inspection from your terminal — checking an index exists, verifying document counts, or running a one-off search. OpenSearch Dashboards provides a full web UI with visualizations, saved queries, and interactive exploration. Use the CLI for fast debugging; use Dashboards for ongoing analytics and dashboard building.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: What happens if the OpenSearch domain is not deployed?
docs.content:
### What happens if the OpenSearch domain is not deployed?

The command looks up the domain endpoint from the deployed stack. If the resource does not exist in the stack or the domain is not yet provisioned, the command fails with an error indicating it could not retrieve the OpenSearch endpoint. Verify the stack is deployed and the `--resource-name` matches a resource in your configuration.

docs.content:
# query redis

`stacktape query redis` lets you inspect a deployed [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) directly from the command line. It supports five read-only operations — `keys`, `get`, `ttl`, `info`, and `type` — so you can check cached values, list keys by pattern, or view server stats without setting up a local Redis client or tunnel.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation info
```

The resource name argument must refer to a `redis` resource defined in your Stacktape configuration. The command resolves the cluster's connection details (host, port, password) from the deployed stack automatically.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Operations

The `--operation` flag selects what to do. If omitted, it defaults to `info`.

| Operation | What it does | Required flags |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| `info` | Returns Redis server information (memory, clients, stats). Optionally filter with `--section`. | — |
| `keys` | Lists keys matching a glob pattern. `--pattern` is optional and defaults to `*`. | — |
| `get` | Returns the value stored at a specific key. | `--key` |
| `ttl` | Returns the remaining time-to-live (in seconds) for a key. | `--key` |
| `type` | Returns the data type of a key (string, list, set, hash, zset, etc.). | `--key` |

All operations are read-only. You cannot write, delete, or modify data through this command.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Accessing VPC-only clusters

Redis caches deployed inside a VPC are not publicly accessible. To reach them from your local machine, pass `--bastion-resource` to tunnel through a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) in your stack. When `--bastion-resource` resolves a tunnel target, the command starts an SSM port-forwarding session, uses localhost for the query, and closes the tunnel after the query.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion --operation keys --pattern "session:*"
```

If the Redis endpoint is reachable from your machine, omit `--bastion-resource`. For VPC-only clusters, pass a bastion resource name.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### View server info

Returns the full Redis INFO output.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation info
```

Use `--section` to pass a Redis INFO section such as `server`, `memory`, or `stats`. The command passes the section string directly to Redis.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation info --section memory
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### List keys by pattern

Lists keys matching a glob pattern. The `--pattern` flag is optional and defaults to `*` (all keys). Use `--limit` to cap the number of returned keys.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation keys --pattern "user:*" --limit 20
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Get a key's value

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --key "session:abc123"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Check a key's TTL

Returns the remaining time-to-live in seconds. A value of `-1` means the key has no expiration; `-2` means the key does not exist.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation ttl --key "session:abc123"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Check a key's type

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation type --key "user:42"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Query through a bastion tunnel

When your Redis cache is VPC-only, pass `--bastion-resource` to route the connection through a bastion host.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion --operation get --key "config:feature-flags"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Agent mode

When running inside an AI coding agent or CI pipeline, pass `--agent` to switch to agent-oriented output. In agent mode, `query redis` prints the Redis result as a JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `operation`, and the operation-specific result fields. Agent mode also disables interactive terminal UI.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --key "session:abc123" --agent
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
# query sql

Run read-only SQL queries against a deployed [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) directly from the command line. Use `query sql` when you need to check a row, verify a migration, or inspect table structure in a deployed PostgreSQL or MySQL database without setting up a local database client.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
## Usage

Query a table in a deployed database:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

Query a database through a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host):

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SHOW TABLES" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
## What it does

The `query sql` command connects to a deployed Stacktape `relational-database` resource, executes a read-only SQL query, and prints the results. Stacktape resolves the database connection string — including host, port, username, and password — from your deployed stack's SSM parameters automatically. You don't need to look up credentials or endpoints.

The command validates that the SQL string starts with an allowed read-only prefix before sending it to the database. Accepted prefixes are `SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXPLAIN`, and `\d` (PostgreSQL meta-commands). Any SQL that does not start with one of these prefixes is rejected.

When the deployed database exposes a `readerConnectionString` SSM parameter, `query sql` uses it. Otherwise it uses the primary `connectionString` parameter. This means read queries are automatically routed away from the writer instance when a reader endpoint is available.

The command passes SSL connection options to the database client automatically.


> **Warning:** This command is for ad-hoc inspection, not bulk data export. Results are capped by the `--limit` flag (default: 1000 rows). For persistent database access with a local client like `psql` or DataGrip, use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) instead.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `<sql>` (required)

The SQL query to execute, passed as the second positional argument. Wrap it in double quotes on the command line. The command accepts queries starting with `SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXPLAIN`, or `\d`.

Select specific columns:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT id, email, created_at FROM users WHERE active = true LIMIT 20" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

Inspect table structure in PostgreSQL:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'users'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

List tables in MySQL:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SHOW TABLES" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `<resource-name>` (required)

The first positional argument: the name of the relational database resource as defined in your Stacktape configuration. The resource must be a `relational-database` — other resource types are not supported by this command.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--bastion-resource`

Name of a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) resource to tunnel through. Use `--bastion-resource` when you want `query sql` to tunnel through a Stacktape bastion host to reach a VPC-only database. Stacktape opens an SSM port-forwarding session for the duration of the query and tears it down automatically afterward.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT count(*) FROM orders" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion
```

If you need a persistent tunnel (for example, to connect a local GUI client), use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) instead.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--limit`

Maximum number of rows to return. Default: **1000**. The output indicates whether results were truncated.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM events" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --limit 50
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--timeout`

Maximum time to wait for the query to finish, in milliseconds. Default: **30000** (30 seconds). Increase this for queries against large tables or complex joins.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM large_table" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --timeout 60000
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--agent`

Switches output to structured JSON for programmatic consumption. In agent mode, `query sql` writes a JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `engine`, `sql`, `rows`, `fields`, `rowCount`, and `truncated`. Use this when calling `query sql` from scripts or AI coding assistants.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 5" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Check if a migration ran

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT * FROM _prisma_migrations ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 5" --stage staging --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Count rows in a table

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2025-01-01'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Describe a PostgreSQL table

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'users'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Explain a slow query

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id WHERE users.email LIKE '%@example.com'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Query through a bastion host

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT * FROM products WHERE stock = 0" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource bastion
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
## Output

In interactive mode, `query sql` prints results as a formatted ASCII table with column headers. When no rows match, it prints "No rows returned."

In agent mode (`--agent`), the output is a structured JSON object containing:

- `ok` — `true` on success
- `resource` — the resource name argument
- `engine` — `postgres` or `mysql`
- `sql` — the executed query string
- `rows` — array of row objects
- `fields` — array of column name strings
- `rowCount` — number of rows returned
- `truncated` — `true` if `rowCount` hit the `--limit` cap

docs.title: query sql
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: What SQL statements does `query sql` accept?
docs.content:
### What SQL statements does `query sql` accept?

The command accepts SQL whose trimmed text starts with `SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXPLAIN`, or `\d` (PostgreSQL meta-commands). Any SQL that does not start with one of these prefixes is rejected before it reaches the database. This is intended for read-only inspection of deployed databases from the CLI.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: What database types does it work with?
docs.content:
### What database types does it work with?

The `query sql` command works with deployed Stacktape `relational-database` resources whose connection string uses the `postgresql://` or `mysql://` protocol. The engine is detected automatically from the connection string, and the appropriate database client driver is used.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: Do I need to know the database password?
docs.content:
### Do I need to know the database password?

No. Stacktape resolves the full connection string — including host, port, username, and password — from the deployed stack's SSM parameters at query time. You only need the resource name and stage. The connection uses SSL automatically.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: When should I use `query sql` vs `bastion tunnel`?
docs.content:
### When should I use `query sql` vs `bastion tunnel`?

Use `query sql` for quick, one-off inspections: checking a row, verifying a migration, counting records. Use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) when you need a persistent connection for a local database client (psql, DataGrip, TablePlus) or need to run write operations. The `query sql` command is read-only by design.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: Can I query a database that is only reachable inside a VPC?
docs.content:
### Can I query a database that is only reachable inside a VPC?

Yes, if your stack includes a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host). Pass `--bastion-resource` and Stacktape opens an SSM port-forwarding session for the duration of the query, then tears it down automatically afterward. Without a bastion resource in the stack, `query sql` cannot reach a VPC-only database.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: What happens if my query returns too many rows?
docs.content:
### What happens if my query returns too many rows?

Results are capped by the `--limit` flag, which defaults to 1000 rows. The output includes a `truncated` indicator when the limit is reached. Increase `--limit` if you need more rows, but keep in mind that large result sets are printed to the terminal. For bulk data exports, use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) with a dedicated database client.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: Does `query sql` use the reader or writer endpoint?
docs.content:
### Does `query sql` use the reader or writer endpoint?

When the deployed database exposes a `readerConnectionString` SSM parameter, `query sql` uses it. Otherwise it uses the primary `connectionString` parameter. This routes read queries away from the writer instance when a reader endpoint is available.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: How do I get machine-readable output for scripts or AI agents?
docs.content:
### How do I get machine-readable output for scripts or AI agents?

Pass `--agent` to switch from the formatted ASCII table to a structured JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `engine`, `sql`, `rows`, `fields`, `rowCount`, and `truncated`. This is the format to parse when calling `query sql` from scripts or AI coding assistants.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
# rollback

`stacktape rollback` puts a deployed stack back on an earlier release. It deploys that release's CloudFormation template with its stored Lambda zips and container images, so nothing is rebuilt.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Usage

Roll back to the release before the current one:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production
```


> **Warning:** Rollback restores infrastructure and code, not data. Database migrations and objects your app wrote stay as they are, so code rolled back past a schema migration can fail. Plan that recovery separately.


Every deploy that changed something is a release, including fast deployments that only updated code. `--region` is the only required flag; `--stage` and `--project` pick the stack, and no config file is needed. A stack stuck in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` can't take a rollback: use [`stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover) instead. A stack in `UPDATE_FAILED` works with either command.

Roll back to a specific version:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --target-version v000003
```

Roll back multiple steps:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --rollback-steps 3
```

List available versions before deciding:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --list-versions
```

docs.title: rollback
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--target-version`

Specifies the exact deployment version to roll back to, for example `v000003`. Versions commonly use values like `v000001`, `v000003`; when `--rollback-steps` is used, Stacktape calculates a six-digit zero-padded target. Use `--list-versions` to see which versions are available in your deployment bucket.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--rollback-steps`

Number of stored releases to step back from the current one. Defaults to `1` (the previous release). For example, if the current release is `v000008` and all older releases are still stored, `--rollback-steps 3` targets `v000005`. Releases removed by `previousVersionsToKeep` are skipped. If neither `--target-version` nor `--rollback-steps` is provided, the command rolls back one version.

Targeting the current release re-applies it. Use this when a fast deployment failed partway and left some functions or services on other code.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--list-versions`

When previous versions exist, the command prints the current version and the available rollback versions, then exits without rolling back. If no previous versions exist, it reports that none were found. Use this to inspect what's available before committing to a rollback.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--config`

Rollback doesn't read a config file. The flag is accepted, but it isn't needed.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## How rollback works

Stacktape keeps the CloudFormation template and the deployment artifacts of each release in the stack's deployment bucket. When you run `rollback`, it copies the stored template into a new release and asks CloudFormation to deploy it:

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Flow
1. **Version resolution**: The target version is --target-version, or the release --rollback-steps steps back among the stored releases.
2. **Artifact verification**: Stacktape verifies that artifacts for the target version are available in the deployment bucket before proceeding.
3. **Safety check**: The command reads rollback safety metadata from the deployed stack, when present, and prints warnings for directives, TypeScript transforms, custom directives, or after:deploy hooks.
4. **Template preparation**: The old CloudFormation template is downloaded and stored as a new release. The function code and container images it uses are copied under the new release, so CloudFormation updates every function and container service to the restored code, including those a fast deployment changed.
5. **Deployment**: CloudFormation applies the rollback template. Lambda zips and container images are reused, not rebuilt. Every container service runs a rolling deployment, even one whose code did not change.
6. **Bucket content restoration**: If the stack includes static hosting with bucket-synced content, Stacktape attempts to restore the bucket contents from a version manifest.


Each rollback is a new release: rolling back from `v000008` to `v000005` produces `v000009`. To roll forward again, deploy as usual or roll back to the release you came from.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Safety warnings

The rollback command reads rollback safety metadata from the deployed stack and warns about situations where a template-only rollback may not fully restore the previous behavior:

- **Directives that embed local or external state** — directives such as `$File` are reported by name. The rolled-back template contains values from the original deploy time, not from your current local files. This is expected behavior for a rollback.
- **TypeScript transforms** — if rollback safety metadata reports that the config uses TypeScript transforms, Stacktape warns that those transforms are not captured in the CloudFormation template.
- **`after:deploy` hooks** — when rollback safety metadata reports `after:deploy` hooks, Stacktape warns that they will not be re-executed during rollback. If the original deployment relied on post-deploy scripts (database seeding, cache warming), you may need to run them manually.
- **Custom directives** — custom directive results were baked into the template at deploy time and are not re-evaluated during rollback.

If the stack was deployed before rollback support was added, the safety metadata may be missing. The rollback still proceeds, but with a warning that results may be unpredictable if the config used `$File`, TypeScript transforms, custom directives, or `after:deploy` hooks.

Shared-layer fast deployments check that the old handler can run on the new layer before attaching it. They do not require the new handler to run on the old layer. CloudFormation restores code and layers separately during rollback: across an edit that added a used export, restoring the old layer first can briefly fail invocations until the old handler is restored. The forward deployment prints a note when it detects this incompatibility. Rollbacks across several releases can also cross incompatible chunk generations. The final restored code and layers are consistent; rollback does not guarantee uninterrupted invocations during that transition.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Version availability

Use `--list-versions` to see which versions are still available. If a target version is not found in the deployment bucket, Stacktape reports that it was not found, lists the versions that are available, and notes that old versions may have been cleaned up based on the `previousVersionsToKeep` setting.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Bucket-synced content

If the stack includes static hosting with bucket-synced content, Stacktape attempts to restore the bucket contents from a version manifest stored during the original deployment. If Stacktape cannot restore bucket-synced content, it warns that stacks with static websites may need to be redeployed from the original commit.

docs.content:
### Rollback in CI/CD

`--agent` prints JSONL and never prompts:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --rollback-steps 1 --agent
```

docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: rollback
headingPath: What is the difference between `rollback` and `stack recover`?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between `rollback` and `stack recover`?

Use `rollback` when the deploy worked but the app is broken: it deploys an earlier release as a new one. Use [`stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover) when the deploy itself failed and left the stack in `UPDATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`: it runs CloudFormation's own recovery.

docs.title: rollback
headingPath: How far back can I roll back?
docs.content:
### How far back can I roll back?

As far as the stored releases go. `previousVersionsToKeep` decides how many older releases keep their artifacts; once they're removed, you can't roll back to that release. `--list-versions` shows what is still available.

docs.content:
# script run

`stacktape script run` executes a script defined in the `scripts` section of your Stacktape configuration. It takes the script name as a positional argument (`script run <script-name>`), requires `--stage`, accepts additional environment variables via `--env`, and can optionally assume a deployed resource's IAM role with `--assume-role-of-resource`. Use `script run` when you need to execute a named script from the `scripts` section without deploying the full stack.

docs.title: script run
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape script run myMigration --stage production
```

`script run` requires the script name and `--stage`. Pass `--region` when you do not rely on a configured default (set via [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set)).

docs.title: script run
docs.content:
## Examples

Add `--region` when you want to override or avoid relying on a configured default region:

```bash
stacktape script run migrate --stage staging --region eu-west-1
```

Pass extra environment variables to a seed script:

```bash
stacktape script run seed --stage dev --env SEED_FILE=./data/seed.json --env VERBOSE=true
```

Run a script while assuming the IAM role of a deployed resource (so the script operates with that resource's AWS permissions):

```bash
stacktape script run exportData --stage production --assume-role-of-resource dataProcessor
```

Use a custom config path when the configuration is not at the default location:

```bash
stacktape script run cleanup --stage dev --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```


> **Info:** If `assumeRoleOfResource` is also defined in the script's configuration properties, the CLI flag takes precedence.

docs.title: script run
docs.content:
## Errors

If the script name does not match any key in the `scripts` section of your configuration, the command throws `stpErrors.e20({ scriptName })`. The command looks up the script by key in `scripts`, so the script name must exactly match a key defined in your configuration.

# secret get

`stacktape secret get` shows a secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager: its name, creation date and ARN. Use it to check that a secret exists before you reference it with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives).

The value is hidden by default and shows as `<<OMITTED>>`. Add `--show-secrets` to print it, but only where the output stays private: never in a shared CI log or an AI assistant's conversation. The [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) never returns the value.

docs.title: secret get
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape secret get --region eu-west-1
```

In a terminal, the command asks for the secret name. With `--agent`, it can't ask, so pass the name as an argument:

```bash
stacktape secret get my-api-key --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

docs.title: secret get
docs.content:
## Output

The terminal box and the `--agent` result carry the same fields. With `--agent`, the final result event has `name`, `arn`, `created` (an ISO 8601 timestamp) and `value` at `data.result`.

With `--show-secrets`, a value that is valid JSON is pretty-printed in the box and returned as an object in the `--agent` result.

docs.title: secret get
docs.content:
## Examples

Retrieve a secret interactively (you'll be prompted for the name):

```bash
stacktape secret get --region us-east-1
```

Check that a secret exists, without printing its value:

```bash
stacktape secret get DATABASE_PASSWORD --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

Print the value in your own terminal:

```bash
stacktape secret get DATABASE_PASSWORD --region eu-west-1 --show-secrets
```

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
# secret set

`stacktape secret set` creates or updates a secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Once stored, you can reference the secret in your Stacktape configuration using the [`$Secret('secret-name')`](/configuration/directives) directive — keeping sensitive values like API keys, database passwords, and third-party tokens out of your config files and version control.

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Usage

In interactive mode (the default), the command walks you through a guided flow — prompting for the secret name, input method, and value:

```bash
stacktape secret set --region eu-west-1
```

With `--agent` the command prints JSONL and asks nothing, so CI and coding agents pass every value as a flag:

```bash
stacktape secret set my-api-key --region eu-west-1 --value sk-abc123 --agent
```

To store the contents of a file as the secret value, exactly as they are in the file:

```bash
stacktape secret set firebase-creds --region eu-west-1 --file ./firebase-service-account.json --agent
```

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Interactive vs agent mode

The command operates in two modes depending on whether `--agent` is set.

**Interactive mode** (default) prompts you for:

1. The secret name.
2. How to provide the value — either by typing it directly (masked input) or by specifying a file path.
3. If a secret with the same name already exists, confirmation before overwriting.

**Agent mode** (`--agent`) prints JSONL and never prompts. It requires the secret name and either `--value` or `--file`. If the secret already exists, the command fails unless you pass `--force-update`.

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Updating existing secrets

When a secret with the given name already exists in the target region:

- **Interactive mode** — you are prompted to confirm the update.
- **Agent mode** — the command fails with an error unless `--force-update` is passed.

To update an existing secret without prompts:

```bash
stacktape secret set my-api-key --region eu-west-1 --value new-value --force-update --agent
```

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Important flags

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--region` | **(required)** AWS region where the secret is stored. |
| `<secret-name>` | Positional argument. Name of the secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Required in agent mode; prompted in interactive mode. |
| `--value` | The value to store. Mutually exclusive with `--file`. |
| `--file` | Path to a file whose contents are stored as the secret value. Mutually exclusive with `--value`. |
| `--force-update` | Overwrite an existing secret without confirmation. Only relevant in agent mode. |
| `--agent` | Run in non-interactive mode with JSONL output. Requires the secret name and one of `--value` or `--file`. |

# stack history

`stacktape stack history` lists recent recorded Stacktape operations with their status. Each entry shows success or failure status, timestamps, and error descriptions for failed operations. Use filters to narrow results by project, stage, or the current API-key user. It needs a Console sign-in: [`stacktape login`](/cli/login), or `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` in CI. The history comes from the operations the Console recorded.

docs.title: stack history
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape stack history
```

`stack history` returns the 25 most recent operations across all projects and stages in your organization. You must be logged in with a valid API key — run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) first if you haven't already.

docs.title: stack history
docs.content:
## Filtering results

Filter by project name to see operations for a single project.

```bash
stacktape stack history --project my-api
```

Filter by stage to see operations for a specific stage across all projects.

```bash
stacktape stack history --stage production
```

Combine `--project` and `--stage` to narrow results to a single project and stage.

```bash
stacktape stack history --project my-api --stage production
```

Show only operations triggered by your own API key.

```bash
stacktape stack history --current-user-only
```

docs.title: stack history
docs.content:
## Controlling output size

By default, `stack history` returns the 25 most recent operations. Use `--limit` to change this.

```bash
stacktape stack history --limit 50
```

docs.title: stack history
docs.content:
## Machine-readable output

Use `--agent` or `--json` to get machine-readable output suitable for scripts or AI coding agents. See the flags reference below for details on each output format.

```bash
stacktape stack history --agent
```

docs.content:
# stack list

`stacktape stack list` lists CloudFormation stacks deployed in a specified AWS region and identifies which ones are Stacktape-managed. It shows each stack's name, status, timestamps, and actual or forecasted spend when budget data is available — giving you a quick inventory of what's running in your account.

docs.title: stack list
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape stack list --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: stack list
docs.content:
## What it does

When you run `stack list`, Stacktape queries CloudFormation for all stacks in the specified region (excluding stacks in `DELETE_COMPLETE` state) and enriches the results with spend data when available. Each stack entry includes:

- **Stack name** and stack ID
- **Status** (e.g. `CREATE_COMPLETE`, `UPDATE_COMPLETE`, `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`)
- **Creation time** and **last update time**
- **Whether it's a Stacktape-managed stack** — the `isStacktapeStack` field is derived from the CloudFormation `TemplateDescription` using Stacktape's `isStacktapeStackDescription` helper, which recognizes descriptions set by Stacktape during deployment
- **Actual and forecasted spend** (when budget data is available)

This is useful for auditing what's deployed, finding forgotten stacks that are still incurring cost, or verifying a deployment landed in the correct region.

docs.title: stack list
docs.content:
## Important flags

The only required flag is `--region`, which determines which AWS region to query.

Use `--profile` to specify which AWS credentials profile to use, or `--aws-account` to target a specific AWS account connected in the Stacktape Console.

Use `--agent` to get JSON output for programmatic consumption. For `stack list`, agent mode prints the full result as a single pretty-printed JSON array (via `JSON.stringify` with indentation) and disables the interactive terminal UI. This differs from the generic `--agent` flag description in the API reference above, which describes JSONL output — `stack list` uses a JSON array instead.


> **Info:** The `--stage` and `--project` flags are accepted by the CLI parser but are not used in the stack-listing logic. The command lists all non-deleted stacks returned for the selected AWS region and account.

docs.title: stack list
docs.content:
## Examples

List all stacks in `us-east-1`:

```bash
stacktape stack list --region us-east-1
```

List stacks using a specific AWS profile:

```bash
stacktape stack list --region eu-west-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

Get JSON output for scripting or AI agent consumption:

```bash
stacktape stack list --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

Use a specific AWS account connected in the Stacktape Console:

```bash
stacktape stack list --region eu-west-1 --aws-account my-production-account
```

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
# stack recover

`stacktape stack recover` recovers a CloudFormation stack stuck in `UPDATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` state by triggering CloudFormation's native rollback mechanism. Only `--region` is required. Use it when a failed deployment leaves your stack unable to accept new updates — this is a recovery command, not a version rollback. To revert to a previous deployment version, use [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) instead.

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
## Usage

Run `stacktape stack recover` with the `--region` flag to trigger a CloudFormation rollback on a stuck stack.

```bash
stacktape stack recover --region eu-west-1
```

Only `--region` is required. Pass `--stage`, `--project`, or `--config` when you need to target a specific stack instead of relying on configured defaults or config file discovery.

A typical invocation targeting a specific stack:

```bash
stacktape stack recover --region eu-west-1 --stage production --project my-api
```

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
## What it does

When a Stacktape deployment fails, CloudFormation can leave the stack in one of these states:

- **`UPDATE_FAILED`** — a stack update failed partway through and kept the resources that updated. Deploying again continues the update. `stack recover` instead uses CloudFormation's native rollback mechanism to return the stack to the last known good state.
- **`CREATE_FAILED`** — a first deployment failed and kept the resources it created. Deploying again continues it. There is no earlier state to return to, so use [`delete`](/cli/delete) to remove it: `stack recover` would delete its resources but leave an empty stack that still has to be deleted.
- **`UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`** — a previous rollback itself failed. `stack recover` retries CloudFormation's native rollback path and can pass logical resource IDs through `--resources-to-skip` for resources that cannot be restored.

After the rollback succeeds, Stacktape attempts to clean up rolled-back deployment artifacts.


> **Info:** This command does NOT roll back to a previous deployment version. It rolls back the CloudFormation stack to the last known good state. To revert to an earlier version of your configuration, use [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) instead.

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
## stack recover vs rollback

The Stacktape CLI provides two distinct rollback commands for different scenarios.

| Scenario | Command |
|----------|---------|
| Update failed (`UPDATE_FAILED`) and you want to undo it rather than continue it | `stack recover` |
| Stack stuck in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` | `stack recover` |
| Want to revert to a specific previous deployment version | [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) |
| Stack is healthy but you want to undo the last deploy | [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) |

Use `stack recover` as a recovery tool when your stack is in `UPDATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`. Use [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) when you want to deploy a previous deployment version; it downloads that deployment's template and deploys it, which also works over `UPDATE_FAILED`.

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
### --resources-to-skip

When a rollback itself fails (`UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`), specific resources may be preventing the rollback from completing — for example, a resource that was manually deleted outside of CloudFormation or depends on an external service that changed state. Pass their logical resource IDs to skip them during the retry:

```bash
stacktape stack recover --region eu-west-1 --stage production --resources-to-skip MyCustomResource AnotherBrokenResource
```


> **Warning:** Use `--resources-to-skip` only for logical resource IDs that prevent rollback from completing. After rollback, inspect the skipped resources before deploying again.

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
### --stage

Identifies which stage's stack to roll back when provided. Can also be resolved from configured defaults or a config file.

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
### --profile

Selects the AWS profile for authentication. Useful when managing stacks across multiple AWS accounts.

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content:
## Examples

Recover a stuck stack in eu-west-1:

```bash
stacktape stack recover --region eu-west-1 --stage production --project my-api
```

Retry a failed rollback, skipping a resource that cannot be restored:

```bash
stacktape stack recover --region us-east-1 --stage staging --resources-to-skip BrokenLambdaPermission
```

Use debug logging to see detailed rollback progress:

```bash
stacktape stack recover --region eu-west-1 --stage production --debug
```

docs.title: stack recover
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: stack recover
headingPath: What's the difference between UPDATE_FAILED and UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED?
docs.content:
### What's the difference between UPDATE_FAILED and UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED?

`UPDATE_FAILED` means a stack update failed partway through and kept what it had updated. The next deploy continues from there, or `stack recover` returns the stack to the last known good state. `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` means CloudFormation already attempted that rollback and the rollback itself failed; in this case, retry with `--resources-to-skip` to bypass the resources blocking it.

docs.title: stack recover
headingPath: My rollback keeps failing on a specific resource. What do I do?
docs.content:
### My rollback keeps failing on a specific resource. What do I do?

Pass that resource's logical ID to `--resources-to-skip` so CloudFormation skips it during the rollback retry. This is common when a resource was deleted outside of CloudFormation or depends on an external service whose state changed. After the rollback completes, inspect the skipped resources before deploying again, since they were left in their failed state.

docs.title: stack update-modules
docs.content:
# stack update-modules

`stacktape stack update-modules` updates CloudFormation infrastructure module private types in your AWS account to the latest compatible version. Stacktape currently offers updates for `atlasMongo`, `upstashRedis`, and `ecsBlueGreen` CloudFormation private types. Run this command when an upstream API change for one of these modules requires the registration in your account to be updated, or when an error message or Stacktape support explicitly tells you to update a module.

docs.title: stack update-modules
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape stack update-modules --region eu-west-1
```

The command is interactive — after running it, you select which module to update from a prompt. There is no CLI flag to specify the module directly, so the command requires interactive terminal input. The three available modules are:

- `atlasMongo`
- `upstashRedis`
- `ecsBlueGreen`

Once you select a module, Stacktape initializes the CloudFormation registry, loads private types and packages for the selected module, and registers the newest available private type version.


> **Info:** This command updates the CloudFormation private type registration in your AWS account for a specific region. If you use the same module in multiple regions, run the command once per region.

docs.title: stack update-modules
docs.content:
## Examples

Update modules in `us-east-1`.

```bash
stacktape stack update-modules --region us-east-1
```

Specify an AWS profile with the `--profile` argument.

```bash
stacktape stack update-modules --region eu-west-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

Enable debug logging to troubleshoot registration failures.

```bash
stacktape stack update-modules --region eu-west-1 --debug
```

docs.title: status
docs.content:
# status

`stacktape status` displays detailed information about a deployed stack, including its outputs (URLs, endpoints, resource identifiers) and the list of AWS resources in the stack. Use it after [deploying](/cli/deploy) to discover endpoints, verify resource creation, or feed stack data into scripts and CI pipelines. It needs a Console sign-in: [`stacktape login`](/cli/login), or `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` in CI. It reads the stage's record in the Console. Without an account, open the stack `<project>-<stage>` in the AWS CloudFormation console, in the stage's region, to see its outputs and resources.

docs.title: status
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape status --region eu-west-1 --project my-project --stage prod
```

Alternatively, pass the stack name directly.

```bash
stacktape status --region eu-west-1 --stack-name my-project-prod
```

The `--region` flag is the only required argument. You identify the target stack in one of two ways: provide `--stack-name` directly (formatted as `projectName-stage`), or provide both `--project` and `--stage` together. If neither combination is supplied, the command exits with an error: *"Provide either --stack-name OR both --project and --stage"*.

With `--agent`, `status` skips the interactive stack-details view and uses the CLI's JSONL protocol. The final `result` event contains a versioned `stacktape.info-stack.v1` document at `data.result`, including the resolved stack name, region, outputs, Stacktape resource map, and CloudFormation resources. Read the final result event rather than parsing informational log messages.

The `--aws-account` flag selects which connected AWS account to query. The account must first be connected in the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account). Omit it when the default account selection is sufficient.

docs.title: status
docs.content:
## Examples

Inspect a production stack to retrieve its outputs (URLs, resource identifiers).

```bash
stacktape status --region us-east-1 --project my-api --stage prod
```

Use the combined stack name instead of separate project and stage flags.

```bash
stacktape status --region us-east-1 --stack-name my-api-prod
```

Get versioned JSONL output for a CI pipeline, coding agent, or script.

```bash
stacktape status --region eu-west-1 --project my-api --stage staging --agent
```

The stable command document is nested in the final event:

```json
{
  "type": "result",
  "ok": true,
  "data": {
    "result": {
      "schemaVersion": "stacktape.info-stack.v1",
      "stackName": "my-api-staging",
      "region": "eu-west-1",
      "description": null,
      "stackOutput": {},
      "stackInfoMap": null,
      "resources": []
    }
  }
}
```

Query a stack in a specific connected AWS account.

```bash
stacktape status --region us-west-2 --project payments --stage prod --aws-account production-account
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
# synth

`stacktape synth` turns your configuration into a CloudFormation template and writes it to a file, `compiled-template.yaml` by default. Use it to read the template or hand it to other tools. It doesn't create or change a stack.

The file isn't exactly what a deploy sends to CloudFormation. `synth` doesn't build your code, so the code locations are empty, and a deploy adds a few resources that `synth` doesn't write. To take over a deployed stack, save its deployed template instead, as [Stop using Stacktape](/getting-started/evaluate/stop-using-stacktape) shows.

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

This reads your Stacktape configuration, resolves all resources, finalizes the CloudFormation template, and writes it to `compiled-template.yaml`. Both `--stage` and `--region` are required so the command can resolve a concrete stack context.

To write the template to a custom path, use `--out`.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --out ./infra/template.yaml
```

`synth` needs no deployed stack and no Stacktape account.

docs.title: synth
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --out

Controls where the synthesized template is saved. Defaults to `compiled-template.yaml`. Use this when you want the template in a specific location for CI artifacts, version control, or external tooling.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage prod --region us-east-1 --out ./output/prod-template.yaml
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --config

Points to your Stacktape configuration file when it is not in the default location. The path is relative to the current working directory.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --keep-temp-files

When set, Stacktape preserves temporary files generated during synthesis under `.stacktape/[invocation-id]`. Useful for debugging the synthesis pipeline when the final template doesn't match your expectations.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --keep-temp-files
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --project

Specifies the Stacktape project name for the operation. Pass the same value you would use with [`deploy`](/cli/deploy).

```bash
stacktape synth --stage prod --region us-east-1 --project my-app
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
## Examples

Synthesize a production template and save it to a specific directory:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage prod --region us-east-1 --out ./artifacts/prod.yaml
```

Synthesize with debug-level logging to troubleshoot configuration resolution:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --debug
```

Synthesize using a specific AWS profile:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

Synthesize and keep temporary files for inspection:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --keep-temp-files --out ./debug-template.yaml
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
## synth vs validate vs diff

| Command | What it does | Writes to AWS | Needs a deployed stack |
|---------|-------------|---------------|------------------------|
| [`synth`](/cli/synth) | Writes the CloudFormation template to a file | Nothing | No |
| [`validate`](/cli/validate) | Checks the config and, with `--thorough`, the template | A temporary template object with `--thorough` | No |
| [`diff`](/cli/diff) | Shows what a deploy would change | Missing secrets, a template and a temporary change set | Yes |

Use `synth` when you need the template file on disk for inspection or downstream tooling. Use [`validate`](/cli/validate) for a quick pass/fail check without writing artifacts. Use [`diff`](/cli/diff) when you want to compare your current config against what is already deployed.

docs.title: synth
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: synth
headingPath: Why are --stage and --region required if nothing is deployed?
docs.content:
### Why are --stage and --region required if nothing is deployed?

Stacktape needs both values before synthesis so it can resolve a concrete stack context. Your configuration may use the stage and region in resource names, conditional logic, or directive expressions, so different stages can produce different templates. Pass the same values you would use for [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) or [`validate`](/cli/validate).

docs.title: synth
headingPath: Can I feed the synthesized template into CloudFormation linting or policy tools?
docs.content:
### Can I feed the synthesized template into CloudFormation linting or policy tools?

Yes. The file is a finished CloudFormation template, so linters, policy scanners and your own scripts can read it. A common CI step runs `synth` and then a scanner on the file.
