docs.content:
# upgrade

`stacktape upgrade` updates the CLI to the latest published version, or to the version you name. It finds out how the CLI was installed and runs the matching update, or prints the command when the CLI is a project dependency. It needs no Stacktape account and no AWS credentials.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape upgrade
```

When you are on the latest version already, the command says so and changes nothing. A preview version upgrades to the newest preview, or to a stable release once one is newer.

Install an exact version, newer or older:

```bash
stacktape upgrade 4.0.1
```

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
## What it runs

| Installed with | What `upgrade` does |
|---|---|
| The installer script | Downloads the installer for your platform and runs it (PowerShell on Windows, `sh` on macOS and Linux) |
| `npm`, `pnpm` or `bun` globally | Runs `npm install -g stacktape@<version>` or the pnpm or Bun equivalent |
| A project dependency (`node_modules`) | Prints the update command, because it changes your lockfile. Run it in the project. |
| Something else | Prints a command to run yourself |

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
# validate

`stacktape validate` checks your configuration and builds the CloudFormation template in memory, without deploying. Run it before a deploy or as a CI step to catch config errors early.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Usage

The command needs a stage and a region. It checks the configuration file, resolves every resource, reports [security findings](#security-findings-by-stage-purpose) and builds the template in memory. It doesn't load your organization's [guardrails](/guardrails/overview); `deploy`, `diff` and the other commands that change a stack check them.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The command does not require a deployed stack and doesn't change your stack. Its only write to AWS is the temporary template object that [`--thorough`](#validation-levels) can upload, deleted after the check.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Validation levels

Each level adds checks to the one before it. The default needs no packaging, `--with-package` builds your workloads, and `--thorough` also asks CloudFormation to check the template.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
### Default — config, resources, and template

Stacktape loads the configuration, resolves all resources and builds the template in memory. This is the fastest level. It catches broken resource references, invalid property values and missing secrets.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
### With packaging — add `--with-package`

The `--with-package` flag runs workload packaging as part of validation. Stacktape packages all Lambda functions and container workloads, which catches packaging errors surfaced by the normal packaging step — such as missing entry files or misconfigured build settings. Use this when you have changed packaging settings or entry file paths.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --with-package
```

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
### Thorough — add `--thorough`

The `--thorough` flag includes workload packaging and calls CloudFormation `ValidateTemplate`. CloudFormation accepts a template of up to 51,200 bytes with the request; a larger one (an ordinary web-service stack is already larger) is uploaded to a temporary object in the stack's deployment bucket, validated from there and deleted. Before the first deploy the stack has no deployment bucket, and `validate` does not create one. A larger template then gets a warning: the `--agent` result reports `checked.cloudformation: false` and lists the warning under `warnings`. The first deploy validates it. This check requires AWS credentials and does not create or modify a stack; its only write is that temporary object.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --thorough
```


> **Info:** The `--thorough` flag implies `--with-package`. You do not need to pass both.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Security findings by stage purpose

`validate` also checks the configuration for security findings, the same ones [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) reports to the Stacktape Console: a database reachable from the internet, a public bucket, an IAM statement that allows every action, a credential pasted into an environment variable, and similar. A finding never fails validation.

How severe a finding is depends on whether the stage is production. A password-protected database open to the internet is a reasonable default for a dev or preview stage, so it is `LOW` there and `HIGH` in production. Rules that only matter once real users depend on the stack, such as deletion protection, backups, termination protection and running two container instances, are not reported for other stages; `validate` lists them separately so you know what to fix before production.

| Finding | Production | Other stages |
|---------|------------|--------------|
| Database or OpenSearch domain reachable from the internet | `HIGH` | `LOW` |
| Public load balancer without a web application firewall | `MEDIUM` | `LOW` |
| Queue without a dead-letter queue | `LOW` | `INFO` |
| Database without deletion protection, data store without backups | `MEDIUM` | listed under "before production" |
| Stack without termination protection, container service with one instance | `LOW` | listed under "before production" |
| Public bucket, wide IAM statement, secret in an environment variable | same in every stage | same in every stage |

Wide IAM statements keep their severity because dev stages often share the AWS account with production, so a role that can do anything in the account reaches production too.

A stage is production when [`stackConfig.stageType`](/configuration/stages-and-environments#production-and-non-production-stages) is `production`. Without that setting, `deploy` uses the type you chose when you created the stage in the Stacktape Console; `validate` does not contact the Console, so it skips this step unless you pass `--aws-account`. Otherwise the stage name decides: `prod`, `production`, `prd` and `live`, alone, as a segment (`prod-eu`) or followed by a number (`prod2`), count as production, and names with a rehearsal marker (`pre-prod`, `prod-test`) do not. The same answer decides incident handling and the delete-production permission in the Console. Set `stageType` when your production stage has another name, so `validate` and `deploy` always agree:

```yaml
stackConfig:
  stageType: production
```

For a non-production stage, the output looks like this:

```text
Security posture: 1 low (stage `dev` is non-production by its name).
  [LOW] mainDatabase: Database reachable from the internet (HIGH in production)
Also fix before production (not reported for this stage):
  [LOW] web: Production container service runs a single instance
  [LOW] Production stack without termination protection
```

With `--agent`, the result's `security` object carries `stage` (`name`, `purpose` and `decidedBy`: `stackConfig.stageType`, `stacktape-console` or `stage-name`), `findings` with each finding's `severity` for this stage and, when production rates it higher, its `productionSeverity`, `productionOnlyFindings`, and `exposure`. `deploy` returns the same object, reports the stage's `findings` to the Console, and only counts the production-only findings in its output.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Missing secrets

A `$Secret` whose secret does not exist yet in the region is a finding, not a failure: `validate` reports it and checks the rest of the configuration, with a placeholder reference in the template. This is the normal state after [`init`](/cli/init), which keeps a generated database or Redis password in a secret it does not create.

```text
[!] Secret my-app-cache does not exist in eu-west-1 yet. It holds a generated database password: stacktape dev creates it when it starts, and stacktape deploy creates it before it deploys (in a terminal it asks first). To create it yourself, run stacktape secret set my-app-cache with a JSON value that has a `password` key.
```

Any other missing secret, such as an API key, has to be created with [`secret set`](/cli/secret-set) before `deploy` or `dev` can run; both stop until it exists. With `--agent`, the result lists them in `missingSecrets`, each with its `name`, the `jsonKeys` the configuration reads and whether Stacktape `generated` its value.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## When to use validate

The `validate` command is a fast pre-deploy check that confirms your configuration synthesizes correctly. Use it when you want a validation gate instead of a written template file.

- **Before deploying.** Run `stacktape validate` to catch configuration errors in seconds without waiting for a full CloudFormation deployment to fail.
- **In CI pipelines.** Add `validate` (or `validate --thorough`) as a CI step on pull requests. This prevents broken configs from reaching [`deploy`](/cli/deploy).
- **After config refactors.** When you reorganize resources, rename stages, or change packaging modes, `validate` confirms the config still synthesizes correctly.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Inspecting the validated template

By default, `validate` produces only a pass/fail result. Add `--out <path>` to write the template after every requested validation step succeeds. When packaging is enabled, this is the packaged template and includes generated Lambda layers and their function references.

Use [`synth`](/cli/synth) when you only need the faster, un-packaged template compilation. Use [`diff`](/cli/diff) when you need to see what a deployment would change against a live stack.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Important flags

| Flag | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `--with-package` | Runs workload packaging as part of validation, catching packaging errors for Lambda functions and container workloads. |
| `--thorough` | Validates packaging and asks CloudFormation to validate the template. Templates over 51,200 bytes go through the stack's deployment bucket; before the first deploy they are reported as not checked. Implies `--with-package`. |
| `--out` | Writes the template only after the requested validation steps succeed. With packaging enabled, the file includes generated artifact and layer references. |
| `--stage` | Required. The stage name used for template synthesis (e.g., `dev`, `staging`, `production`). |
| `--region` | Required. The AWS region used for template synthesis. |
| `--config` | Path to your Stacktape configuration file if it is not in the default location. |
| `--agent` | Prints JSONL (one JSON object per line) and turns off prompts, for CI and coding agents. |

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Examples

Validate config for a production stage in `us-east-1`.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage production --region us-east-1
```

Validate with a specific config file path.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

Run the most thorough validation, including packaging and CloudFormation validation, before merging a pull request.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage ci --region eu-west-1 --thorough --out ./validated-template.yaml
```

Use JSONL output for CI or AI-agent consumption.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

docs.title: validate
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: validate
headingPath: Do I need AWS credentials to run validate in CI?
docs.content:
### Do I need AWS credentials to run validate in CI?

Stacktape normally needs an AWS identity because the account id participates in deterministic names and synthesized ARNs. `--thorough` additionally calls CloudFormation's `ValidateTemplate` API, and for a template over 51,200 bytes writes and deletes a temporary object in the stack's deployment bucket. Use a CI profile scoped to the intended account that can read the stack and write to that bucket.

| Option | Required | Type | Description | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-r, --region` | yes | `string` | AWS Region — The AWS region for the operation. For a list of available regions, see the [AWS documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/rande.html). Inside a project whose config declares `region`, the flag is optional and overrides the config. | `us-east-2`, `us-east-1`, `us-west-1`, `us-west-2`, `ap-east-1`, `ap-south-1`, `ap-northeast-3`, `ap-northeast-2`, `ap-southeast-1`, `ap-southeast-2`, `ap-northeast-1`, `ca-central-1`, `eu-central-1`, `eu-west-1`, `eu-west-2`, `eu-west-3`, `eu-north-1`, `me-south-1`, `sa-east-1`, `af-south-1`, `eu-south-1` |

When there are several, the command stops and asks you to choose one with this option. | - |

| `--log-level` | no | `string` | Log Level — The level of logs to print to the console. • `info`: Basic information about the operation. • `error`: Only errors. • `debug`: Detailed information for debugging. | `info`, `debug`, `error` |
| `-o, --out` | no | `string` | Output File — The path to the file where the operation output will be saved. | - |

For commands that use a connected AWS account, `--profile` (or `AWS_PROFILE`) selects the connected account the profile belongs to, unless `--aws-account` is set. The command fails if that account is not connected. | - |
| `--project` | no | `string` | Project Name — The name of the Stacktape project for this operation. Commands that target a stack take it from `projectName` in the project's config when the flag is absent. | - |
| `--quiet` | no | `boolean` | Quiet — Hide progress, banners, success messages and hints. Command output, warnings and errors are still printed. | - |
| `--thorough` | no | `boolean` | Thorough — If `true`, validates workload packaging and asks AWS CloudFormation to validate the synthesized template. A template over 51,200 bytes is validated from a temporary object in the stack's deployment bucket; before the first deploy there is none, so the result reports checked.cloudformation false with a warning. | - |
| `--with-package` | no | `boolean` | With Package — If `true`, validates workload packaging in addition to resolving the configuration and template. | - |

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`synth`](/cli/synth) — compiles the configuration into an un-packaged CloudFormation template and writes it to a file. Use `validate --with-package --out ...` when you need the packaged template.
- [`diff`](/cli/diff) — shows a preview of changes that would be applied to a deployed stack. Requires a deployed stack, unlike `validate`.
- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) — deploys or updates a stack. Running `validate` before `deploy` catches errors before they reach CloudFormation.
- [`package`](/cli/package) — packages workloads and writes artifacts to disk. The `--with-package` flag on `validate` runs workload packaging as part of validation, while `package` is the dedicated command for preparing packaged outputs for inspection or deployment.

docs.title: version
docs.content:
# version

`stacktape version` prints the currently installed version of Stacktape. It requires no arguments, no configuration file, and no API key. Use it to verify your installation or check whether you need to [upgrade](/cli/upgrade).

docs.title: version
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape version
```

The command outputs the installed version number and exits. No AWS credentials, project configuration, or login are required.

`stacktape --version` and `stacktape -v` print the same output.

docs.title: version
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: version
headingPath: Does `stacktape version` require an API key or login?
docs.content:
### Does `stacktape version` require an API key or login?

No. The `version` command runs entirely locally and does not contact the Stacktape API. You can run it before logging in or configuring any credentials.

docs.title: version
headingPath: How do I check if my Stacktape version is out of date?
docs.content:
### How do I check if my Stacktape version is out of date?

Run `stacktape version` to see what you have installed, then run [`stacktape upgrade`](/cli/upgrade) to move to the latest release (or `stacktape upgrade 4.0.1` for a specific version). Re-run `stacktape version` afterward to confirm the new version is active.

docs.content:
# whoami

`stacktape whoami` shows the current user, organization, connected AWS accounts, and accessible projects for your configured API key. Use it to verify your authentication is set up correctly and confirm which organization and projects you can access.

docs.title: whoami
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape whoami
```

This command requires a valid API key. If you haven't logged in yet, run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) first.

The output includes:

- **User** — your name, email, and user ID.
- **Organization** — the organization tied to your API key, including your displayed role, such as Owner, Admin, Developer, or Viewer.
- **Connected AWS accounts** — each account's name, AWS account ID, and connection state.
- **Projects** — all projects you can access in the current organization.
- **Permissions** — the result can include project-scoped API key metadata, including `isProjectScoped` and `permissions`, when the API returns those fields.

docs.title: whoami
docs.content:
## Examples

Verify your identity and check which organization you're operating in.

```bash
stacktape whoami
```

Get machine-readable JSON output (one JSON object per line) for scripting or CI pipelines.

```bash
stacktape whoami --json
```

Enable debug-level logging to troubleshoot API key issues.

```bash
stacktape whoami --debug
```

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.content:
# Configuration files

A Stacktape project has one configuration file in its root, `stacktape.ts` or `stacktape.yml`. It lists the resources of your app (functions, containers, databases, buckets) and how they connect. [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) writes one for you; this page explains what is in it.

docs.title: Configuration files
Configuration files
docs.content:
## TypeScript or YAML

Both formats produce the same infrastructure. TypeScript is the better default: your editor checks every property, and you can use conditions, loops, functions and imports. YAML suits a small config that does not change per stage. In YAML, each resource has a `type` and `properties`; in TypeScript, each type is a class whose constructor takes those properties.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | TypeScript | YAML |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type checking and autocompletion | yes | With the VS Code extension |
| Per-stage values | Any code | Directives such as $Stage() |
| Loops and generated resources | yes | no |
| Reuse across files | Imports | Variables in one file |
| Transforms of the generated template | yes | no |


To move from YAML to TypeScript, rewrite the resources with the same names and property values, then compare the output with [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) before you deploy. Keep only one config file in the directory.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.content:
## Project name and region

Declare the project name and region in the first argument of `defineConfig`, or as top-level keys in YAML. Commands run inside the project then need only `--stage`: `stacktape deploy --stage dev`, `stacktape logs api --stage dev`, `stacktape status --stage dev`.

Stacktape reads these two values before it runs the config, because it needs the region and project to pick credentials. Write them as plain strings: a variable, an environment variable or another computed value is rejected with an error that shows the supported form.

A `--project` or `--region` flag overrides the config for one command. Without a region in the config, it comes from `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, then the machine-wide default (`stacktape defaults set`), then the AWS profile. Commands that do not load the config, such as `stacktape secret get`, take only the region from it and never fail because of it.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.content:
## The defineConfig callback

The callback receives the context of the command that runs the config. Use it for values that differ per stage or region.

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stage` | `string` | The stage, for example `dev` or `production` |
| `region` | `string` | The AWS region, for example `eu-west-1` |
| `projectName` | `string` or `undefined` | Always set when the config declares `projectName`; otherwise the value of `--project` or the machine-wide default, if any |
| `command` | `string` | The CLI command, such as `deploy`, `delete` or `dev` |
| `cliArgs` | `Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>` | The options of the current command. See [Command-line options in the config](#command-line-options-in-the-config) |
| `awsProfile` | `string` | The local AWS profile the command uses |
| `user` | `{ id, name, email }` or `undefined` | The signed-in Stacktape user. Undefined without a Console account and for local commands such as `package`, `synth` and `validate` |

Do not base resource names or sizes on `user`: the same stage deployed from CI or without an account would then change.

docs.title: Configuration files
Configuration files
Configuration files
docs.content:
## Top-level fields

The only required field is `resources`.

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `resources` | Your infrastructure: functions, containers, databases, buckets and so on. See [Declaring resources](/configuration/resources) |
| `scripts`, `hooks` | Commands you run by hand or before and after `deploy`, `delete` and `dev`. See [Hooks and scripts](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) |
| `variables` | Values reused across the config with `$Var()`. See [Variables and reuse](/configuration/variables-and-reuse) |
| `directives` | Your own functions that compute config values at deploy time. See [Directives](/configuration/directives) |
| `deploymentConfig` | Rollback, termination protection and artifact retention. See [Deploying stacks](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks) |
| `stackConfig` | Outputs, tags, VPC and NAT settings, tracing, and whether the stage is production |
| `providerConfig` | Credentials for MongoDB Atlas and Upstash |
| `cloudformationResources` | Raw CloudFormation resources. See [Overrides and escape hatches](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches) |

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.content:
## Which file is used

The CLI looks for `stacktape.ts`, `stacktape.yml`, `stacktape.yaml` or `stacktape.js` in the current directory (or in `--cwd`). Use `--config` for a file elsewhere:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --config ./infrastructure/stacktape.ts
```

When the directory has more than one of these files, for example a `stacktape.yml` left next to its `stacktape.ts` rewrite or a `stacktape.js` your TypeScript build wrote, commands stop with `CONFIG_FILE_AMBIGUOUS` instead of guessing. Pass `--config`, or delete or rename the file you no longer use.

Use `stacktape.ts` for `defineConfig` and the resource classes. A `stacktape.js` file is loaded as plain JavaScript: it must export the config object itself (the same shape as the YAML file) or a function that returns it. `defineConfig` and transforms work only in `stacktape.ts`.

To check a config without deploying, run [`stacktape validate`](/cli/validate). It loads the config, resolves resources and builds the CloudFormation template in memory.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.content:
## Directives

Directives are values that Stacktape resolves when it runs a command, such as a secret or the URL of another resource. You write them as strings like `$Secret('db-password')`. In TypeScript, the common ones (`$Secret`, `$ResourceParam`, `$Stage`, `$Region`, `$SsmParam`) are also functions you can import from `stacktape`.

| Directive | What it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `$Secret()` | A secret from AWS Secrets Manager |
| `$ResourceParam()` | A parameter of a resource in this stack, such as a URL or ARN |
| `$StackOutput()` | An output of another stack |
| `$Stage()`, `$Region()` | The current stage or region |
| `$Format()` | A string built from other values |
| `$Var()` | A value from the `variables` section |
| `$File()` | The contents of a file |

In TypeScript you often do not need `$Var()`, `$Format()` or `$File()`: constants, template literals and `readFileSync` do the same. Directives that read deployed state, such as `$Secret()` and `$ResourceParam()`, are still needed. See [Directives](/configuration/directives) for the full list.

docs.content:

| `LambdaFunction` | `function` |
| `EdgeLambdaFunction` | `edge-lambda-function` |
| `WebService` | `web-service` |
| `PrivateService` | `private-service` |
| `WorkerService` | `worker-service` |
| `MultiContainerWorkload` | `multi-container-workload` |
| `BatchJob` | `batch-job` |
| `NextjsWeb` | `nextjs-web` |
| `RelationalDatabase` | `relational-database` |
| `DynamoDbTable` | `dynamo-db-table` |
| `Redis` | `redis` |
| `MongoDbAtlasCluster` | `mongo-db-atlas-cluster` |
| `UpstashRedis` | `upstash-redis` |
| `OpenSearchDomain` | `open-search-domain` |
| `HttpApiGateway` | `http-api-gateway` |
| `ApplicationLoadBalancer` | `application-load-balancer` |
| `NetworkLoadBalancer` | `network-load-balancer` |
| `Bucket` | `bucket` |
| `HostingBucket` | `hosting-bucket` |
| `EfsFilesystem` | `efs-filesystem` |
| `SqsQueue` | `sqs-queue` |
| `SnsTopic` | `sns-topic` |
| `EventBus` | `event-bus` |
| `UserAuthPool` | `user-auth-pool` |
| `WebAppFirewall` | `web-app-firewall` |
| `Bastion` | `bastion` |
| `StateMachine` | `state-machine` |

Nested objects, such as packaging, database engines and events, follow the same rule: `type` and `properties` in YAML, a class in TypeScript. Each resource page lists its options.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
# Connecting resources

List a resource in a workload's `connectTo`, and Stacktape gives the workload access to it: IAM permissions, `STP_*` environment variables with the connection details and, for databases and Redis, the security group rules. Use it whenever a function, container or script talks to another resource in the same stack.

The access `connectTo` grants is fixed per resource type and cannot be narrowed. A [bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) target, for example, allows reading, writing and deleting objects. For read-only access, leave the target out of `connectTo`, pass its name with [`$ResourceParam()`](/configuration/directives) and add only the actions you need with [`iamRoleStatements`](#custom-permissions-with-iamrolestatements).

docs.title: Connecting resources
Connecting resources
headingPath: Complete Lambda and DynamoDB API example

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
## What connectTo does

When you add a resource name to `connectTo`, Stacktape performs up to three actions depending on the target resource type:

1. **Grants IAM permissions**: the consuming resource's execution role gets a policy allowing it to interact with the target (e.g., read/write objects for buckets, send/receive messages for queues). Network-bound resources like relational databases and Redis caches don't use IAM for data-plane access.

2. **Opens security group access**: for [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) and [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis), Stacktape creates security group rules allowing the consuming resource to reach the target on the correct port. See the [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) pages for VPC placement details.

3. **Injects environment variables**: Stacktape injects connection parameters as `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]` environment variables into the consuming resource. The exact set of injected variables depends on the target resource type, documented in the tables below.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
## Environment variable naming

Stacktape converts the resource name and parameter name to `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` with the `STP_` prefix:

```
STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAMETER_NAME]
```

A resource named `myDatabase` with parameter `connectionString` becomes `STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`. A resource named `uploads` with parameter `name` becomes `STP_UPLOADS_NAME`. CamelCase names are split at word boundaries: `jobQueue` → `JOB_QUEUE`, `usersTable` → `USERS_TABLE`.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
## Injected variables

The tables below document the environment variables injected by `connectTo` for each supported target resource type. Each table assumes an illustrative resource name shown in the heading: your actual variable names follow the `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]` pattern based on the name you give the resource in your config. Additional parameters beyond what is listed here may be accessible via [`$ResourceParam()`](/configuration/directives).

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Relational database

Assuming a resource named `myDatabase`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `connectionString` | `STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING` | Full connection string |
| `host` | `STP_MY_DATABASE_HOST` | Database hostname |
| `port` | `STP_MY_DATABASE_PORT` | Database port |
| `readerConnectionString` | `STP_MY_DATABASE_READER_CONNECTION_STRING` | Reader endpoint connection string (Aurora only) |
| `readerHost` | `STP_MY_DATABASE_READER_HOST` | Reader endpoint hostname (Aurora only) |


> **Tip:** Use [`$Secret()`](/configuration/secrets) for the database password in your config to keep credentials out of source control. Additional database parameters like `dbName` and `masterUserName` are available via [`$ResourceParam()`](/configuration/directives).

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Aurora DSQL

Assuming a resource named `database`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `endpoint` | `STP_DATABASE_ENDPOINT` | Public TLS endpoint |
| `port` | `STP_DATABASE_PORT` | PostgreSQL port (`5432`) |
| `databaseName` | `STP_DATABASE_DATABASE_NAME` | Default database (`postgres`) |
| `username` | `STP_DATABASE_USERNAME` | Built-in role (`admin`) |
| `region` | `STP_DATABASE_REGION` | Region used to sign an IAM token |
| `id` | `STP_DATABASE_ID` | Cluster ID |
| `arn` | `STP_DATABASE_ARN` | Cluster ARN |

DSQL does not expose a static password or connection string. Generate a short-lived IAM token for each new connection and keep TLS enabled. `connectTo` grants `dsql:DbConnectAdmin` on the connected cluster; see [Aurora DSQL](/resources/databases/dsql) for the explicit least-privilege path.

docs.title: Connecting resources
Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Bucket

Assuming a resource named `uploads`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `STP_UPLOADS_NAME` | Bucket name |
| `arn` | `STP_UPLOADS_ARN` | Bucket ARN |


> **Tip:** Additional bucket parameters are available via [`$ResourceParam()`](/configuration/directives). See the [referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) page for the full list.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Hosting bucket

A [hosting bucket](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) exposes the same S3 `name` and `arn` variables as a regular bucket, using the hosting resource's name in the variable prefix. `connectTo` automatically grants access to the underlying S3 bucket; you do not need to know or reference its nested resource name.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### EFS filesystem

Assuming a resource named `sharedFiles`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `STP_SHARED_FILES_ID` | EFS filesystem ID |
| `arn` | `STP_SHARED_FILES_ARN` | EFS filesystem ARN |

`connectTo` deliberately does not mount the filesystem. A mount needs a local path and root-directory decision that Stacktape cannot safely infer. Configure the workload's EFS `volumeMounts` when it needs filesystem access; use `connectTo` alone when code only needs the ID or ARN.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### DynamoDB table

Assuming a resource named `usersTable`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `STP_USERS_TABLE_NAME` | Table name |
| `arn` | `STP_USERS_TABLE_ARN` | Table ARN |
| `streamArn` | `STP_USERS_TABLE_STREAM_ARN` | DynamoDB Streams ARN |
| `endpoint` | `STP_USERS_TABLE_ENDPOINT` | Dev mode only: address of the local DynamoDB Local |

In [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview), local tables run in DynamoDB Local. A workload, local script or frontend connected to them also gets `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_DYNAMODB`, which the AWS SDK reads, so `new DynamoDBClient({})` reaches the local tables without code changes. A workload connected to both a local and a deployed table does not get it, because one endpoint cannot serve both; pass `STP_<TABLE>_ENDPOINT` as the `endpoint` of the client for the local table instead.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Redis cache

Assuming a resource named `cache`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `host` | `STP_CACHE_HOST` | Primary host endpoint (the configuration endpoint of a sharded cluster) |
| `port` | `STP_CACHE_PORT` | Port number |
| `connectionString` | `STP_CACHE_CONNECTION_STRING` | Full URL with the `default` user's password |
| `readerHost` | `STP_CACHE_READER_HOST` | Reader endpoint (clusters without sharding) |
| `readerPort` | `STP_CACHE_READER_PORT` | Reader port (clusters without sharding) |
| `readerConnectionString` | `STP_CACHE_READER_CONNECTION_STRING` | Full URL of the reader endpoint (clusters without sharding) |

The deployed cluster uses TLS, so its connection string starts with `rediss://`. In [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) the local Redis has no TLS, and the connection string starts with `redis://`. Code that connects with `STP_CACHE_CONNECTION_STRING` therefore works in both, while code that builds its own URL from the host and port has to switch TLS itself. The local Redis has no reader endpoint.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### AgentCore resources

AgentCore targets inject their resource identifiers and grant only the data-plane permissions needed to use that target:

| Target | Injected parameters | Access granted |
|---|---|---|
| [Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime) | `id`, `arn`, `endpointName`, `endpointArn` | Invoke the runtime and configured endpoints |
| [Memory](/resources/ai/agentcore-memory) | `id`, `arn` | Create, read, search, update, and delete events and memory records |
| [Gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway) | `id`, `arn`, `url` | Invoke the gateway |
| [Browser](/resources/ai/agentcore-browser) | `id`, `arn` | Start, use, inspect, and stop browser sessions |
| [Code Interpreter](/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter) | `id`, `arn` | Start, invoke, inspect, and stop code-interpreter sessions |

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### WebSocket API Gateway

Assuming a gateway named `realtime`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `apiId` | `STP_REALTIME_API_ID` | API Gateway ID |
| `url` | `STP_REALTIME_URL` | Public `wss://` client URL |
| `managementEndpoint` | `STP_REALTIME_MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINT` | HTTPS endpoint used by `ApiGatewayManagementApiClient` |
| `canonicalDomain` | `STP_REALTIME_CANONICAL_DOMAIN` | AWS DNS target, useful with external DNS |

Connecting to a WebSocket gateway grants only `execute-api:ManageConnections`, scoped to that API and Stacktape's managed stage. Lambda functions that own a WebSocket route receive this wiring automatically; use explicit `connectTo: [realtime]` for other producers that need to send messages to clients.

Stacktape does not create a connection registry. Add a [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) when your application needs broadcasts, rooms, presence, or user-to-connection lookup. See [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway) for the cleanup pattern.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Kafka cluster

Assuming a cluster named `events`:

| Parameter | Example env var | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `arn` | `STP_EVENTS_ARN` | Amazon MSK cluster ARN |
| `name` | `STP_EVENTS_NAME` | Physical MSK cluster name |
| `bootstrapServers` | `STP_EVENTS_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS` | Comma-separated IAM/TLS broker endpoints |

`connectTo` grants Kafka IAM access scoped to the cluster, its topics, and consumer groups, including `CreateTopic`
but excluding `AlterTopic` and `DeleteTopic`. It also opens port 9098 from deployed workloads. A Lambda function used
as a direct Kafka client must set `joinDefaultVpc: true`; Lambda Kafka triggers have separate event-source networking.
See [Kafka cluster](/resources/messaging/kafka-cluster).

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Additional connectTo targets

The tables above cover resource types with documented `connectTo` environment variables. Beyond those, `connectTo` also accepts **IAM-permission-only targets**: resource types where `connectTo` adds the required IAM permissions to the consuming workload's execution role but does not have a documented set of injected environment variables. These include:

- [Multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload)
- [State machines](/resources/orchestration/state-machine)
- [OpenSearch domains](/resources/databases/opensearch)
- [Kinesis streams](/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream)

For these targets, use [`$ResourceParam()`](/configuration/directives) to pass specific parameters as environment variables manually.

In the type definitions, `connectTo` targets fall into three categories: **role-affecting** targets (including AWS API resources and AgentCore resources) that modify the consuming workload's IAM role, **security-group-affecting** targets (relational databases and Redis caches) that open network access, and **environment-only** targets such as EFS that expose identifiers without guessing additional configuration.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
### Script-only variables

[Scripts](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) have their own documented `connectTo` environment-variable set that differs from workload `connectTo`. In addition to the variables shared with workloads, script `connectTo` documents these script-specific parameters. Notably, a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) target injects `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_URL` only for scripts: workload `connectTo` does not inject a URL for web services.

| Resource type | Script-only parameters |
|---|---|
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | `JDBC_CONNECTION_STRING`. Aurora also adds `READER_JDBC_CONNECTION_STRING` |
| [Web service](/resources/compute/web-service) | `URL` |
| Upstash Kafka topic | `TOPIC_NAME`, `TOPIC_ID`, `USERNAME`, `PASSWORD`, `TCP_ENDPOINT`, `REST_URL` |

docs.title: Connecting resources
Connecting resources
docs.content:
## Permissions granted

Stacktape generates IAM policies at deploy time based on the target resource type. The access categories below reflect the documented behavior for each target:

| Target resource | Access granted |
|---|---|
| [Bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) | Read, write, and delete objects; list bucket contents |
| [Hosting bucket](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) | Read, write, and delete objects in its underlying S3 bucket; list bucket contents |
| [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) | CRUD operations (get, put, update, delete) + query and scan |
| [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) | Send, receive, and delete messages |
| [SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic) | Publish and subscribe |
| [Event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) | Publish events |
| [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) | Invoke the function |
| [Batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) | Submit, list, and terminate jobs |
| [User auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool) | Full Cognito User Pool control |
| [MongoDB Atlas cluster](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas) | Temporary credential-less access |
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | Network access (security group rules, not IAM) |
| [Aurora DSQL](/resources/databases/dsql) | Connect as the built-in `admin` role on the target cluster (`dsql:DbConnectAdmin`) |
| [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) | Network access (security group rules, not IAM) |
| [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime) | Invoke the runtime and its configured endpoints |
| [AgentCore Memory](/resources/ai/agentcore-memory) | Use events and short- and long-term memory records |
| [AgentCore Gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway) | Invoke the gateway |
| [AgentCore Browser](/resources/ai/agentcore-browser) | Use browser sessions and streams |
| [AgentCore Code Interpreter](/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter) | Use code-interpreter sessions |
| [EFS filesystem](/resources/storage/efs-filesystem) | No access change from `connectTo`; use an explicit volume mount for IAM and network wiring |
| [Email sender](/resources/messaging/email-sender) | `ses:SendEmail` and `ses:SendRawEmail`, scoped to the exact identity and configuration set |
| [Kafka cluster](/resources/messaging/kafka-cluster) | IAM cluster/topic/group access and port 9098 network access; no topic deletion or alteration |

[Relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) and [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis) are network-bound resources: data-plane access is controlled through VPC security groups rather than IAM policies. Stacktape opens the correct port between the consuming resource and the target automatically.

[Multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload), [state machines](/resources/orchestration/state-machine), [OpenSearch domains](/resources/databases/opensearch), [Kinesis streams](/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream), and [event buses](/resources/messaging/event-bus) are also valid `connectTo` targets that affect the consuming workload's IAM role. For the final deployed policy, inspect the generated CloudFormation template, for example with [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth).


> **Info:** The exact IAM policy statements generated at deploy time may include additional supporting actions (e.g., listing, describing). For the authoritative policy, inspect the generated CloudFormation template or the deployed stack's IAM roles in the AWS Console.

## Resources that use connectTo

The following list covers resources where the `connectTo` property is available: these are **consumers** that can connect to other resources. The supported **target** resources and what each target provides are documented in the [injected variables](#injected-variables) and [permissions granted](#permissions-granted) sections above.

- [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function)
- [Web service](/resources/compute/web-service)
- [Private service](/resources/compute/private-service)
- [Worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service)
- [Multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload)
- [Batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job)
- [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime)
- SSR frontends: see each resource's page for `connectTo` on the server workload: [Next.js](/resources/frontend/nextjs), [Astro](/resources/frontend/astro), [Nuxt](/resources/frontend/nuxt), [SvelteKit](/resources/frontend/sveltekit), [SolidStart](/resources/frontend/solidstart), [TanStack Start](/resources/frontend/tanstack-start), [Remix](/resources/frontend/remix)
- [Deployment scripts](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts)
- Scripts (`local-script`, `local-script-with-bastion-tunneling`, `bastion-script`)

[Edge Lambda functions](/resources/compute/edge-function) are not listed as `connectTo` consumers in the type definitions. Check the [edge function page](/resources/compute/edge-function) for what access mechanisms are available and any limitations specific to CloudFront edge runtimes.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
## VPC and networking

Production stages get a VPC of their own; non-production stages of an account and region share one, the [shared non-production network](/configuration/shared-network). When you connect to [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) or [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis), Stacktape creates security group rules that allow the consuming resource to reach the target on the correct port. Workloads that need to reach VPC-bound databases or Redis caches must be placed in the same VPC: see the [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), and [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) pages for VPC placement configuration.


> **Warning:** Lambda functions placed in a VPC lose direct internet access. If your function needs to call external APIs while also connecting to a VPC database, set `stackConfig.nat` (see below) or use a database with internet-accessible settings for development stages.

docs.title: Connecting resources
headingPath: NAT: internet access from private subnets
docs.content:
### NAT: internet access from private subnets

Workloads in the private subnets reach the internet through the stack's NAT, and their outbound traffic leaves through one static Elastic IP per availability zone, which you can allowlist with external services. Three kinds of resources use it:

- container workloads with `usePrivateSubnetsWithNAT: true`; they cannot run without NAT, so that flag requires `stackConfig.nat`;
- Lambda functions (and SSR frontends) with `joinDefaultVpc: true`, which have no internet access at all until `stackConfig.nat` is set, and use it automatically once it is;
- AgentCore runtimes that connect to a VPC-only database or Redis.

`stackConfig.nat` chooses the kind of NAT:

```yaml
stackConfig:
  nat: ha-ec2 # or ec2, or gateway
```

| | `ec2` | `ha-ec2` | `gateway` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | One small EC2 instance (`t4g.nano` by default), managed by Stacktape | One such instance per availability zone (two by default) | AWS-managed NAT Gateway per zone |
| Cost | About $7 per month, no per-GB charge | About $7 per month per zone, no per-GB charge | About $32 per month per zone, plus $0.045 per GB processed |
| Throughput | 5 Gbps burst on `t4g.nano`; pick a larger `instanceSize` for sustained load | Same, per zone | Up to 100 Gbps |
| When an instance fails | AWS replaces it; about three minutes without outbound internet | Stacktape routes that zone through another zone's instance within about a minute, then back once the replacement is healthy. Outbound calls from that zone fail during that minute and open connections are reset | AWS handles it, no visible impact |
| Updates | The instance is replaced when a newer Amazon Linux image or a new `instanceSize` is deployed, with the same short outage | Zones are replaced one at a time, with the same short failover per zone | None needed |

Use `ec2` for development stages, `ha-ec2` for production stacks whose outbound traffic is moderate and can tolerate a minute of failed outbound calls once in a long while, and `gateway` for high sustained throughput or when every minute of outbound connectivity matters. You can switch kinds on a deployed stack: the VPC, subnets and route tables stay, the previous NAT keeps serving until the new one is ready, and the switch itself only resets the connections open at that moment. The Elastic IPs change, so update any allowlists afterwards.

The object form sets the instance size (`ec2`, `ha-ec2`) and the number of zones (`ha-ec2`, `gateway`):

```yaml
stackConfig:
  nat:
    type: ha-ec2
    instanceSize: t4g.small
    availabilityZones: 3
```

Each failover raises an incident in the Console that says what happened, which zone was affected and that it recovered on its own, so nobody has to go looking in AWS. Stacktape reaches the instances through AWS Systems Manager only; they have no SSH access.

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Connecting resources
headingPath: How does connectTo differ from setting environment variables myself?
docs.content:
### How does connectTo differ from setting environment variables myself?

An `environment` entry with `$ResourceParam()` passes the value but grants no IAM permissions and opens no security group. `connectTo` does all three. You can combine both on one workload.

docs.title: Connecting resources
headingPath: Can I connect to resources in a different stack?
docs.content:
### Can I connect to resources in a different stack?

Not with `connectTo`; it takes resources of the same config. Export the value from the stack that owns the resource and import it in the other one:

```yaml

docs.title: Connecting resources
headingPath: Stack that owns the resource (project shared-infra, stage production)
docs.content:
# Stack that owns the resource (project shared-infra, stage production)
stackConfig:
  outputs:
    - name: OrdersQueueUrl
      value: $ResourceParam('ordersQueue', 'url')
      export: true
    - name: OrdersQueueArn
      value: $ResourceParam('ordersQueue', 'arn')
      export: true
```

```yaml

docs.title: Connecting resources
docs.content:
# Stack that uses it
resources:
  worker:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/worker.ts
      environment:
        - name: ORDERS_QUEUE_URL
          value: $CfStackOutput('shared-infra-production', 'OrdersQueueUrl')
      iamRoleStatements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action: ['sqs:SendMessage']
          Resource: [$CfStackOutput('shared-infra-production', 'OrdersQueueArn')]
```

`$CfStackOutput` makes CloudFormation import the export, so the owning stack cannot remove or change that output while another stack uses it. `$StackOutput` reads the value once at deploy time instead, with no such link. Permissions and network access are not part of the export: add `iamRoleStatements`, and for a private database put both stacks in a network that can reach it. See [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments#sharing-resources-across-stages).

docs.title: Connecting resources
headingPath: What happens if I remove a resource from connectTo?
docs.content:
### What happens if I remove a resource from connectTo?

The next deploy removes the workload's permissions, `STP_*` variables and security group rules for it. The resource itself stays.

docs.title: Connecting resources
headingPath: Why does the deploy say my function cannot connect to VPC-only resources?
docs.content:
### Why does the deploy say my function cannot connect to VPC-only resources?

A Lambda function runs outside your VPC unless you set `joinDefaultVpc: true`. A Redis cluster, a Kafka cluster and a relational database with `accessibilityMode: vpc` or `scoping-workloads-in-vpc` are reachable only from inside it, so the CLI stops with `CONFIG_FUNCTION_VPC_REQUIRED` before it deploys. Set `joinDefaultVpc: true` on the function. A function in the VPC has no internet access until you set [`stackConfig.nat`](#nat-internet-access-from-private-subnets), so add it if the function also calls external APIs.

If the function is in the VPC and still times out, check that you connect with the injected `STP_*` values rather than an address from another stage, and that the database is in the same network as the function.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
# Directives

Directives are built-in functions (prefixed with `$`) that inject dynamic values into your Stacktape configuration. They let you reference secrets, resource outputs, stage names, files, and cross-stack values without hardcoding anything. Directives bridge the gap between static config and the dynamic reality of deployments where values like database URLs exist only after resources are created.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
## Why directives exist

A Stacktape configuration file describes your entire infrastructure declaratively. But some values are inherently dynamic:

- A database connection string is only known after the database is provisioned.
- A secret should never be committed to source control.
- The stage name determines which domain prefix to use.
- A shared infrastructure stack exports values that dependent stacks consume.

Directives solve these problems by deferring value resolution to the right moment: either when Stacktape parses your config (local directives) or when CloudFormation deploys your resources (runtime directives).

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
## Local vs runtime directives

Stacktape divides directives into two categories based on **when** they resolve:

| Category | Resolved when | Use for |
|----------|---------------|---------|
| **Local** | Stacktape parses your config (before deployment) | Stage name, region, file contents, string formatting, CLI args, git info |
| **Runtime** | CloudFormation deploys resources | Secrets, resource parameters, cross-stack imports, runtime string composition |

Runtime directives are supported in `resources`, `scripts` and `cloudformationResources` properties that become part of the synthesized template. Directives introduced by supported overrides and transforms are also resolved. Local directives work anywhere, including variables and top-level settings.


> **Warning:** Avoid runtime directives where config parsing needs a concrete local value. Compose runtime values inside template properties, for example with `$CfFormat`.

docs.title: Directives
Directives
headingPath: Pass deployment context to your app

docs.title: Directives
docs.content: ## Local directives reference

docs.title: Directives
Directives
Directives
docs.content:
### $Format()

In YAML configs, `$Format()` is the directive-based way to interpolate strings using `{}` placeholders. Each `{}` is replaced with the corresponding positional argument. The number of `{}` placeholders must match the number of additional arguments. Example: `$Format('{}-api.example.com', $Stage())` produces `dev-api.example.com` when the stage is `dev`.

In TypeScript configs, prefer template literals for ordinary local string composition. For example, `` `${stage}-api.example.com` `` achieves the same result. The `stage` value is available from the `defineConfig` callback parameter: `defineConfig(({ stage }) => { ... })`.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
### $Var()

`$Var()` references the `variables` section in directive-based (YAML) config. In YAML, access nested properties with dot notation: `$Var().myProperty.nested`.

In TypeScript config, use regular JavaScript variables instead: that is clearer and keeps values type-checkable. For example, `const instanceSize = 'db.t4g.micro';` and use `instanceSize` wherever needed.

docs.title: Directives
Directives
docs.content:
### $FileRaw()

Reads a file as a raw UTF-8 string without parsing. Use it when you need the literal file content: for example, embedding a JSON config as a string environment variable or reading a template file.

docs.title: Directives
Directives
docs.content:
### $CliArgs()

Accesses additional CLI arguments passed after `--` in the deploy command. Accepts a second optional argument as a default value if the argument isn't provided.

Pass custom arguments when deploying:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1 -- --featureFlag true --apiVersion v2
```

In your config, reference them with `$CliArgs('featureFlag')`. The optional second argument provides a fallback: `$CliArgs('featureFlag', 'false')` returns `'false'` if `--featureFlag` wasn't passed.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
### $StackOutput()

References an exported output from another deployed CloudFormation stack. The referenced stack must already be deployed. This is a **local** directive: it fetches the value at config-parse time by querying CloudFormation.

Arguments: `$StackOutput('stackName', 'outputName')` with an optional third argument for `region` when importing from a stack in another AWS region.

The `stackName` is the full CloudFormation stack name. The `outputName` must match the CloudFormation output key of the referenced stack. Use [`stacktape status`](/cli/status) to discover available output keys for a deployed stack.


> **Warning:** The referenced output must be exported from its stack. Unexported outputs cannot be referenced and will cause a deployment error. The referenced stack must also be deployed before the stack that uses the directive.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
### $Profile()

Returns the name of the AWS profile being used for the current deployment. Useful when you need to pass profile information to scripts or hooks.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
### $AwsAccountId()

Returns the AWS account ID of the target account. Use it when you need the account ID for ARN construction or cross-account references.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
### $This()

`$This()` is a YAML-only directive that returns the raw configuration object. In YAML, access nested properties with dot notation: `$This().resources.myApi`. In TypeScript, this directive has no import: reference variables and resource objects directly since they are already in scope.

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
## Runtime directives reference

Runtime directives resolve during CloudFormation deployment. Depending on the directive, Stacktape emits CloudFormation-time values such as dynamic references (`$Secret`, `$SsmParam`) or intrinsic functions (`$CfFormat`, `$CfStackOutput`). The actual values are only available when AWS provisions your resources.
