| `$Profile()` | Local | None | AWS profile name |
| `$AwsAccountId()` | Local | None | Target AWS account ID |
| `$Format()` | Local | `(template, ...values)` | String interpolation with `{}` placeholders |
| `$Var()` | Local | None (access via `.property`) | Reference the `variables` section |
| `$This()` | Local | None (access via `.property`) | Reference the raw config object |
| `$File()` | Local | `(filePath)` | Parse .env, JSON, YAML, or INI file |
| `$FileRaw()` | Local | `(filePath)` | Read file as raw string |
| `$GitInfo()` | Local | `(property)` | Git repository information |
| `$CliArgs()` | Local | `(argName, defaultValue?)` | CLI arguments passed after `--` |
| `$StackOutput()` | Local | `(stackName, outputName, region?)` | Exported output from another deployed stack |
| `$Secret()` | Runtime | `(secretName, jsonKey?)` | AWS Secrets Manager value, or one key of a JSON secret |
| `$SsmParam()` | Runtime | `(paramName)` | SSM Parameter Store value |
| `$ResourceParam()` | Runtime | `(resourceName, param)` | Parameter from a Stacktape resource |
| `$CfResourceParam()` | Runtime | `(logicalId, attribute)` | Parameter from a raw CF resource |
| `$CfFormat()` | Runtime | `(template, ...values)` | Runtime string interpolation via `Fn::Sub` |
| `$CfStackOutput()` | Runtime | `(stackName, outputName, region?)` | Cross-stack import with deletion lock |

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: When to use directives vs alternatives
docs.content:
## When to use directives vs alternatives

Not every dynamic value needs a directive. Consider the alternatives:

| Need | Best approach |
|------|--------------|
| Pass a database URL to your code | Use [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) — it grants required IAM permissions and injects commonly needed environment variables |
| Compose strings from stage/region | In TypeScript: use template literals. In YAML: use `$Format()` |
| Share values across resources | In TypeScript: use a variable. In YAML: use `variables` + `$Var()` |
| Read config from a file | In TypeScript: use `import` or `readFileSync`. In YAML: use `$File()` |
| Reference a secret credential | `$Secret()` — no alternative; secrets must never be in source control |
| Build a string from multiple resource outputs | `$CfFormat()` — the only way to compose runtime values into a string |
| Consume an output from another stack | `$StackOutput()` or `$CfStackOutput()` depending on whether you need deletion protection |

docs.title: Directives
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
### What's the difference between $Secret and $SsmParam?

`$Secret` resolves values from AWS Secrets Manager, which is designed for credentials and sensitive data. `$SsmParam` resolves values from SSM Parameter Store, which supports both plain `String` and encrypted `SecureString` types and is commonly used for configuration values, feature flags, and non-credential settings. Use `$Secret` for database passwords, API keys, and tokens. Use `$SsmParam` for configuration that changes between environments or is managed by other AWS tools.

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: Can I use $ResourceParam to reference a resource in a different stack?
docs.content:
### Can I use $ResourceParam to reference a resource in a different stack?

No. `$ResourceParam` only references resources within the same stack. For cross-stack references, use `$StackOutput` (local resolution, no deletion protection) or `$CfStackOutput` (runtime resolution with deletion protection). Both require the referenced output to be exported from its source stack: unexported outputs cannot be referenced and cause a deployment error. See [Referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) for per-resource parameter details.

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: Why can't I use $Secret in the variables section?
docs.content:
### Why can't I use $Secret in the variables section?

Runtime directives like `$Secret` produce CloudFormation intrinsic functions that only resolve during deployment. The `variables` section is processed locally before the CloudFormation template is generated. If you need a secret value in multiple places, reference `$Secret('name')` directly in each resource property, or use `$CfFormat` to compose it with other values within a resource.

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: How do I pass custom values at deploy time without changing the config?
docs.content:
### How do I pass custom values at deploy time without changing the config?

Use `$CliArgs()` to read arguments passed after `--` in the deploy command. For example, `stacktape deploy --stage prod -- --dbSize db.r6g.large` lets your config read `$CliArgs('dbSize')`. The optional second argument is a fallback used when the flag isn't passed: `$CliArgs('dbSize', 'db.t4g.micro')`. This is useful for values that change per-deploy but shouldn't be committed.

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: What happens if a referenced secret doesn't exist?
docs.content:
### What happens if a referenced secret doesn't exist?

In a terminal, `stacktape deploy` lists the missing secrets and SSM parameters and asks for their values before it changes anything. In a pipeline or for a coding agent, it fails and names them; create them with [`stacktape secret set`](/cli/secret-set) first. Database passwords are generated for you. See [Secrets](/configuration/secrets#when-a-secret-does-not-exist).

docs.title: Directives
docs.content:
### How does $CfStackOutput prevent accidental deletion?

`$CfStackOutput` produces a CloudFormation `ImportValue` intrinsic function. AWS CloudFormation prevents any stack whose outputs are imported by another stack from being deleted. You must delete the consuming stack first (or remove the `$CfStackOutput` reference) before the shared stack can be removed. Use `$StackOutput` instead if you don't need this deletion protection.

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: Can I import an output from a stack in another region?
docs.content:
### Can I import an output from a stack in another region?

Use `$StackOutput`, not `$CfStackOutput`. `$StackOutput` fetches the value at config-parse time, so its optional `region` argument lets it read an export from a stack in a different region. `$CfStackOutput` produces a CloudFormation `ImportValue`, which only resolves within the deployment region: cross-region imports don't work with it. Use [`stacktape status`](/cli/status) to find the exact `outputName` (it must match the stack's CloudFormation `OutputKey`).

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: How do I access JSON properties from $Secret?
docs.content:
### How do I access JSON properties from $Secret?

Pass a top-level key as the second argument to read one value from a JSON secret: `$Secret('my-secret', 'apiKey')`, where `my-secret` is the secret name and `apiKey` is a top-level key in the JSON object. Nested key traversal is not supported. The secret value must be valid JSON: if it isn't, Stacktape reports a parsing error.

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: How do runtime directives resolve in dev mode?
docs.content:
### How do runtime directives resolve in dev mode?

During local resolution, for example in [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview), runtime directives do not emit CloudFormation references. `$ResourceParam()` reads the value from the deployed stack. `$Secret()` fetches the secret from Secrets Manager, and `$SsmParam()` fetches the parameter from SSM. So `stacktape dev` needs the referenced values to exist in AWS.

docs.title: Directives
headingPath: How do I keep one config for development and production?
docs.content:
### How do I keep one config for development and production?

For string values, use `$Stage()` directly or compose stage-specific names with `$Format()`, or template literals in TypeScript. Because `defineConfig` takes a function, you can use normal conditionals for bigger differences, such as a smaller database in `dev`. Create separate [secrets](/configuration/secrets) per stage for sensitive values that differ. See [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments).

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
# Hooks and scripts

Scripts are named commands in your config, such as a frontend build or a seed script. Run them with [`stacktape script run`](/cli/script-run), or attach them to hooks so they run before or after `deploy`, `delete`, `dev` and `bucket sync`. Hooks run on your machine or CI runner. For database migrations, use a [release command](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands) instead.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
## Choose the right tool

Stacktape can run your own code at three points of a deploy. Pick by when the code has to run and what should happen when it fails.

| | [Release command](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands) | [Hooks](#hooks) | [Deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Runs | In a one-off ECS task in your VPC, with the service's new image | On your machine or CI runner | As a Lambda function in your stack |
| When | During the deploy, before services and functions get the new code | Before or after `deploy`, `delete`, `dev` and `bucket sync` | After every other resource is deployed (`after:deploy`), or first in a stack delete (`before:delete`) |
| If it fails | The deploy stops; running code keeps serving | `before*`: the command stops before anything changes. `after*`: the new version stays live and the command exits with an error | The deploy fails; the changes stay unless automatic rollback is on |
| Use it for | Database migrations | Builds, tests, seeding, notifications | Work that must run in AWS on every deploy, whoever deploys |

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
### Order within a deploy

1. `beforeDeploy` hooks run on your machine. A failure stops here.
2. Stacktape packages and uploads your code.
3. Release commands run, then services and functions get the new code.
4. `after:deploy` deployment scripts run, once everything else in the stack is deployed.
5. `afterDeploy` hooks run on your machine.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
## Scripts

A Stacktape script is a named task in the `scripts` section of your config. Scripts can run shell commands or JS/TS/Python files. Use [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) to auto-inject resource connection details as environment variables. Run scripts manually with [`stacktape script run`](/cli/script-run) or attach them to [hooks](#hooks) for automatic execution.

Stacktape supports three script types, each suited to different execution and network requirements:

| Type | Runs on | Best for |
|------|---------|----------|
| `local-script` | Your machine or CI runner | Builds, migrations using local tools, seeding, linting |
| `local-script-with-bastion-tunneling` | Your machine, tunneled through a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) | Running local tools against private VPC resources (databases, Redis) |
| `bastion-script` | The bastion EC2 instance in your VPC | Direct VPC network access without local tool requirements |

**`local-script` is the right default** for most tasks. Use bastion tunneling when your resources have no public endpoint and you need local CLI tools like `prisma` or `psql`. Use bastion scripts when you need direct VPC access and only need basic shell commands.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
Hooks and scripts
Hooks and scripts
Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
## Running scripts manually

Run any defined script with [`stacktape script run`](/cli/script-run):

```bash
stacktape script run seedBucket
```

See the [`script run` CLI reference](/cli/script-run) for the complete command options.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
### Lifecycle events

Hooks correspond to the before and after phases of the deploy, delete, dev, and bucket sync commands:

| Hook | When it fires | Common use |
|------|------|------|
| `beforeDeploy` | Before deployment starts | Builds, linting, tests, asset preparation |
| `afterDeploy` | After deployment completes | Seeding, cache warming, notifications |
| `beforeDelete` | Before stack deletion | Data exports, backups |
| `afterDelete` | After stack deletion | External cleanup, notifications |
| `beforeBucketSync` | Before syncing bucket contents | Pre-processing assets |
| `afterBucketSync` | After syncing bucket contents | Cache invalidation, notifications |
| `beforeDev` | Before dev mode starts | Dependency installation, local setup |
| `afterDev` | After dev mode exits | Cleanup |

`stacktape delete` runs `beforeDelete` and `afterDelete` only when it can load the config, so run it in the project directory if you rely on them.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
### When a hook fails

A failed hook stops the command with an error, and the hooks listed after it don't run. A `beforeDeploy` failure therefore stops the deploy before anything changes.

An `afterDeploy` hook runs after the deployment finished. When it fails, the stack stays deployed on the new version and nothing is rolled back, but `stacktape deploy` exits with an error, so a CI job fails. Fix the problem and run the script again with [`stacktape script run`](/cli/script-run).

In the Console, Slack and email, the deploy is still reported as succeeded, because the new version is live. Everyone who is notified about failed deploys also gets a "Deployed, but a hook failed" message that names the hook.

Set `onFailure: continue` on a hook whose failure should not fail the command, such as a notification. The failure is then printed as a warning:

```yaml
hooks:
  afterDeploy:
    - scriptName: migrate
    - scriptName: notifyTeam
      onFailure: continue
```

A hook cannot roll a deploy back. To keep the old version when a check fails, run the check where it can stop the rollout: a [release command](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands) runs before services and functions get the new code, and an `after:deploy` [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts) with `deploymentConfig.autoRollback: true` makes CloudFormation roll the whole deploy back.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
### Conditional execution

Hook entries can use `skipOnCI` and `skipOnLocal` to control where they run.

- **`skipOnCI: true`** skips the hook in CI, such as GitHub Actions or GitLab CI. Use it for local-only actions like opening a browser.
- **`skipOnLocal: true`** runs the hook only in CI. Use it for smoke tests, test reports or notifications, as `smokeTest` does above.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
## Environment variables in scripts

Scripts commonly receive environment variables from `connectTo` and `environment`, configured inside the script's `properties`.

**`connectTo`** auto-injects connection details for each listed resource as environment variables. The exact variables depend on the resource type: see [connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for the full per-resource injection table.

**`environment`** lets you define additional variables explicitly. Values support [directives](/configuration/directives) like `$Secret()`, `$ResourceParam()`, and `$Var()`, so you can inject secrets and computed values at execution time.

**`assumeRoleOfResource`** injects temporary AWS credentials matching the IAM role of a deployed resource, granting the script the same permissions as that resource. The resource must be deployed before the script runs. Most AWS SDKs and CLIs automatically pick up the injected credentials.

docs.title: Hooks and scripts
docs.content:
## Deployment scripts

A [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts) is different: it is a resource, a Lambda function that CloudFormation runs as part of the stack. It runs no matter who or what deploys, and it can reach the VPC without a bastion when you set `joinDefaultVpc: true`.

```yaml
resources:
  syncSearchIndex:
    type: deployment-script
    properties:
      trigger: after:deploy
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./scripts/sync-search-index.ts
      connectTo:
        - search
      timeout: 300
```

- **Every deploy runs it.** A stack with an `after:deploy` script always deploys through CloudFormation, so [fast deploys](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#fast-deployments) are off for it.
- **A failure fails the deploy.** Without [automatic rollback](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#automatic-rollback), the stack stays in `UPDATE_FAILED` with the new code running. With `deploymentConfig.autoRollback: true`, CloudFormation returns the whole stack to the previous version.
- **A `before:delete` failure stops the delete.** The stack ends in `DELETE_FAILED`; fix the script and delete again.
- **It runs for at most 15 minutes**, the Lambda limit.

Run one by hand with [`stacktape deployment-script run`](/cli/deployment-script-run). Options and examples are on the [Deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts) page.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
# Overrides and escape hatches

Stacktape turns your config into a CloudFormation template. When you need something its properties do not cover, you can change the generated resources or add your own, and keep deploying with Stacktape:

- **[Overrides](#overrides)** set a property of a generated resource, such as reserved concurrency on a Lambda function. They work in YAML and TypeScript.
- **[Transforms](#transforms)** are TypeScript functions that change a generated resource's properties, for example to append to a list. They work only in `stacktape.ts`.
- **[Raw CloudFormation resources](#raw-cloudformation-resources)** add any AWS resource type to the stack.
- **[AWS CDK constructs](#aws-cdk-constructs)** add a group of resources written with the CDK.

Check the resource's own properties first: they are validated and keep working across Stacktape versions. An override is tied to the generated template, so test it again after upgrading Stacktape.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## Understanding child resources

Each Stacktape resource creates one or more CloudFormation resources internally: called "child resources." For example, a Lambda function creates an `AWS::Lambda::Function`, an `AWS::IAM::Role`, and an `AWS::Logs::LogGroup`. A [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) creates an ECS task definition, an ECS service, IAM roles, security groups, and potentially load balancer resources.

Overrides and transforms name a child resource by its CloudFormation logical ID: the key it has under `Resources` in the generated template. The logical ID combines the Stacktape resource name with the child's kind, so a Lambda function named `api` has the child `ApiFunction`.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
### Finding child resource names

Run [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) to generate the CloudFormation template locally and find the logical ID of the child resource you want to change:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

This writes a `compiled-template.yaml` file. Use it to verify that your overrides produce the expected CloudFormation properties. For a deployed stack, [`stacktape status`](/cli/status) lists the child resources too:

```bash
stacktape status --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
### Common child resource names

The table below lists commonly overridden child resources of a resource named `api` (or `db`, `uploads`, `mainTable`). Replace the first part of the logical ID with the PascalCase name of your resource.

| Stacktape resource type | Logical ID of the child resource | AWS resource type |
|---|---|---|
| Lambda function `api` | `ApiFunction` | `AWS::Lambda::Function` |
| Lambda function `api` | `ApiRole` | `AWS::IAM::Role` |
| Lambda function `api` | `ApiLogGroup` | `AWS::Logs::LogGroup` |
| Web service `api` | `ApiTaskDefinition` | `AWS::ECS::TaskDefinition` |
| Web service `api` | `ApiRole` | `AWS::IAM::Role` |
| Relational database `db` | `DbDbInstance` | `AWS::RDS::DBInstance` |
| Relational database `db` | `DbDbParameterGroup` | `AWS::RDS::DBParameterGroup` |
| Bucket `uploads` | `UploadsBucket` | `AWS::S3::Bucket` |
| DynamoDB table `mainTable` | `MainTableGlobalTable` | `AWS::DynamoDB::GlobalTable` |
| HTTP API Gateway `api` | `ApiApi` | `AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Api` |


> **Warning:** The table above is not exhaustive, and the children of a resource depend on its configuration. An override whose target is not a child of the resource is rejected, and the error lists the valid logical IDs.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## Overrides

Stacktape resource overrides let you set specific CloudFormation properties on child resources. The `overrides` property accepts an object where each key is the logical ID of a child resource (such as `ApiFunction`) and the value is an object of CloudFormation properties to set.

The properties are relative to the child resource's `Properties`: write `ReservedConcurrentExecutions`, not `Properties.ReservedConcurrentExecutions`. For nested properties, use a nested object or a dot-notation path such as `TimeToLiveSpecification.Enabled`. Overrides apply your specified keys on top of what Stacktape generates for each child resource.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
Overrides and escape hatches
Overrides and escape hatches
Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## Transforms

Transforms are functions that receive the current CloudFormation properties of a child resource and return modified properties. They're more flexible than overrides because you can compute values, conditionally modify properties, or append to arrays without knowing the full existing configuration.

Transforms are TypeScript functions, so they work only in a `stacktape.ts` config written with `defineConfig`. A YAML config can use overrides, but not transforms.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
### How transforms work

Each transform function receives the `Properties` object of a CloudFormation resource and must return the modified properties:

```typescript
type CfResourceTransform = (props: Record<string, any>) => Partial<Record<string, any>>;
```

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
Overrides and escape hatches
Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: When to use transforms over overrides
docs.content:
### When to use transforms over overrides

Use transforms when you need to:
- **Append to arrays**: add layers, environment variables, or mount points without clobbering existing entries
- **Conditionally modify**: change a property only if it meets a condition
- **Compute derived values**: set a property based on another property's current value

Use overrides when you know the exact final value and it doesn't depend on existing configuration.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## Overrides vs transforms

| Aspect | Overrides | Transforms |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | Static key-value pairs | JavaScript function |
| Config format | TypeScript and YAML | TypeScript (native functions) and YAML (function strings) |
| Use case | Set known property values | Compute, append, or conditionally modify |
| Merge behavior | Recursive merge for existing top-level objects; directly assigned arrays replace their target | Full control — you return the final object |
| Stacktape validation | CloudFormation property values are not Stacktape-validated; verify with `synth` | No Stacktape validation on returned properties; verify with `synth` |

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## Raw CloudFormation resources

The `cloudformationResources` top-level config property lets you add any AWS CloudFormation resource directly to your stack. This is the escape hatch for AWS services Stacktape doesn't have a built-in resource type for: SES configuration sets, custom CloudWatch dashboards, Secrets Manager secrets, or any of the 750+ CloudFormation resource types.

Raw CloudFormation resources are merged into the final template as-is. They don't benefit from Stacktape's automatic IAM permissions, [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) integration, or simplified configuration.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
### Referencing CloudFormation resources from Stacktape

Use the [`$CfResourceParam`](/configuration/directives) directive to reference attributes of raw CloudFormation resources. Import `$CfResourceParam` from `stacktape` and call it with the logical resource name and the CloudFormation attribute to retrieve (for example, `$CfResourceParam('AlertTopic', 'TopicArn')` to get the ARN of an SNS topic. The available attributes depend on the CloudFormation resource type) check the [AWS CloudFormation Resource Reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-template-resource-type-ref.html) for each resource type's return values. To get the value `Ref` returns, such as the physical ID, use that value's name rather than `Ref`: `$CfResourceParam('ImageFunction', 'FunctionName')` for an `AWS::Lambda::Function`, or `BucketName` for an `AWS::S3::Bucket`. An unknown attribute fails with an error that lists the accepted names. The CodeBlock example above shows this pattern in a complete `defineConfig` config.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
### Referencing Stacktape resources from CloudFormation

Use the [`$ResourceParam`](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) directive inside `cloudformationResources` to reference attributes of Stacktape-managed resources. For example, to create a Lambda invocation permission that references both a Stacktape-managed Lambda function and a raw CloudFormation SNS topic, use `$ResourceParam('processor', 'arn')` to get the function ARN and `$CfResourceParam('AlertTopic', 'TopicArn')` to get the topic ARN. Both directives are importable from the `stacktape` package and can be used as values in `cloudformationResources` property definitions.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
### DependsOn for ordering

Use the standard CloudFormation `DependsOn` property to control creation order between raw resources. Add `DependsOn: ['AlertTopic']` to a resource definition within `cloudformationResources` to ensure it is created after the specified dependency. This follows standard CloudFormation ordering semantics.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
### Limitations of raw CloudFormation resources

- **No automatic IAM permissions**: you must manage roles and policies yourself
- **No `connectTo` support**: environment variables and security group rules aren't injected automatically
- **No Stacktape-level validation**: CloudFormation errors surface only at deploy time
- **Property updates may require resource replacement**: some CloudFormation properties can't be updated in-place

For more complex raw CloudFormation usage patterns, see [Raw CloudFormation resources](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources).

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## AWS CDK constructs

For complex escape-hatch scenarios where raw CloudFormation is too verbose, Stacktape supports embedding [AWS CDK](https://aws.amazon.com/cdk/) constructs directly in your stack using the `AwsCdkConstruct` resource type. Write a CDK construct class in TypeScript or JavaScript, and Stacktape synthesizes and deploys it alongside your other resources.

CDK constructs are the right choice when you need multiple interrelated AWS resources with complex logic: for example, a custom CloudWatch monitoring dashboard with dynamic widgets, a VPC peering setup, or a multi-step Step Functions workflow that Stacktape's built-in [state machine](/resources/orchestration/state-machine) doesn't cover. For a single additional resource (like an SNS topic or a Secrets Manager secret), raw CloudFormation in `cloudformationResources` is simpler.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## Inspecting the generated template

To verify that your overrides, transforms, and raw resources produce the expected CloudFormation output, use [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth):

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

This writes the final CloudFormation template to `compiled-template.yaml`. Inspect it before deploying to catch errors early: CloudFormation deployment failures are slower to debug than template inspection.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content:
## Best practices

- **Try native properties first.** Overrides are a last resort. Check the resource's API reference for the property you need before reaching for an override.
- **Use transforms for array modifications.** If you need to append to an existing array (layers, environment variables, mount points), a transform is safer than an override because it preserves whatever Stacktape already configured.
- **Keep overrides minimal.** Each override is a maintenance obligation: Stacktape may change its internal resource structure in future versions.
- **Check the result before deploying.** Inspect the output of `synth` after adding overrides or transforms. Overrides bypass Stacktape's validation; `stacktape validate --thorough` also asks CloudFormation to check the template.
- **Prefer CDK constructs for multi-resource setups.** If you need more than 2-3 related raw CloudFormation resources with cross-references, a CDK construct is cleaner and benefits from CDK's type-safe APIs.
- **Document why, not what.** When using overrides, add a code comment explaining why the override is needed: the code already shows what it does.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: Should I use overrides or transforms?
docs.content:
### Should I use overrides or transforms?

An object override for an existing top-level object recursively merges into it. A directly assigned array replaces that array, and a dot path sets its target. Nested arrays inside merged objects follow lodash merge semantics. Use transforms when you need explicit control over nested arrays, appending entries or removing existing keys.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: Can I use overrides and transforms in YAML configs?
docs.content:
### Can I use overrides and transforms in YAML configs?

Overrides, yes: they are plain objects keyed by the child resource's logical ID. Transforms, no: they are functions, and only a `stacktape.ts` config can hold them. Move the config to TypeScript if you need one.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: Will overrides break when Stacktape updates?
docs.content:
### Will overrides break when Stacktape updates?

Possibly. If Stacktape changes how it structures a child resource internally, your override could target a property that no longer exists or behaves differently. This is rare in patch updates but can happen in major versions. Pin your Stacktape version in production and test overrides after upgrading. Running `synth` after an upgrade shows whether your overrides still produce the expected output.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: What attributes can I reference with $CfResourceParam?
docs.content:
### What attributes can I reference with $CfResourceParam?

Use the name of the value returned by CloudFormation `Ref`, such as `FunctionName` for `AWS::Lambda::Function` or `BucketName` for `AWS::S3::Bucket`; do not pass the literal `Ref`. Other return-value names depend on the resource type. Invalid names are rejected with the accepted names. See the [CloudFormation resource reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-template-resource-type-ref.html) for each type's return values.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: Do raw CloudFormation resources get automatic IAM permissions?
docs.content:
### Do raw CloudFormation resources get automatic IAM permissions?

No. Unlike Stacktape-managed resources (which get baseline IAM permissions automatically and support [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) integration) raw CloudFormation resources require you to manage IAM roles and policies manually. You'll need to add your own `AWS::IAM::Role` or `AWS::IAM::Policy` resources in `cloudformationResources`, or use overrides on existing Stacktape-managed roles to add additional policy statements.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: When should I use a CDK construct instead of raw CloudFormation?
docs.content:
### When should I use a CDK construct instead of raw CloudFormation?

Use CDK constructs when you need multiple interrelated resources with complex configuration logic: for example, a CloudWatch dashboard with dynamic widgets, a custom VPC peering setup, or a Step Functions state machine with many states. CDK provides type-safe APIs, intelligent defaults, and handles cross-resource references cleanly. For a single additional resource (like an SNS topic or a Secrets Manager secret), raw CloudFormation is simpler and has less tooling overhead.

docs.title: Overrides and escape hatches
headingPath: Can I override resources conditionally based on the stage?
docs.content:
### Can I override resources conditionally based on the stage?

Yes. Since TypeScript configs are executable code, you can use standard conditionals. Read the stage from the `defineConfig` callback's `stage` parameter, or use the [`$Stage()` directive](/configuration/directives), then conditionally include overrides. For example, you might enable enhanced RDS monitoring only in production by checking the stage name before adding the `MonitoringInterval` override.

docs.content:
### Relational database

[Relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) expose the richest set of parameters. Standard RDS engines provide host, port, and connection strings. Aurora engines additionally expose reader endpoints for read scaling. Read replica parameters are available when replicas are explicitly configured.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
docs.content:
## Referenceable Parameters: `relational-database`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `connectionString` | Fully-formed connection string that can be used to access the primary instance. For aurora databases, this is connectionString to cluster endpoint, which can be used for both reads and writes. Includes **host**, **port**, **username**, **password** and **dbName**. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "connectionString")` |
| `jdbcConnectionString` | Fully-formed connection string in JDBC form that can be used to access the primary instance. Includes **host**, **port**, **username**, **password** and **dbName**. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "jdbcConnectionString")` |
| `host` | Hostname (address) of the primary instance that can be used for both reads and writes. For aurora databases, this is hostname of a cluster endpoint, which can be used for both reads and writes. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "host")` |
| `port` | Port of the database. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "port")` |
| `dbName` | Name of the automatically created database (can be configured using the `dbName` property). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "dbName")` |
| `readerHost` | Hostname (address) used for reads only. (only available for `aurora-postgresql` and `aurora-mysql` engines). If you have multiple instances, it is advised to use readerHost for reads to offload the primary (read/write) host. ReaderHost automatically balances requests between available instances. Connections are auto-balanced among available reader hosts. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readerHost")` |
| `readerConnectionString` | Same as **connectionString** but targets readerHosts (only available for `aurora-postgresql` and `aurora-mysql` engines). Connections are auto-balanced among available reader hosts. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readerConnectionString")` |
| `readerJdbcConnectionString` | Same as **readerConnectionString** but in JDBC format (only available for `aurora-postgresql` and `aurora-mysql` engines). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readerJdbcConnectionString")` |
| `readReplicaHosts` | Comma-separated list of read replica hostnames (only available if read replicas are configured). Read replicas can only be used for read operations. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readReplicaHosts")` |
| `readReplicaConnectionStrings` | Comma-separated list of connection strings (URLs) used to connect to read replicas (only available when read replicas are configured). Read replicas can only be used for read operations. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readReplicaConnectionStrings")` |
| `readReplicaJdbcConnectionStrings` | Same as **readReplicaConnectionStrings** but in JDBC format (only available when read replicas are configured). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readReplicaJdbcConnectionStrings")` |

docs.content:
## Using parameters in practice

The `$ResourceParam` directive is most commonly used in environment variables and stack outputs. The examples below show the primary patterns for wiring resource outputs into your configuration.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
Referenceable parameters
Referenceable parameters
docs.content:
### Difference from connectTo

[`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) is a higher-level abstraction for wiring resources together. For supported resource types (databases, buckets, queues, Lambda functions, and others documented on the [connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) page), `connectTo` grants IAM permissions, opens security group rules for network-accessible resources like databases and Redis, and injects a predefined set of environment variables automatically.

`$ResourceParam` gives you access to individual parameters without side effects: no permissions are granted and no security groups are modified. Use `$ResourceParam` when you want to:

- Choose your own environment variable name for a resource parameter
- Use a resource parameter outside an environment variable (e.g. in stack outputs or other resource properties)
- Reference one of the documented parameters directly from a resource type

Use `connectTo` when you want Stacktape's documented IAM, networking, and environment-variable wiring. For most workload-to-resource wiring, start with `connectTo` and add `$ResourceParam` for any additional parameters you need.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
docs.content:
### How is $ResourceParam different from connectTo?

[`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) is a higher-level abstraction that, for supported resource types, grants IAM permissions, opens security group rules, and injects a predefined set of environment variables. `$ResourceParam` gives you access to individual parameters without any side effects: no permissions are granted and no security groups are modified. Use `connectTo` for standard access patterns; use `$ResourceParam` for specific values, non-standard wiring, or resource types not covered by `connectTo`.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
headingPath: Can I reference resources from other stacks?
docs.content:
### Can I reference resources from other stacks?

`$ResourceParam` references resources defined in the same Stacktape configuration. To share a value with another stack, add it to `stackConfig.outputs` with `export: true` and read it there with `$CfStackOutput()`. [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments#sharing-resources-across-stages) shows a full example.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
headingPath: What happens if I reference a parameter that doesn't exist?
docs.content:
### What happens if I reference a parameter that doesn't exist?

If you reference a resource name not defined in your config, or a parameter name not supported by that resource type, the configuration is invalid. Check the parameter tables on this page to confirm the parameter name is supported for the resource type you are referencing.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
docs.content:
### Are CDN parameters always available?

CDN-related parameters (`cdnDomain`, `cdnUrl`, `cdnCustomDomains`, `cdnCustomDomainUrls`) are only available on resources that have a `cdn` configuration block attached. Several resource types expose CDN parameters when configured: including [buckets](/resources/storage/s3-bucket), [hosting buckets](/resources/frontend/static-hosting), [web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [Application Load Balancers](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer), and [HTTP API Gateways](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway). Check the per-resource parameter table above for the exact CDN parameter names exposed by each type.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
headingPath: How do relational database parameters differ between engine types?
docs.content:
### How do relational database parameters differ between engine types?

Standard RDS engines (Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB) expose core parameters: host, port, connection string, JDBC connection string, and database name. Aurora engines (Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL) additionally expose reader endpoints (reader host and reader connection strings) for distributing read traffic. Read replica parameters are a separate set, available only when read replicas are explicitly configured. See the [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) resource page and the parameter table above for the full list.

docs.title: Referenceable parameters
headingPath: Can I use $ResourceParam in hooks and scripts?
docs.content:
### Can I use $ResourceParam in hooks and scripts?

Yes. [Scripts](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) and lifecycle hooks can use `$ResourceParam` to reference resource outputs: the `environment` and `parameters` properties of a script accept directives like `$ResourceParam()`, which resolve at deploy time. A common pattern is passing a database connection string into a seeding script. A service's [`releaseCommand`](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands) gets the service's own environment variables.

docs.title: Declaring resources
docs.content:
# Declaring resources

A Stacktape resource is a named piece of infrastructure (an API, a database, a container service, a queue) that Stacktape provisions and manages in your AWS account. You define resources in the `resources` object of your configuration, and Stacktape handles the underlying AWS setup: CloudFormation resources, IAM permissions, networking, and environment variable injection.

docs.title: Declaring resources
docs.content:
## Why resources exist

One resource stands for all the AWS pieces it needs. A [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) is a few lines in your config: the packaging, `cpu` and `memory`. From that, Stacktape creates an ECS cluster, a Fargate task definition and service, an HTTP API Gateway that finds the containers through Cloud Map, a security group, a log group and the IAM roles. You don't write task definitions, target groups or roles yourself.

You stay in control of the underlying AWS resources through [overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches), but you don't need to think about them until you have an edge case that the abstraction doesn't expose directly.

docs.title: Declaring resources
Declaring resources
docs.content:
## Which resources exist

The [resource catalog](/resources) lists every resource with the AWS service it creates and what it is for, and helps you choose between similar ones, such as a web service and a Lambda function.

docs.title: Declaring resources
Declaring resources
Declaring resources
docs.content:
## How resources map to AWS

Each Stacktape resource produces one or more CloudFormation resources. When you run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy), Stacktape resolves your configuration (variables, directives, secrets), translates each resource into CloudFormation definitions with the necessary IAM roles and security groups, and submits the resulting template to AWS for provisioning.

You can inspect the generated template with [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) before deploying. After deploying, use [`stacktape status`](/cli/status) to see deployed resource details.


> **Info:** Stacktape automatically adds `projectName`, `stage`, and `stackName` tags to every AWS resource in your stack. Custom tags defined in `stackConfig.tags` are merged on top: useful for cost tracking and access control in AWS Cost Explorer. Tag names starting with `stp:` are reserved for Stacktape's own tags, and a config that uses one fails validation.

docs.title: Declaring resources
docs.content:
## Overrides

Most Stacktape resources expose an `overrides` property that lets you modify the underlying CloudFormation resources directly. This is the escape hatch for edge cases where Stacktape's abstraction doesn't expose a specific AWS property you need. A few resource types that don't map to CloudFormation (such as MongoDB Atlas clusters) do not support overrides.

Overrides use dot-notation paths to target specific CloudFormation properties on child resources. You can find resource logical IDs with `stacktape status`.

For full details, see [Overrides and escape hatches](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches).

docs.title: Declaring resources
docs.content:
## The stack as a unit

All resources defined in one configuration file deploy together as a single CloudFormation stack. This means:

- They share a lifecycle: deploy, update, and delete together.
- By default, Stacktape creates a VPC for stacks that need VPC networking. You can share or reuse a VPC across stacks with `stackConfig.vpc.reuseVpc`.
- Cross-resource references resolve at deploy time.
- A failed deployment keeps what it created or updated, and the next deployment continues from the failure. With `deploymentConfig.autoRollback`, it rolls back all changes instead.

One stack per [stage](/configuration/stages-and-environments) is the standard pattern. A typical project has a `dev` stage for development and a `production` stage for live traffic: same config, different stages, separate AWS resources.

docs.title: Declaring resources
docs.content:
## Resources vs cloudformationResources

The `resources` section uses Stacktape's typed abstractions: you get IntelliSense, automatic IAM wiring, `connectTo` integration, and managed lifecycle. The `cloudformationResources` section accepts raw CloudFormation resource definitions for anything Stacktape doesn't abstract.

Raw CloudFormation resources don't participate in `connectTo`. If you need to expose values from raw resources to other stacks, define a `stackConfig.outputs` entry with `export: true` and reference it from another stack with the `$CfStackOutput()` directive.


> **Warning:** Renaming a resource deletes it and creates a new one: CloudFormation reads `ordersDb` → `mainDatabase` as "delete ordersDb, create mainDatabase", and the data is gone. `stacktape deploy` asks for confirmation before it deletes or replaces a database, table, bucket, user pool, OpenSearch domain or EFS file system, and [`stacktape diff`](/deployment-and-lifecycle/previewing-changes) shows it before you deploy. Turn on `deletionProtection` for production databases.

docs.title: Declaring resources
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Declaring resources
headingPath: How many resources can I put in one stack, and when should I split?
docs.content:
### How many resources can I put in one stack, and when should I split?

Each Stacktape resource produces multiple CloudFormation resources underneath (IAM roles, security groups, log groups, etc.), so there is a practical ceiling on how many fit in one stack. A typical web application (API + database + queue + bucket) stays well within limits, so start with one stack per service boundary. Split into separate projects when you hit CloudFormation limits, when teams need independent deploy cycles, or when blast-radius concerns justify isolation.

docs.title: Declaring resources
headingPath: Do resources cost money when idle?
docs.content:
### Do resources cost money when idle?

It depends on the resource type. Serverless resources like Lambda functions and DynamoDB tables (on-demand mode) follow a pay-per-request model. Container-based services (web service, private service, worker service) run continuously and incur charges based on allocated CPU and memory. Relational databases and Redis caches charge while the instance is running. Check each resource's dedicated page for pricing details specific to that resource type.

docs.title: Declaring resources
headingPath: Can I reference resources across different stacks?
docs.content:
### Can I reference resources across different stacks?

Yes. Use `stackConfig.outputs` with `export: true` to expose values from one stack, then reference them from another stack using the `$CfStackOutput` directive. This pattern is common for shared infrastructure like VPCs or databases used by multiple services.

docs.title: Declaring resources
headingPath: Can I use AWS services that Stacktape doesn't have a built-in resource for?
docs.content:
### Can I use AWS services that Stacktape doesn't have a built-in resource for?

Yes. Use [raw CloudFormation resources](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources) via the `cloudformationResources` section, or embed [CDK constructs](/resources/advanced/aws-cdk-constructs) for higher-level abstractions. Both approaches let you add any AWS resource while keeping it in the same stack and deployment lifecycle.

docs.title: Declaring resources
headingPath: How does Stacktape handle VPC networking?
docs.content:
### How does Stacktape handle VPC networking?

Stacktape sets up the network when your stack includes resources that need one, such as relational databases and Redis. Production stages get a VPC of their own; non-production stages of an account and region share one, the [shared network](/configuration/shared-network). Resources that don't need a VPC (Lambda functions by default, DynamoDB, S3 buckets) work without one. To use an existing VPC, set `stackConfig.vpc.reuseVpc`.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.content:
# Secrets

Keep API keys, passwords and tokens in AWS Secrets Manager in your account, and reference them in the config with `$Secret('name')`. The config holds only the name, so you can commit it. Secrets belong to an AWS region: every stack in that region can use them.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.content:
## Create a secret

```bash
stacktape secret set stripe-key --region eu-west-1
```

The command asks for the value without showing it. Use the region you deploy to. In a script, pipe the value in, or pass `--value` or `--file`; see [`secret set`](/cli/secret-set).

You can also create, view, edit and delete secrets on the **Secrets** page of the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview), per AWS account and region.


> Screenshot: The New secret dialog in the Console: name, AWS account, region, value, optional description and the Create secret button Caption: New secret creates the secret in the AWS account and region shown in the dialog.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.content:
## Use it in a container

For web services, private services, worker services, multi-container workloads and Batch jobs, put secrets in `secrets`, not in `environment`. ECS or AWS Batch then fetches the value right before the container starts, so it never appears in the CloudFormation template or the task definition. Your code reads it as a normal environment variable, here `process.env.STRIPE_KEY`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { $Secret, WorkerService, defineConfig, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const worker = new WorkerService({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/worker.ts' }),
    resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 },
    environment: { LOG_LEVEL: 'info' },
    secrets: [{ name: 'STRIPE_KEY', valueFrom: $Secret('stripe-key') }]
  });

  return { resources: { worker } };
});
```


Example (YAML):

```yaml
resources:
  worker:
    type: worker-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/worker.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      environment:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          value: info
      # stp-focus
      secrets:
        - name: STRIPE_KEY
          valueFrom: $Secret('stripe-key')
      # stp-end-focus
```


Each `valueFrom` is exactly one `$Secret(...)` or `$SsmParam(...)` directive. SSM parameters used here must be `SecureString`. Stacktape lets the container read only the secrets and parameters it references. Keep the default AWS managed key on these secrets and parameters. With your own KMS key, the task fails to start: the values are fetched by the task execution role, which Stacktape creates without `kms:Decrypt`, and `iamRoleStatements` go to a different role (the one your code runs with). To use your own key anyway, allow `kms:Decrypt` in the key policy for callers in your account that come through Secrets Manager or SSM (the `kms:CallerAccount` and `kms:ViaService` conditions).


> **Warning:** `$Secret()` under a container's `environment` makes CloudFormation write the value into the task definition, where anyone who can describe the task definition reads it. Use `secrets`.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.content:
## Use it elsewhere

Lambda functions have no separate secrets field. `$Secret()` in a function's `environment` works, but the value is stored in the function's configuration, visible to anyone who can read it in the AWS console. For sensitive keys, read the secret from Secrets Manager in your code instead.

Database fields take `$Secret()` directly, for example `credentials.masterUserPassword` of a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database). The value goes to AWS as a CloudFormation dynamic reference (`{{resolve:secretsmanager:...}}`), never as plain text in the template.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.content:
### JSON secrets

When a secret holds a JSON object, pass the key as the second argument: `$Secret('stripe', 'apiKey')` reads `apiKey` from `{ "apiKey": "...", "webhookSecret": "..." }`. The first argument is the exact secret name, so a name such as `billing.api` works too. Stacktape 3 configs that write `$Secret('stripe.apiKey')` keep working. The deploy fails with an error when the value is not valid JSON or the key is empty.

docs.title: Secrets
headingPath: When a secret does not exist
docs.content:
## When a secret does not exist

Before it changes anything, `stacktape deploy` (and `stacktape diff`) checks every secret the config references in the target region:

- **In a terminal**, it lists the missing secrets and asks for their values, then creates them.
- **In a pipeline or for a coding agent**, it stops with an error that names them. Create them with `stacktape secret set` and run it again.
- **Database passwords** (`masterUserPassword` of a database, `defaultUserPassword` of Redis, the MongoDB Atlas admin password) are generated with secure random values. A terminal asks first; a pipeline generates them without asking.

A secret scheduled for deletion that the config still references is restored.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.content:
## Update and rotate

Each deploy pins the secret version that was current at that moment. Changing the value in Secrets Manager does not change running workloads; deploy again to roll out the new version. This applies to rotation too: Stacktape does not set up rotation, and after AWS rotates a secret, the next deploy picks up the new version.

`$SsmParam()` in a container's `secrets` is the exception. ECS and Batch read the parameter when a task starts, without a version, so a task that starts after you change the parameter (a restart, a scale-out, a new job) gets the new value while older tasks keep the old one. A deploy notices the new version and replaces all running tasks. A rollback to an earlier deploy still reads the current value. Everywhere else, `$SsmParam()` is pinned to the version number at deploy time.

Commands that run locally read the current value instead: [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview), scripts and hooks. Commands that connect to a deployed database, such as `stacktape query-sql`, use the version in the deployed connection string, so their credentials match the database.

[`stacktape secret get --show-secrets`](/cli/secret-get) prints the current value. Before deleting a secret with [`stacktape secret delete`](/cli/secret-delete), remove every `$Secret()` reference to it and deploy, or delete the stacks that use it. Otherwise their next deploy fails.

docs.title: Secrets
headingPath: Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store
docs.content:
## Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store

`$SsmParam()` reads a parameter from SSM Parameter Store instead. A standard SecureString parameter costs nothing to store and suits credentials that do not rotate. Secrets Manager charges per secret and per API call ([pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/secrets-manager/pricing/)), and supports rotation and JSON keys.

| | `$Secret()` | `$SsmParam()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Store | AWS Secrets Manager | SSM Parameter Store |
| JSON keys | Yes | No |
| Encryption | Always, with KMS | SecureString parameters, with KMS |
| Pinned per deploy | The version ID | The version number, except in container `secrets` |

For values that are not secret, such as public URLs, feature flags or sizes, use plain config values or [variables](/configuration/variables-and-reuse).

For different values per stage, use different secret names, such as `staging-stripe-key` and `production-stripe-key`, and build the name from `stage` in a TypeScript config.

docs.title: Shared non-production network
docs.content:
# Shared non-production network

Non-production stages of an AWS account and region share one VPC, the `stacktape-network` stack, instead of creating a VPC each. A new stage's first deploy skips creating a VPC, subnets and an internet gateway, and a team with many preview and feature stages stays under the AWS default limit of 5 VPCs per region.

When a stage in it needs outbound internet ([`stackConfig.nat`](/configuration/connecting-resources#nat-internet-access-from-private-subnets)), it uses one shared NAT instance, the `stacktape-network-nat` stack: one `t4g.nano` for every non-production stage, about $7.70 per month in total. The first stage that needs each shared stack creates it while the stage builds, which takes about a minute for the network and about three minutes for the NAT; later stages only use them, and the shared stacks are removed after a day without stages. The shared NAT's size is fixed, so a stage's `nat.instanceSize` does not apply in the shared network.

docs.title: Shared non-production network
docs.content:
## How a stage is placed

Every deploy prints where the stage runs and why:

```text
Network: shared non-production network `stacktape-network` (the stage name `pr-42` marks a non-production stage).
Network: own VPC (the stage name `acme` does not say whether it is production). Set `stackConfig.stageType` or `stackConfig.vpc.shared` to choose.
```

The first deploy that creates networked resources decides, in this order:

1. `stackConfig.vpc.shared: true` or `false` decides.
2. Otherwise `stackConfig.stageType`, then the stage type chosen in the Stacktape Console: non-production stages join the shared network, production stages get a VPC of their own.
3. Otherwise the stage name: names with `dev`, `staging`, `test`, `qa`, `uat`, `preview`, `sandbox`, `pr`, `feature`, `feat`, `e2e` or `ci` join the shared network; `prod`, `production`, `prd` and `live` get their own VPC.
4. A name that says neither (`main`, `acme`, or one with both kinds of word, such as `pre-prod`) asks once, "Is stage acme production?", when you deploy from a terminal. In CI, agents, MCP and remote runners nothing is asked: the stage gets a VPC of its own, and the output says how to choose. The answer is not stored for you: add the `stackConfig.stageType` line the deploy prints so paging, permissions and security checks classify the stage the same way.

Stages with `vpc.reuseVpc`, [MongoDB Atlas](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas) clusters, Kafka clusters with function triggers, or `stackConfig.nat` set to `gateway` or `ha-ec2` always get a VPC of their own, and the output says why.

docs.title: Shared non-production network
docs.content:
## Placement is fixed

Stages deployed before this behavior existed keep their VPC. A deployed stage cannot move between the shared network and a VPC of its own, because its databases, caches, load balancers and functions would be replaced; to move it, delete the stage and deploy it again. A stage that later becomes production (through `stageType`, the Console or a rename) keeps running in the shared network, and every deploy warns about it until you set `stackConfig.vpc.shared: true` to keep it there.

docs.title: Shared non-production network
docs.content:
## Isolation between stages

Each stage keeps its own security groups, and every workload of the stage also carries a stage security group. In the shared network, databases, Redis and OpenSearch in `accessibilityMode: vpc`, internal load balancers and Service Connect ports admit only that stage group, so one stage cannot reach another stage's resources by private IP. `connectTo` works as before. What you give up in the shared network: reaching another stage's resources by private IP (use `reuseVpc` for that), choosing the CIDR, peering or a transit gateway per stage, and a NAT IP of the stage's own. Anyone who can deploy to the account can still change the shared network; the separation prevents accidental access, not a hostile deployer.

docs.title: Shared non-production network
docs.content:
## Functions with no private access

Functions that reach nothing private deploy in seconds. AWS creates network interfaces for each combination of subnets and security groups that VPC functions use. A new combination takes about 4 minutes on the first deploy, and deleting its last function waits up to 20 minutes for AWS to release them. In the shared network, a function with `joinDefaultVpc` therefore runs in the network's no-access security group when it connects to nothing private: no `connectTo` target that admits functions by security group (database, Redis, OpenSearch, Kafka) and no EFS mount, in a stage with no `accessibilityMode: vpc` database, Redis or OpenSearch, no internal load balancer and no Service Connect port. Nothing admits that group, so such a function reaches no stage's private resources, its own stage's included; its outbound access does not change. Every such function in the account and region shares the same network interfaces, so it is created in seconds and deleting it waits for nothing. Other functions keep the stage's security groups. A deployed function keeps its security group, because moving it would create network interfaces again; it moves to the no-access group only when its group changes anyway, for example when it is new or its connections change. The network keeps two idle functions in that group, `stacktape-network-keeper-public` and `stacktape-network-keeper-private`, and the janitor invokes them every hour, because AWS removes the network interfaces of functions that are not invoked for about 14 days. They cost nothing in practice.

docs.title: Shared non-production network
docs.content:
## Removal of the shared stacks

The shared stacks go away on their own. The network stack includes a small function, the janitor, that checks the shared stacks every hour. Once no stage has used the shared NAT for 24 hours, it removes the NAT; once no stage has used the network for 24 hours, it deletes the network's idle keeper functions and, on a later run once AWS has released their network interfaces, removes the network, its own function included. Deleting a stage never waits for this. The day of grace keeps the NAT for preview and feature stages that come and go, instead of creating it again, about three minutes, for the next one. A stage uses a shared stack while its stack imports it, which lasts until AWS has deleted the stage completely, and each deploy of a stage in the shared network counts as a use too. A failed first deploy, or a stage that stops using `nat`, is cleaned up the same way. The janitor keeps a shared stack whose VPC holds something Stacktape did not create, such as an instance or an endpoint you added, and says so in its log group, `/aws/lambda/stacktape-network-janitor`. A deploy that starts while a shared stack is being removed waits for the removal and creates the stack again. The janitor runs within the Lambda free tier and costs well under a cent per month without it.

docs.title: Shared non-production network
Stages and environments
docs.content:
# Stages and environments

A stage is a named deployment of your project, such as `dev`, `staging` or `production`. Each stage is a separate
CloudFormation stack with its own application resources: databases, functions, queues and buckets. Non-production
stages in the same AWS account and region usually share one VPC; see
[Shared network for non-production stages](/configuration/shared-network).

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
## Why stages exist

Most teams need at least two copies of their infrastructure: one to develop against and one for production. With
stages you keep one `stacktape.ts` and branch on `stage` where sizing, secrets or features differ. For example, `dev`
runs one small container and `production` runs two larger ones with a multi-AZ database.

A deploy to `dev` doesn't touch production's databases, functions or storage. A common CI setup deploys `main` to
`production` and each feature branch to a short-lived stage.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content: ## How stages work

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Stack naming

Stacktape derives the CloudFormation stack name from your project name and stage:

```
{projectName}-{stage}
```

A project named `my-api` deployed to stage `dev` creates a stack called `my-api-dev`. The same project deployed to
`production` creates `my-api-production`.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Stage name constraints

A stage name has at least 2 characters and contains only lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens. The project name, a hyphen and the stage form the CloudFormation stack name, which can have at most 128 characters. Examples of valid stage names: `dev`, `staging`, `production`, `pr-42`, `dev-john`.


> **Warning:** Keep stage names short. The combined project name + stage forms the CloudFormation stack name and the names of AWS
  resources. When a resource name would be longer than AWS allows, Stacktape shortens it and adds a short hash. The
  stack works the same, but these names are harder to recognize in the AWS console.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Deploying a stage

Pass the `--stage` flag to [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) to target a specific stage.

Deploy a development stage:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

Deploy production:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

Deleting a stage removes only that stage's resources.

docs.title: Stages and environments
Stages and environments
Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Config callback parameters

The `defineConfig` callback receives an object whose `stage` property is the stage name passed via `--stage`. See the [configuration files](/configuration/configuration-files) page for the full `defineConfig` API and any other properties exposed on the callback object.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Using $Stage() in directives

When composing directive strings that need the stage value at deploy time (rather than at config-evaluation time), use
the [`$Stage()` directive](/configuration/directives). This is mainly useful in YAML configs or when building
CloudFormation-level expressions. In TypeScript configs, you can typically use the `stage` parameter directly since it's
already available as a JavaScript variable.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content: ## Common patterns

docs.title: Stages and environments
Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Feature branch stages

Create a temporary stage for any feature branch. Deploy it, test it, and delete it when the branch merges.

Deploy a feature branch stage:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage feat-42 --region eu-west-1
```

Delete the stage after the branch merges:

```bash
stacktape delete --stage feat-42 --region eu-west-1
```

Feature branch stages are disposable by design. Each one gets its own database, its own API endpoint, and its own
resources. Keep stage names short: abbreviate branch names if needed.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Preview environments for pull requests

Stages are a good fit for per-PR preview environments. See [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) and [Stacks per Git branch](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) for setup details.

docs.title: Stages and environments
Stages and environments
Stages and environments
Stages and environments
docs.content:
## Sharing resources across stages

To let several stages or projects share one database, put it in its own project, deploy that project once, and export what the others need. Here the `shared-infra` project runs one database for all non-production stages (stage `dev`) and one for production:

docs.title: Stages and environments
Stages and environments
docs.content:
## Setting defaults

If you always deploy to the same stage and region during development, use [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set) to set default values for stage and region. See the [CLI reference](/cli/defaults-set) for details.

```bash
stacktape defaults set
```

Once configured, you can deploy without passing `--stage` and `--region`:

```bash
stacktape deploy
```

Override the defaults when deploying to a different stage:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region us-east-1
```

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content: ## Managing deployed stages

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Listing stacks

Use [`stacktape stack list`](/cli/stack-list) to list deployed stacks in a region. See the [CLI reference](/cli/stack-list) for available options.

```bash
stacktape stack list --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
### Deleting a stage

Use [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) to delete a stage's stack.

```bash
stacktape delete --stage feat-42 --region eu-west-1
```

Deletion removes the stage's CloudFormation stack. Other stages remain completely unaffected.

A stage that [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) created stays a dev stack after dev mode stops, and `stacktape deploy` refuses it. Use a separate stage name for dev mode (for example `local`), or delete the dev stack with `stacktape delete --stage <stage>` before deploying that stage.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content:
## Best practices

**Use consistent stage names.** Pick a naming convention (`dev`, `staging`, `production`) and stick to it across all
projects. Consistent names simplify CI/CD pipelines and make `$Secret('db-password-' + stage)` patterns predictable.

**Keep dev stages minimal.** Use the smallest instance sizes and lowest scaling in development. The multi-tier lookup
pattern shown above makes this automatic and keeps development costs low without manual intervention.

**Make staging mirror production.** The whole point of a staging stage is to catch issues before production. Use the
same instance types, same scaling ranges, and same configuration: just with test data and lower traffic.

**Separate secrets per stage.** Never reuse production credentials in development. Stage-interpolated secret names
(`db-password-dev`, `db-password-production`) enforce this by convention.

**Delete ephemeral stages promptly.** Feature branch and PR preview stages accumulate if not cleaned up. See
[Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) and [Stacks per Git branch](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) for setting up preview-stage workflows, or manually run
[`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete).

**Add safeguards in production.** Enable multi-AZ for databases, add a
[web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall), configure
[alarms](/observability/alarms), and set [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets). Use conditional resource inclusion
to add these only in production.

docs.title: Stages and environments
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Stages and environments
headingPath: How do I access the stage name in my config?
docs.content:
### How do I access the stage name in my config?

The `defineConfig` callback receives an object with a `stage` property. Use standard TypeScript logic to branch on the stage value: ternary operators, lookup objects, or if statements all work. In directive strings that need the stage at CloudFormation deploy time, use the [`$Stage()` directive](/configuration/directives).

docs.title: Stages and environments
headingPath: Can I include resources only in certain stages?
docs.content:
### Can I include resources only in certain stages?

Yes. Since `defineConfig` returns a plain JavaScript object, you can conditionally add keys to the `resources` object using `if` statements or any other control flow. Resources not included in the returned object are simply not created for that stage. This is commonly used to skip databases in preview stages or add WAFs only in production.

docs.title: Stages and environments
headingPath: Are stages fully isolated from each other?
docs.content:
### Are stages fully isolated from each other?

Their application resources are separate, and deploying or deleting one stage does not touch the others. Two things are shared:

- **The network.** Non-production stages of an account and region usually run in one VPC, the [shared network](/configuration/shared-network). Each stage has its own security groups, so one stage cannot reach another stage's databases by private IP. Where a stage runs is decided on its first deploy and doesn't change later, even when the stage becomes production.
- **The AWS account.** Anyone with deploy credentials for the account can reach every stage in it. To keep production away from people who deploy previews, deploy it to its own AWS account.

docs.title: Stages and environments
headingPath: What happens when I deploy to an existing stage?
docs.content:
### What happens when I deploy to an existing stage?

Deploying to an existing stage updates that stage's CloudFormation stack rather than creating a new one. CloudFormation computes the diff between the current and desired state and applies only the changes needed. Deleting a stage removes only that stage's stack: other stages are unaffected.

docs.title: Stages and environments
headingPath: Can different stages use different AWS regions?
docs.content:
### Can different stages use different AWS regions?

Yes. The region is a separate parameter from the stage, so you can deploy `dev` to `eu-west-1` and `production` to `us-east-1`. The stack name is derived from `{projectName}-{stage}`, and region-scoped resources (like secrets and ACM certificates) must exist in the target region. Create stage-appropriate secrets in each region you deploy to.

docs.title: Stages and environments
headingPath: How do I keep development costs low across stages?
docs.content:
### How do I keep development costs low across stages?

Vary resource sizing by stage. Branch on the `stage` parameter to give dev and preview stages the smallest instance sizes and lowest scaling, while production gets larger instances and multi-AZ: the multi-tier lookup pattern shown above makes this automatic. You can also conditionally skip expensive resources (like a database) in ephemeral `pr-*` stages, or have several services in the same stage share one database via the [`$CfStackOutput` directive](/configuration/directives).

docs.title: Variables and reuse
docs.content:
# Variables and reuse

To avoid repeating values such as ports, sizes or domain prefixes, use ordinary constants, functions and imports in a TypeScript config. In YAML, use the `variables` section and reference values with `$Var().variableName`. For values computed at deploy time, define a custom directive.

docs.title: Variables and reuse
docs.content:
## TypeScript-native reuse

The [`defineConfig`](/configuration/configuration-files) callback returns your configuration as plain TypeScript. You can use any language feature (constants, conditionals, loops, imports, spread operators) to reduce duplication and add stage-aware logic.

docs.title: Variables and reuse
Variables and reuse
Variables and reuse
Variables and reuse
Variables and reuse
docs.content:
### Other TypeScript patterns

Beyond constants, stage branching, and factory functions, several other standard TypeScript patterns work inside `defineConfig`:

- **Object spreading**: define a shared object (e.g. `const sharedEnv = { LOG_LEVEL: 'info', NODE_ENV: 'production' }`) and spread it into each resource's `environment`: `environment: { ...sharedEnv, SERVICE_NAME: 'api' }`. This keeps shared values in one place while letting each resource add its own overrides. Works equally well for tags, scaling configuration, or VPC settings.

- **Conditional resources**: use conditional spread syntax inside `defineConfig` to include resources only for certain stages. For example, return `{ resources: { api, ...(isProduction ? { metricsExporter } : {}) } }` where `metricsExporter` is a `LambdaFunction` declared earlier in the callback. Resources not spread into the returned object are not created: other stages skip them entirely.

- **Dynamic resource generation**: use `Array.map()` or a `for` loop to create multiple resources from a data array. The `resources` object accepts any string keys, so `Object.fromEntries()` combined with `Array.map()` can generate one `LambdaFunction` per route from a data array. Adding a new route means adding one entry to the array.

docs.title: Variables and reuse
Variables and reuse
headingPath: When to use variables vs TypeScript constants
docs.content:
### When to use variables vs TypeScript constants

| Approach | Best for | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TypeScript `const` | Most cases | Full type safety, autocomplete, conditional logic, refactoring support |
| `variables` + `$Var()` | YAML configs | No type checking, no autocomplete, but works without TypeScript tooling |

The `variables` property defines reusable values referenced with `$Var().variableName` anywhere in the config. In TypeScript configs, language-level constants cover the same need and additionally support type checking and conditional logic; `variables` is the primary mechanism in YAML where those language features are not available.

docs.title: Variables and reuse
Variables and reuse
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Variables and reuse
headingPath: Can I use environment variables in my stacktape.ts?
docs.content:
