### Can I use environment variables in my stacktape.ts?

Yes. Since `stacktape.ts` is a regular TypeScript file, you can read `process.env` values when the config is evaluated. Use `process.env` for truly external values like CI tokens or build-time feature flags that you don't want to commit to the repository.

docs.title: Variables and reuse
headingPath: What happens to variables at runtime?
docs.content:
### What happens to variables at runtime?

Variables and constants defined in `stacktape.ts` exist only when the config is evaluated before deployment. They do not automatically appear as runtime values in your deployed Lambda functions or containers. To pass a value to a running workload, set it in the resource's `environment` property: which maps to environment variables available at runtime.

docs.title: Variables and reuse
headingPath: How do Stacktape config variables compare to CloudFormation parameters?
docs.content:
### How do Stacktape config variables compare to CloudFormation parameters?

Stacktape `variables` (and TypeScript constants) are resolved at config evaluation time, before the CloudFormation template is generated. CloudFormation parameters are resolved at deploy time by the CloudFormation service itself. Stacktape's approach means your entire config is fully resolved before deployment starts, which makes the template deterministic and easier to debug. For values that must remain secret until deploy time, use the [`$Secret()` directive](/configuration/secrets) instead of `variables`.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
# In-place code swap

Set `codeSwap: true` on a web service to let `stacktape deploy` update eligible code inside its running containers. It is off by default and can be used in any stage, including production, within the task cap. Stacktape still builds and pushes an image for every code change, so image fallback and rollback stay available.

```yaml configExample="complete"
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      codeSwap: true
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 1024
      scaling:
        minInstances: 1
        maxInstances: 2
```

Deploy as usual with `stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1`. The first deploy installs the supervisor and uses an image rollout. Later code-only changes can swap inside the same tasks. The CLI reports whether it swapped code or used an image deploy, and explains a fallback.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
## Can your service use it

A code change swaps in place only when all of these hold. Otherwise the deploy uses a normal image rollout and the CLI says why.

- The service is a web service on x86 Fargate, behind the default HTTP API Gateway or an application load balancer (`loadBalancing.type: application-load-balancer`). Several services per stack can opt in.
- It has no `internalHealthCheck`, network load balancer, blue/green deployment, side containers, tracing sidecar or remote sessions, and does not run on EC2 or arm64.
- Its scaling fits within **10 simultaneous tasks**, including the deployment surge (see [Task limit](#task-limit)).
- The app listens on `PORT`, can write to its working directory and keeps its child processes under its own process tree. State that must survive a deploy lives outside the process and its release directory.
- The change touches only your code. Dependency, environment, runtime and base image changes, and `--full`, use an image rollout.
- Node.js and Python with installed dependencies need local Docker caching; a registry-cache builder uses images.

Custom Dockerfiles, prebuilt images, Bun and Deno always use image rollouts. Behind the default HTTP API Gateway, WebSocket connections are not possible and SSE responses are buffered; use an application load balancer for them.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
### Node.js

Use `js-bundle` packaging. Dependencies are either bundled or kept in a separate generated install in the image. A change to that install uses an image rollout.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
### Python

Use `buildpack` packaging with a complete, hash-locked `requirements.txt`: every dependency, including transitive ones, pinned with `==` and a SHA-256 hash. Generate it with:

```bash
uv pip compile requirements.in --generate-hashes --output-file requirements.txt
```

The build installs with `--require-hashes`; an incomplete lock falls back to an image rollout. Also required:

- The start command runs `uvicorn`, `gunicorn` or `python` directly, without shell chains or an absolute `/app` source path.
- No local or URL dependencies, custom build or install commands, or custom Railpack configuration. Other dependency managers use images.
- The app reads its files relative to the working directory. Each swap starts the command from a new release directory, so an absolute `/app/...` path still reads the image's files.

A swap ships the source and assets the buildpack selects, with the same exclusions as the image. The interpreter and virtualenv stay in the image; a change to the installed environment, interpreter or system libraries uses an image rollout. Projects that install their own source or compile it during the build use images.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
### Task limit

Each service's autoscaling maximum, scheduled overrides and deployment surge must fit within 10 simultaneous tasks; unknown bounds use images. `minimumHealthyPercent` must be 100, and the surge must allow at least one replacement. With the default 200% maximum, use `maxInstances: 5` or fewer. A custom CloudFormation transform that breaks the role or capacity checks is refused before deployment.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
### Several services

A deploy prepares every changed service before switching any. If one changed service cannot swap, all changed services use image rollouts, and a failure during switching does the same. Unchanged services keep their tasks. Services switch independently, so there is no single moment when all endpoints change; keep the API between your services compatible across versions.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
## Memory and failed requests

During a switch, **the old and new processes share the task's memory**. A sudden increase in the new code's memory use can kill a candidate after it starts serving, failing some in-flight requests. Memory screening and OOM preferences reduce the risk; they do not isolate the processes or guarantee that the old process survives extreme pressure.

Before starting a candidate, each task reads its kernel lifetime peak and checks:

`2 × 1.25 × peak + 64 MiB ≤ 0.9 × memory limit`

An unknown or unreadable peak, an unsupported memory layout, or a failed screen causes an image deploy. The lifetime peak includes startup, workers, caches and overlap from earlier swaps. A successful swap can therefore raise the peak enough that the next edit uses images. Increase `resources.memory` (for example, from 512 to 1024 MiB), reduce memory use, or continue with image deploys. A larger limit is not a promise that any new code will fit.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
## Completion and fallback

A small supervisor owns the HTTP port, starts the candidate, verifies proxy reachability, switches new requests, then waits for the old process to drain and exit. The old process gets up to **65 seconds** to finish requests that were already in flight, about the time an image deploy allows (a 35 s HTTP API routing drain or a 30 s load balancer deregistration delay, plus the 30 s default stop timeout). It receives `SIGTERM` as soon as its last request finishes, so a swap with no open requests does not wait. Requests still open after 65 seconds are closed. The application then has its `stopTimeout` (default 2 s) to exit before it is killed. Without an authored application check, **any complete HTTP response, including 500, counts as reachability**. There is no default application health check and no fixed observation window.

Behind an application load balancer, the supervisor also runs the target group's health check. Before the switch, the candidate must answer `GET` on `loadBalancing.properties.healthcheckPath` (default `/`) with status 200 within `healthcheckTimeout` (default 4 s); it gets up to 30 seconds to pass. The same check runs on the new code right after the switch, every second while the old process drains, and once more before completion. The load balancer's own checks reach whichever process serves, with no gap during the switch. If a check fails, the task switches back to the old process and the deploy uses an image, which the load balancer and ECS then check as usual.

The CLI reports success only after every current task completes, the fleet remains healthy and routable, old process trees exit (except one that only holds long-lived connections), and release history is durable. Candidate failure, OOM, task replacement or fleet changes prevent swap success and trigger image convergence. If candidate cleanup cannot be confirmed, the command fails and the next deploy repairs the service, as described below. A later crash is an ordinary application incident; use your existing monitoring and rollback procedure.

Dependency, environment, runtime, supervisor and base configuration changes use image deploys. `--full` also forces an image rollout. Scaling without a new task revision keeps the committed code; replacement tasks load that code before reporting ready. Opted-in image rollouts and new tasks pay the ECS supervisor-readiness delay. Normal services without the opt-in keep their existing resources and behavior.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
### WebSocket and SSE connections

WebSocket connections and Server-Sent Events streams do not delay a swap. Two kinds of connection count as long-lived: a connection upgraded through the HTTP `Upgrade` mechanism, such as a WebSocket, and a response whose `Content-Type` is `text/event-stream` (parameters such as `charset` are ignored). The supervisor classifies an event stream when its response headers arrive. Every other request counts as ordinary and keeps the old process waiting as described above. This includes streamed `text/plain` or NDJSON responses (such as AI SDK text streams), long polling, downloads, gRPC and any request whose response headers have not been sent yet.

When only long-lived connections remain, the swap completes and the CLI exits. It reports how many connections still run on the previous code. They stay on the old process until they close or the same 65-second deadline passes, as on an old task after an image deploy. Then WebSocket clients receive close code 1001 (going away), event streams end, and the old process gets its `stopTimeout` to exit. Clients must reconnect to reach the new code. A browser `EventSource` reconnects automatically; WebSocket clients need their own reconnect logic.

While the old process holds these connections, it is the first choice of the kernel's out-of-memory killer, and the swap can no longer revert to it. If it crashes or is killed, only its connections end; the swap stays complete. A redeploy within 65 seconds closes the remaining connections early, before the next candidate starts. A task stop closes them at the end of the task's routing drain.

docs.title: In-place code swap
docs.content:
## Rollback, disabling and interrupted deploys

Use [`stacktape rollback`](/deployment-and-lifecycle/rollbacks) to deploy a retained release's exact image as a new task revision. Rollback uses images rather than reversing a swap. Deployment artifact retention follows `deploymentConfig.previousVersionsToKeep`; the current committed bundle stays available for task replacement. Successful deploys remove status rows for tasks ECS confirms have stopped. Live task status has no expiry.

Set `codeSwap: false` or remove it, then deploy, to return to image-only operation. [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) also removes the runtime table and code bundles.

A stack runs one deploy, rollback or delete at a time. Once a stack is opted in, the operation holds the stack's lock from its start, because preparing a swap already starts new code in the running tasks. If you interrupt the CLI (Ctrl+C, or a cancelled CI job) before it starts changing the stack, it aborts any prepared swap and releases the lock. After it has started changing the stack, and whenever the CLI is killed, the lock stays until it expires, within two minutes. A command that starts before then waits and names the holder. Once the lock expires, it takes over and repairs an interrupted swap through an image deploy; it never reports the interrupted attempt as a successful swap. If that repair also stops before it finishes, the following command repairs the swap the same way.

The application has permission to write its own supervisor status. A malicious application can forge its own completion and cause a false success report. It cannot write the release record or another task's status. Code bundles, images, release records and task status stay in your AWS account; this feature adds no external data service.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
# Deploying stacks

[`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) builds your code, turns your config into a CloudFormation template and creates or updates the stack in your AWS account. Each stage of a project is one CloudFormation stack. When only code changed, the deploy updates the changed functions and containers directly, which takes seconds instead of minutes.

A deploy that fails keeps what it already created. Fix the error and deploy again; it continues from where it stopped. See [When a deployment fails](#when-a-deployment-fails).

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
## Run a deploy

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The CLI reads the config file in the current directory: `stacktape.ts`, `stacktape.yml`, `stacktape.yaml` or `stacktape.js`. If there is more than one, or the file is elsewhere, pass `--config`. When the config declares `projectName` and `region`, as the one [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) writes does, `--stage` is enough:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev
```

Flags override the config. The region can also come from `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, from a default saved with [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set), or from your AWS profile. A stage name has at least two characters: lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens. See [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments).

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--stage`, `-s` | The stage to deploy. Each stage is its own stack. |
| `--region`, `-r` | The AWS region. |
| `--config`, `-c` | Path to the config file. |
| `--full` | Deploy through CloudFormation even when only code changed. |
| `--yes`, `-y` | Confirm deleting or replacing a database or another data store without asking. |
| `--auto-rollback` | Roll the stack back if this deploy fails, instead of keeping what it created. |
| `--no-cache` | Build everything again, ignoring cached artifacts. |
| `--skip-release-command` | Do not run [release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands) in this deploy. |
| `--profile`, `-p` | The AWS profile to use. |

The [`deploy` reference](/cli/deploy) lists every option.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content: ## What a deploy does

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
## Flow
1. **Validate**: Read the config, check guardrails, ask for missing secrets and SSM parameters.
2. **Package**: Bundle functions and build container images, in parallel.
3. **Upload**: Upload artifacts to the stage’s S3 bucket and images to ECR.
4. **Release command**: Run due release commands, such as database migrations.
5. **Deploy**: Update changed code directly, or create or update the stack through CloudFormation.
6. **Post-deploy**: Sync hosting buckets, invalidate CDN caches, run afterDeploy hooks, print URLs.


**Validate.** The CLI checks the config and any [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) of your organization. When the config references a [secret](/configuration/secrets) or SSM parameter that does not exist in the region, an interactive terminal asks for its value. A pipeline or a coding agent fails instead and names the missing values. Database passwords referenced with `$Secret()` can be generated for you.

**Package and upload.** [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) are bundled and [container workloads](/resources/compute/web-service) build images from your source or Dockerfile. Unchanged artifacts come from the cache. See [Packaging](/packaging/overview).

**Release command.** A [release command](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands) runs before services get the new code, on fast and full deploys, when its inputs changed. A failed command stops the deploy.

**Deploy.** For a new stage, CloudFormation creates the stack. For an existing one, it works out what to create, update or delete and runs independent changes in parallel. An update is finished once the new resources are in place. Resources the update removed or replaced, such as a CDN distribution, are then deleted in the background, which can take several minutes. The next deploy, delete or rollback of the stage waits for that. If AWS could not delete an old resource, the next operation reports it once, because the resource then stays in your account.

**Post-deploy.** Stacktape syncs [hosting buckets](/resources/frontend/static-hosting), invalidates [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) caches, runs your `afterDeploy` [hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts), sends notifications to [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) and prints the URLs of your resources. After the first deploy of a stage, a signed-in terminal inside a Git repository offers to set up [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

Before a CloudFormation deploy, the CLI prints how many resources it will create, update, replace and delete. It asks for confirmation only when the deploy would delete or replace a database, DynamoDB table, S3 bucket, user pool, OpenSearch domain or EFS file system. A run that cannot ask (a pipeline, a coding agent) stops there unless you pass `--yes`. Use `--yes` only where someone already approves deploys outside Stacktape. To see AWS's property-level view before you deploy, run [`stacktape diff`](/deployment-and-lifecycle/previewing-changes).

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
## Fast deployments

Every `stacktape deploy` picks the mode itself and prints why when it uses CloudFormation.

- **Fast deploy.** Only the code of functions or container services changed. A function update takes seconds. A container service runs a normal rolling deployment and the CLI finishes a few seconds after the new containers are healthy and registered with the load balancer or API Gateway. The old containers drain in the background ([how containers are replaced](/resources/compute/web-service#how-deploys-replace-containers)).
- **Full deploy.** Everything else goes through CloudFormation: new or removed resources, configuration, environment variables, permissions, routes.

A deploy uses CloudFormation when:

- the stack is new, or the template changes anything other than function code or container images built by Stacktape,
- stack settings changed, such as tags or termination protection,
- a changed function uses an alias (`deployment` or provisioned concurrency), or a changed container service uses blue/green deployment,
- the stack has an `after:deploy` [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts), which runs through CloudFormation on every deploy,
- the last deploy failed and left the stack in `CREATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_FAILED`,
- you pass `--full`.

A web service behind an HTTP API Gateway without an `internalHealthCheck` gives the fast deploy no health signal. The CLI then finishes once the new containers run and API Gateway can find them, and says that application health is unchecked. Add an [`internalHealthCheck`](/resources/compute/web-service) if you want the deploy to wait for a healthy app.

Both modes create a release that [`stacktape rollback`](/deployment-and-lifecycle/rollbacks) can return to. A deploy that changes nothing creates no release, even with `--full`. If some fast updates fail, Stacktape still finishes the others and lists which workloads run the new code; deploying again updates the rest. After a fast deploy, the CloudFormation template still references the previous code until the next full deploy. Rollback restores the exact code of a release either way.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
## When a deployment fails

By default, a failed deploy keeps everything it created or updated, and the next deploy continues from the failure. The CLI prints the stack state and what you can do.

| What failed | State | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The first deploy of a stage | `CREATE_FAILED` | Fix the error and deploy again. It creates what is missing and retries what failed; resources that already exist, such as a database, stay. To remove everything instead, run [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete). |
| An update | `UPDATE_FAILED` | Fix the error and deploy again. Or return the whole stack to the last successful deploy with [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover). |
| The deploy succeeded but the app is broken | `UPDATE_COMPLETE` | Return to an earlier release with [`stacktape rollback`](/deployment-and-lifecycle/rollbacks), or deploy a fix. |

After a failed update, the resources that updated keep their new configuration and the ones that failed return to their previous state. The stack can run a mix of old and new configuration, so fix a failed production deploy promptly or recover it. When the next deploy succeeds, Stacktape removes the artifacts the failed attempts left behind.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
### Resources that must be replaced

CloudFormation can replace a resource (for example a container's task definition, which every container change replaces) only in a deploy that it may roll back. Stacktape handles this for you:

- An update of a healthy stack that replaces resources rolls back if it fails. The CLI says so before it deploys.
- When the fix for a failed deploy replaces resources that the failed deploy created, such as the task definition of a new service that never started, Stacktape removes them and what depends on them, then deploys the full config, which creates them again. They never served traffic, so nothing is interrupted. It stops instead if this would remove a database or another data store.
- When the fix would replace resources of the last successful deploy, Stacktape stops before changing anything. Run [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover) (or [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) for a stage that never deployed successfully), then deploy again.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
### Automatic rollback

Set `deploymentConfig.autoRollback: true`, or pass `--auto-rollback` for one deploy, to have CloudFormation undo a failed deploy instead. A failed update then returns the whole stack to its previous state. A failed first deploy deletes the new stack together with the deployment bucket and image repository Stacktape created for it, so the next attempt starts from nothing. Automatic rollback is always on when `deploymentConfig.triggerRollbackOnAlarms` or `monitoringTimeAfterDeploymentInMinutes` is set, because rollback alarms need it. [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) rolls back by default.

A stack already in `CREATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_FAILED` can only be continued without rollback, so the deploy that continues it never rolls back.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
## Dev mode and deploy

[`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) creates its own kind of stack, and `stacktape deploy` refuses a stage that has one. Use separate stage names:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage local
```

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev
```

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
## Deploy from Git

To deploy on every push without writing a pipeline, use [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) in the Stacktape Console. To run `stacktape deploy` in your own pipeline, see [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd). The [CI/CD overview](/ci-cd-and-gitops/overview) compares the two.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
## Stack states

| State | Meaning | What you can do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CREATE_COMPLETE`, `UPDATE_COMPLETE` | The last deploy succeeded | Deploy, delete |
| `CREATE_FAILED` | The first deploy failed and kept what it created | Fix and deploy again, or delete |
| `UPDATE_FAILED` | An update failed and kept what it updated | Fix and deploy again, or [`stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover) |
| `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` | An update failed and rolled back | Fix and deploy again, delete |
| `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` | The first deploy failed and rolled back | Delete, then deploy again |
| `*_IN_PROGRESS` | An operation is running | Wait for it to finish |

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
### Stack is in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE

The first deploy failed with automatic rollback on, and CloudFormation removed everything it created. The empty stack still holds the name. Delete it, then deploy again:

```bash
stacktape delete --stage dev
```

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev
```

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
### Stack name too long

The stack name is the project name, a dash and the stage. CloudFormation allows at most 128 characters, and the CLI refuses a longer name before it deploys; the error says how long the stage can be. Shorten generated stage names in CI, for example by trimming the branch name. A name under that limit can still be too long for some AWS resource names. Stacktape then shortens those names with a hash and prints a warning. Everything works the same; only the names in the AWS console are harder to read.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
headingPath: Missing secrets fail the deploy in CI
docs.content:
### Missing secrets fail the deploy in CI

A pipeline cannot answer the prompt for a missing secret, so the deploy fails and lists the secrets it needs. Create each one once in the region you deploy to, then run the pipeline again:

```bash
stacktape secret set my-api-key --region eu-west-1
```

The command asks for the value without echoing it. For a script, pass `--value` or `--file`; see [`secret set`](/cli/secret-set).

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
### No changes to deploy

The template and code match what is deployed. Check that you saved the config, that you deploy the right stage and region, and that your change touches something Stacktape deploys.

docs.title: Deploying stacks
docs.content:
### Deploys are slow

- **Large container images.** Use a multi-stage [Dockerfile](/packaging/containers/dockerfile) or [`js-bundle`](/packaging/containers/js-bundle) packaging for Node.js services.
- **Many resources.** CloudFormation creates dependent resources one after another. A new database or CDN takes several minutes.
- **Slow local builds.** Use a machine with more CPU and memory, or deploy from the Console's [build runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners).

Run the deploy with `--log-level debug` to see how long each phase takes.

docs.title: Deleting stacks
docs.content:
# Deleting stacks

[`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) removes a stage: its CloudFormation stack, every resource in it, and the deployment bucket and image repository that hold its artifacts. Use it for development stages, closed pull request previews and environments you no longer need.


> **Warning:** There is no undo. Databases, buckets and caches are deleted with their data unless the AWS resource keeps a snapshot or backup. Export what you need first.

docs.title: Deleting stacks
docs.content:
## Delete a stage

```bash
stacktape delete --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

Run it in the project directory, or pass `--project` when you run it elsewhere. The command does not need the config file; without one, it simply skips your [`beforeDelete` and `afterDelete` hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts). It shows the stack name, when the stack was created and how many resources it has, then asks for confirmation. In a script or pipeline, pass `--yes`.

When the command finishes, everything that costs money is gone. AWS may still be removing free leftovers, such as a disabled CloudFront distribution or the network interfaces of functions in a VPC; the command lists them. A `stacktape deploy` of the same stage waits until they are gone and then creates the stage again.

docs.title: Deleting stacks
docs.content:
## What happens, in order

1. **Checks.** Your organization's [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) are checked. The command stops if the stack has termination protection, or if a resource has deletion protection on, such as a database with `deletionProtection: true`. Nothing has been deleted at this point.
2. **`beforeDelete` hooks.** They run when the config is available. Use one to export data.
3. **Artifacts.** Stacktape empties the deployment bucket and image repository, because CloudFormation cannot delete a bucket or repository that still has content.
4. **Stack.** CloudFormation deletes the stack's resources in dependency order. To save time, Stacktape starts deleting slow resources (RDS and Aurora instances, DynamoDB tables, Redis and Valkey clusters, OpenSearch domains, load balancers) itself, instead of waiting for the services that use them. It leaves alone anything CloudFormation would keep or snapshot, anything with deletion protection, and databases with read replicas.
5. **External artifact store.** For stacks that `stacktape deploy` created, the deployment bucket and image repository are not part of the stack. Stacktape deletes them after CloudFormation has accepted the stack delete.

If CloudFormation refuses the delete, for example because another stack imports one of this stack's outputs, Stacktape deletes nothing further and prints CloudFormation's reason.

docs.title: Deleting stacks
docs.content:
## What is kept

- **Resources with a retain or snapshot policy.** For example, an RDS final snapshot stays and is billed until you delete it.
- **The shared network.** Stages in the shared non-production network leave the network and its NAT in place. They are removed automatically once no stage has used them for a day.
- **Shared resources used by other stages or projects.** The command lists them.
- **Secrets.** Secrets you created with `stacktape secret set` stay. Passwords that dev mode generated for a dev stage also stay, because another stage may use them; the command names them so you can delete them with [`secret delete`](/cli/secret-delete).

docs.title: Deleting stacks
Deleting stacks
docs.content:
## When a delete fails

If CloudFormation cannot delete a resource, the stack ends in `DELETE_FAILED` and the CLI prints the resource and AWS's error. When this happens after `stacktape delete` finished (while AWS was removing free leftovers), the next `stacktape deploy` of the stage stops with CloudFormation's reason. Fix the cause and run `stacktape delete` again.

| Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Another stack imports an output of this stack | Remove the import from the other stack, or delete that stack first |
| A security group is used by a resource in another stack | Update or delete the other stack first |
| An IAM role is referenced by a policy outside the stack | Remove the outside reference |
| Deletion protection was turned on outside Stacktape | Turn it off in the AWS console |

docs.title: Deleting stacks
docs.content:
## Delete or keep a stage

Container services ([web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [private services](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service)) and [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) cost money every hour they run, used or not. [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and on-demand [DynamoDB tables](/resources/databases/dynamodb) cost nothing without traffic. A stage made of the latter can stay; a stage with containers or a database is worth deleting when nobody uses it.

Delete pull request previews when the pull request closes. [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) can do this for you, and [Stacks per Git branch](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) shows how to do it in your own pipeline.

docs.title: Gradual deployments
docs.content:
# Gradual deployments

A gradual deployment moves traffic to the new version in steps, for example 10% first and the rest after 5 minutes, instead of switching everything at once. It works for [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), and for [web services](/resources/compute/web-service) and [multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) behind an [application load balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer). AWS CodeDeploy shifts the traffic.

Shifting traffic alone does not detect a broken version. A rollout goes back to the old version only when a test function you write reports a failure, or when a CloudWatch alarm you name fires. See [What rolls a rollout back](#what-rolls-a-rollout-back).

docs.title: Gradual deployments
headingPath: Turn it on for a function

docs.title: Gradual deployments
headingPath: Turn it on for a web service

docs.title: Gradual deployments
docs.content:
## Strategies

| Strategy | Functions | Services | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Canary10Percent5Minutes` | Yes | Yes | 10%, then the rest after 5 minutes |
| `Canary10Percent10Minutes` | Yes | No | 10%, then the rest after 10 minutes |
| `Canary10Percent15Minutes` | Yes | Yes | 10%, then the rest after 15 minutes |
| `Canary10Percent30Minutes` | Yes | No | 10%, then the rest after 30 minutes |
| `Linear10PercentEvery1Minute` | Yes | No | 10% more every minute |
| `Linear10PercentEvery1Minutes` | No | Yes | 10% more every minute |
| `Linear10PercentEvery2Minutes` | Yes | No | 10% more every 2 minutes |
| `Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes` | Yes | Yes | 10% more every 3 minutes |
| `Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes` | Yes | No | 10% more every 10 minutes |
| `AllAtOnce` | Yes | Yes | Everything at once, after the test function |

The one-minute linear strategy is spelled `Minute` for functions and `Minutes` for services; these are AWS's names. Percentages and intervals are fixed.

Start with `Canary10Percent5Minutes`. Use a longer canary when your traffic is low and 5 minutes would not send enough requests to the new version to notice errors. Use a linear strategy when problems show only under load, such as connection pools running out. Use `AllAtOnce` to get the test function without a slow rollout.

docs.title: Gradual deployments
docs.content:
## What rolls a rollout back

- **The `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` reports `Failed`**, or does not report within an hour. No production traffic has reached the new version yet.
- **The `afterTrafficShiftFunction` reports `Failed`.** By then all traffic is on the new version; for a function, CodeDeploy points it back to the old version.
- **A CloudWatch alarm listed in `deploymentConfig.triggerRollbackOnAlarms` fires** while CloudFormation updates the stack, which includes the shift. CloudFormation then rolls the whole stack back. This is how you roll back on errors seen by real traffic: create an alarm on the function's or the load balancer's error rate and list its ARN. See [Automatic rollback](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#automatic-rollback).

Without one of these, a version that returns errors still gets all the traffic when the strategy ends.

docs.title: Gradual deployments
Gradual deployments
docs.content:
## Configuration reference

The reference below covers functions. Services take the same `strategy`, `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` and `afterTrafficShiftFunction`, plus `testListenerPort`; see the [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) and [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) references.

docs.title: Gradual deployments
docs.content:
### Definition: `LambdaDeploymentConfig`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/function` with definition name `LambdaDeploymentConfig`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `strategy` | yes | `string: "AllAtOnce" \| "Canary10Percent10Minutes" \| "Canary10Percent15Minutes" \| "Canary10Percent30Minutes" \| "Canary10Percent5Minutes" \| "Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes" \| "Linear10PercentEvery1Minute" \| "Linear10PercentEvery2Minutes" \| "Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes"` | - |
| `afterTrafficShiftFunction` | no | `string` | - |
| `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` | no | `string` | - |

docs.title: Multi-region deployments
docs.content:
# Multi-region deployments

A Stacktape stack lives in one AWS region. To run in several regions, deploy the same config once per region. Each deploy creates an independent stack with its own compute, databases and network; Stacktape does not connect them.

Most apps do not need this. A single region with a [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) in front serves static and cacheable content fast worldwide. Go multi-region when dynamic requests are too slow for distant users, when regulations require data to stay in a country or region, or when a regional AWS outage must not take your product down. Every region adds the full cost of its stack, plus replication and routing you set up yourself.

docs.title: Multi-region deployments
docs.content:
## Deploy to two regions

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --region us-east-1
```

The same stage name can exist in several regions; the stacks do not collide. If the config declares a `region`, `--region` overrides it for that command.

Stacktape supports these regions: `us-east-1`, `us-east-2`, `us-west-1`, `us-west-2`, `ca-central-1`, `sa-east-1`, `eu-west-1`, `eu-west-2`, `eu-west-3`, `eu-central-1`, `eu-north-1`, `eu-south-1`, `ap-east-1`, `ap-south-1`, `ap-northeast-1`, `ap-northeast-2`, `ap-northeast-3`, `ap-southeast-1`, `ap-southeast-2`, `me-south-1` and `af-south-1`. The CLI refuses others, even when your account has them enabled. Regions that AWS launched as opt-in, such as `ap-east-1` or `me-south-1`, also need to be enabled in your account, and not every AWS service is available in every region.

docs.title: Multi-region deployments
Multi-region deployments
docs.content:
## Patterns

- **Active-active.** Every region serves traffic. Route users to the nearest region with Route 53 latency or geolocation routing, and replicate data between regions. The most expensive and the most complex.
- **Active-passive.** One region serves traffic and the other waits, often scaled down. Route 53 failover routing switches traffic when health checks fail. Only one region writes data, so consistency is simpler, but a failover takes the DNS TTL plus the health check time.
- **One region per audience.** EU customers use `eu-west-1`, US customers `us-east-1`, each with its own data. No replication is needed. This is the usual answer to data-residency requirements.

docs.title: Multi-region deployments
docs.content:
## Data and DNS

Each region's databases, buckets and caches are separate. Stacktape does not replicate between them. AWS offers:

| Strategy | Consistency | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DynamoDB global tables | Eventual | Sessions, preferences, feature flags |
| Aurora Global Database | One writer, asynchronous replicas | Read-heavy apps that write in one region |
| S3 Cross-Region Replication | Eventual | Uploads, static assets, backups |
| Replication in your app | What you build | Selective or business-specific sync |

Replication costs extra: replicated writes in DynamoDB, the secondary Aurora cluster, cross-region data transfer.

Each regional stack can have its own [custom domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains). Routing between regions (latency, geolocation, weighted or failover records) lives outside the regional stacks. Create it in Route 53 directly, or in a separate stack with [raw CloudFormation resources](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources).

docs.title: Multi-region deployments
Multi-region deployments
docs.content:
## Operate each region

Every command takes the region of the stack it works on:

```bash
stacktape logs api --stage production --region us-east-1
```

Logs, metrics and alarms belong to their region. To remove a region, delete its DNS records first, then run `stacktape delete` with that region, so no record points at a stack that is being deleted.

docs.title: Previewing changes
docs.content:
# Previewing changes

[`stacktape diff`](/cli/diff) shows what a deploy would create, update, replace or remove in a deployed stage, without deploying. CloudFormation itself assesses the change, so it is the most reliable way to catch a replaced database or load balancer before it happens.

Use it before deploying to production, on stages with data, and in pull request checks. On a development stage you can usually deploy directly: `diff` packages your code just like a deploy, so it is not much faster.

docs.title: Previewing changes
docs.content:
## Run a preview

```bash
stacktape diff --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

The stage must already be deployed. For a stage that does not exist yet there is nothing to compare, so deploy it. Like `deploy`, the command takes the project and region from the config when it declares them, and `--config` for a config file elsewhere.

`diff` never executes the change. It does write a few things to AWS to compute it:

- It creates [secrets](/configuration/secrets) and SSM parameters that the config references but that do not exist yet. In a terminal it asks for their values; in a pipeline it fails and lists them, like `deploy`.
- It builds your functions and container images on your machine, using the build cache.
- It uploads the template to the deployment bucket and deletes it when done.
- It creates a CloudFormation change set, reads it and deletes it without executing it.

Change sets are free; the main cost is the build time.

docs.title: Previewing changes
docs.content:
## Read the output

Each changed resource gets one line with an action, followed by up to three highlights of what changed inside it (for example `Lambda::Function: Code, MemorySize`).

| Symbol | Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` | new | The resource will be created. |
| `~` | updated | The resource is updated in place. |
| `!` | replaced | CloudFormation creates a new resource and deletes the old one. |
| `-` | removed | The resource will be deleted. |

Below a resource, `Will replace` lists parts that CloudFormation must replace. `May replace` lists parts where it can only tell at deploy time.


> **Warning:** A replaced database, DynamoDB table, Redis cluster or bucket is a new, empty resource. Treat `May replace` on these like `Will replace`, and back up the data or change the config before you deploy.


`NO CHANGES DETECTED` means the config matches the stage. `NO MEANINGFUL STACKTAPE RESOURCE CHANGES` means CloudFormation reported only internal changes (for example a dependency it re-evaluates) that change nothing in your resources.

docs.title: Previewing changes
docs.content:
## Preview in a pull request

Run `diff` against the stage the pull request will deploy to, and post its output where reviewers see it. In CI the output is plain text automatically. Look for `replaced`, `removed`, `Will replace` and `May replace`.

```bash
stacktape diff --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

The job needs the same AWS access as a deploy, and every referenced secret must already exist, because a pipeline cannot answer the prompt. [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd) shows the credential setup. Coding agents get the result as JSON lines that include a summary of the changes.

docs.title: Previewing changes
docs.content:
## Unexpected changes

- **A resource that depends on one you changed.** CloudFormation can report a dependent resource as updated even when nothing changes for it.
- **A rebuilt container image with a new digest.** The service shows as updated even without a source change.
- **A secret or SSM parameter value changed** since the last deploy. Resources that reference it show as updated.

docs.title: Previewing changes
headingPath: diff, synth and the deploy plan
docs.content:
## diff, synth and the deploy plan

- `stacktape diff` needs a deployed stage and shows what AWS would change, including replacements.
- [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) writes the CloudFormation template without comparing it to anything. Use it to read the template or to audit it.
- `stacktape deploy` prints a count of resources to create, update, replace and delete before it changes the stack. It asks for confirmation when a data store would be deleted or replaced. See [Deploying stacks](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#what-a-deploy-does).

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
# Release commands

Set `releaseCommand` on a service, a function or a server-rendered site to run a command once during a deploy, before your services and functions get the new code. Use it for database migrations. By default, it runs on every deploy that changes the image; with [`runWhenChanged`](#run-it-only-when-something-changed), only when your migration files change.

```yaml configExample="complete"
resources:
  database:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      credentials:
        masterUserPassword: $Secret('database-password')
      engine:
        type: postgres
        properties:
          version: '17'
          primaryInstance:
            instanceSize: db.t4g.micro
      accessibility:
        accessibilityMode: vpc
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: .
          startCommand: npm start
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      connectTo:
        - database
      releaseCommand: npx prisma migrate deploy
```

Stacktape runs the command in a one-off ECS task. The task uses the image you are about to deploy, with the same environment variables, secrets, IAM role and network access as the service, so it reaches a database with no public address without a bastion. The deploy waits for the task and prints its logs. If the command fails, the deploy stops and your running containers keep serving the old code.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## What your commands must allow

- **The old code runs against the new schema until the rollout finishes.** Keep migrations compatible with it. To remove a column, stop using it in one deploy and remove it in a later one.
- **A retry runs the command again.** Stacktape records a run only when the whole deploy succeeds, so a deploy that fails after the command succeeded runs it again on the next attempt. Migration tools handle this already, because they record what they applied.
- **Nothing reverses the command.** Neither a failed deploy nor [`stacktape rollback`](/deployment-and-lifecycle/rollbacks) changes the database back. A rollback does not run the command either, because an old command must not run against a newer database. The old code has to work with the schema that is there.

docs.title: Release commands
headingPath: Run it only when something changed
docs.content:
## Run it only when something changed

By default, the command runs on each deploy that changes the image. Use `runWhenChanged` to run it only when the listed files or directories changed:

```yaml
releaseCommand:
  command: npx prisma migrate deploy
  runWhenChanged:
    - prisma/migrations
```

A deploy that changes none of the listed paths skips the command and takes no extra time. Use this with tools that apply only what is in one folder. Don't use it with a command that reads anything else that can change. Paths are relative to the project root, and each one must exist.

The command also runs when the environment variables or secrets of the service change through a CloudFormation deployment, even if the listed paths stayed the same. A replaced database therefore gets its schema.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## How it affects deploy time

| Deploy | Added time |
|---|---|
| The command does not run | None |
| Fast deployment, the command runs | About 15 to 30 seconds for the task to start, plus the command |
| Full deployment, the command runs | The same, inside the CloudFormation update |
| A function or site, the command runs | The image build, the task start and the command, inside a CloudFormation update |

A code-only deploy stays a [fast deployment](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks), and it runs the command before it updates any service. With [code swap](/deployment-and-lifecycle/code-swap), the command runs from the new image and the swap follows.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `command` | | The shell command. It runs through `/bin/sh -c` in place of the image's entry point. If the image needs its entry point, call it in the command. An image without a shell cannot run a release command. |
| `runWhenChanged` | | Files or directories that decide whether the command runs. |
| `timeout` | `3300` | Seconds the command can run, up to 3300. After that, the task stops and the deploy fails. |
| `container` | The main container | The container to run in. Required for a [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) with several containers. Not allowed on a function or site. |

Containers that the chosen container depends on run too, but only the chosen container decides when the task ends. Load balancers, health checks and scaling don't apply to the task.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## Several commands

Each service can have its own release command. They run one at a time, in the order of the resources in your config. Every container service and function waits until all of them finished.

One exception: if a command refers to a workload, for example through an environment variable with its URL, that workload has to be updated first, so it can get new code before the command finishes. The deploy prints a warning that names it.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## Functions and server-rendered sites

A [function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and a server-rendered site, such as [`nextjs-web`](/resources/frontend/nextjs), take `releaseCommand` too. Their packages hold only bundled code, so Stacktape builds an image of the whole project and runs the command from the project root in a one-off ECS task. The task gets the resource's environment variables and its access to the resources in `connectTo`, and it runs in the stack's VPC, so it reaches a database with no public address.

```yaml
resources:
  database:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      credentials:
        masterUserPassword: $Secret('database-password')
      engine:
        type: postgres
        properties:
          version: '17'
          primaryInstance:
            instanceSize: db.t4g.micro
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      connectTo:
        - database
      releaseCommand:
        command: npx prisma migrate deploy
        runWhenChanged:
          - prisma/migrations
```

Three things differ from a service:

- **Building the image needs Docker** on the machine that deploys, each time the command is due. Set `runWhenChanged`: without it, each change of the project builds the image and runs the command.
- **A deploy that runs the command goes through CloudFormation.** A deploy that skips it stays a fast deployment.
- **The task has 1 vCPU and 2 GB of memory**, whatever the function has. Nothing runs between deploys, so it costs only the seconds the command takes.

If the machine that deploys has no Docker, run the migration from an [`afterDeploy` hook](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) instead.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## `js-bundle` services

A `js-bundle` image contains only the bundled code, not your migration tool or migration files. For these services, Stacktape builds a second image of the whole project, used only by the release command. It builds it only when the command is due, so ordinary code deploys keep the fast bundle. Use `runWhenChanged` with these services: without it, each code change builds the second image and runs the command.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## Skipping and interrupting

Pass `--skip-release-command` to deploy without running the command, for example when you ran it yourself or when you need to deploy a fix for it. A skipped run is not recorded, so the next deploy without the flag runs the command if its inputs still differ from the last successful run.

If you cancel a deploy while the command runs, its task keeps running, because stopping a migration partway can leave the database half migrated. The next deploy waits for that task to finish before it runs the command again or changes anything, and prints which task it waits for. It stops waiting after the command's `timeout`.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## Logs

The output appears in the deploy output, prefixed with the service name. It is also kept in the `stp-release` log group of the service, even when the service's own logging is disabled. Use the `logs-release-command` link in the stack details to open it.

docs.title: Release commands
docs.content:
## When to use something else

Use an [`afterDeploy` hook](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts#hooks) for a command that needs the new code to be live, such as seeding through your API or warming a cache. A hook runs on your machine or CI runner, after the deploy, and a failed hook fails the command without undoing the deployment.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
# Rollbacks

Stacktape has two recovery commands. [`stacktape rollback`](/cli/rollback) puts a previous release back when the last deploy succeeded but broke your app. [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover) undoes a deploy that failed and left the stack in `UPDATE_FAILED`. Neither rebuilds your code: rollback reuses the artifacts stored with the release.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
## Which command to use

| Situation | Command |
| --- | --- |
| The last deploy succeeded, but the app is broken | `stacktape rollback` |
| A deploy failed and you want to fix it and continue | `stacktape deploy` after the fix |
| An update failed and you want to undo it | `stacktape stack recover` |
| The first deploy of a stage failed and you want it gone | `stacktape delete` |

A failed deploy keeps what it created by default, so deploying the fix is usually the fastest way forward. See [When a deploy fails](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#when-a-deployment-fails).

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: Roll back to an earlier release
docs.content:
## Roll back to an earlier release

Every deploy that changes something creates a release: `v000001`, `v000002` and so on. Stacktape keeps its CloudFormation template and its artifacts (function code, layers, container images) in the stage's deployment bucket and image repository.

Go back one release:

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

List the releases you can return to:

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1 --list-versions
```

Go back to a specific release, or a number of releases back:

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1 --target-version v000003
```

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1 --rollback-steps 3
```

The rollback deploys the old template as a new release. Rolling back from `v000005` to `v000003` creates `v000006` with the code and template of `v000003`, so the next deploy continues from `v000006`. Bucket contents synced by [hosting buckets](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) are restored to what they were at that release; if that fails, the CLI warns and you redeploy the site from its commit.

Passing the current release as `--target-version` repairs a stage where a failed fast deploy left some workloads on newer code.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: Roll back to an earlier release
What is checked before the rollback
docs.content:
### What is checked before the rollback

Stacktape reads the target release's template and checks that what it needs still exists:

- The template, Lambda code, layers and Lambda container images must exist. If one was removed, the rollback stops before changing anything and names it. Roll back to a newer release that is still complete.
- A missing container image of an ECS service only produces a warning, and the rollback continues. New tasks of that service will fail to start because they cannot pull the image. If you see this warning, check that service after the rollback, or deploy a fix instead.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: Roll back to an earlier release
What a rollback does not undo
docs.content:
### What a rollback does not undo

- **Release commands and database changes.** A rollback does not run or reverse [release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands) or migrations. The database keeps its current schema, so the old code must work with it. Make migrations backward compatible if you want to be able to roll back.
- **Values fixed at deploy time.** `$File()` and other directives that read local or external state, custom directives and TypeScript transforms ran when the release was first deployed. The rollback uses those old results. The CLI warns when the release used any of them.
- **`afterDeploy` hooks.** They do not run during a rollback.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: Roll back to an earlier release
How many releases you can return to

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
## Recover a failed update

When an update fails without [automatic rollback](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#automatic-rollback), the stack stays in `UPDATE_FAILED` with a mix of old and new configuration. `stacktape stack recover` asks CloudFormation to return it to the last successful deploy, then deletes the artifacts the failed deploy uploaded:

```bash
stacktape stack recover --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

You do not need it when the stack already rolled back on its own (`UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`), or when the stack is healthy and you want an earlier release (use `stacktape rollback`). A failed first deploy has no earlier state to return to; run [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) instead.

CloudFormation cannot always restore the previous state. It fails, for example, when someone deleted a resource outside CloudFormation or when the old configuration is no longer valid. The stack then needs manual recovery in the AWS CloudFormation console before Stacktape can deploy it again.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.content:
# Quickstart

Stacktape deploys your app into your own AWS account. The CLI reads your project, writes one configuration file and
deploys it as a CloudFormation stack. You don't need a Stacktape account.

docs.title: Quickstart
headingPath: Run it in your app's directory
docs.content:
## Run it in your app's directory

Open a terminal in the root of the app you want to deploy and run the command for your system. It installs the CLI
and starts `stacktape init`. The standalone CLI doesn't need Node.js.


Example (macOS):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/macos.sh | sh -s -- init
```


Example (Linux):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/linux.sh | sh -s -- init
```


Example (Windows):

```powershell
iex "& { $(irm https://installs.stacktape.com/windows.ps1) } init"
```


Example (npm):

```bash
npx stacktape@latest init
```


The macOS, Linux and Windows installers put the CLI in `~/.stacktape/bin` and add it to your `PATH`. Open a new
terminal before you run `stacktape` yourself. To only install it, leave out the trailing `init`.

`npx stacktape@latest init` runs the CLI without installing it. The later commands on this site start with
`stacktape`. To have that command, install the CLI with `npm install -g stacktape`, or put `npx` in front of each
command.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.content:
## What happens next

`stacktape init` opens a wizard in your browser. Keep the command running while you use it. The wizard has four steps:

1. **Start.** Choose what reads your code: Claude Code, Codex or files only. Then click **Analyze my project**.
2. **Analyze.** You see every file it opens. An agent can read your source code, and it sends the files it reads to
   its own model provider. Files only reads manifests and config files and sends nothing to an AI provider, but it
   leaves more settings for you to check. No code is sent to Stacktape.
3. **Review.** You get the resources it proposes, the line of code behind each one and the monthly price. Change any
   choice, pick YAML or TypeScript and the region, and save the file.
4. **Deploy.** This step is optional. The wizard shows the exact AWS account and stack, deploys after you confirm and
   gives you the live URL.

Nothing is created in AWS before you confirm the deploy. [Deploy an existing app](/getting-started/deploy-an-existing-app)
walks through every screen.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.content:
## What you need

- **An AWS account, with credentials on your machine.** Only the deploy needs them, and the wizard checks them before
  it does anything. If you have never used AWS from the terminal, [set up AWS credentials](/getting-started/aws-credentials)
  first.
- **Claude Code or Codex (optional).** With one installed, init can read your source code, not only manifests, so
  fewer settings fall back to defaults. See [who reads your code](/getting-started/deploy-an-existing-app#1-start-choose-who-reads-your-code).
- **Docker, for most apps that are not JavaScript or TypeScript functions.** Stacktape builds container images and
  Python, Go or Java functions on your machine, with Docker. See [Packaging](/packaging/overview).

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.content:
## No app yet?

Start from a starter project instead. Run this in the directory where the new project folder should go:

```bash
stacktape init --starter-project
```

The CLI asks which starter, where to put it and which config format to use. Then it prints the commands that deploy
it. See [Start a new project](/getting-started/start-a-new-project).

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.content:
## What it costs

- The CLI is free and open source under the MIT license.
- AWS bills you for the resources in your account. The wizard shows the monthly estimate before you deploy, and one
  command removes everything when you're done.
- The [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) is optional. It's free while your organization's AWS spend
  managed by Stacktape stays at or under $200 a month.

Prefer to write the configuration yourself? [Configuration files](/configuration/configuration-files) explains the
format. You can still deploy it with the same commands.

docs.title: Add the Console
docs.content:
# Add the Console

The Stacktape Console is the hosted part of Stacktape, for what a team shares. You add it to stacks you already
deployed. Connecting doesn't redeploy, rename or replace anything.

It's free while the AWS spend Stacktape manages for your organization stays at or under $200 a month. Above that, the
Flexible plan costs 19–25% of that spend; see [Free plan cost limit](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription#free-plan-cost-limit)
for the warning, the grace period and what pauses. AWS bills your AWS account for the resources, as before.

You don't need the Console to deploy. The CLI works without an account; see
[Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli).

docs.title: Add the Console
docs.content:
## What you get

- **Deploy history** of every stage: who deployed what and when.
- **Costs** per project, stage and resource, and [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) with alerts.
- **Alerts** in Slack or by email, [uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) and
  [error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) with incidents.
- **Team access**: members with roles, limited to the projects and AWS accounts you choose, and organization keys for
  CI.
- **Git deployments**: push to deploy and pull request previews, built on runners in your AWS account. See
  [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).
- **Organization rules**: [guardrails](/guardrails/overview), security reports and the audit log.

docs.title: Add the Console
docs.content:
## Connect from the init wizard

After a successful deploy, the wizard shows **Add dev to the Stacktape Console** below the live address.


> Screenshot: Add dev to the Stacktape Console, free up to $200 a month of AWS spend, with Connect to the Console and Not now, and a note that the stack is not redeployed Caption: The Console offer in the init wizard after a successful deploy.


1. Click **Connect to the Console**. A new tab opens the Stacktape sign-in.
2. Sign in, or create an account. Check that the tab shows the same code as the wizard, and approve.
3. If your account belongs to more than one organization, pick one.
4. The wizard connects the AWS account it deployed to. This usually takes a minute or two.
5. When it says **Connected to the Stacktape Console**, click **Open dev in the Console**.

Your app keeps running the whole time. **Not now** skips the offer; you can connect later from the terminal.

docs.title: Add the Console
docs.content:
## Connect from the terminal

Run this with the AWS credentials of the account your stacks are in:

```bash
stacktape connect
```

Add `--profile my-dev-account` to use a profile other than the default one. The command:

1. **Signs you in**, if this machine isn't signed in yet. Choose **Sign in with the browser**. The CLI prints an
   address and a code and opens the address. Sign in or create an account, check the code and approve.
2. **Connects the AWS account** of your credentials to your organization. It creates a small CloudFormation stack in
   your account with an IAM role that the Console uses. If it can't create the stack with your credentials, it opens
   AWS CloudFormation in your browser instead: check the box that allows creating IAM resources and choose **Create
   stack**.
3. **Finds the Stacktape stacks** already in the account and adds them to the Console as projects and stages.

It ends with `Nothing was redeployed or changed.` and the link to your projects. Open the link to see your stages.

If a region couldn't be read, the CLI says which one. An Owner or Admin can run **Find existing stacks** on the **AWS
accounts** page of the Console later.

docs.title: Add the Console
headingPath: Who can connect an AWS account
docs.content:
### Who can connect an AWS account

An Owner or Admin of the organization. When you create an account, you're the Owner of its new organization. A
Developer or Viewer gets `Your role in <organization> cannot connect AWS accounts` and needs an Owner or Admin to run
`stacktape connect` with credentials for that account.

docs.title: Add the Console
headingPath: What the connection can do in your AWS account
docs.content:
### What the connection can do in your AWS account

The connection's IAM role has administrator access, so the Console can deploy from Git, read logs and metrics and
manage your stacks. It's the standard AWS way to give a service access to an account, with short-lived credentials
and no access keys stored by Stacktape. To remove it, delete the connection in the Console or delete its
CloudFormation stack in AWS. See [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions) and
[Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account).
[What leaves your AWS account](/observability/overview#what-leaves-your-aws-account) lists the data each Console
feature sends to Stacktape.

docs.title: Add the Console
docs.content:
## What changes after connecting

- The CLI on this machine is signed in. Your deploys are recorded in the Console, and Console features in your config
  work.
- A deploy prints the Console link of the stage when it finishes.
- Error tracking for a stage starts with its next deploy, because the deploy adds the log subscription it needs.
  Deploy each stage once more to turn it on.
- Some features send data from your AWS account to Stacktape. Error tracking, for example, sends each error with its
  log line, after masking secrets and tokens. Your logs and secrets themselves stay in your account. Each feature's
  page says what leaves it.

docs.title: Add the Console
docs.content:
## CI with the Console

A pipeline uses an API key instead of a browser sign-in. Owners and Admins create an
[organization key](/stacktape-console/api-keys#create-an-organization-key) on the API keys page and store
it as the `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret of the pipeline. Unlike a personal key, it keeps working when people leave. If
the organization has more than one connected AWS account, pass `--aws-account <name>` to the deploy. See
[Deploy from your CI](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd).

docs.title: Add the Console
docs.content:
## Work without the Console again

Run [`stacktape logout`](/cli/logout). The CLI goes back to working without an account. Nothing you deployed changes.
In CI, remove `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` from the pipeline.

A stage served on a default `*.stacktape-app.com` domain keeps it, but the CLI won't deploy that stage without an
account, because the deploy would remove the domain. Add your own domain first, or deploy it signed in.

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
# After the first deploy

Your app runs in your AWS account as one CloudFormation stack. This page covers the commands you use from here on:
check the app, read its logs, ship a change, add stages and remove what you don't need.

The commands below run in the project directory. The config written by `stacktape init` declares the project name and
region, so a stage is all they need. For a starter, add the `--project` and `--region` values from the commands init
printed, for example `--project hono-api --region eu-west-1`.

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
## Check that it works

Open the URL from the end of the deploy. The wizard lists it under **It's live**, and the terminal prints it after the
deploy. HTTP APIs, web services and websites get an HTTPS address from AWS, or your own domain once you
[add one](/resources/networking/custom-domains).

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
## Read the logs

```bash
stacktape logs api --stage dev
```

`api` is the resource name: its key under `resources` in your config. The command prints the last 100 log lines from
the past hour and keeps printing new ones until you press Ctrl+C. Use `--since 6h` to look further back and
`--filter ERROR` to show only matching lines. See [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) and [Logs](/observability/logs).

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
## Ship a change

Edit your code, then run the same deploy:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev
```

When only the code of functions or container services changed, Stacktape updates them directly instead of through
CloudFormation. A function update takes seconds. Changes to the configuration, such as a new resource or an
environment variable, go through CloudFormation and take longer. To see what a deploy would change first, run
`stacktape diff --stage dev`.

To change the infrastructure, edit `stacktape.yml` (or `stacktape.ts`). [Resources](/configuration/resources),
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) and [Secrets](/configuration/secrets) cover the common
changes.

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
## Add another stage

A stage is another copy of the app from the same config, for example `staging` next to `dev`:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage staging
```

Each stage is its own stack, named `<project>-<stage>`, with its own resources, URLs and data. Non-production stages
in one AWS account and region share one network (VPC), but each keeps its own security groups. Production stages get a
network of their own. A stage's first deploy decides which, from its name or `stackConfig.stageType`; see
[Shared network for non-production stages](/configuration/shared-network).
To vary sizes or settings by stage, see [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments).

To keep production in a separate AWS account, deploy it with that account's credentials, for example
`--profile my-prod-account`.

docs.title: After the first deploy
After the first deploy
docs.content:
## Find the stack in AWS

Everything Stacktape deploys is a regular AWS resource in your account. Open **CloudFormation** in the AWS console,
pick the region and open the stack `<project>-<stage>`. The **Resources** tab lists everything in it, with links to
each service. The stack keeps working if you stop using Stacktape.

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
## Delete the stage

When you're done with a stage, delete it:

```bash
stacktape delete --stage dev
```

This removes the stack and everything in it, including databases and the data in them, and the stage's deployment
bucket. Your code and config file stay. Back up any data you want to keep first: a delete can't be undone. See
[`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete).

A database that `stacktape init` added has `deletionProtection: true`, so the delete stops before it removes anything
and names the database. To delete it anyway, set `deletionProtection: false` on the database in your config, run
`stacktape deploy --stage dev`, then run the delete again.

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
## If a deploy fails

First find the error:

- **The build failed.** The error is in the output of the command, the wizard's log or the CI job.
- **AWS refused a resource.** The CLI prints `Stack action ... failed.` and one line per resource that failed, with
  AWS's reason. If you no longer have that output, open **CloudFormation** in the AWS console, pick the region, open
  the stack `<project>-<stage>` and its **Events** tab. The first event with a `FAILED` status has the reason.
- **The app started and then stopped.** Read its logs: `stacktape logs <resource name> --stage dev`.
- **With the Console**, each deploy and its error stay in the stage's deploy history, and
  [`stacktape stack history`](/cli/stack-history) lists them in the terminal.

Common causes are a missing IAM permission, an AWS quota and an invalid value in the config.

By default, a failed deploy keeps what it already created or updated. Fix the error and deploy again to continue from
where it stopped. To remove a failed first deploy instead, run `stacktape delete`. With `--auto-rollback`,
CloudFormation undoes a failed deploy by itself. See [When a deployment fails](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#when-a-deployment-fails).

If you lose your connection during a deploy, CloudFormation keeps going in AWS. Check the stack in the CloudFormation
console before you deploy again.

A stage created by [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) can't be deployed with `stacktape deploy`. Use
another stage name for the deploy.

docs.title: After the first deploy
docs.content:
## Where to go next

- **[Add the Console](/getting-started/add-the-console).** Deploy history, costs, alerts and team access for your
  stages. Free while the AWS spend it manages stays at or under $200 a month.
- **[Deploy from CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/overview).** Deploy on every push from GitHub Actions, GitLab or another CI,
  or let the Console deploy from Git.
- **[Run it locally with dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview).** Run your code on your machine against a
  small stack in AWS, and see changes without a deploy.
- **[Prepare for production](/getting-started/going-to-production).** Domains, alarms, rollouts and budgets before
  real users arrive.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
docs.content:
# Set up AWS credentials

Stacktape deploys into your own AWS account with the AWS credentials on your machine. It finds them the same way the
AWS CLI does, so if the AWS CLI works for you, Stacktape works too. Reading your project and writing the config don't
need credentials. Only the deploy does.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
docs.content:
## Check what you already have

If you have the [AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html) installed,
run:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity
```

It prints the AWS account ID and the identity your credentials belong to. If it's the account you want to deploy to,
you're done. For a named profile, add `--profile my-dev-account`.

If it fails or prints another account, set up credentials with one of the two ways below.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
docs.content:
## Which AWS account to use

Use an account for development, not the one your production runs in. A separate account keeps experiments away from
production data and makes it clear what they cost. If you don't have an AWS account yet,
[create one at AWS](https://portal.aws.amazon.com/billing/signup).

Don't deploy with the root user of the account, the email address you signed up with. Create an identity for daily
work, as described below.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
headingPath: If your company uses IAM Identity Center (SSO)
docs.content:
## If your company uses IAM Identity Center (SSO)

Many companies sign in to AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center, often with a start URL like
`https://my-company.awsapps.com/start`. Ask whoever manages your AWS accounts for the URL and a role in a development
account, then run:

```bash
aws configure sso
```

It asks for a session name, the start URL and its region, opens your browser to sign in, and lets you pick the
account and role. At the end it asks for a profile name, for example `my-dev-account`.

SSO sessions expire. When a command says your credentials are expired, sign in again:

```bash
aws sso login --profile my-dev-account
```

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
headingPath: If you have your own AWS account
docs.content:
## If you have your own AWS account

For a personal account without IAM Identity Center, create an IAM user with an access key:

1. Sign in to the [AWS Management Console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/) and open **IAM**.
2. Go to **Users** and click **Create user**. Give it a name, for example `stacktape-dev`.
3. Under permissions, choose **Attach policies directly** and select **AdministratorAccess**. See
   [what permissions you need](#what-permissions-you-need).
4. Open the new user, go to **Security credentials** and click **Create access key**. Choose **Command Line Interface
   (CLI)** as the use case.
5. Copy the access key ID and the secret access key. AWS shows the secret only once.

Then save the key as a profile on your machine. Either command works and stores it in `~/.aws/credentials`:

```bash
stacktape aws-profile create
```

