```bash
aws configure --profile my-dev-account
```

An access key works until you delete it. Keep it out of your repository, and delete it in IAM when you no longer need
it.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
headingPath: Tell Stacktape which credentials to use
docs.content:
## Tell Stacktape which credentials to use

Stacktape picks credentials in this order:

1. `--profile <name>` on the command.
2. The `AWS_PROFILE` environment variable.
3. AWS keys in environment variables, such as `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`.
4. A profile saved with [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set).
5. The `default` profile in `~/.aws`, and the rest of the standard AWS credential chain.

The init wizard takes the profile from the environment, so start it like this:

```bash
AWS_PROFILE=my-dev-account stacktape init
```

For other commands, pass the flag:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev --profile my-dev-account
```

On Windows PowerShell, set the variable first with `$env:AWS_PROFILE = "my-dev-account"`.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
docs.content:
## What permissions you need

A deploy creates a CloudFormation stack with everything in your config: functions, containers, databases, buckets and
the IAM roles they run with. The identity that deploys needs permission to create all of it, including IAM roles.

In a development account, the **AdministratorAccess** policy is the simple answer. In an account with restricted
permissions, ask whoever manages it for a role that can create the resources in your config and their IAM roles. If a
permission is missing, the deploy stops with the AWS error that names it.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
docs.content:
## What it costs

Credentials cost nothing. AWS bills the account for the resources you deploy. To get an email before a bill grows, set
a budget in **Billing and Cost Management** → **Budgets** in the AWS console.

docs.title: Set up AWS credentials
docs.content:
## Back to your deploy

If the init wizard is waiting, click **Check again** on its [Deploy step](/getting-started/deploy-an-existing-app#4-deploy).
For a starter project, run the deploy command init printed; see [Deploy](/getting-started/start-a-new-project#4-deploy).

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
# Deploy an existing app

`stacktape init` reads your project, works out the AWS setup it needs and writes it to one file. You see every
resource and its monthly price before the file is saved. Nothing is created in AWS until you confirm the deploy. This
guide follows the wizard screen by screen.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## Before you start

- [Install the CLI](/getting-started#run-it-in-your-apps-directory). The installer can start `init` for you.
- Open a terminal in the root of your app, the directory with its `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod` or
  `Dockerfile`. For an app inside a monorepo, use the app's own directory.
- Commit your work first, so you can see what init changes. It adds one config file and, for a TypeScript config,
  updates `package.json`.
- AWS credentials are needed only for the last step. You can set them up when the wizard asks. See
  [Set up AWS credentials](/getting-started/aws-credentials).

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## Start the wizard

```bash
stacktape init
```

The CLI starts the wizard on your machine and opens it in your browser. The link works once, for this session. Leave
the command running while you use the wizard and press Ctrl+C when you're done.

To read an app from another directory, pass `--project-directory ./apps/api`. To get the address without opening a
browser, for example to open it in a different browser, pass `--no-browser`.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
headingPath: 1. Start: choose who reads your code
docs.content:
## 1. Start: choose who reads your code

The first screen is **Put this project on AWS**. It shows the directory it will read and does nothing until you click
**Analyze my project**.

Under **Options** you choose what reads the code:

- **Claude Code or Codex**, when installed. The agent runs on this machine with read-only tools, under the account you
  already have with it. It sends the files it chooses to read to its own model provider, as it always does. Nothing
  goes to Stacktape. It usually takes under a minute. With Claude Code you can also pick the model.
- **Files only, no agent.** The built-in scanner reads manifests, Compose files, Dockerfiles, Procfiles, Render, Fly.io
  and Heroku manifests, and Serverless Framework, SAM, SST, CDK and Terraform declarations. Nothing is sent to an AI
  provider. It takes a second and falls back to defaults more often.


> Screenshot: The Start screen with Options open: Claude Code or Files only, no agent, and for Claude Code the model: Your default, Opus, Sonnet or Haiku Caption: Options on the Start screen: the agent that reads your code and, for Claude Code, the model.


An installed agent is the default. To skip agent detection, start with `stacktape init --coding-agent none`.

If the app already runs on Heroku, Render, Fly.io, SST or the Serverless Framework, init reads those files too and
deploys a separate copy. [Move to Stacktape](/getting-started/evaluate/move-to-stacktape) covers the data, secrets and
DNS that you move yourself.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## 2. Analyze

The built-in scan always runs first. If it answers everything, the wizard says your agent was not needed and no tokens
were spent. Otherwise the agent reads your project and you watch each file it opens. From `.env` files, only the
variable names are kept.


> Screenshot: The Analyze screen: the agent in use, the number of files read so far and a list of each file it read Caption: The Analyze screen lists each file the agent reads.


If the analysis finds no server, worker or website, the wizard says so and has nothing to save. Run `stacktape init`
in the app's own directory, or click **Analyze again with Claude Code** (or Codex) if you started with files only.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## 3. Review: your app on AWS

**Here's your app on AWS** shows what will be created, in three tabs:

- **Diagram**: the resources and how they connect.
- **What & why**: each resource, with the line of your code that led to it under **Where we saw this**.
- **stacktape.yml** (or **stacktape.ts**; **File** on a narrow screen): the configuration that will be saved.

Below the tabs:

- **Decided for you** lists what your code didn't say and the answer the wizard picked for it. Change any of it and
  the file and the price follow.
- **Important choices** appears when they apply: how much traffic to size for, what happens when one machine fails,
  how much backup history to keep and who can reach the SQL database. Each option shows what it adds to the price.
- **Before you deploy** lists what only you can provide: secrets your app reads, settings your code reads with no
  default, and anything else the deploy still needs.


> Screenshot: The Review step for a Next.js app with Postgres: the monthly estimate at AWS list prices, the What & why tab with each resource, its price and a Where we saw this link, and Decided for you with one alarm the wizard added Caption: Review shows the monthly estimate, each resource with its price and the reason for it, and what the wizard decided for you.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### What it will cost

The sentence above the tabs gives the monthly total, and each resource shows its own price. Prices come from AWS list
prices for the region you pick. Usage charges, such as requests and data transfer, come on top. A resource without a
known price says **Price unavailable**.

To calculate the price, the wizard sends the generated configuration and the region to Stacktape's price estimator.
The configuration contains no source code and no secret values.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### Save the file

1. In the file tab, choose **YAML** or **TypeScript**. YAML is the default.
2. Pick the region. It's saved in the file as `region`, and every command in this project deploys there. The wizard
   preselects the region your AWS setup uses, or `eu-west-1`.
3. Click **Save stacktape.yml & continue**, or **Save stacktape.ts & continue**.

The file declares the project name and region, so later commands only need a stage. Saving needs no AWS credentials
and no Stacktape account.

If your project already has a `stacktape.yml`, `stacktape.yaml` or `stacktape.ts`, init leaves it alone and writes
`stacktape.generated.yml` (or `.ts`) beside it. Deploy that file with `--config stacktape.generated.yml`, or merge it
into yours. An old `stacktape.js` is not detected: move or delete it. With two config files in one directory, every
command stops with an error until you pass `--config`.

For a TypeScript config in a project with a `package.json`, init adds the `stacktape` package as a dev dependency
pinned to your CLI version and prints the install command for your package manager. Run it, so your editor has the
types.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## 4. Deploy

The deploy is optional. **Ready to deploy** shows where the stack will go:

- **AWS account on this machine**, the **AWS identity** and the **AWS profile** (or environment variables) it comes
  from.
- **Region**, from the file.
- **Stage**, `dev` by default. A stage is one environment of the app, such as `dev` or `production`. Each stage is a
  separate stack.

If the account is not the one you want, stop the command and start again with the right profile:

```bash
AWS_PROFILE=my-dev-account stacktape init
```

If the wizard says **This machine has no AWS credentials yet**, or **AWS did not accept the credentials on this
machine**, set them up as in [Set up AWS credentials](/getting-started/aws-credentials) and click **Check again**.
Nothing on the page is lost.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### Before you deploy

- **Secrets.** For each secret, the wizard gives you a command such as `stacktape secret set stripe_api_key --region
  eu-west-1`. Run it in your terminal. It asks for the value, so the value never lands in the file or your shell
  history.
- **Settings nothing sets yet.** If your app needs one of them to start, add it under `environment` in the saved file.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
headingPath: Optional: try it on this machine first
docs.content:
### Optional: try it on this machine first

Under **Optional**, **Try it on this machine first** has a **Build and start it here** button. It builds your services
in Docker and starts them without network access and with placeholder settings, to catch an app that won't start
before it reaches AWS. It runs your project's code, including install scripts. If it finds a startup failure, the
deploy waits until you fix it or set the result aside. The check needs Docker. Skipping it doesn't skip Docker for the
deploy: a config that builds a container image or a Python, Go or Java function builds it with Docker on this
machine.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### Check the target, then deploy

1. Click **Check exact AWS target**. This is read-only. It shows the stack name, AWS account and region.
2. Read what it found:
   - **This will create a new stack**: nothing with this name exists in that account and region.
   - **This will update a stack that already exists**: the deploy makes that stack match your file, and removes
     anything in it the file doesn't define.
   - A stack that another tool or another Stacktape project owns, or one that AWS is still changing, is blocked. The
     wizard says why and, where a command fixes it, gives you the command.
3. Click **Create new stack** or **Update existing stack**.


> Screenshot: What the deploy does after the target check: This will create a new stack, with the stack name, AWS account and region, and the Create new stack button Caption: The target check names the stack, the AWS account and the region before you confirm.


The deploy usually takes a few minutes. A first deploy with a new database takes 10 to 15 minutes. The wizard shows
each phase, warnings and the full log.

If the deploy fails for a reason that could come from how your code was read, such as a wrong start command, the agent
reads the project again with the error in hand, the file is rebuilt and the deploy runs again. This happens at most
twice. Problems with the AWS account itself, such as expired credentials or a missing permission, are shown as they
are. With files only, there is no repair.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### It's live

**It's live** lists the public HTTPS address of each resource that has one. Open it to check your app, then
[check the database](#check-the-database) if it has one. Below it:

- **Add dev to the Stacktape Console**: optional, see [below](#add-the-console).
- **Ship a change**: the command that deploys again after you edit your code.
- **Deploy on every push**: if your project pushes to GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, **Add a GitHub Actions pipeline**
  (or GitLab CI/CD, Bitbucket Pipelines) writes a CI file and lists the secrets to add to your repository.
- **Done experimenting? Remove this deployment**: the command that deletes everything the deploy created, including
  any database and its data. Your code and config file stay. A database the wizard added is protected from deletion,
  so turn that off first; see [Delete the stage](/getting-started/after-the-first-deploy#delete-the-stage).

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### Check the database

A health route can answer while every database query fails, so check the data path too:

1. **The connection.** In the saved file, find the variable your app reads its database address from. Init sets it
   from the new database, for example:

   ```yaml
   environment:
     - name: DATABASE_URL
       value: $ResourceParam('mainDatabase', 'connectionString')
   ```

   If your app reads another name, change `name` and deploy again. [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources)
   lists the other values, such as `host` and `port`.
2. **The schema.** A new database is empty. If init found your migration tool, the file runs it on every deploy: as
   `releaseCommand` on a container service, or as a script under `hooks.afterDeploy`. If it found the tool but no
   command, **Before you deploy** asks you to set one. See [Release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands).
3. **A real query.** Open a page or call an endpoint that reads or writes data. If it fails, the error is in the
   logs: `stacktape logs <resource name> --stage dev`.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## Deploy from your terminal instead

Under **Optional**, **Run it from your terminal instead** has the same deploy as a command, for example:

```bash
stacktape deploy --config stacktape.yml --project my-app --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

It creates the stack or updates it, and shows the account and target before it changes anything. In the project
directory, `stacktape deploy --stage dev` does the same, because the file names the project and region.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## What the deploy costs

AWS charges your AWS account for the resources from the moment they exist. The estimate on the Review step is what
they cost per month before usage. Stacktape charges nothing for the CLI or for a deploy without an account.

Some resources cost money even with no traffic, such as a database or an always-on container. If you're only trying
Stacktape, remove the stage when you're done. See [Delete the stage](/getting-started/after-the-first-deploy#delete-the-stage).

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## Add the Console

After a successful deploy, the wizard offers **Add dev to the Stacktape Console**: deploy history, costs, alerts and
team access for the stage, free up to $200 a month of AWS spend. **Connect to the Console** signs you in (or creates an
account) in a new tab, then connects the AWS account. Your app is not redeployed. **Not now** skips it, and
`stacktape connect` does the same later. See [Add the Console](/getting-started/add-the-console).


> Screenshot: The end of a deploy: the live stage with its public address and an Open button, then Add dev to the Stacktape Console with Connect to the Console and Not now Caption: After the deploy: the live address, then the offer to add the stage to the Console.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
## Without a browser

On Linux without a display, for example over SSH, and in CI, init runs in the terminal. You can ask for it anywhere
with `--headless`:

```bash
stacktape init --headless
```

It reads the project, prints the resources and what it decided for you, prints the monthly estimate and writes the
file. It doesn't ask questions and doesn't deploy. Review the file, then run `stacktape deploy --stage dev`. Add
`--config-format typescript` for a TypeScript file, and `--coding-agent none` to skip the agent.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content: ## If something goes wrong

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
headingPath: The wizard found nothing to deploy
docs.content:
### The wizard found nothing to deploy

Your app is probably in a subdirectory. Run `stacktape init` there, or pass `--project-directory`. If you used files
only, try again with an agent: it reads source code, not only manifests.

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### AWS rejects the credentials

AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) sessions expire. Run `aws sso login --profile <name>` and click **Check again**. The
wizard explains other errors. The identity also needs permission to create the resources in your file. See
[Set up AWS credentials](/getting-started/aws-credentials#what-permissions-you-need).

docs.title: Deploy an existing app
docs.content:
### The target is blocked

A stack with the same name already exists and belongs to another tool or another Stacktape project, or AWS is still
working on it. Pick another stage name, or wait and click **Check again**. A failed first deploy can leave a stack that
AWS only allows deleting; the wizard gives you the delete command.

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
# Evaluate Stacktape

This page is for the person who decides whether Stacktape fits the team for the next few years. Each section gives the
short answer and links to the page with the details.

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
headingPath: What it is and what it isn't
docs.content:
## What it is and what it isn't

Stacktape turns one configuration file into a CloudFormation stack in your own AWS account. It has two parts:

- **The CLI** is open source under the MIT license. It writes the config with you (`stacktape init`), packages your
  code, deploys and deletes stacks, runs dev mode and reads logs, metrics and secrets. It works with your AWS
  credentials and needs no Stacktape account.
- **The Console** is an optional hosted service for teams: deploy history, costs, error tracking, incidents, uptime
  checks, Git deployments, team access and an audit log.

Stacktape is not a hosting provider. Your app runs on AWS services in your account: Lambda, ECS on Fargate, RDS,
DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront and others; see the [resource catalog](/resources). It supports only AWS. It has no
Kubernetes and no runtime of its own between your code and AWS. When the catalog doesn't cover something, you can add
[raw CloudFormation, CDK constructs or overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches) to the same stack.

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## What runs where

| Part | Where it runs | Who pays |
|---|---|---|
| Your app: functions, containers, databases, buckets, CDN | Your AWS account, one CloudFormation stack per stage | You pay AWS |
| MongoDB Atlas and Upstash resources, if you use them | The provider's account | You pay the provider |
| The CLI, builds and deploys | Your machine or your CI | Free |
| Git deployment build runners | An EC2 instance in your AWS account | You pay AWS |
| Uptime check probes and the error detector | Small Lambda functions in your AWS account | You pay AWS |
| The Console and its database | Stacktape's AWS account, in `eu-west-1` (Ireland) | Stacktape |
| The Console connection | An IAM role in your account that Stacktape assumes | Free |

Your stacks keep running if you stop using the CLI or the Console. See [Stop using Stacktape](/getting-started/evaluate/stop-using-stacktape).

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## Who does what in production

Take an API container with a Postgres database, as in the [example on the home page](/).

- **AWS** runs the servers under Fargate and RDS, applies database maintenance in the maintenance window and replaces
  failed hardware.
- **Stacktape** turns your config into the stack: network, security groups, IAM roles, the load balancer or API
  gateway, logs and the alarms you configure. It builds your code and deploys it. With the Console, it also groups
  errors into incidents and runs uptime checks.
- **Your team** decides the sizes and scaling limits, sets backup retention and tests a restore, approves production
  deploys in its own pipeline and answers alerts. Your team also owns the AWS account: who can sign in to it and what
  it may spend.

[Going to production](/getting-started/going-to-production) lists what to set up before real users arrive.

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## What leaves your AWS account

Without the Console, Stacktape receives two things: anonymous CLI usage telemetry, which one environment variable
turns off, and the generated config that `stacktape init` sends to the price estimator. A coding agent you pick in init
sends the files it reads to its own provider.

With the Console, some features send operational data to Stacktape: errors with their masked log line, alarm state
changes, uptime results, monthly cost reports and security findings. Application logs, build artifacts and secrets
stay in your account. The Console stores what it receives in `eu-west-1`. Error samples are kept with no time limit.
[What leaves your AWS account](/observability/overview#what-leaves-your-aws-account) lists every feature, field and
retention period.

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## Access and security

- **AWS access.** Without the Console, Stacktape has no access to your account. Connecting the Console creates an IAM
  role that only Stacktape's AWS account can assume, with an external ID and sessions of at most 12 hours. The role has
  `AdministratorAccess`, so the Console can deploy anything a stack contains. Each workload runs with its own role
  that allows only what its config declares. See [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions).
- **People.** Members are Owners, Admins, Developers or Viewers. Developers and Viewers see only the projects and AWS
  accounts you give them. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).
- **Sign-in.** Owners and Admins can require two-factor sign-in on every plan. Single sign-on (SAML or OIDC) and SCIM come with
  the Flexible plan. See [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on).
- **Audit.** The audit log keeps Stacktape events for 400 days and shows AWS CloudTrail events from the last 90 days.
  Every AWS call the Console makes for a person carries their identity. See [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log).

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## Accounts, stages and isolation

A stage, such as `dev` or `production`, is a separate CloudFormation stack with its own functions, containers,
databases and URLs. Three things matter when you plan accounts:

- **Non-production stages share a network.** In one AWS account and region, they run in one shared VPC. Each stage has
  its own security groups, so one stage can't reach another stage's databases by private IP. Production stages get a
  VPC of their own. The first deploy decides this, and a stage that becomes production later stays where it is. See
  [Shared network for non-production stages](/configuration/shared-network).
- **AWS access covers the whole account.** A developer who gets AWS access to one project's account can reach every
  other project's stacks in that account. The Console limits what people see in the Console, not what their AWS
  credentials can do.
- **Separate accounts are the boundary.** Keep production in its own AWS account. An agency keeps one account per
  client and gives each person only their clients' accounts. Service control policies in AWS Organizations then limit
  everything in an account, Stacktape's role included.

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## CI/CD

- **Your own pipeline.** GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Bitbucket, CircleCI or any other CI runs `stacktape deploy` with
  AWS credentials, for example an OIDC role. No Stacktape account is needed. Approvals, environments and release
  gates stay in your CI. `stacktape init` can write the pipeline file. See [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd).
- **Git deployments in the Console.** A push deploys a stage, and each pull request can get a preview stage that is
  deleted when it closes. Builds run on a runner in your AWS account, one per project, account and region. See
  [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).
- **Before a deploy.** `stacktape diff` shows what would change. A failed deploy keeps what it already created unless
  you turn on automatic rollback; see [Rollbacks](/deployment-and-lifecycle/rollbacks).

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## Scaling, networking and databases

- **Compute.** Containers run on ECS Fargate with minimum and maximum instance counts and CPU or memory targets.
  Functions run on Lambda. Batch jobs and workers cover background work. See [Web service](/resources/compute/web-service#scaling).
- **Databases.** Relational databases run on RDS or Aurora, with Multi-AZ, read replicas, backups kept up to 35 days
  and deletion protection. DynamoDB, Redis, OpenSearch and MongoDB Atlas are also available. See
  [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database).
- **Private networking.** A database accepts connections from the internet, with credentials, unless you choose
  otherwise. `accessibilityMode` limits who can connect, and `forceDisablePublicIp` removes the public IP address. On
  Aurora, decide the public IP when you create the database. See
  [Accessibility](/resources/databases/relational-database#accessibility).
- **Regions.** Each stage deploys to one region. Several regions are several stages, and Stacktape doesn't replicate
  data between them. See [Multi-region deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/multi-region-deployments).

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## What it costs

- **The CLI** is free.
- **The Console** is free while the AWS spend Stacktape manages for your organization stays at or under $200 a month.
  Above that, the Flexible plan costs one rate on the month's managed spend, from 25% down to 19%. Enterprise runs a
  single-tenant Console in your own AWS account, at an agreed price. See
  [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).
- **AWS** bills your account for the resources, as it would without Stacktape. `stacktape init` estimates the monthly
  price from AWS list prices before the first deploy, and requests and data transfer come on top. Databases,
  containers, NAT and load balancers cost money every hour they exist, including in preview stages. See
  [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview).

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## Maturity and support

- **Source.** The CLI's code and history are public on [GitHub](https://github.com/stacktape/stacktape), under the MIT
  license. Version 4 is the current major version; [Upgrading from v3](/getting-started/upgrading-from-v3) describes
  the changes.
- **Status.** [status.stacktape.com](https://status.stacktape.com) shows current incidents and maintenance, and their
  history.
- **Support.** Every plan can write to [support@stacktape.com](mailto:support@stacktape.com). The Flexible plan adds a
  shared Slack channel with the founders. Enterprise adds up to 24x7 premium support, with response times agreed in
  advance. No plan comes with a published SLA.
- **AWS problems.** An outage of an AWS service in your account goes through your own AWS Support plan.

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## Lock-in and the way out

Everything Stacktape deploys is a regular CloudFormation stack in your account, and `stacktape synth` writes its
template to a file. You can leave the Console and keep the CLI with one command, or take over the stacks and stop
using Stacktape altogether. [Stop using Stacktape](/getting-started/evaluate/stop-using-stacktape) walks through both,
including the helper resources and secrets you would keep or replace.

To bring an app that runs on Heroku, Render, Fly.io, SST or the Serverless Framework, see
[Move to Stacktape](/getting-started/evaluate/move-to-stacktape).

docs.title: Evaluate Stacktape
docs.content:
## Run a pilot

1. Create an AWS account for the pilot, or use a development account.
2. Run `stacktape init` in one real service and deploy it. Compare the estimate with your current bill for it.
3. Connect the Console (free) to see deploy history, costs and error tracking for that stage.
4. Deploy a change from your CI, roll it back and restore the database from a backup.
5. Run `stacktape synth` and read the template you would own if you left.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
# Move to Stacktape

Stacktape deploys your app as a new stack in your own AWS account. It never takes over what another platform or tool
runs. A move is a copy next to the old app, then the secrets, the data and the DNS, then retiring the old setup. You
can switch back until the last step.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
## What init reads

`stacktape init` reads the other platform's files together with your code. It writes the services, workers and
databases they describe into the Stacktape config, and you review it before anything is deployed.

| From | What init takes | What you set yourself |
|---|---|---|
| Heroku: `Procfile`, `app.json` | Web and worker processes, the port, the `release` command as the migration, add-ons such as Heroku Postgres and Redis, variable names | Dyno sizes and counts. `heroku.yml` isn't read |
| Render: `render.yaml` | Web, worker and private services, cron jobs on their schedule, databases, Key Value, build and start commands, Dockerfiles, variables that point at databases and services | Plans, instance counts, region, health check path, pre-deploy command |
| Fly.io: `fly.toml` | The app, its Dockerfile, each process as a service, the internal port, variable names | Region, VM sizes, health checks, volumes, release command |
| SST (v3): `sst.config.ts` | Databases, Redis, buckets, queues, topics, DynamoDB tables with sizes and versions, Next.js and other sites, functions, cron jobs, API routes, queue subscribers and `link` | `environment` values. SST v2 apps are recognized but not imported |
| Serverless Framework: `serverless.yml` | Functions with runtime, memory, timeout and environment, `http`, `httpApi`, `schedule`, `sqs`, `sns` and `s3` events, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, S3, ElastiCache and RDS from `resources` | Plugins, layers, Step Functions, `custom` and `params`. Keys init doesn't know are listed as import notes |

It also reads Docker Compose files, AWS SAM templates, CDK apps in TypeScript or JavaScript, and the databases,
caches, queues and buckets in Terraform files. For all of them:

- **The region** comes from your AWS setup, not from the old platform. Without one it's `eu-west-1`.
- **Sizes** carry over only for AWS database and cache instance classes, such as `db.t4g.small`. Everything else
  gets a default that you see and can change on the Review step.
- **Secrets travel as names.** Init copies the values of a few harmless settings, such as `NODE_ENV`, `LOG_LEVEL` or a
  port. Every other variable becomes a secret that you set before the deploy. Values in `.env` files are read only to
  recognize your database host, then dropped.
- **Databases are new.** A database declared in the old platform's files becomes a new, empty AWS database. When a
  `.env` file points at a hosted database, such as Heroku, Render, Supabase, Neon or Upstash, the wizard offers to keep
  using it instead. Then nothing is created, and your app reads the address from a secret.
- **The old platform is untouched.** Init doesn't read, change or delete its resources.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content: ## Move a running app

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
### 1. Deploy a copy

Run `stacktape init` in the repository and deploy a stage such as `staging`. See
[Deploy an existing app](/getting-started/deploy-an-existing-app). The old app keeps serving your users.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
### 2. Copy the secrets

**Before you deploy** lists each secret the app needs. Copy each value from the old platform and store it in your AWS
account:

```bash
stacktape secret set stripe_api_key --region eu-west-1
```

Heroku shows values with `heroku config`. Fly.io doesn't show secret values again, so take them from where your team
keeps them.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
### 3. Decide where the data lives

You have two options:

- **Keep the old database for now.** Put its connection string in a secret and use that secret for your app's
  variable. The old provider must accept connections from AWS, and every query crosses the internet, so expect more
  latency. This lets you move the app first and the data later.
- **Move the data.** Stop writes on the old app, for example with a maintenance mode. Dump the database with your
  usual tool, such as `pg_dump`, and restore it into the new one. A database that isn't open to the internet is
  reachable through a [bastion tunnel](/cli/bastion-tunnel). For a large database, AWS Database Migration Service can
  copy it continuously, which shortens the pause.

Files move with `aws s3 sync` or your provider's export. Caches usually start empty.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
### 4. Run the migrations

If init found your migration tool, the config runs it on each deploy, as a `releaseCommand` or a script after the
deploy. A `release` line in a Procfile becomes that command. Release commands in `fly.toml` and `render.yaml` are not
carried over: set them as described in [Release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands).

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
### 5. Test the copy

Open the AWS address from the end of the deploy. Check a page or an endpoint that reads and writes data, not only a
health route. Then add a [CI pipeline](/ci-cd-and-gitops/overview) that deploys the new stage.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
### 6. Switch DNS

Add your domain to the new resources with `customDomains` and deploy. Lower the TTL of the old records a day before,
then point the hostname at the new stack. If you move the domain's DNS to Route 53, copy its existing records first.
See [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains).

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
headingPath: 7. Keep a way back, then retire the old app
docs.content:
### 7. Keep a way back, then retire the old app

Until you retire the old app, switching back is a DNS change. If you moved the data, writes made after the switch
exist only in the new database, so plan how you would copy them back. When traffic has moved and the old DNS records
have expired, take a last backup of the old database and delete the old app.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
## From SST or Serverless Framework

Both already run in your AWS account. Stacktape creates its own stack next to theirs and doesn't adopt their
resources, so the new stack starts with new tables, buckets and databases.

- **Move the data** as above: DynamoDB export and import, `aws s3 sync`, or a database dump.
- **Or keep using an old resource.** Pass its name to the app in `environment` and allow access with
  [`iamRoleStatements`](/configuration/connecting-resources#custom-permissions-with-iamrolestatements).
- **Before you remove the old stack**, check which of its resources hold data and whether the old tool deletes them.

docs.title: Move to Stacktape
docs.content:
## What usually takes the time

- Reviewing what init decided for you, especially sizes, scaling and the settings it left at defaults.
- Collecting the secret values.
- Moving the data, and the write pause it needs.
- Waiting for DNS.
- Health checks, instance counts, regions and volumes, which init doesn't carry over.

docs.title: Stop using Stacktape
docs.content:
# Stop using Stacktape

You can step back in two ways: leave the Console and keep deploying with the open-source CLI, or stop using Stacktape
and manage the CloudFormation stacks yourself. Your app keeps running in both cases. Some steps only work while
Stacktape can still deploy, so read the whole page before you start.

We wrote this page from the CLI's source code and haven't run the full takeover on a live stack yet. Before you rely on
it for production, try it on a disposable stage: take it over, ship one code change with your own tooling, then delete
it.

docs.title: Stop using Stacktape
headingPath: Leave the Console, keep the CLI
docs.content:
## Leave the Console, keep the CLI

1. **Remove what only the Console provides.** Take uptime checks, alarm channels of type `console-channel` and
   `slack-app`, and `deploymentConfig.errorTracking` out of the config. Give each resource on a default `*.stacktape-app.com` domain a
   [custom domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains), then deploy each stage while you're still signed in. The
   default domain's DNS record is in Stacktape's zone, so only a signed-in deploy can remove it.
2. **Sign out.** Run [`stacktape logout`](/cli/logout). In CI, remove `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` from the pipeline.
3. **Deploy each stage once more.** A stage deployed while signed in keeps sending errors, alarm state changes and
   uptime results to Stacktape. A deploy without an account removes that. Until you remove the features from step 1,
   the CLI refuses this deploy and says which feature is left.
4. **Disconnect the AWS account.** In the Console, choose **Disconnect account** on **Configuration → AWS accounts**,
   then delete the connection stack, `stacktape-<connection ID>` in `eu-west-1`. See
   [Revoke access](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions#revoke-access).
5. **Remove the uptime probes.** They live outside your stacks, in each region that probed: the
   `stacktape-uptime-prober` function with its role and schedule, a bucket named `stp-uptime-prober-*` and SSM
   parameters under `/stacktape/uptime-checks/`. Nothing deletes them for you.

What the Console already stored stays with Stacktape. Error issues, for example, have no time limit; see
[where errors are stored](/observability/error-tracking#where-errors-are-stored-and-for-how-long).

docs.title: Stop using Stacktape
docs.content: ## Stop using Stacktape

docs.title: Stop using Stacktape
docs.content:
### Before you leave

Do these while the CLI can still deploy:

1. **Leave the Console first**, if you use it. See the steps above.
2. **Deploy each stage with `--full`:**

   ```bash
   stacktape deploy --stage production --full
   ```

   When only code changes, a normal deploy updates functions and containers directly, without CloudFormation. The
   stack's template can then still name older code. `--full` sends everything through CloudFormation, so the template
   describes the code that runs.
3. **Save the deployed template.** In the AWS console, open **CloudFormation**, the stack `<project>-<stage>` and its
   **Template** tab, or run:

   ```bash
   aws cloudformation get-template --stack-name my-app-production --query TemplateBody --output text > template.yaml
   ```

   Don't use `stacktape synth` for this. It doesn't build your code, so it leaves the code locations empty, and a
   deploy adds a few resources that synth doesn't write.

docs.title: Stop using Stacktape
docs.content:
### What you take over

**The stack.** Update it with your saved template, with `aws cloudformation deploy` or change sets. It has no
parameters. Its stack policy refuses to replace or delete databases with deletion protection, and it has termination
protection if your config set `deploymentConfig.terminationProtection`. The `StpDeploymentVersion` and
`StpStackInfoMap` outputs and the `stp:*` tags are only for Stacktape.

**Shipping code.** Stacktape built your code and uploaded it. That becomes your build's job:

- Function code is a zip in the deployment bucket, `stp-deployment-bucket-<hash>`. Upload the new zip under a new key
  and change the function's `Code.S3Key` in the template.
- Container images are in the ECR repository `<hash>-stp-multi-container-workload-repo`. Push a new tag and change the
  image in the task definition.
- Functions at the CDN edge get their code through a custom resource. Change its `artifactS3Key` property.

The bucket and the repository are not part of the stack, so they stay when the stack goes. Untagged images expire after
a day. Nothing prunes old zips and tagged images any more.

**The service function.** Each stack has a function named `<stack>-stpService-CR`. CloudFormation calls it to create,
update and delete the stack's custom resources: the `Custom::Stp*` types and the `AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource`
entries, such as SQS queues, EventBridge rules and CDN edge functions. It also tags resources every two hours and
delivers alarm notifications. It runs in your account and its source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Keep it. To
remove it, you would replace each custom resource with its native CloudFormation type, and CloudFormation would
create those resources again.

**Registered resource types.** Blue/green container deployments, MongoDB Atlas and Upstash use CloudFormation types
that Stacktape registered in your account and region: `Stacktape::ECSBlueGreenV1::Service`, `MongoDB::StpAtlasV1::*`
and `Upstash::DatabasesV1::Database`, with execution roles named `stp-*`. They stay registered and keep working. Keep
them while a stack uses them.

**Secrets.** Secrets you created with `stacktape secret set` are ordinary Secrets Manager secrets with the name you
gave them, outside the stack. The template points at one version of each secret. After you change a value, put the
new version ID in the template and update the stack. The stack's `<Name>CurrentSecretVersionId` output shows the
version it uses. Some generated values are SSM SecureString parameters under `/stp/<region>/<stack>/`.

**Domains and certificates.** `stacktape domain add` created the Route 53 hosted zone and the ACM certificates, in
your region and in `us-east-1`, outside the stack. They stay, and ACM keeps renewing the certificates while their
validation records exist. The DNS records of your resources are in the stack.

**The shared network.** Non-production stages use the `stacktape-network` stack and, with NAT, `stacktape-network-nat`.
A function inside the network stack deletes both after 24 hours without stages. It doesn't call Stacktape.

**Your workflow.** Replace the CLI commands with AWS tools:

| Stacktape | AWS |
|---|---|
| `stacktape deploy` in CI | Your build, an upload to S3 or ECR, then `aws cloudformation deploy` |
| `stacktape logs` | `aws logs tail` or CloudWatch Logs Insights |
| `stacktape secret set` | `aws secretsmanager put-secret-value`, then update the template |
| `stacktape bastion tunnel`, `stacktape container exec` | `aws ssm start-session`, `aws ecs execute-command` |
| `stacktape dev` | Your own local setup |

Alarms are CloudWatch alarms in the stack and keep working.

docs.title: Stop using Stacktape
Going to production
docs.content:
# Going to production

Your app is deployed. Before real users arrive, add alarms, database backups, a budget, your own domain, gradual rollouts and, for a team, guardrails. Each section says what to configure and links to the full guide.

Most of it is configuration that works with the CLI alone. Budgets and guardrails are [Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) features; each section says so, and what to use without the Console.

Deploy production as its own stage, for example `--stage production`, ideally in a separate AWS account from development.

docs.title: Going to production
Going to production
docs.content:
## Database backups

AWS takes a daily backup of a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database). `automatedBackupRetentionDays` sets how many days are kept: `1` by default, up to `35`. For production, keep at least `7`, so you can still recover from a problem you find days later. Set `deletionProtection: true` so a deploy or a delete can't remove the database. A database added by `stacktape init` has deletion protection on, and **Keep recovery copies** on the Review step sets 7 days of backups. See [Backups and maintenance](/resources/databases/relational-database#backups-and-maintenance).

docs.title: Going to production
docs.content:
## Budgets

Budgets catch surprise AWS bills. In the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console), a budget sets a monthly spending limit for one connected AWS account and alerts your [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) when the account's spend crosses percentages of it (80% and 100% by default). Forecast alerts, on by default, also warn you when AWS forecasts that the month's spend will cross a percentage.

A budget watches the whole AWS account. It cannot filter by project or stage. If you want separate limits for production and development, run them in separate AWS accounts. See [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) for setup details.

Without the Console, create a budget in the AWS console under **Billing and Cost Management** → **Budgets**. It can email you when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold.


> **Tip:** Create a budget for every AWS account that runs production stages. Even a generous limit catches mistakes such as a runaway Lambda loop or an oversized database instance before they become expensive. Set the limit to your expected monthly bill and keep the default 80% and 100% alerts.

docs.title: Going to production
Going to production
docs.content:
## Gradual deployments

Instead of switching all traffic to a new version instantly, gradual deployments shift traffic incrementally — catching regressions before they affect all users. Stacktape supports canary and linear strategies for [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and [web services](/resources/compute/web-service) (and other container workloads — see [Gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments) for the full list).

**Lambda functions** support nine deployment strategies. Canary strategies (`Canary10Percent5Minutes`, `Canary10Percent10Minutes`, `Canary10Percent15Minutes`, `Canary10Percent30Minutes`) send 10% of traffic to the new version first, then shift the rest after the specified wait period. Linear strategies (`Linear10PercentEvery1Minute`, `Linear10PercentEvery2Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes`) shift 10% of traffic at regular intervals until complete. `AllAtOnce` provides an instant switch with no gradual rollout.

Lambda deployments also support optional `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` and `afterTrafficShiftFunction` hooks — references to Lambda functions in your config that run smoke tests before traffic begins shifting and validation after all traffic has moved. If the `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` hook signals failure, the deployment rolls back.

**Web services** and other container workloads expose gradual deployments through the `deployment` property, which requires `application-load-balancer` load balancing. Container workloads support five strategies: `Canary10Percent5Minutes`, `Canary10Percent15Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery1Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes`, and `AllAtOnce`. Container deployments also support `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` and `afterTrafficShiftFunction` hooks. See [Gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments) for rollback behavior and hook configuration.

docs.title: Going to production
Going to production
Going to production
docs.content:
## Multi-region deployments

Deploy the same stack to multiple AWS regions for lower latency or regional compliance. Each region gets its own independent stage — deploy with `--region eu-west-1` and `--region us-east-1` as separate commands or CI pipelines. Stacktape does not automatically replicate data between regions; you handle cross-region data strategy (DynamoDB global tables, Aurora Global Database, or application-level replication).

Multi-region adds operational complexity and cost — you manage separate deployments, cross-region data consistency, and region-specific monitoring. Use it when you have users on multiple continents and latency matters, or when regulations require data residency in specific regions. For most apps, a single region with a [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) provides good global performance at lower cost. See [Multi-region deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/multi-region-deployments) for patterns and tradeoffs.

docs.title: Going to production
docs.content:
## Guardrails

Guardrails are a [Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) feature. They define organization-wide policy rules that restrict what deployments can do — which stages and regions are allowed, what resource types and sizes are permitted, and which security settings are required. They prevent teams from deploying configurations that violate your standards.

Available guardrail types cover four categories:

| Category | Guardrail types |
|----------|----------------|
| **Deployment** | Stage restriction, region restriction, command restriction, resource type restriction, resource count limit |
| **Security** | Require VPC-only databases, require WAF on application load balancers, require custom domains on web services and hosting buckets |
| **Data protection** | Require deletion protection on relational databases, require dead-letter queues on SQS queues |
| **Resource limits** | Function memory limit, function timeout limit, container CPU/memory limit, database engine restriction, database instance size restriction |

Guardrails are most valuable once your team has more than one person deploying, or when you run both production and development stages and want to enforce stricter rules on production. For solo developers or early-stage projects, you can skip guardrails and revisit when your team or compliance requirements grow. See [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) for configuration details and per-type documentation.

docs.title: Going to production
docs.content:
## Verify before go-live

Before sending real traffic, run through these concrete checks:

1. **Confirm alarms notify correctly.** Trigger a test error in your function or service and verify the notification reaches your on-call channel. An alarm without `notificationChannels` fires silently in CloudWatch — check that every production alarm has at least one target configured. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) to confirm CloudWatch is receiving log data.

2. **Check database backups.** Confirm `deletionProtection: true` and at least 7 days of `automatedBackupRetentionDays` on every production database. In the AWS console, **RDS** → your database → **Maintenance & backups** shows the latest backup.

3. **Set a budget.** Create a budget for your production AWS account with a monthly limit matching your expected spend: under **Budgets** in the Stacktape Console, or in AWS Budgets without it. Keep alerts at 80% and 100% of the limit, and turn on forecast alerts so you hear about a trend before it reaches the limit.

4. **Verify your custom domain resolves.** Open your custom domain in a browser and confirm the TLS certificate is valid (lock icon, no warnings). With DNS in Route 53, Stacktape creates the records. With external DNS, check that the CNAME record points to the AWS hostname.

5. **Test a gradual deployment.** Deploy a small change and watch the CLI output, or the deployment in the Console. Confirm that traffic shifts according to your chosen strategy, and use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) to check that the new version handles requests.

6. **Review guardrails (Console).** Confirm deletion protection is required for production databases, VPC-only access is enforced where needed, and resource limits match your team's standards. See [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) for the full list of policy rules.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
# Use the CLI without an account

The Stacktape CLI is open source under the MIT license and works without a Stacktape account. It deploys with your own AWS credentials, straight to AWS. It also sends anonymous usage telemetry, which you can turn off (see [Telemetry](#telemetry)). You can deploy, update, roll back and delete stacks, run dev mode, and read logs and secrets without signing up for anything.

The [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) adds what a team shares: deploy history, costs, alerts, error tracking and access control. It is free while your organization's managed AWS spend is up to $200 a month. You can connect it later with one command, and your existing stacks appear in it without a redeploy.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
How the CLI chooses its mode
docs.content:
## How the CLI chooses its mode

- **Signed in.** When the CLI has a Stacktape API key, from [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) or the `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` environment variable, it works with the Console.
- **Without an account.** Otherwise, stack commands run on your local AWS credentials and don't depend on any Stacktape service. No command asks you to sign in first.

A stack is the same in both modes. The same configuration gives the same stack name, the same deployment bucket and the same resources. The only differences are additions that Console features need, such as organization-wide alarms.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
## Deploy without an account

The CLI uses the AWS credentials it finds the same way the AWS CLI does: environment variables such as `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` or `AWS_PROFILE`, the default profile in `~/.aws`, or an AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) session. Pass `--profile` to pick a profile.

```bash
aws sso login --profile my-dev-account
stacktape deploy --project my-app --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --profile my-dev-account
```

The stack goes to the AWS account those credentials belong to. Resources get AWS URLs or the [custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains) you configure.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
## What works without an account

| Feature | Without an account | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Deploy, update, roll back and delete stacks | Works | Runs against AWS with your credentials |
| Dev mode, scripts, bastion tunnels and container sessions | Works | Runs on your machine and in your AWS account |
| Logs, metrics, secrets and parameters | Works | Read from your AWS account |
| Synthetic tests | Works | CloudWatch Synthetics runs them in your AWS account; the Console adds a page with each run |
| Alarms in your configuration, with `slack`, `ms-teams`, `discord`, `email` or `webhook` channels | Works | CloudWatch alarms live in your AWS account, and the stack delivers these notifications itself |
| Deploys and pull request previews from your own CI pipeline | Works | Your pipeline runs `stacktape deploy` and `stacktape delete` with AWS credentials; see [CI/CD without an account](#cicd-without-an-account) |
| Deploy history, costs and team access | Needs the Console | Stored by Stacktape and shared by your team |
| Alarm channels of type `console-channel` and `slack-app`, and deploy notifications | Needs the Console | The Console delivers these alerts |
| Uptime checks | Needs the Console | The probes run in your AWS account, but the Console decides when a check is down and alerts you |
| Error tracking, incidents and incident AI | Needs the Console | Stacktape stores and groups the events |
| Default `*.stacktape-app.com` domains, including the one a load balancer without its own domain needs for HTTPS | Needs the Console | Stacktape owns that domain |
| Git deployments: push to deploy, Console-managed pull request previews and Stacktape-managed runners | Needs the Console | The Console receives the Git events and runs the jobs |
| Organization-wide guardrails, security reports and the audit log | Needs the Console | They apply to, and are shared by, the whole organization |

Commands that are Console features by nature, such as `stacktape org list`, `stacktape project create`, `stacktape error list`, `stacktape incident list`, `stacktape whoami` and `stacktape deploy --runner ec2`, ask you to sign in and say why.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
When the configuration uses a Console feature
docs.content:
### When the configuration uses a Console feature

When a configuration uses something only the Console provides, validation stops before anything is deployed. The error names the resources and how to fix it, for example:

```
Uptime checks (`homepageCheck`) need the Stacktape Console (free up to $200/month of AWS spend). Run: stacktape connect — your stacks are added as they are, no redeploy. Or remove the uptime-check resources.
```

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
## Connect the Console later

Run `stacktape connect` from a terminal where your AWS credentials are set. It signs you in, connects the AWS account of your credentials to your organization and adds the Stacktape stacks already in that account to the Console. It never redeploys, renames or replaces anything. [Add the Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) explains each step, what it creates in your account and how to go back with `stacktape logout`.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
## CI/CD without an account

Give the pipeline AWS credentials and run the CLI. No Stacktape API key is needed. With GitHub Actions, use an IAM role that trusts GitHub's OIDC provider:

```yaml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-deploy
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: npx stacktape deploy --project my-app --stage production --region eu-west-1 --yes
```

Other CI providers work the same way: set AWS credentials in the job, then run `stacktape deploy`. See [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd) for more providers.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
## Hints about the Console

Without an account, the CLI sometimes prints one dim line that mentions the Console, for example after the first successful deploy of a project:

```
Deploy history, costs and alerts for this stage, shared with your team: stacktape connect (free)
```

The CLI also prints a hint when a deploy waits because someone else is deploying the same stage. It first says who holds the lock.

A hint never opens a browser or asks a question. It appears only in an interactive terminal, after the command's result, and each hint at most once per project on this machine. It never appears in CI, in JSON output, in quiet mode or after a failure. Set `STP_NO_HINTS=1` to turn hints off.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
## Telemetry

Without an account, the CLI sends anonymous usage data, so we can see which commands fail and fix them. The first time you run the CLI, it tells you what it sends and how to turn it off, before it sends anything.

It sends only these fields:

- the command name
- whether the command succeeded, and the error code or class if it failed
- the CLI version, operating system and CPU architecture
- whether it runs in CI
- a random installation ID

It never sends project, stack, stage or AWS account names or IDs, file paths, configuration contents, or error messages.

Telemetry is off when `STP_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` is set, and always off in CI.

`stacktape init` also records anonymous outcome statistics of the analysis: which frameworks it found, whether the deploy worked and how long the analysis took. They never include code, names or files, and the same variables turn them off.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
### When you're signed in

When you are signed in, the CLI sends usage statistics and reports of its own crashes, so we can see which commands fail and fix them. Set `STP_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` to turn both off.

- **After every command:** the command name, the names of the options you used (not their values), how long it took, whether it succeeded, the error code if it failed, your operating system, locale, time zone and the CLI version.
- **When the CLI crashes:** the error type, message and stack trace, the command, your operating system, CPU architecture and whether it ran in CI. The CLI prints an error ID you can give our support. Errors in your configuration, code or AWS account are not reported this way; only failures of the CLI itself are.
- **Identity:** a random ID of your machine. After `stacktape login`, events are linked to your Stacktape user and organization, and your account's email and name are attached to your user.

Before a crash report leaves your machine, the CLI masks tokens and other credentials, email and IP addresses, AWS account IDs and the user name in home-directory paths. Error messages can still contain other text, such as file or resource names. The CLI never sends configuration values, source code, environment variables or AWS credentials. Stacktape processes this data in [PostHog](https://posthog.com) in the EU.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content:
## License

The CLI is open source under the [MIT license](https://github.com/stacktape/stacktape/blob/main/LICENSE). Its source is on [GitHub](https://github.com/stacktape/stacktape). The Stacktape Console is a proprietary hosted service.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
Do I need a Stacktape account to deploy?
docs.content:
### Do I need a Stacktape account to deploy?

No. The CLI deploys with your own AWS credentials. You need an account only for Console features such as deploy history, alerts, error tracking and Git deployments.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
Will connecting the Console change my stacks?
docs.content:
### Will connecting the Console change my stacks?

No. `stacktape connect` finds the stacks already in your AWS account and shows them in the Console without deploying. Later deploys add only what the Console features you use need.

docs.title: Use the CLI without an account
headingPath: Use the CLI without an account
Does the CLI contact Stacktape when I'm not signed in?
docs.content:
### Does the CLI contact Stacktape when I'm not signed in?

A deploy never depends on a Stacktape service. The CLI still makes these requests:

- the anonymous telemetry described above, unless you turn it off
- a check for a newer CLI version, and short notices such as planned maintenance
- downloads of Stacktape's public CloudFormation resource types from a public S3 bucket, when a stack uses them. No sign-in is involved.
- from `stacktape init`, the monthly price estimate: it sends the generated configuration and the region to Stacktape's public price estimator. Your source code is never sent.

The telemetry, the version check and the price estimate never stop a command when they fail.

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
# Start a new project

Starter projects are working apps with their Stacktape configuration already written: APIs, full-stack apps, workers,
AI agents and more. `stacktape init` copies one into a new directory and prints the commands that deploy it.

This guide uses the Hono API starter, a small TypeScript API that runs in a Lambda function behind an HTTP API Gateway.
It deploys in a few minutes and costs close to nothing while nobody calls it. The steps are the same for every starter.

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
## 1. Create the project

Run this in the directory where the project folder should go:

```bash
stacktape init --starter-id hono-api \
  --initialize-project-to ./hono-api --config-format yaml
```

- `--starter-id` is the starter's ID. Each card in [Starter projects](/getting-started/starter-projects) shows it.
- `--initialize-project-to` is the new directory. If it exists and isn't empty, the CLI warns you and asks
  `Continue?`. Answering yes deletes everything in it.
- `--config-format` is `yaml` or `typescript`.

To choose interactively, run `stacktape init --starter-project`. The CLI asks three things: **Choose a starter
project**, **Where to create the project?** (`stacktape-project` by default, `.` for the current directory) and
**Config format**.

The CLI downloads the starter from GitHub and prints a summary:

- where the project is and which config file it has,
- the resources and their monthly price, when it can be estimated,
- the region it picked and why,
- the commands to run next.

The last part looks like this:

```text
Navigate to the project:
  cd ./hono-api
Run hybrid-local dev mode (deploys minimal, free dev stack to AWS):
  stacktape dev --project hono-api --stage local --region eu-west-1
Deploy to AWS:
  stacktape deploy --project hono-api --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The region is the one your AWS setup uses, from `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` or `AWS_REGION`, your Stacktape defaults or your AWS profile, or
`eu-west-1` when none is set. Change `--region` in the commands if you want another one.

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
## 2. Look at what you got

```text
hono-api/
├── src/index.ts      the API: GET /, GET /posts and POST /posts
├── stacktape.yml     two resources: apiGateway and api
└── package.json
```

`stacktape.yml` declares an HTTP API Gateway (`apiGateway`) and a Lambda function (`api`) that bundles
`src/index.ts`. Every request to the gateway goes to the function.

You don't need to run `npm install` first. The deploy installs dependencies when they changed.

docs.title: Start a new project
headingPath: 3. Set the secrets, if the starter has any
docs.content:
## 3. Set the secrets, if the starter has any

Some starters need values only you have, such as an API key for an external service. For those, the summary lists one
command per secret before the deploy command:

```bash
stacktape secret set <name> --region eu-west-1
```

It asks for the value and stores it as a secret in your AWS account. The Hono starter has no secrets. Database
passwords are generated by the deploy, so they are never on this list.

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
## 4. Deploy

Deploying needs AWS credentials on your machine. If you don't have them yet, see
[Set up AWS credentials](/getting-started/aws-credentials).

```bash
cd ./hono-api
stacktape deploy --project hono-api --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The CLI says which AWS credentials it uses, builds the function, uploads it to your AWS account and creates a
CloudFormation stack named after the project and stage, `hono-api-dev`. The first deploy of this starter takes a few
minutes. Starters with a database or a container service take longer.

When it's done, the CLI prints the URL of the API Gateway.

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
## 5. Check that it works

Open the URL in your browser, or call it:

```bash
curl https://<api-id>.execute-api.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/
```

```json
{ "message": "Hello from Hono on AWS Lambda!" }
```

`/posts` returns two sample posts. If you get an error, read the function's logs:

```bash
stacktape logs api --project hono-api --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

`api` is the resource name from `stacktape.yml`. [After the first deploy](/getting-started/after-the-first-deploy)
covers redeploying, more stages and deleting the stack.

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
## What it costs

AWS bills your AWS account for the resources. The Hono starter is pay-per-request: Lambda and HTTP API Gateway charge
per request and have a free tier, so a test deployment that nobody calls costs close to nothing. Starters with a
database, a container service or a load balancer cost money every hour they exist. Check the monthly price in the
summary before you deploy, and [delete the stage](/getting-started/after-the-first-deploy#delete-the-stage) when you're
done trying it.

The CLI is free. You don't need a Stacktape account.

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
## Starters with TypeScript configs

With `--config-format typescript`, the project gets a `stacktape.ts` that imports from the `stacktape` npm package.
Keep that package on the same version as your CLI (`stacktape version` prints it):

```bash
npm install --save-dev stacktape@<cli-version>
```

docs.title: Start a new project
docs.content:
## Dev mode

The summary also prints a `stacktape dev` command. Dev mode runs your code on your machine against a small stack in
AWS, so you see changes without a full deploy. It uses its own stage, `local`, because a stage created by dev mode
can't be deployed with `stacktape deploy`. See [Dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview).

docs.title: Starter projects
docs.content:
# Starter projects

Each starter is a working app with its Stacktape configuration. Pick the one closest to what you're building, create
it with the command on its card and deploy it to your AWS account. Most starters come with both a YAML and a
TypeScript config. The CLI asks which one you want and keeps only that one.

```bash
stacktape init --starter-id <starter-id>
```

[Start a new project](/getting-started/start-a-new-project) walks through creating, deploying and checking one. The
cards link to each starter's source on GitHub, which is also a good reference when you configure your own app.


Browse the current starter projects at https://docs.stacktape.com/getting-started/starter-projects or scaffold one with `stacktape init --starter-id <starter-id>`.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
# Upgrading from v3

Stacktape v4 makes deliberate breaking changes. A v3 configuration usually needs a few renames before v4 accepts it, some CLI flags and commands are gone, the first v4 deployment of a stack changes more than an ordinary deployment, and the Stacktape Console changes for everyone at the same time.

This guide is for upgrading a project from v3.7 to v4. Start with [Before you upgrade](#before-you-upgrade), follow [the upgrade, step by step](#the-upgrade-step-by-step), and read the other sections when that procedure points you to them. Most projects need only the packaging renames and a slower first deployment.

Your deployed stacks keep running while you upgrade: nothing in AWS changes until you deploy a stack with v4.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Before you upgrade

Do these before the v4 release reaches your machines and CI, or right now if it already has.

1. **Pin the Stacktape version everywhere you install it.** The v4 release replaces the install scripts at `installs.stacktape.com`, so every unpinned `curl … | sh` or `irm … | iex`, CI jobs included, and `stacktape upgrade` on a v3 CLI install v4. Pin v3 until each project is migrated:


Example (macOS):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/macos.sh | STACKTAPE_VERSION=3.7.1 sh
```


Example (Linux):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/linux.sh | STACKTAPE_VERSION=3.7.1 sh
```


Example (Windows):

```powershell
$env:STACKTAPE_VERSION='3.7.1'; irm https://installs.stacktape.com/windows.ps1 | iex
```


Example (npm):

```bash
npm install --save-exact stacktape@3.7.1
```


   A project that runs the CLI from its `stacktape` npm package (`npx stacktape`) stays on the version in its lockfile. Use an exact version, not a range such as `^3.7.1`.

2. **Export configurations stored in the Stacktape Console.** The Console update that ships with v4 deletes every configuration template stored in the Console, and the history of configurations it generated for you. This cannot be undone, and a pinned v3 CLI does not keep them: `--templateId` stops working because the Console no longer has the templates. If you deploy with `--templateId`, or want to keep a template, save it as a file in your repository before the Console update: copy it from the template editor in the Console, or run `stacktape init --templateId <id>` with the v3 CLI in an empty directory. That command writes `stacktape.yml` without asking, so running it in your project would overwrite the configuration you have. Your deployed stacks are not affected.

3. **Plan to upgrade the whole toolchain of a project at once.** A project's deployments must all use v4 once one has: the CLI on every developer machine, the project's `stacktape` npm package and lockfile, and the CLI version pinned in CI. A v4 CLI evaluates a TypeScript configuration with the project's installed `stacktape` package, so an old package produces a v3 configuration that v4 rejects. An older CLI that deploys a stack after v4 has deployed it can also delete images that v4's container helpers need. Deployments the Console runs for you (Git pushes and Console runners) use the CLI version the Console chooses, which is v4 after the Console update, unless the project was set to a specific Stacktape version. If you are not sure, ask [support@stacktape.com](mailto:support@stacktape.com) to check your projects.

4. **Choose a quiet time for the first v4 deployment of each stage.** It rebuilds and re-uploads every function, replaces running containers once, and can replace AWS Batch compute environments. See [what the first v4 deployment changes](#what-the-first-v4-deployment-changes).

5. **Tell your team about the Console changes.** Everyone may have to sign in to the CLI again, people who used an authenticator app set it up again, and Developers and Viewers keep access only to some AWS accounts. See [Stacktape Console changes](#stacktape-console-changes).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Which sections apply to you

| If your project or team uses… | Read |
|---|---|
| Any `packaging` (every function and container) | [Packaging](#packaging) |
| `serviceName` in the configuration | [Project name](#project-name) |
| Alarms with `notificationTargets` | [Alarm notifications](#alarm-notifications) |
| `usePrivateSubnetsWithNAT` or `stackConfig.vpc.nat` | [NAT](#nat) |
| `redis-cluster` | [Redis caches](#redis-caches) |
| `aurora-postgresql-serverless` or `aurora-mysql-serverless` | [Aurora Serverless v1](#aurora-serverless-v1) |
| CDN `cookies`, `headers` or `queryString` options | [CDN cache and forwarding options](#cdn-cache-and-forwarding-options) |
| `$ResourceParam(<website>, 'url')` or `connectTo` on a website with several custom domains | [Website URLs](#website-urls) |
| `$Secret(...)` | [Secrets with a JSON key](#secrets-with-a-json-key) |
| `disableAutoRollback`, `--disableAutoRollback` | [Automatic rollback](#automatic-rollback) |
| A TypeScript configuration (`stacktape.ts`) | [TypeScript configurations](#typescript-configurations) |
| `connectTo: ['aws:ses']` or `AWS_SES` | [Sending email with SES](#sending-email-with-ses) |
| `afterDeploy` hooks | [After-deploy hooks fail the deployment](#after-deploy-hooks-fail-the-deployment) |
| Scripts or CI that call the CLI, including `--agent` | [CLI changes](#cli-changes) |
| More than one `stacktape.*` file in a project directory | [Several configuration files in one directory](#several-configuration-files-in-one-directory) |
| Java, Ruby or Go functions | [Lambda runtimes](#lambda-runtimes) |
| Container services | [Container services](#container-services) |
| AWS Batch jobs | [Batch jobs](#batch-jobs) |
| Lambda functions in a VPC (`joinDefaultVpc`) | [Functions in a VPC](#functions-in-a-vpc) |
| The Stacktape Console | [Stacktape Console changes](#stacktape-console-changes) |

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## The upgrade, step by step

Upgrade one project at a time, and one stage before the others.

1. **Install v4** on your machine and update the project's package. Name the version, so you get a v4 release and not an older default, and keep the CLI and the package on the same version:


Example (npm):

```bash
npm install --save-exact stacktape@4.0.0
```


Example (macOS):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/macos.sh | STACKTAPE_VERSION=4.0.0 sh
```


Example (Linux):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/linux.sh | STACKTAPE_VERSION=4.0.0 sh
```


Example (Windows):

```powershell
$env:STACKTAPE_VERSION='4.0.0'; irm https://installs.stacktape.com/windows.ps1 | iex
```


   Use a later 4.x version in place of `4.0.0` when there is one. `stacktape version` prints what you have.

2. **Update the configuration** using the [configuration changes](#configuration-changes) that apply to it. v4 rejects the old names and prints the property it does not accept.

3. **Validate** the configuration against a non-production stage. Name the stage, region and AWS account explicitly:

   ```bash
   stacktape validate --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --aws-account my-staging-account
   ```

   Validation checks the configuration and builds the CloudFormation template. It does not start your application or deploy anything.

4. **Review the change plan** with [`stacktape diff`](/cli/diff), using the same flags. Look for resources that would be replaced or deleted. The first v4 deployment always updates functions, container task definitions and some helper resources; [what the first v4 deployment changes](#what-the-first-v4-deployment-changes) lists what to expect. A database, bucket or table listed as replaced means a configuration change went wrong: compare the resource names and settings with the v3 configuration before deploying. `stacktape deploy` also stops and asks for confirmation before replacing or deleting a Stacktape resource that holds data, but not for resources in `cloudformationResources`.

5. **Deploy the non-production stage** and check that the application works: open its endpoints, run a job, read its logs with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs).
