6. **Update CI**: install v4 with a pinned version (`STACKTAPE_VERSION=4.0.0`, or the package version in the lockfile), replace [removed commands and flags](#cli-changes), and pass `--aws-account` (see [Target AWS account](#target-aws-account)).

7. **Deploy production**, at a quiet time.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Going back to v3

There is no automatic way back. A configuration updated for v4 does not work with v3, and the v4 Console no longer supports some things v3 relies on: stored templates, configuration generation in `init`, and AWS account connection from the CLI. To go back for one stack, revert the configuration and the package to their v3 versions and deploy with a pinned v3.7.1 CLI. Expect that deployment to change the stack again: it rebuilds the functions, replaces the containers and moves functions in a VPC back to their own security groups, which can interrupt their database connections for about four minutes. Before you rely on this, try it on a non-production stage.

Data in databases, buckets and tables is not affected either way. A database migration your application ran during the upgrade is not reverted by redeploying.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Configuration changes

v4 rejects the old names: `stacktape validate` and `stacktape deploy` stop and name the property they do not accept. Make these changes before the first v4 deployment.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Alarm notifications

On the `alarms` of functions, databases, load balancers, HTTP APIs and SQS queues, `notificationTargets` is now `notificationChannels`. The channel objects inside are unchanged.

Before:

```yaml
alarms:
  - trigger:
      type: lambda-error-rate
      properties:
        thresholdPercent: 5
    notificationTargets:
      - type: slack
        properties:
          conversationId: C0123456789
          accessToken: $Secret('slack-bot-token')
```

After:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging, $Secret } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    alarms: [
      {
        trigger: { type: 'lambda-error-rate', properties: { thresholdPercent: 5 } },
        notificationChannels: [
          {
            type: 'slack',
            properties: { conversationId: 'C0123456789', accessToken: $Secret('slack-bot-token') }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


Example (YAML):

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/api.ts
      alarms:
        - trigger:
            type: lambda-error-rate
            properties:
              thresholdPercent: 5
          notificationChannels:
            - type: slack
              properties:
                conversationId: C0123456789
                accessToken: $Secret('slack-bot-token')
```


v4 also accepts `{ type: console-channel, properties: { channelName: <name> } }`, which sends to an [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels) set up in the Console, so the token stays out of the configuration.

In v4, inline channels such as `slack` are delivered by the stack's own service Lambda from your AWS account, when the alarm fires and when it recovers. Their tokens and webhook URLs are no longer sent to the Stacktape Console. A stack still deployed with v3 keeps sending them with each alarm event until you redeploy it with v4; the Console delivers those notifications but does not store the channel settings.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### NAT

`stackConfig.vpc.nat` moved to `stackConfig.nat`, and NAT is no longer created implicitly. In v3, a container with `usePrivateSubnetsWithNAT: true` gave the stack NAT Gateways. In v4, the stack needs `stackConfig.nat`; without it, validation stops with `CONFIG_NAT_REQUIRED`.

To keep the NAT Gateways you have, and with them the Elastic IPs your partners may allowlist, set `gateway` with the number of availability zones you had (2 if you did not set it):

Before:

```yaml
stackConfig:
  vpc:
    nat:
      availabilityZones: 3
```

After:


Example (YAML):

```yaml
stackConfig:
  nat:
    type: gateway
    availabilityZones: 3
```


`stackConfig.nat: gateway` alone means two zones. v4 has no single-gateway option: if you had `availabilityZones: 1`, `type: gateway` with two zones keeps the existing gateway and its IP, and adds a second gateway (about $32 per month) with a new IP that you need to allowlist too.

v4 also offers cheaper NAT instances, `ec2` and `ha-ec2`. Switching to them on a deployed stack changes the outbound IPs. See [NAT: internet access from private subnets](/configuration/connecting-resources#nat-internet-access-from-private-subnets) for the trade-offs. Once a stack has NAT, its [VPC Lambda functions use it too](#functions-in-a-vpc).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Redis caches

`type: redis-cluster` is now `type: redis`, and the node settings (`instanceSize`, replicas, sharding, `port`, `logging`) moved under `engine.properties`. To keep a deployed cache unchanged, use `engine.type: redis` and set `version` to the version it runs: the former `engineVersion`, or `6.2` if it was not set. The CLI rejects `redis-cluster` and prints this replacement for your settings. TypeScript configurations replace `RedisCluster` with `Redis`.

The cache keeps its endpoint and data. New caches use Valkey (`engine.type: valkey` or `valkey-serverless`). Changing an existing cache to Valkey is an in-place migration that cannot be reversed, so do it separately from the upgrade if at all. See [Redis](/resources/databases/redis#migrating-from-redis-cluster).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Aurora Serverless v1

AWS retired Aurora Serverless v1 on 31 March 2025, and v4 no longer deploys it. The `aurora-postgresql-serverless` and `aurora-mysql-serverless` engine types, and the `AuroraServerlessEnginePostgresql` and `AuroraServerlessEngineMysql` classes, fail validation with a migration error.

For a new database, use `aurora-postgresql-serverless-v2` or `aurora-mysql-serverless-v2` (`AuroraServerlessV2EnginePostgresql`, `AuroraServerlessV2EngineMysql`) with `minCapacity` and `maxCapacity` between 0.5 and 128 ACUs. Serverless v2 does not pause when idle, and `pauseAfterSeconds` does not exist on it.

Do not only change the engine type of a deployed v1 database. The v2 engine type uses a different engine mode, and CloudFormation replaces the cluster when the engine mode changes, so editing the type alone puts your data at risk. Keep that stack on v3, take a snapshot, and email [support@stacktape.com](mailto:support@stacktape.com) to plan the move.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### CDN cache and forwarding options

Each `cookies`, `headers` and `queryString` option under `cdn.cachingOptions.cacheKeyParameters` and `cdn.forwardingOptions` (including those in `routeRewrites`) now sets exactly one choice. A choice without a list, such as `all` or `none`, must be `true`.

v3 accepted `{ all: false }` and applied `all` anyway. v4 rejects `false`, an empty object and several choices at once, and names the valid choices. Replace a `false` value with the choice you mean, for example `none: true`. Selectors that already set one choice, such as `{ all: true }` or `{ whitelist: [session] }`, are unchanged and produce the same cache and origin request policies.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Website URLs

The `url` parameter of `nextjs-web`, `astro-web`, `nuxt-web`, `sveltekit-web`, `solidstart-web`, `tanstack-web` and `remix-web` is now always one URL: the first of the website's `customDomains`, or its default Stacktape URL when it has none. In v3, a website with several custom domains returned all of them joined by `, `, which broke code that parsed `url` as a URL. This value reaches `$ResourceParam('<website>', 'url')` and the `STP_<WEBSITE>_URL` variable of resources that list the website in `connectTo`.

With zero or one custom domain, nothing changes. If you need every custom domain, use the new `customDomainUrls` parameter: the custom domain URLs in configured order, joined by `, `.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Secrets with a JSON key

`$Secret('secret-name', 'key')` is the documented way to read one key of a JSON secret. The first argument is the exact secret name, so it can contain dots. You do not have to change anything: `$Secret('secret-name.key')` keeps working and reads the same secret and key as in v3. Use the two-argument form for a secret whose name contains a dot. See [Secrets](/configuration/secrets#json-secrets).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Automatic rollback

`deploymentConfig.disableAutoRollback` is removed. v4 no longer rolls back a failed deployment by default (see [Failed deployments keep what they created](#failed-deployments-keep-what-they-created)), so:

- if you had `disableAutoRollback: true`, delete it;
- to keep v3's behaviour, set `autoRollback: true`.


Example (YAML):

```yaml
deploymentConfig:
  autoRollback: true
```


Stacks with `triggerRollbackOnAlarms` or `monitoringTimeAfterDeploymentInMinutes` keep rolling back automatically.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Sending email with SES

The `aws:ses` entry in `connectTo` and the `AWS_SES` constant are removed. v4 resolves every `connectTo` entry as a resource in your configuration. Declare an [email sender](/resources/messaging/email-sender) for the identity you send from, and connect to it. For an identity you verified outside Stacktape, set `manageIdentity: false` so the deployment uses it instead of creating one. The connection grants permission to send email, where `aws:ses` granted every SES action; give automation that needs other SES actions its own IAM statements.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Values that v4 rejects

v4 checks some values that v3 accepted:

- **Container scaling below one instance.** `scaling.minInstances` and `maxInstances` must be at least 1. v3 accepted `minInstances: 0`; set it to 1.
- **Stack tags starting with `stp:`.** Stacktape uses this prefix for its own tags. Rename such tags in `stackConfig.tags`.
- **Database log settings that do not fit the engine.** Remove `logging` options for another engine.
- **State machine definitions with Stacktape metadata.** `Parallel` branches and `Map` item workflows must be Amazon States Language workflows with `StartAt` and `States`, and each state needs a valid `Type`. Other ASL fields, such as `QueryLanguage` or `ItemProcessor`, and `null` paths are passed to AWS unchanged.
- **SQS triggers with a function timeout longer than the queue's visibility timeout.** AWS rejects this combination; raise the queue's `visibilityTimeoutSeconds` or lower the function's `timeout`.
- **`Condition` and `DependsOn` in `cloudformationResources`** must be a condition name and a resource name (or a list of names), as CloudFormation requires.
- **`budgetControl`**, from Stacktape 3.5 and earlier (3.6 removed it). Delete it and set the budget in the Stacktape Console under Budgets. The next deploy deletes the AWS budget it created.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Scripts

`pipeStdio` on `local-script` and `local-script-with-bastion-tunneling` is replaced by `stdioMode`. A configuration that still sets it fails validation with `CONFIG_SCRIPT_PIPE_STDIO_REMOVED`, which names the script. Replace `pipeStdio: false` with `stdioMode: ignore`, and delete `pipeStdio: true`, which is the default (`stdioMode: capture`). Use `stdioMode: inherit` for a script that needs keyboard input. See [hooks and scripts](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Removed resource parameters

The `MultiContainerWorkload` class no longer has a `logGroupArn` property, and `$ResourceParam('<workload>', 'logGroupArn')` is rejected. Stacktape never published this parameter, so a v3 configuration using it could not deploy.

A multi-container workload has one log group per container. To reference one, use [`$CfResourceParam`](/configuration/directives) with the log group's CloudFormation logical ID: the workload name and the container name in PascalCase, followed by `LogGroup`. For the `app` container of a workload named `orders`, use `$CfResourceParam('OrdersAppLogGroup', 'Arn')`. A container with `logging.disabled` has no log group. Run [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) to check the logical IDs in the generated template.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### User auth pool token lifetimes

v3 sent `accessTokenValiditySeconds` and `idTokenValiditySeconds` to Cognito without a unit, so Cognito read them in hours and accepted only 1 to 24. v4 sends them in seconds. A value from 1 to 24 keeps its meaning in hours, and the CLI warns you to write it in seconds: replace `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 1` with `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 3600`. Unset lifetimes stay at 1 hour, and deploying updates the user pool client in place. See [token lifetimes](/resources/security/user-auth-pool#token-lifetimes).

The CLI does not warn about `overrides`. If you set `AccessTokenValidity` or `IdTokenValidity` on the user pool client through `overrides`, the value is now read in seconds, so a value that meant hours fails to deploy. Set the matching unit in the same override, or replace the override with `accessTokenValiditySeconds` or `idTokenValiditySeconds`. For a pool named `auth`:

```yaml
resources:
  auth:
    type: user-auth-pool
    overrides:
      AuthUserPoolClient:
        AccessTokenValidity: 2
        TokenValidityUnits:
          AccessToken: hours
```

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Packaging

v4 replaces the v3 packaging types with a smaller set:

| v3 type | v4 type | v4 class |
|---|---|---|
| `stacktape-lambda-buildpack`, JavaScript or TypeScript entry file | `js-bundle` | `JsBundleLambdaPackaging` |
| `stacktape-lambda-buildpack`, Python, Java, Go, Ruby or .NET entry file | `buildpack` | `BuildpackLambdaPackaging` |
| `stacktape-image-buildpack`, JavaScript or TypeScript entry file | `js-bundle` | `JsBundleImagePackaging` |
| `stacktape-image-buildpack`, other languages | `buildpack` | `BuildpackImagePackaging` |
| `nixpacks` | `buildpack` | `BuildpackImagePackaging` |
| `external-buildpack` | `buildpack` or `dockerfile` | `BuildpackImagePackaging` or `DockerfilePackaging` |
| `custom-dockerfile` | `dockerfile` | `DockerfilePackaging` |
| `custom-artifact` | `custom-artifact` (unchanged) | `CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging` |
| `prebuilt-image` | `prebuilt-image` (unchanged) | `PrebuiltImagePackaging` |

In TypeScript configurations, rename the classes in both the `new ...Packaging(...)` calls and the `import` list. The v3 classes were `StacktapeLambdaBuildpackPackaging`, `StacktapeImageBuildpackPackaging`, `CustomDockerfilePackaging`, `NixpacksPackaging` and `ExternalBuildpackPackaging`.

Before:


Example (TypeScript (v3)):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, StacktapeLambdaBuildpackPackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new StacktapeLambdaBuildpackPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/api.ts',
      languageSpecificConfig: { outputModuleFormat: 'esm' }
    })
  });
  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


After:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/api.ts',
      outputModuleFormat: 'esm'
    })
  });
  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


#### JavaScript and TypeScript Lambda functions

Rename the type to `js-bundle` and move the options from `languageSpecificConfig` up one level.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/api.ts
          languageSpecificConfig:
            nodeVersion: 22
            outputModuleFormat: esm
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/api.ts
          nodeVersion: 22
          outputModuleFormat: esm
```

See [JS Bundle for Lambda](/packaging/function/js-bundle).

#### Python, Java, Go, Ruby and .NET Lambda functions

Rename the type to `buildpack`. Rename `languageSpecificConfig` to `python`, `java` or `dotnet`, depending on the language. Delete the version fields and set the function's `runtime` instead. Go and Ruby have no options, so delete their `languageSpecificConfig`.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  processor:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/process.py
          languageSpecificConfig:
            pythonVersion: 3.12
            packageManagerFile: ./pyproject.toml
            minify: false
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  processor:
    type: function
    properties:
      runtime: python3.12
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/process.py
          python:
            packageManagerFile: ./pyproject.toml
```

v3 ignored the runtime when it built a function: without a version field, it built for Python 3.12, Java 11, Ruby 3.3 or .NET 8. v4 builds for the function's runtime. Set `runtime` explicitly; see [Lambda runtimes](#lambda-runtimes) for the defaults that changed.

See [Buildpack for Lambda](/packaging/function/buildpack).

#### Rust Lambda functions

v3 had no Rust support, so Rust functions used `custom-artifact` with a hook that ran cargo-lambda. In v4, you can delete the hook and use `buildpack`.

Before:

```yaml
hooks:
  beforeDeploy:
    - scriptName: buildRust
scripts:
  buildRust:
    type: local-script
    properties:
      executeCommand: cargo lambda build --release --output-format zip
resources:
  resizer:
    type: function
    properties:
      runtime: provided.al2023
      packaging:
        type: custom-artifact
        properties:
          packagePath: ./target/lambda/resizer/bootstrap.zip
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  resizer:
    type: function
    properties:
      runtime: provided.al2023
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/main.rs
```

#### JavaScript and TypeScript container services

Rename the type to `js-bundle` and move the options from `languageSpecificConfig` up one level. `requiresGlibcBinaries` and `customDockerBuildCommands` stay where they are.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-image-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/server.ts
          requiresGlibcBinaries: true
          languageSpecificConfig:
            emitTsDecoratorMetadata: true
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/server.ts
          requiresGlibcBinaries: true
          emitTsDecoratorMetadata: true
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

The v4 image installs nothing beside the runtime by default. v3 images ran `tini` and shipped `curl` and `openssl`:

- ECS and AWS Batch now start the init process (`initProcessEnabled`), so stop signals still reach your server.
- `curl` is installed only when the container's `internalHealthCheck` command calls it. If a script in the image calls `curl`, or your code runs the `openssl` command, add it with `customDockerBuildCommands`, for example `apk add --no-cache curl`.
- The OpenSSL libraries that Prisma loads are still in the image. When your code, or a package installed beside the bundle, uses Prisma, the Alpine image also gets the `openssl` command, which Prisma 5 needs to choose its query engine.

See [JS Bundle for Containers](/packaging/containers/js-bundle).

#### Python and other non-JavaScript container services

Rename the type to `buildpack`. The container `buildpack` builds the whole project directory, so replace `entryfilePath` with `sourceDirectoryPath`. Replace `runAppAs` with a `startCommand` that starts the server on `$PORT`, and add the server (for example `uvicorn` or `gunicorn`) to the project's dependencies.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-image-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./app/main.py:app
          languageSpecificConfig:
            runAppAs: ASGI
            packageManagerFile: ./pyproject.toml
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: .
          startCommand: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

For a WSGI app, use gunicorn, for example `gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT app.main:app`. When a FastAPI, Flask or Django project uses the conventional module layout, the start command is detected and `startCommand` can be omitted.

The v4 images are Debian-based and larger than the v3 Alpine images, and they detect native dependencies differently. Test that the application starts and shuts down in the new image. See [Buildpack for Containers](/packaging/containers/buildpack).

#### Nixpacks

Rename the type to `buildpack` and `startCmd` to `startCommand`. Nixpacks phases have no direct equivalent: move install and build commands to `installCommand` and `buildCommand`, and use `railpackConfig` for anything else.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: nixpacks
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
          startCmd: node dist/server.js
          phases:
            - name: build
              cmds:
                - npm run build
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
          startCommand: node dist/server.js
          buildCommand: npm run build
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

A PHP application that used Nixpacks builds with `buildpack` too; check that the detected PHP version and extensions match what it needs, or switch it to a Dockerfile.

#### External buildpacks

Cloud Native Buildpacks and the pack CLI are no longer supported. Try `buildpack`, which detects most projects without configuration. If you depended on a specific builder or buildpack, write a Dockerfile and use `dockerfile`.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: external-buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
          builder: paketobuildpacks/builder-jammy-base
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

#### Custom Dockerfiles

Rename the type to `dockerfile`. The properties are unchanged.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  worker:
    type: worker-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: custom-dockerfile
        properties:
          buildContextPath: ./worker
          dockerfilePath: Dockerfile.prod
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  worker:
    type: worker-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: dockerfile
        properties:
          buildContextPath: ./worker
          dockerfilePath: Dockerfile.prod
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

See [Dockerfile](/packaging/containers/dockerfile).

#### Removed packaging properties

- `languageSpecificConfig`: its options are direct properties of `js-bundle`, or `python`, `java` and `dotnet` on the Lambda `buildpack`.
- `pythonVersion`, `javaVersion`, `rubyVersion` and `dotnetVersion` on Lambda functions: set the function's `runtime`.
- `packageManager`, `minify` and `runAppAs` for Python Lambda functions.
- `entryfilePath`, `runAppAs`, `languageSpecificConfig`, `requiresGlibcBinaries` and `customDockerBuildCommands` for non-JavaScript container services. Use `sourceDirectoryPath`, `startCommand`, `aptPackages` or a Dockerfile.
- `startCmd`, `phases`, `providers`, `buildImage`, `startRunImage` and `startOnlyIncludeFiles` from `nixpacks`. Use `startCommand`, `installCommand`, `buildCommand`, `aptPackages` or `railpackConfig`.
- `builder` and `buildpacks` from `external-buildpack`.
- PHP Lambda functions. Run PHP as a container with [`buildpack`](/packaging/containers/buildpack).

#### Files that v4 refuses to package

v4 stops packaging when the project contains a symbolic link that points outside the package or to nothing, or a path with a backslash on Linux or macOS. v3 followed or rewrote these. Copy the files the link points to into the project, or fix the link. This mostly affects monorepos that link packages from outside the project directory.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content: ## CLI changes

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Command and flag spelling

v4 commands and flags use standard spelling: words separated by spaces, and lowercase flags with dashes. For example, `stacktape secret set my-key --region eu-west-1` replaces `stacktape secret:set --region eu-west-1 --secretName my-key`. Most old spellings, such as colon commands (`info:stack`) and camelCase flags (`--projectName`), still work. Run `stacktape help <command>` to see the current names.

These v3 commands were renamed. The old names still run the new command and print a warning, so scripts keep working; replace them when convenient:

| v3 command | v4 command |
|---|---|
| `compile-template` | `synth` |
| `preview-changes` | `diff` |
| `package-workloads` | `package` |
| `secret:create` | `secret set` |
| `projects:list` | `project list` |
| `debug:logs` | `logs` |
| `debug:metrics` | `metrics` |
| `debug:alarms` | `alarm list` |
| `debug:sql`, `debug:dynamodb`, `debug:redis`, `debug:opensearch` | `query sql`, `query dynamodb`, `query redis`, `query opensearch` |
| `debug:aws-sdk` | `aws call` |
| `debug:container-exec` | `container exec` |

`codebuild:deploy` was removed and fails with `CLI_COMMAND_REMOVED`. Run `stacktape deploy` in the CI job, or use `deploy --runner ec2` after you set up a [Console runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Removed flags

`deploy` still accepts the first three flags and prints a warning, so scripts keep working. The others stop the command.

| v3 flag | What to do |
|---|---|
| `--hotSwap`, `--hs` | Accepted and ignored. `deploy` updates code-only changes directly without it; see [Fast deployments are automatic](#fast-deployments-are-automatic). Delete it when convenient. |
| `--disableAutoRollback`, `--dar` | Accepted as `--auto-rollback=false`, which is now the default. Use `--auto-rollback` for v3's behaviour. See [Automatic rollback](#automatic-rollback). |
| `--disableDriftDetection`, `--ddd` | Accepted and ignored. `deploy` no longer checks for drift. |
| `--templateId`, `--ti` | Fails with `CLI_ARGUMENT_REMOVED`. Use a configuration file in the repository and pass its path with `--config` if it is not in the project root. See [Before you upgrade](#before-you-upgrade). |
| `--awsAccount` on `compile-template`/`synth` or `package-workloads`/`package` | Fails with `CLI_ARGUMENT_REMOVED`. These commands use local AWS credentials (`--profile` or AWS keys in the environment) when the configuration needs AWS. Delete it. |
| `--devMode`, `--dm` | Delete it. Use [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev). |
| `dev --container`, `dev --resourceName` | Use `dev --resources <name>` (and `--skip-resources`). |

Two parsing rules changed:

- An option with one dash must be one letter: `-r eu-west-1` works, `-pn shop` does not. Use the long form, `--project shop`.
- A boolean flag takes its value after `=`: `--watch=false`. `--flag true` and `--flag false` as separate words still work for commands without positional arguments, such as `deploy`; for others the second word is read as a positional argument.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Target AWS account

v3 stack commands ignored `--profile` and `AWS_PROFILE` for accounts connected with Stacktape-managed access. They deployed to `--aws-account`, the saved default, or the organization's only connected account. In v4, when `--aws-account` is not set, `--profile`, `AWS_PROFILE` or AWS keys in the environment choose the connected account they belong to. If they belong to an account that is not connected, the command stops before changing anything.

Check scripts and CI jobs that set an AWS profile or AWS keys, for example for an S3 upload in an earlier step. Pass `--aws-account <name>` to Stacktape commands in them, or remove the AWS settings. See [Choosing the account for a CLI command](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account#choosing-the-account-for-a-cli-command).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### `--agent` no longer confirms operations

In v3, `--agent` also answered every confirmation, as if you had passed `--yes`. In v4 it only selects machine-readable output and turns off prompts. An operation that asks for confirmation needs `--yes`: deleting a stack, a deploy whose update may delete stateful resources such as a database, creating a project that does not exist yet, `project delete`, `org delete` and `dev network delete`. Without `--yes`, such a command run with `--agent`, with `--json` or without a terminal stops before it changes anything and fails with `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED`. An explicit `--yes=false` is respected.

Add `--yes` where a script or CI job intends the operation, for example `stacktape delete --stage preview --region eu-west-1 --agent --yes`. `stacktape dev --agent` takes `--yes` too, to create a project that does not exist yet.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: Interrupted commands exit with a non-zero code
docs.content:
### Interrupted commands exit with a non-zero code

v3 exited with code 0 when a command was interrupted, so `stacktape deploy && ./next-step.sh` continued after you pressed Ctrl+C or CI cancelled the job. In v4 an interrupted command exits with 130 for Ctrl+C (SIGINT) or a declined confirmation, 143 for SIGTERM, 129 for SIGHUP and 131 for SIGQUIT. The `--json` result stays `ok: false` with code `USER_INTERRUPTION`. This includes long-running commands that you usually end with Ctrl+C, such as `logs --follow`, `bastion tunnel` and `stacktape dev`. Stopping a dev session with `stacktape dev stop` is not an interruption: both the command and the stopped session exit with 0.

If a script treats an interrupted command as success on purpose, check for these codes explicitly.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: Several configuration files in one directory
docs.content:
### Several configuration files in one directory

v3 picked one file by precedence (`stacktape.ts`, then `stacktape.yml`, then the others) and printed a warning when a directory held more than one of `stacktape.ts`, `stacktape.yml`, `stacktape.yaml` and `stacktape.js`. v4 stops with `CONFIG_FILE_AMBIGUOUS` instead, because the files can name different projects, stages or regions. This often happens after converting `stacktape.yml` to `stacktape.ts`, or when a TypeScript build writes `stacktape.js` next to `stacktape.ts`. Delete or rename the file you no longer use, or pass `--config <file>` in every script and CI job. A directory with a single configuration file works as before.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Secrets in command output

Every command replaces secret values with `<<OMITTED>>` unless you pass `--show-secrets`. Secret values are database and Redis connection strings, Upstash passwords and tokens, AppSync API keys, user pool client secrets and Convex keys. This changes:

- `deploy --agent`: `data.result.stackInfo` now holds `<<OMITTED>>` for them; v3 returned them. So does the stack-info file `deploy` writes.
- `secret get`: prints the secret's name, ARN and creation date, and its value only with `--show-secrets`. With `--agent`, the result is `{ name, arn, created, value }` at `data.result`, where v3 printed the value in a log line.
- `aws-profile list --agent`: returns the secret access key masked, as its table shows it, unless you pass `--show-secrets`.
- Local scripts: their captured output and their error replace the secrets Stacktape gives them (`$Secret`, `$SsmParam` and secret `connectTo` parameters) with `[redacted]`. A script with `stdioMode: inherit` writes to your terminal unchanged.

If a script or CI job reads a secret from one of these commands, add `--show-secrets` to that command and keep its output out of shared logs. The [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) never returns secret values and refuses `--show-secrets`.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Scripts that read CLI output

The `--json` (JSONL) output keeps its v3 envelope: lines with `event`, `log`, `output` or `result`, and `ok`, `code`, `message` and `data.result`. Error codes are more specific: `result.code` is now a code such as `CONFIG_NAT_REQUIRED` instead of a category such as `CONFIG`. Some renamed commands return different data; for example, `diff` returns `changes`, `resourceChanges` and `changePlan`. Human-readable output is redesigned, so do not match its text. A failed command still exits with code 1; an interrupted one now exits with 130 or 143 (see [Interrupted commands exit with a non-zero code](#interrupted-commands-exit-with-a-non-zero-code)).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Environment variables

`STACKTAPE_API_KEY`, `STP_DISABLE_TELEMETRY`, `STP_DISABLE_NOTIFICATIONS` and the AWS variables work as before. `STACKTAPE_TUNNEL_SERVER` no longer does anything: `stacktape dev` connects deployed functions to your machine through a small shared instance in your account (see [`dev network`](/cli/dev-network)). The `STP_CODEBUILD*` variables belonged to the removed CodeBuild runner.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What the first v4 deployment changes
docs.content:
## What the first v4 deployment changes

The first deployment of a stack with v4 is an ordinary CloudFormation update, but it changes more than a usual deployment. Expect it to take longer, and deploy at a quiet time.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What the first v4 deployment changes
docs.content:
### Your data is kept

Databases, buckets, DynamoDB tables, Redis caches, EFS file systems, user pools, Kinesis streams and SQS queues keep their CloudFormation logical IDs and physical names, so they are neither replaced nor deleted. Default domains keep their names as well. This holds as long as the configuration keeps the project name, stage and resource names, and no replacement-sensitive setting changed. Stacktape checks it before every deployment: the change plan printed by `stacktape deploy` lists every resource it would replace or delete, and it stops for confirmation when a Stacktape resource that holds data would be replaced or deleted. Resources you define in `cloudformationResources` are not part of this check, so review them in the change plan yourself.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What the first v4 deployment changes
docs.content:
### Lambda functions

- **Every function and layer is rebuilt and uploaded once.** v4 packages functions differently, so the first build cannot use the v3 cache, and each function publishes a new version.
- **Functions with `deployment` or `provisionedConcurrency` get their configuration on the alias.** In v3, a change to only the environment, memory, timeout or similar settings of such a function did not reach the alias that serves traffic. v4 publishes a new version and moves the alias, so the first v4 deployment applies any such setting that never reached it, runs the gradual deployment and allocates provisioned concurrency again. Check that the function's configuration is what you want live.
- **JavaScript source maps leave the package.** Bundled functions no longer carry `.map` files, so stack traces in CloudWatch show the deployed file names. Stacktape [error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) still maps them to your source. To keep the maps in the package, set `keepSourceMapsInPackage: true` in the `js-bundle` packaging.

#### Lambda runtimes

A function without `runtime` gets the default for its language, and three defaults changed:

| Language | v3 default | v4 default | To keep the v3 runtime |
|---|---|---|---|
| Java | `java21` | `java25` | `runtime: java21` |
| Ruby | `ruby3.3` | `ruby4.0` | `runtime: ruby3.3` |
| Go | `provided.al2` | `provided.al2023` | `runtime: provided.al2` |

Node.js (`nodejs24.x`), Python (`python3.13`) and .NET (`dotnet10`) keep their defaults. v4 also builds each function for its runtime, where v3 built for Python 3.12, Java 11, Ruby 3.3 or .NET 8. Set `runtime` explicitly on existing functions, and test those with native dependencies.

#### Functions in a VPC

- **Security groups are shared.** Functions with `joinDefaultVpc: true` that connect to the same databases, caches or file systems now share one security group, instead of one each. The first v4 deployment keeps each function's old group while it moves, and the next deployment deletes it. AWS creates network interfaces for each new combination of subnets and security groups, which adds about four minutes to that deployment. `overrides` or `$CfResourceParam` references that target a function's own security group (`<Function>SecurityGroup`) no longer apply; run [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) to find the shared group's logical ID.
- **Functions use the stack's NAT.** In a stack with `stackConfig.nat`, VPC functions now run in the private subnets and reach the internet through the NAT. In v3 they stayed in public subnets without internet access. Their outbound traffic leaves from the NAT's IP addresses.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What the first v4 deployment changes
docs.content:
### Container services

- **Containers are replaced once.** The default container `stopTimeout` is 30 seconds instead of 2, and a load balancer gives an old container 30 seconds instead of 5 to finish its requests. The first v4 deployment therefore registers new task definitions and replaces the running containers, as a code change would. Set `stopTimeout: 2` on a container to keep the v3 shutdown window.
- **Unused scaling policies are removed.** A service whose `minInstances` equals `maxInstances` (the default is 1 and 1) loses its CPU and memory scaling policies and their CloudWatch alarms, because they could never change its instance count. The service keeps its scalable target and its instance count. Services whose `overrides` change the scalable target or a scaling policy keep both policies.
- **Web services behind the default HTTP API get a drain container.** Their tasks gain a small container that delays the application's stop signal by 35 seconds, so API Gateway stops sending requests before the application exits. It uses one of ECS's 10 container slots and 16 MiB of memory, and stopping a task takes about 36 seconds longer. The first rollout still stops the previous tasks without this delay; keep a shutdown delay in your application or deploy at a quiet time. The CLI copies the helper's image into the stack's ECR repository. Deployer roles with restricted permissions need `ecr:BatchGetImage`, `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability`, `ecr:InitiateLayerUpload`, `ecr:UploadLayerPart`, `ecr:CompleteLayerUpload` and `ecr:PutImage` on that repository, even when every application image is prebuilt.
- **A code-only deployment does not check application health by default.** It finishes when the new tasks run and the HTTP API can reach them. Add an `internalHealthCheck` so that a failing application fails and rolls back the deployment. See [web-service health checks](/resources/compute/web-service#health-checks).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What the first v4 deployment changes
docs.content:
### Batch jobs

Batch jobs now run on Amazon Linux 2023 instances, because AWS Batch stopped creating compute environments with its Amazon Linux 2 images on 30 June 2026. A compute environment last deployed by v3.0.10 or later keeps Amazon Linux 2: changing the image would make CloudFormation replace the environment and could interrupt jobs running on it. AWS keeps such environments running but no longer patches their image. An older environment, or one that a later change replaces anyway (such as a change to the stack's `tags`), moves to Amazon Linux 2023. CloudFormation then deletes the old environment, which can interrupt jobs still running on it, so deploy such a change when no jobs run; the change plan lists the compute environment as replaced. Amazon Linux 2023 requires IMDSv2 and uses cgroup v2; see [compute resources](/resources/compute/batch-job#compute-resources).

The first v4 deployment also gives each batch job an execution role with `AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy`, which the ECS agent uses to pull the job's image from ECR, write its logs and read its secrets. The job's own role is unchanged.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What the first v4 deployment changes
docs.content:
### Error tracking and security scanning

v4 turns on two features that send operational data to the Stacktape Console:

- **[Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking)** subscribes the log group of every function and `js-bundle` container to Stacktape's error detector, which runs in your account. The detector sends each error's message, stack frames and log line to the Console, with known kinds of sensitive values, such as tokens, passwords and email addresses, masked. Your logs stay in your account.
- **[Security scanning](/stacktape-console/security-scanning)** checks the stack's configuration and lists its dependencies during each deployment, and reports findings to the Console. It never blocks a deployment. The dependency list stays in your account's deployment bucket; the first scan downloads the Trivy scanner (about 50 MB) to the machine that deploys.

Each subscription filter is a CloudFormation resource: one per function and per container, plus one shared permission. A stack close to CloudFormation's limit of 500 resources per stack can exceed it; the CLI then stops before deploying and says how many resources error tracking added. If your v3 stack has more than about 480 resources, decide before the first v4 deploy. Turn error tracking off, or limit it to some stages, in `deploymentConfig`:


Example (YAML):

```yaml
deploymentConfig:
  errorTracking:
    stages:
      - production
  securityScanning:
    enabled: false
```


AWS allows two subscription filters per log group, so a log group that already has two of your own cannot take Stacktape's. Deployer roles with restricted permissions also need permission to create subscription filters.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What the first v4 deployment changes
docs.content:
### Helper resources that are removed

- **Development and debugging roles.** The stack's `<stack name>-dev-agent` IAM role and its `DevAgentRoleArn` output are deleted: only `stacktape dev` uses that role, and its dev stacks keep it. The read-only `<stack name>-debug-agent` role, which `aws call`, `query dynamodb` and `query opensearch` use, now reads only the stack's own resources in the stack's region. It no longer reads Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store values, other stacks' databases and caches, or the account-wide `aws/spans` trace log group. Automation that assumed either role for anything else needs its own role.
- **The tagging schedule.** On stacks without databases, load balancers or private service discovery, the deployment deletes Stacktape's internal tagging schedule (an EventBridge rule and its Lambda permission), which had nothing to tag.
- **The stack budget.** A stack last deployed by Stacktape 3.5 or earlier can have an AWS budget that tracks its monthly cost (in accounts where Stacktape's cost allocation tag is active), with email alerts only if the configuration set `budgetControl`. The deployment deletes it. Set budgets and their alerts in the Stacktape Console under Budgets.
- **CDN edge functions.** On stacks with a CDN, it deletes Stacktape's origin-response Lambda@Edge function unless a bucket sets custom metadata headers, the only case that uses it. It also deletes the origin-request Lambda@Edge function unless a bucket cache behaviour uses URL normalization or SPA routing without a custom origin-request handler. When no edge function remains, its internal artifact bucket is removed too. AWS may keep detached Lambda@Edge replicas for a few hours; this does not fail the update. After AWS releases the replicas, delete any retained function in `us-east-1` with `aws lambda delete-function --profile <profile> --region us-east-1 --function-name <name>`.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What changes after the first deployment
docs.content: ## What changes after the first deployment

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What changes after the first deployment
Failed deployments keep what they created
docs.content:
### Failed deployments keep what they created

v3 rolled a failed deployment back: a failed update returned the stack to its previous state, and a failed first deployment deleted the stack, including a database that had already taken minutes to create. In v4, a failed deployment keeps every resource it created or updated, unless it replaced existing resources: CloudFormation can only replace resources in a deployment it may roll back. The stack stays in `CREATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_FAILED`, and the next `stacktape deploy` continues from the failure.

To undo a failed update, run [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover); to remove a failed first deployment, run `stacktape delete`. A failed deployment can leave part of the application on the new version and part on the old one, so check the application after a failure. To keep v3's behaviour, see [Automatic rollback](#automatic-rollback). See [when a deployment fails](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#when-a-deployment-fails).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What changes after the first deployment
docs.content:
### After-deploy hooks fail the deployment

In v3, `deploy` reported success when an `afterDeploy` hook failed. In v4, the failure makes `stacktape deploy` exit with an error, so the CI job fails, and the hooks after it don't run. The stack is already deployed and stays on the new version; deploying again does not undo anything.

Keep this for hooks that must succeed, such as database migrations. For a hook that may fail without consequences, such as a notification, set `onFailure: continue`:


Example (YAML):

```yaml
hooks:
  afterDeploy:
    - scriptName: migrate
    - scriptName: notifyTeam
      onFailure: continue
```


See [When a hook fails](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts#when-a-hook-fails).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What changes after the first deployment
docs.content:
### Fast deployments are automatic

`stacktape deploy` updates functions and containers directly when only their code changed, without a CloudFormation update; v3 did this only with `--hotSwap`. Automation that waits for a CloudFormation stack update after every deployment no longer sees one for code-only changes. Use the CLI's result instead, or pass `--full` to deploy through CloudFormation every time. See [fast deployments](/cli/deploy#fast-deployments).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What changes after the first deployment
New non-production stages share a network
docs.content:
### New non-production stages share a network

A new non-production stage, such as `staging` or a preview stage, joins a VPC shared by the non-production stages in the same AWS account and region, instead of creating its own. Stages deployed before v4 keep their own VPC. A stage cannot move between the two after its first deployment. To give a new stage its own VPC, set `stackConfig.vpc.shared: false` before you deploy it the first time. See [Shared network for non-production stages](/configuration/shared-network), which also lists the permissions a restricted CI role needs.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: What changes after the first deployment
Deploy each upgraded stack only with v4
docs.content:
### Deploy each upgraded stack only with v4

After v4 deploys a stack, deploy it only with v4, from CI and from every developer machine. A v3 CLI rebuilds functions and containers in the v3 format and can delete images that v4's container helpers need.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Stacktape Console changes

The Console is updated to v4 for everyone at the same time as the v4 release, whichever CLI version you use.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: Configuration templates and generation are removed
docs.content:
### Configuration templates and generation are removed

Configurations live in your repository. The Console no longer stores configuration templates or offers the configuration editor, and the update deletes stored templates and the history of generated configurations. Export the ones you need [before the update](#before-you-upgrade).

A v3 CLI keeps deploying with a local configuration file, but these v3 features stop working against the v4 Console: `init` from a template (`--templateId`) and `init` that analyses the project to generate a configuration, connecting an AWS account from the CLI, and setting up Git deployments after a deploy. Use [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) from v4, and connect AWS accounts and Git providers in the Console.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Signing in to the Console

The Console has a new sign-in system.

- **Email and password:** sign in with your current password. The first sign-in moves it to the new system.
- **Google:** sign in with Google as before. Your account is linked by its email address.
- **GitHub:** new; you can link it in [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings).
- **Authenticator app:** if you used one, the first sign-in still asks for its code. Authenticator secrets cannot be moved, so the Console then asks you to set up the authenticator app, or a passkey, again. Until you do, your sign-ins do not count as two-factor, and an organization that requires two-factor sign-in asks you to set it up. SMS codes are no longer offered.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### CLI logins expire

A login made with `stacktape login` now lasts at most 90 days, and ends after 30 days without use. With the Console update, older or unused logins end at once, and the CLI reports that the API key has expired: run `stacktape login` again. API keys created in the Console for CI are not affected.

On Linux and Windows, the first v4 command on a machine moves the stored login into the operating system's credential store, and a v3 CLI on the same machine then asks you to log in again. On macOS, the login stays in `~/.stacktape`. See [`login`](/cli/login).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: Developers and Viewers reach only their AWS accounts
docs.content:
### Developers and Viewers reach only their AWS accounts

Before v4, every member of an organization reached every connected AWS account. Now Owners and Admins reach all accounts, and Developers and Viewers only the accounts chosen for them on the Members page. The update gives each Developer and Viewer the accounts their projects have deployed to, so day-to-day work continues. Someone who works with an account their projects never deployed to gets "Your access does not include the AWS account" until an Owner or Admin adds it.

CI that deploys with a person's API key stops working when that person loses access or leaves. Use an [organization key](/stacktape-console/api-keys#create-an-organization-key) instead. See [Project and AWS account access](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#project-and-aws-account-access).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Removed Console features

- **CodeBuild runners.** Deployments from Git and from the Console run on [EC2 runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) in your account. Projects that used CodeBuild need an EC2 runner.
- **Old GitLab and Bitbucket connections.** GitLab connections made with a personal or group access token and Bitbucket connections made with OAuth are removed, and projects that used them are no longer linked to a Git connection. Connect GitLab or Bitbucket again in the Console; to make such a project deploy on push again, email [support@stacktape.com](mailto:support@stacktape.com). GitHub connections are unchanged.
- **Hosted MCP server.** Remove the hosted Stacktape MCP server from your coding agent and run `stacktape mcp add`. See [Moving from the hosted MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup#moving-from-the-hosted-mcp-server).
- **Alarm rules in the Console.** Existing organization-wide alarm rules keep working as legacy rules, but the Console no longer creates or edits them. Use `stacktape alarm export` to [move them into stack configuration](/observability/alarms#migrating-legacy-console-alarm-rules).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Upgrading from a v4 preview

If you used a `4.0.0-preview` release, these changed since then:

- `deploymentConfig.issues` is now `deploymentConfig.errorTracking`, and the old name is rejected. The `issues:*` commands are now `error list`, `error ignore`, `error resolve` and `error reopen`; the old commands still work. Issue IDs and status values are unchanged.
- In the `--agent` result of `validate` and `deploy`, one `security` object replaces the `securityFindings` and `securityExposure` fields of `4.0.0-preview.10`: read `security.findings` and `security.exposure`. See [security findings by stage purpose](/cli/validate#security-findings-by-stage-purpose).
- The default Python runtime is `python3.13`, not `python3.14`. Set `runtime: python3.14` to keep it.
- An `agentcore-gateway` needs an explicit `authorizer`. A JWT authorizer moves under `properties` with `type: jwt` (`authorizer: { type: jwt, properties: { discoveryUrl: ... } }`). A gateway meant to be open sets `authorizer: { type: none }`.
- AgentCore timing fields name their unit: on a runtime, `lifecycle.maxLifetime` is now `maxLifetimeSeconds` and `lifecycle.idleRuntimeSessionTimeout` is `idleTimeoutSeconds`. On a memory, `expirationDays` and `eventExpiryDuration` are replaced by one `eventRetentionDays` (default 30). Values are unchanged.

docs.title: Database guardrails
docs.content:
# Database guardrails

These guardrails decide which SQL engines and instance sizes your team can use, and which Stacktape resource types are
off-limits. They appear under **Database restrictions** on **Security → Guardrails**.
[Guardrails overview](/guardrails/overview) explains who they bind and how to set them up.

Private network access and deletion protection for databases are on
[Security and data protection guardrails](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection).

docs.title: Database guardrails
docs.content:
## Allowed database engines

Every [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) must use one of the engines you list. Other
database types, such as DynamoDB, OpenSearch, Redis or Aurora DSQL, aren't checked; block them with
[Blocked resource types](#blocked-resource-types).

The engine identifiers are the values of `engine.type`:

| Family | Identifiers |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | `postgres`, `aurora-postgresql`, `aurora-postgresql-serverless-v2` |
| MySQL and MariaDB | `mysql`, `mariadb`, `aurora-mysql`, `aurora-mysql-serverless-v2` |
| Oracle | `oracle-ee`, `oracle-se2` |
| SQL Server | `sqlserver-ee`, `sqlserver-ex`, `sqlserver-se`, `sqlserver-web` |

To standardize on PostgreSQL, list all three PostgreSQL identifiers, so teams can still choose between a fixed instance,
Aurora and Aurora Serverless.

docs.title: Database guardrails
docs.content:
## Allowed database instance sizes

Every provisioned database instance must use one of the sizes you list, such as `db.t4g.medium`, `db.r6g.large`. The
check covers the primary instance and read replicas of standard RDS engines and the instances of Aurora clusters. Aurora
Serverless v2 has no instance size and isn't checked.

The list is an allowlist: a size nobody reviewed, including a new one AWS adds later, stays blocked until you add it.
Rules created before allowlists blocked listed sizes instead; they still work until you edit them.

docs.title: Database guardrails
docs.content:
## Blocked resource types

No config may declare a resource of the types you list, for example `open-search-domain` or `redis`. Any Stacktape
resource type can be listed, not only databases:

```text
Blocked by the organization guardrail "Blocked resource types". Resource `search` uses blocked type
`open-search-domain`. Blocked resource types: `open-search-domain`.
```

Use it for services your organization hasn't approved, or that cost more than a team should start on its own. A rule
that lists the old `redis-cluster` type also blocks `redis`.

docs.title: Deployment guardrails
docs.content:
# Deployment guardrails

These guardrails decide where and how your team can deploy: which stages and regions, which commands, and whether
public endpoints must use your own domain. They appear under **Deployment restrictions** on **Security → Guardrails**.
[Guardrails overview](/guardrails/overview) explains who they bind and how to set them up.

docs.title: Deployment guardrails
docs.content:
## Stage restriction

Commands may target only the stage names you list, such as `production`, `staging`, `dev`. A deploy, delete or any
other guarded command for a stage that isn't listed stops:

```text
Blocked by the organization guardrail "Stage restriction". Stage `pr-42` is not allowed. Allowed stages: `production`,
`staging`.
```

The rule compares the exact stage name. Use it to keep stage names to a convention. It doesn't check what was deployed
to another stage first, so it can't require a staging deploy before production; put that order in your
[CI pipeline](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd). Pull request previews (`pr-<number>`) can't be listed one by one, so an
organization that uses previews usually doesn't restrict stages.

docs.title: Deployment guardrails
docs.content:
## Region restriction

Commands may target only the AWS regions you list, such as `eu-west-1`, `eu-central-1`. The rule compares the stack's
region. It doesn't cover global AWS services such as CloudFront, IAM and Route 53, and it doesn't stop anyone from
using AWS directly. For a data residency
requirement, also restrict regions with an AWS Organizations service control policy.

docs.title: Deployment guardrails
docs.content:
## Command restriction

The commands you list don't run for anyone in the organization. You can block `deploy`, `delete`, `dev`, `rollback`,
`stack recover`, `script run` and `deployment-script run`. `diff` and `validate` always run, so developers can still
check a config.

Blocking `delete` stops only deletes through Stacktape. To stop a stack from being deleted by any tool, use
[Protect stacks from deletion](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#protect-stacks-from-deletion), which turns on
CloudFormation termination protection.

docs.title: Deployment guardrails
docs.content:
## Require custom domains

Every web service and hosting bucket must set `customDomains`, so users reach them on your domain instead of an
address AWS or Stacktape generated. See [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains) for setting them up.

docs.title: Guardrails overview
docs.content:
# Guardrails overview

A guardrail is an organization rule that the Stacktape CLI checks before it changes anything: allowed stages and
regions, blocked commands, size limits, and settings every stack must have, such as private databases or backups. A
deploy that breaks a rule stops before it touches AWS, with an error that names the rule. Owners and Admins set
guardrails in the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console), and they apply to every project of the
organization.

docs.title: Guardrails overview
docs.content:
## What guardrails check, and when

The CLI loads the organization's guardrails when it runs `deploy`, `diff`, `delete`, `dev`, `rollback`,
`stack recover`, `script run` or `deployment-script run`, and checks them against the command, the target stage and
region, and the config. `validate` and `synth` don't check them.

Guardrails bind every run that is signed in to the organization: developers' CLIs, CI with an organization key, and
[Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console). A run with AWS credentials alone, without a Stacktape
account, doesn't load them. Guardrails are a shared team standard, not an access control: to make sure nobody can
deploy outside the rules, also limit what the AWS credentials can do with IAM policies or AWS Organizations service
control policies. See [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions).

Guardrails check what a deploy asks for, not what already runs. A stack that breaks a new rule keeps running; its next
deploy stops until the config complies.

docs.title: Guardrails overview
docs.content:
## Set up a guardrail

1. In the Console sidebar, open **Security → Guardrails** and choose **All rules**.
2. For a rule with a value, such as allowed regions, click **Set up**, enter the values and click **Turn on**. For an
   on/off rule, such as private databases, flip its switch.
3. The **On** tab lists the rules your organization enforces. **Edit** changes a rule's values; **Turn off** removes
   it.

For rules that match a [security scanning](/stacktape-console/security-scanning) check, the row shows which stacks the
rule would block on their next deploy, before you turn it on. You can also turn a finding's check into a guardrail from
the finding's page. Changing guardrails needs the `org:manage-guardrails` permission (Owners and Admins); every member
can see them.

docs.title: Guardrails overview
docs.content:
## All guardrails

| Guardrail | Requires | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Stage restriction | Only the listed stage names | [Deployment](/guardrails/deployment#stage-restriction) |
| Region restriction | Only the listed AWS regions | [Deployment](/guardrails/deployment#region-restriction) |
| Command restriction | The listed commands don't run | [Deployment](/guardrails/deployment#command-restriction) |
| Require custom domains | Web services and hosting buckets use your own domain | [Deployment](/guardrails/deployment#require-custom-domains) |
| Keep SQL and OpenSearch private | Databases and OpenSearch use a VPC access mode | [Security](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#keep-sql-and-opensearch-private) |
| Protect stacks from deletion | CloudFormation termination protection | [Security](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#protect-stacks-from-deletion) |
| Protect databases from deletion | `deletionProtection` on SQL and Aurora DSQL databases | [Security](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#protect-databases-from-deletion) |
| Require recoverable data stores | Backups for SQL databases, DynamoDB and EFS | [Security](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#require-recoverable-data-stores) |
| Require dead-letter queue | A dead-letter queue for every SQS queue | [Security](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#require-dead-letter-queue) |
| Require WAF on application load balancers | A web application firewall on every load balancer | [Security](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#require-waf-on-application-load-balancers) |
| Require two container instances | At least two instances of each container service | [Security](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection#require-two-container-instances) |
| Function memory limit | Function memory at or under a maximum | [Resource limits](/guardrails/resource-limits#function-memory-limit) |
| Function timeout limit | Function timeout at or under a maximum | [Resource limits](/guardrails/resource-limits#function-timeout-limit) |
| Container resource limit | Container vCPU and memory at or under a maximum | [Resource limits](/guardrails/resource-limits#container-resource-limit) |
| Stacktape resource count limit | At most so many resources in one config | [Resource limits](/guardrails/resource-limits#stacktape-resource-count-limit) |
| Allowed database engines | Only the listed SQL engines | [Databases](/guardrails/databases#allowed-database-engines) |
| Allowed database instance sizes | Only the listed instance sizes | [Databases](/guardrails/databases#allowed-database-instance-sizes) |
| Blocked resource types | None of the listed resource types | [Databases](/guardrails/databases#blocked-resource-types) |

All rules apply to the whole organization; there are no per-project or per-stage exceptions. A team that needs
different rules for an experiment uses a separate Stacktape organization.

docs.title: Guardrails overview
docs.content:
## When a deploy is blocked

The CLI stops with a `GUARDRAIL_…` error that starts with the rule's name and says what broke it:

```text
Blocked by the organization guardrail "Keep SQL and OpenSearch private". Database `mainDb` uses accessibility mode
`internet`. It must use `vpc` or `scoping-workloads-in-vpc`.
```

Change the config and deploy again, or ask an Owner or Admin to change the rule. `stacktape diff` shows the same error,
so you can check a fix without deploying.

Guardrails stop a deploy before it happens. [Security scanning](/stacktape-console/security-scanning) reports risky
settings and vulnerable packages after each deploy and never blocks one. [Alarms](/observability/alarms) watch the
running stack.

docs.title: Resource limit guardrails
docs.content:
# Resource limit guardrails

These guardrails set upper limits on sizes, under **Resource limits** on **Security → Guardrails**. They stop mistakes,
such as 10 GB of memory where 1 GB was meant, not spending; for spend, set a [budget](/managing-costs/budgets).
[Guardrails overview](/guardrails/overview) explains who they bind and how to set them up.

docs.title: Resource limit guardrails
docs.content:
## Function memory limit

Every function's `memory` must be at or under the maximum (128 to 10,240 MB). The check covers
[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and [edge functions](/resources/compute/edge-function).
A function that doesn't set `memory` counts as 1,024 MB, so a limit below that blocks functions on their defaults.

```text
Blocked by the organization guardrail "Function memory limit". Function `imageResizer` uses `3008 MB`, exceeding the
`2048 MB` limit.
```

Most functions run well between 256 and 2,048 MB. A ceiling of 2,048 or 3,008 MB catches typos and leaves room for
memory-heavy work such as image processing.

docs.title: Resource limit guardrails
docs.content:
## Function timeout limit

Every function's `timeout` must be at or under the maximum (1 to 900 seconds), for Lambda and edge functions. A function
that doesn't set `timeout` counts as 20 seconds.

A long timeout often means the work belongs in a [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) or a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job). A limit of 30 to 60 seconds covers most APIs and event handlers.

docs.title: Resource limit guardrails
docs.content:
## Container resource limit

Every container workload's `resources.cpu` and `resources.memory` must be at or under the maximums you set. It covers
web, private and worker services and multi-container workloads. Set one value to cap only that one. A workload that
doesn't set `cpu` or `memory`, such as one that runs on EC2 instance types, isn't checked for that value.

docs.title: Resource limit guardrails
docs.content:
## Stacktape resource count limit

A config may declare at most so many resources (1 to 10,000). Each resource in your config counts once, however many
AWS resources it creates. Use it to keep stacks small enough to understand; CloudFormation's own limit of 500 resources
per stack is counted separately, by AWS.

To forbid whole resource types, such as OpenSearch, use [Blocked resource types](/guardrails/databases#blocked-resource-types).

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
docs.content:
# Security and data protection guardrails

These guardrails require settings that protect data and keep services running, in every stack of the organization.
Each is an on/off switch under **Security & data protection** or **Reliability** on **Security → Guardrails**. When
one blocks a deploy, the error names the resource; the fix for each is below. [Guardrails
overview](/guardrails/overview) explains who they bind and how to turn them on.

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
docs.content:
## Keep SQL and OpenSearch private

This guardrail checks the access mode of [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) and
[OpenSearch domains](/resources/databases/opensearch). Their `accessibilityMode` must be `vpc` or
`scoping-workloads-in-vpc`; the default, `internet`, is refused, and so is `whitelisted-ips-only`.

It doesn't check `whitelistedIps`. A relational database in a VPC mode still accepts connections from the addresses
listed there, and keeps a public IP address unless `forceDisablePublicIp` is `true`. For a database that only the VPC
can reach, leave `whitelistedIps` out and turn the public IP off:

```yaml
resources:
  mainDb:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      accessibility:
        accessibilityMode: vpc
        forceDisablePublicIp: true
```

[Aurora DSQL](/resources/databases/dsql) databases are refused while this guardrail is on: they use a public
service endpoint, and Stacktape can't set up the private endpoint they would need yet.

Once a database is private, tools on your machine reach it through a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host),
for example with `stacktape query sql --bastion-resource`. DynamoDB has no network setting and isn't checked.

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
docs.content:
## Protect stacks from deletion

Every stack must set `deploymentConfig.terminationProtection: true`:

```yaml
deploymentConfig:
  terminationProtection: true
```

CloudFormation then refuses to delete the stack from any tool, including the AWS console. A
[command restriction](/guardrails/deployment#command-restriction) on `delete` stops only Stacktape's own command.

While this guardrail is on, a deploy with `terminationProtection: false` is refused too. To delete a stack, an Owner
or Admin first turns the guardrail off, then you deploy with protection off and delete. Guardrails apply to the whole
organization, so other stacks lose the rule meanwhile.

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
docs.content:
## Protect databases from deletion

Every relational database and Aurora DSQL database must set `deletionProtection: true`. AWS then refuses to delete the
database, and `stacktape delete` stops before deleting anything while a protected database is in the stack. A deploy
can't remove or replace it either. To delete it, an Owner or Admin first turns the guardrail off, then you deploy
with `deletionProtection: false` and delete.

```yaml
resources:
  mainDb:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      deletionProtection: true
```

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
docs.content:
## Require recoverable data stores

Data stores must keep backups:

| Resource | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Relational database | `automatedBackupRetentionDays` at least 1 (the default is 1; 0 is refused) |
| DynamoDB table | `enablePointInTimeRecovery: true` |
| EFS filesystem | `backupEnabled: true` |
| Aurora DSQL database | Refused: Stacktape can't check an AWS Backup plan for it yet |

Backups add storage cost. They don't replace trying a restore; see the
[relational database backups](/resources/databases/relational-database#backups-and-maintenance) section.

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
docs.content:
## Require dead-letter queue

Every [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) must have a `redrivePolicy`, so messages that keep failing move to a
dead-letter queue instead of being retried until they expire. A queue that another queue uses as its dead-letter queue
doesn't need one itself.

```yaml
resources:
  orders:
    type: sqs-queue
    properties:
      redrivePolicy:
        targetSqsQueueName: ordersDlq
        maxReceiveCount: 5
  ordersDlq:
    type: sqs-queue
```

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
headingPath: Require WAF on application load balancers
docs.content:
## Require WAF on application load balancers

Every application load balancer must name a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall)
in `useFirewall`. This covers the load balancers you declare and those that web and private services create; on a web
service, `useFirewall` is a property of the service. The internal load balancer of a self-hosted Convex resource has no firewall setting and is skipped.

A web service uses an HTTP API Gateway by default, and `useFirewall` works only with an application load balancer, so
set `loadBalancing` next to it. The firewall must have the `regional` scope.

```yaml
resources:
  firewall:
    type: web-app-firewall
    properties:
      scope: regional
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      loadBalancing:
        type: application-load-balancer
      useFirewall: firewall
```

A firewall adds a monthly AWS WAF charge per web ACL and per rule, plus a charge per million requests.

docs.title: Security and data protection guardrails
docs.content:
## Require two container instances

Every container service must run at least two instances (`scaling.minInstances: 2` or more), so one failing task
doesn't take it down. It roughly doubles the service's baseline compute cost. Self-hosted Convex runs one backend by
design and is skipped.

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      scaling:
        minInstances: 2
        maxInstances: 4
```

Other database rules, such as allowed engines and instance sizes, are on [Database guardrails](/guardrails/databases).

docs.content:
# Deploy your app to your own AWS account

Stacktape is an open-source CLI. It reads your project, writes the infrastructure config with you and deploys it with your own AWS credentials. A Console for teams is optional.

Run it in your project directory:

- macOS: `curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/macos.sh | sh -s -- init`
- Linux: `curl -fsSL https://installs.stacktape.com/linux.sh | sh -s -- init`
- Windows: `iex "& { $(irm https://installs.stacktape.com/windows.ps1) } init"`
- npm: `npx stacktape@latest init`

It opens a wizard in your browser. You review the setup and its monthly price, then deploy. No Stacktape account needed.

- [Quickstart](/getting-started)
- [Starting a new project?](/getting-started/start-a-new-project)

headingPath: A config and what it creates
docs.content:
## A config and what it creates

An API container and a Postgres database that only the API can reach. Init writes a file like this for you, and you can change it by hand. TypeScript configs get type checking and autocomplete.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  WebService,
  JsBundleImagePackaging,
  RelationalDatabase,
  RdsEnginePostgres,
  $Secret
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const database = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '18',
      primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' }
    }),
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: $Secret('db-password')
    },
    accessibility: {
      accessibilityMode: 'scoping-workloads-in-vpc'
    }
  });

  const api = new WebService({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/server.ts'
    }),
    resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 },
    connectTo: [database]
  });

  return { resources: { api, database } };
});
```


Example (YAML):

```yaml
resources:
  database:
    type: relational-database
    properties:
      engine:
        type: postgres
        properties:
          version: '18'
          primaryInstance:
            instanceSize: db.t4g.micro
      credentials:
        masterUserPassword: $Secret('db-password')
      accessibility:
        accessibilityMode: scoping-workloads-in-vpc
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/server.ts
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
      connectTo:
        - database
```


What it creates in your AWS account, in the stack `my-api-dev`:

- `api` (WebService), connected by HTTPS requests:
  - HTTP API Gateway: The public URL
  - ECS on Fargate: Your container, 0.25 vCPU and 512 MB, in the VPC
- `database` (RelationalDatabase), connected by `connectTo`: private, inside the VPC:
  - RDS Postgres 18: db.t4g.micro, reachable only from `api`
- `STP_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING` in the container environment
- Security groups, an IAM role and CloudWatch logs
- A generated database password, kept in AWS Secrets Manager

Deploy it:

1. Create the stack. The first deploy generates the database password.: `stacktape deploy --project my-api --stage dev --region eu-west-1`

docs.content:
### Where it runs

AWS resources are created in your account, one CloudFormation stack per stage. MongoDB Atlas and Upstash resources, if you use them, live with those providers. Stacktape gets access to your AWS account only if you connect the Console. [Using the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli)

docs.title: Start here
docs.content:
### What leaves your account

Without the Console: anonymous CLI telemetry, which you can turn off, and the config init sends for its price estimate. With the Console: alarm state changes, uptime results, monthly cost breakdowns, security findings and errors. Application logs stay in CloudWatch; each recorded error sends a masked copy of its log line. AI features send data to the provider of your own key, and only when you use them. [What each feature sends](/observability/overview#what-leaves-your-aws-account)

docs.title: Start here
docs.content:
### How you would leave

Your stacks are plain CloudFormation in your account and keep running without Stacktape. `stacktape synth` writes the template to a file. To leave, you take over the stacks and replace the few parts the CLI did for you. [Stop using Stacktape](/getting-started/evaluate/stop-using-stacktape)
