docs.content:
### Networking

Non-production stages in one account and region share a VPC, each with its own security groups. Production stages get their own. The first deploy decides, so choose before it. Databases accept internet connections with credentials by default: `accessibilityMode` limits who can connect, and `forceDisablePublicIp` removes the public IP. [Shared network](/configuration/shared-network)

docs.title: Start here
docs.content:
### CI/CD

Your pipeline runs `stacktape deploy` with AWS credentials, no Stacktape account needed. Init can write a GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or Bitbucket pipeline. With the Console, a push deploys and each pull request can get its own preview stage. [CI/CD options](/ci-cd-and-gitops/overview)

docs.title: Start here
docs.content:
### Observability

Logs, metrics and alarms stay in CloudWatch and work from the CLI. The Console adds error tracking, incidents and uptime checks. [Observability](/observability/overview)

docs.title: Start here
docs.content:
### Costs

Init estimates the monthly price from AWS list prices before the first deploy. The Console shows what each stage costs and alerts you on budgets. [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview)

### Access

The Console has roles per organization and project, two-factor sign-in and an audit log on every plan. SSO and SCIM come with the Flexible plan. AWS access covers a whole account: whoever can deploy to it can reach every stack in it, so keep production and each client in their own account. docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
# Debugging Lambda functions

Stacktape [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) runs Lambda functions on real AWS infrastructure while you iterate on code locally. Stacktape deploys a dev stack to run selected functions on AWS. The dev TUI shows logs and supports on-demand rebuilds: giving you a fast edit-test loop without running a full stack deployment.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## How it works

Lambda functions are dev-compatible workloads that deploy to the AWS-backed dev stack and execute on AWS Lambda. Unlike [container workloads](/local-development/dev-mode-overview#what-runs-where) that run locally in Docker, Lambda functions run in their real cloud environment. This surfaces issues that local emulation would miss: you test against AWS Lambda rather than a local approximation.

Stacktape deploys a dev stack when one does not already exist for the target stage. Your selection in the resource picker controls which workloads dev mode starts and renders in the TUI. Unchanged starts reuse the existing dev stack. Restarting after cloud configuration or cloud-image changes, or with missing required outputs, can update it. The dev TUI then launches with log output, keyboard controls for rebuilding functions, and status for any [local databases](/local-development/local-databases) you selected.

1. **Load config**: Stacktape reads your configuration and discovers dev-compatible resources (functions, containers, databases)
2. **Select resources**: Choose which resources to run via the interactive picker or `--resources` / `--skip-resources` flags
3. **Deploy dev stack**: A dev stack is deployed automatically on first run
4. **Start local databases**: Selected databases run as Docker containers on your machine
5. **Connect the dev box**: when deployed functions use local databases, dev mode starts the [dev box](#connecting-to-local-databases) if it is stopped and opens one tunnel per database
6. **Run workloads and stream logs**: Functions are deployed, logs appear in the dev TUI, and you can rebuild on demand

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### First-time setup

The first run deploys a dev stack. Dev mode never updates or deletes a stack it did not create, regardless of its name or status. Choose another stage, or explicitly delete an unwanted stack. A dev stack in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` cannot be updated: delete it explicitly before starting again. A dev stack in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` can restart normally. A stack still rolling back or in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` must finish or recover before an update can proceed.

Use a dedicated stage name for dev mode: `dev`, `dev-local`, or a personal stage like `dev-jane`.


> **Warning:** Dev mode and full deployments share the same stage namespace. Running `stacktape dev --stage production` against an existing `production` deployment will be rejected. Always use a separate stage name for dev mode.


If your config includes `beforeDev` [hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) with a `scriptName`, dev mode registers those hook names in the dev TUI during startup.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Rebuilds

After changing your function code, rebuild it from the dev TUI without leaving the session, or start dev mode with `--watch` to rebuild on save.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+R** | Rebuild. With several workloads, pick one by its number, `a` for all, or Esc to cancel |
| **Ctrl+A** | Rebuild all workloads |
| **Tab** | Switch between the overview and the logs |
| **Ctrl+C** | Stop dev mode |

When you work on one function, rebuild only that one: the others keep running untouched. A rebuild that fails, for example on a syntax error, shows the error and the function keeps its previous code.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Viewing logs

Stacktape provides two ways to view Lambda function logs: real-time streaming in the dev TUI during active development, and historical log fetching with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) for deployed stages.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### Dev TUI log streaming

The Stacktape dev TUI shows logs for running workloads during the dev session, giving you immediate feedback on each invocation. Logs appear within the TUI alongside status information for all running workloads and local resources. This is the primary debugging interface during active development: you see function output, errors, and stack traces without leaving your terminal.


> **Tip:** Structure your Lambda function output as JSON objects. JSON logs are easier to search and filter, both in the dev TUI and later with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) and CloudWatch Logs Insights when investigating production issues.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### Historical logs with logs

Outside of dev mode, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) to fetch logs for a Stacktape resource in a deployed stack. For Lambda debugging, pass the Lambda function resource name with `--resource-name`.

View logs for a specific function:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage production
```

By default, `stacktape logs` uses a one-hour start time and returns up to 100 events.

View the last 30 minutes of logs:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage production --since 30m
```

Filter logs containing a specific pattern:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage production --filter "ERROR"
```

Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query for structured searching:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage production --query "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /error/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20"
```

The `--since` flag accepts relative values (`1h`, `30m`, `1d`, `5s`) and absolute ISO timestamps. Use `--limit` to control how many log events are returned. `--until` sets the upper time boundary for `--query` Logs Insights queries. `--raw` switches the standard log-fetching output to machine-readable JSON; the `--query` path prints formatted results unless agent mode is active.


> **Warning:** CloudWatch Logs Insights queries (via `--query`) are billed by the amount of data scanned. For high-volume functions, use narrow time ranges and specific filters to control cost.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Connecting to local databases

Deployed dev functions reach the [local databases](/local-development/local-databases) on your machine through the **dev box**. A function that uses a local database, through `connectTo` or `$ResourceParam`, gets the database's usual `STP_*` variables pointing at the box, and the box forwards each connection to your machine.

```
dev function (dev network, private subnet) ──► dev box ──► Systems Manager session ──► your machine ──► local database
```

Nothing is published on the internet. Your machine opens the connection to the box, through an AWS Systems Manager session authenticated by your AWS credentials and encrypted. On the box, the relay port of each database admits only dev functions.

The AWS account is the trust boundary. Every dev function in the account's dev network can reach every developer's relay ports, not only the functions of that developer's stage. Local DynamoDB and OpenSearch have no password, and local Redis has one only when its `defaultUserPassword` is set; Postgres and MySQL always have one. The passwords of local databases, including the ones Stacktape generates, are written into the dev functions' environment variables, so they appear in the dev stack's Lambda configuration and CloudFormation template. They are valid only for the databases on your machine. Use a separate AWS account for people who must not reach each other's local databases.

A database's relay port stays open for 2 minutes after its session ends, so a session that restarts finds it open. A function that connects while no session holds the port, for example a schedule that fires during a restart, waits up to 30 seconds for the next session of the stage and then reaches its database. When no session comes back in time, the box closes the connection, and the database client reports a closed connection. A connection is refused when no session has opened the port since the box started, or when the last session ended more than 2 minutes before.

A query takes your machine's round trip to the region plus a few milliseconds; about 45 ms from Central Europe to `eu-west-1`. Bulk transfers are limited to about 0.7 MB/s per developer by Systems Manager, so a query that returns 5 MB takes about 7 s. Seeding or exporting large amounts of data is faster from your machine directly.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### The dev network

The first `stacktape dev` that needs it creates the **dev network** of the AWS account and region, once; every later session and stage reuses it. Creating it takes about 4 minutes, most of it Lambda creating the network interfaces of dev functions. The dev stack deploys meanwhile, so a first start that creates both takes about 5 minutes. The network has:

- a VPC with private subnets, where dev functions that use a local database run, and every dev function with `joinDefaultVpc: true`. All of them share one security group, so new dev stages create their functions in seconds;
- the dev box, a `t4g.nano` EC2 instance. It runs the relay for local databases and gives VPC functions internet access (it is their NAT).

A dev stage no longer creates a VPC or NAT of its own. VPC functions work in dev mode and reach the internet through the box. The exception is a dev stage that still deploys VPC resources itself, such as a database marked `dev.remote`: its VPC functions stay in that stage's VPC and cannot reach local databases.

The dev box costs about $0.01 per hour while a dev session runs. It stops itself 30 minutes after the last session ends, and the next `stacktape dev` starts it again (the TUI shows "Starting the dev box…", which takes about 30 seconds and overlaps the rest of startup). A stopped box costs about $0.75 per month for its disk and the SSM parameter that holds its relay. While it is stopped, dev functions in the network have no internet access: schedules and queue consumers of a dev stage that fire while nobody develops fail until the next session.

See the network with [`stacktape dev network`](/cli/dev-network) and delete it with [`stacktape dev network delete`](/cli/dev-network-delete).

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### Several developers

Each developer runs dev mode against their own stage, and every stage gets its own relay ports. A stage's deployed functions can reach only one session's databases, so one dev session at a time holds a stage. This also applies to one developer running the same stage in two worktrees or on two machines.

A second `stacktape dev` for a stage that another session holds is refused before it deploys anything. The error names the holder: the user, the host and the project directory. Run it again with [`--take-over`](/cli/dev#--take-over) to move all of the stage's ports to the new session at once. The first session's open database connections, such as a warm function's connection pool, are closed. The first session stops itself with a message that names the new one, so it cannot redeploy functions over the new session's. The deployed functions then reach only the new session's databases.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### AWS permissions

The AWS identity that runs `stacktape dev` needs, besides the usual deployment permissions: `cloudformation:DescribeStacks` on the dev network stack, `ec2:DescribeInstances`, `ec2:StartInstances` on the box, `ssm:DescribeInstanceInformation`, `ssm:StartSession` on the dev box and on the `AWS-StartPortForwardingSession` document, `ssm:TerminateSession`, and `ssm:GetParameters`, `ssm:GetParametersByPath`, `ssm:PutParameter`, `ssm:DeleteParameter` and `ssm:DeleteParameters` on `/stacktape/dev-network/*`, where the relay port leases, their port reservations and the record of which session runs each stage are kept. Without the read, a start elsewhere is refused only after the dev network step; without the delete, starts in another directory or on another machine are refused for up to 3 minutes after a session stops.

When a newer Stacktape version brings a new relay, the first session that finds the box running an older one restarts the relay with SSM Run Command, without stopping the box. Other sessions on the box lose their connections for a few seconds and reconnect on their own. This needs `ssm:SendCommand` on the dev box and on the `AWS-RunShellScript` document, and `ssm:GetCommandInvocation`. Without them, dev mode warns and runs with the older relay, and the next session tries again.

When dev mode generates a missing database password for a `$Secret`, it tags the secret with each dev stage that uses it. Creating it needs `secretsmanager:CreateSecret` and `secretsmanager:TagResource`. `stacktape delete` of a dev stage never deletes the secret: it removes the stage's tag (`secretsmanager:ListSecrets`, `secretsmanager:UntagResource`) and prints `Kept generated secret <name>`. Delete it with [`stacktape secret delete`](/cli/secret-delete) when no stage needs it. A deployment that is not a dev session removes the dev tags, and the secret is then the deployment's. Stacktape 4.0.0-preview.11 and earlier scheduled a deleted stage's generated secrets for deletion; a deployment or dev session that uses a secret scheduled this way restores it (`secretsmanager:RestoreSecret`).

Container workloads that run on your machine use the AWS permissions of their role in the dev stack: dev mode assumes the role with your credentials, so they need `sts:AssumeRole` on it. When your IAM permissions don't allow that, the container's start fails with `AWS_ASSUME_ROLE_NOT_PERMITTED` and the policy statement to add, instead of waiting for AWS. The container roles of the dev stack trust your AWS account only for your own IAM user, or the IAM role of your session (an `aws:PrincipalArn` condition), and no other principal. Credentials of a federated user cannot be named this way; for them, dev mode adds the trust after the deploy, and a container's first start on a new stage can then wait several minutes until AWS accepts it.

The first session in an account and region creates the dev network with CloudFormation, using the credentials of whoever runs it. That identity also needs `ssm:GetParameter` on the public Amazon Linux parameter `/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64`, `cloudformation:ListStackResources` on the dev network stack, and the rights to create the network's VPC, subnets, route tables, internet gateway, security groups, launch template, EC2 instance, IAM role and instance profile (with `iam:PassRole`), and the keeper Lambda function. The box starts before CloudFormation has finished its instance profile, which takes about 2 minutes, and the session attaches the profile once it exists. That needs `ec2:AssociateIamInstanceProfile` on the box and `iam:PassRole` on its role (`stacktape-dev-network-…-BoxRole-…`). When the first session is interrupted before it attaches the profile, the next session in the account and region attaches it, so every developer whose session may come next needs these two rights too. `stacktape dev network` and `stacktape dev network delete` also need `lambda:ListFunctions`, and the deletion needs the rights to delete those resources. While the box runs, the deletion asks it for live sessions over Systems Manager, with the same `ssm:DescribeInstanceInformation`, `ssm:StartSession` and `ssm:TerminateSession` rights as a session.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### Skipping the tunnels

`--no-tunnel` keeps deployed functions away from your local databases for one session; they get no database variables. VPC functions still run in the dev network. To connect functions to deployed databases instead, use `--remote-resources`.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Using a database in AWS

Dev mode runs supported databases locally. When a function needs a real AWS database, pass its name in `--remote-resources`:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --remote-resources myDatabase
```

The dev stack then deploys that database in AWS for the dev stage, or reuses the one an earlier session created. It costs what the database costs until you delete the dev stage. It is not the database of a deployed stage such as `production`. See [Local databases](/local-development/local-databases#using-remote-databases).

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Environment cleanup

Stacktape registers cleanup hooks when dev mode starts. When you press `Ctrl+C` or the process receives SIGTERM, Stacktape runs the registered cleanup hooks. Dev mode registers hooks for:

- **Credentials**: temporary credentials used during the dev session
- **Local resources**: Docker containers for local databases
- **Health monitor**: the local resource health monitor
- **Dev server**: the dev server process
- **Tunnels**: the tunnels to the dev box and its Systems Manager session
- **Named proxy**: the named proxy process

The dev TUI prints a cleanup summary showing which workloads, local resources, and tunnels are being stopped.

Dev mode does not change deployed functions at session start or exit: they are deployed with the dev box address, which stays valid. If dev mode exits unexpectedly (process kill, power loss), the next start of the same stage ends the Systems Manager session the old one left open.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Agent mode

For AI-assisted debugging workflows, dev mode supports an `--agent` flag that starts a background daemon with an HTTP API. Agent mode registers rebuild handlers and keeps workload and local-resource state updated for the agent server. See [agent mode in dev](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev) for the supported API surface.

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --agent
```

The agent daemon starts on port 7331 when available. If you do not pass `--agent-port`, Stacktape finds an available port starting at 7331. Use `--agent-port` to request a specific agent port. Stop a running agent with [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop):

```bash
stacktape dev stop --agent-port 7331
```

When agent mode is enabled, dev mode updates agent state with workload and local-resource details and registers rebuild handlers. For endpoint-level details, API documentation, integration with coding assistants, and common workflows, see [agent mode in dev](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev).

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Debugging strategies

Lambda functions in dev mode run on AWS infrastructure rather than locally, so the documented debugging path is log streaming in the dev TUI combined with targeted rebuilds. The strategies below help you get the most out of this workflow.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### Testing HTTP-triggered functions

For Lambda functions with [HTTP API Gateway triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers), invoke the function's endpoint directly with curl, a browser, or any HTTP client while watching logs stream in the dev TUI. For HTTP-triggered Lambda functions, use the URL shown by dev mode when one is available, or inspect the deployed stack outputs for the endpoint.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
### Narrowing the feedback loop

When debugging a specific function, use `--resources <name>` to select it for session rebuilds, watching and logs. Unselected functions are not built: they keep the code they run until you select them again. Rebuild just that function with **Ctrl+R**. Selected Lambda functions are deployed by Stacktape during dev mode, so exercise their configured triggers as you normally would (invoke HTTP endpoints, send messages into queues like [SQS](/resources/triggers/sqs-events), or wait for [schedules](/resources/triggers/schedule-triggers)) and watch the function process events live in the dev TUI.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content:
## Dev mode vs deployed-stack debugging

Stacktape offers two distinct workflows for investigating Lambda function behavior: interactive dev mode for active development, and [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) for historical log analysis on deployed stages. Choose based on whether you are iterating on code or investigating an issue in an existing deployment.

| Aspect | Dev mode (`stacktape dev`) | Deployed stack (`logs`) |
|--------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Log delivery | Streamed in the dev TUI | Follows CloudWatch logs in a terminal by default; `--follow=false` takes a snapshot |
| Code iteration | **Ctrl+R** in the TUI, or `--watch` | Run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) again; a code-only change is a [fast deploy](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#fast-deployments) that takes seconds |
| Database access | Local databases through the dev box, or deployed ones via `--remote-resources` | AWS-deployed databases |
| Interaction model | Interactive TUI with keyboard shortcuts | Follows until stopped, or exits after a snapshot |
| Infrastructure | Dev stack | Full production stack |
| Local resources | Docker-based databases on your machine | Not applicable |
| Best for | Active development and rapid iteration | Investigating issues in deployed stages |

Use dev mode for active development: the rebuild-and-test loop from the TUI is significantly faster than deploying each change. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) for investigating issues in deployed production or staging stacks where you need historical logs without disrupting the running environment. You can also view logs in the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
headingPath: Can I set breakpoints in Lambda functions during dev mode?
docs.content:
### Can I set breakpoints in Lambda functions during dev mode?

Lambda functions in dev mode run on AWS Lambda infrastructure, not on your local machine. The debugging path documented here is log streaming in the dev TUI combined with targeted rebuilds (**Ctrl+R**). The tradeoff is high-fidelity testing against the real Lambda runtime on AWS. Add targeted `console.info(JSON.stringify(...))` statements at key points and rebuild quickly after changes.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
headingPath: Do my Lambda function's event sources work in dev mode?
docs.content:
### Do my Lambda function's event sources work in dev mode?

Lambda functions are included as dev-compatible workloads, and dev mode deploys a dev stack that includes selected functions. To verify a trigger during dev mode, invoke the function's configured entry point (call the HTTP endpoint directly, send a message to a connected queue, or wait for a scheduled trigger) and watch the dev TUI logs for output. See [triggers overview](/resources/triggers/overview) for the available event source types.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
headingPath: Can I debug only some functions while keeping others untouched?
docs.content:
### Can I debug only some functions while keeping others untouched?

Use `--resources myApi,myWorker` to select functions, or `--skip-resources myWorker` to exclude one. Selection limits which functions the running session rebuilds and watches. Updating the dev stack does not build unselected functions, so a broken function you skip does not fail the start: it keeps running the code it ran before, and the session's status lists it with when that code was deployed. Changes to its source are deployed only once you select it again. A function is built anyway when the dev stack has no code for it yet (a new dev stack or function) or when its configuration changed, such as its environment, memory or permissions: its old code never ran with the new configuration. The start output says why. Unselected functions stay in the dev stack with their configured triggers removed. Use a separate stage when another session's triggers need to keep running. Batch jobs cannot be selected or skipped; use a dev-specific configuration to omit them or disable their triggers, and restart dev mode after changing Batch code.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
headingPath: Why does dev mode refuse to start on my stage?
docs.content:
### Why does dev mode refuse to start on my stage?

Dev mode refuses any stack it did not create, regardless of name or status. Use a dedicated stage such as `dev-jane`. A dev stack in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` requires explicit deletion before restarting; see [first-time setup](#first-time-setup).

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
headingPath: How do my local databases connect to functions running on AWS?
docs.content:
### How do my local databases connect to functions running on AWS?

Through the dev box of your account's dev network: functions connect to the box's private address, and the box forwards each connection to your machine over an encrypted Systems Manager session. See [Connecting to local databases](#connecting-to-local-databases).

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
headingPath: How much does running dev mode cost?
docs.content:
### How much does running dev mode cost?

Dev mode deploys a dev stack on real AWS infrastructure, so standard AWS charges apply for the resources it runs (Lambda invocations, API Gateway endpoints, and other deployed resources). The dev box costs about $0.01 per hour while a dev session runs and about $0.75 per month while it is stopped. Selected local databases run on your machine as Docker containers, so no AWS database service charges apply for those during the dev session. Note that `stacktape logs` CloudWatch Logs Insights queries (via `--query`) are billed by the amount of data scanned: use narrow time ranges and specific filters on high-volume functions.

docs.title: Debugging Lambda functions
headingPath: How do I view logs from a Lambda function that's already deployed?
docs.content:
### How do I view logs from a Lambda function that's already deployed?

Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) with `--resource-name` and `--stage` to fetch CloudWatch logs from any deployed stage. In a terminal, it shows the last hour of logs (up to 100 events), then follows new lines. Use `--follow=false` for a snapshot; piped, redirected and agent runs take snapshots unless `--follow` is requested. Add `--filter "ERROR"` to narrow results, or use `--query` for CloudWatch Logs Insights queries that can search structured JSON fields across log streams. You can also view logs in the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
# Dev mode

[`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) runs your app on your machine while it stays connected to AWS. Containers and local copies of your databases run in Docker. Frontends run on their own dev servers. [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) are built on your machine and run in AWS, with their logs in your terminal. You edit code, save, and see the result without a deploy.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## What you need

- **A Stacktape configuration.** `stacktape dev` reads the same `stacktape.ts` you deploy. [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) creates one.
- **Docker running.** Containers and local databases need it. A config with only Lambda functions and no local databases works without Docker.
- **AWS credentials** for the account you develop in. The first run deploys a small dev stack there. A Stacktape account is not needed.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Start dev mode

Run it in the directory with your `stacktape.ts`:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

A picker lists the resources dev mode can run, all of them selected. Deselect what you don't need and press Enter. To skip the picker, name the resources or pass `all`:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --resources all
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --resources myApi,myDatabase
```

The first run deploys the dev stack: IAM roles, secrets and the routing local development needs. When deployed functions use local databases or join the VPC, it also creates the account's [dev network](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#the-dev-network). A first start that creates both takes about 5 minutes. Later starts reuse them.


> **Tip:** Give every developer their own stage, such as `--stage dev-alice` and `--stage dev-bob`. Each stage gets its own dev stack and its own local data. Don't use a stage you deploy: dev mode refuses a stage that `stacktape deploy` created, and `deploy` refuses a dev stage.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Change code and see it

Edit a file and save. Then:

- **With `--watch`**, dev mode rebuilds the changed workload by itself. Containers restart, and Lambda functions get the new code in AWS.
- **Without `--watch`**, press **Ctrl+R** to rebuild. With several workloads running, a picker opens: press a workload's number, or `a` for all. **Ctrl+A** rebuilds everything at once.
- **Frontends** reload through the framework's own hot reload, with or without `--watch`.

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --resources all --watch
```

A rebuild deploys code only. After you change the configuration, such as a new resource, an environment variable or a connection, dev mode tells you to restart, and refuses rebuilds until you do. The restart updates the dev stack.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Stop dev mode

Press **Ctrl+C**. The dev stack stays in AWS for the next start, and your local database data stays in `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/`. A dev session started with `--agent` runs in the background: stop it with [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop).

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## What runs where

| Resource | Where it runs | After a change |
|---|---|---|
| Containers: [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service), [private service](/resources/compute/private-service) and [workloads of several containers](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) | Docker on your machine | Rebuilt with `--watch` or **Ctrl+R** |
| [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) | AWS, built on your machine | Code updated in AWS with `--watch` or **Ctrl+R**. Logs stream to your terminal. |
| SSR frontends: [Next.js](/resources/frontend/nextjs), [Astro](/resources/frontend/astro), [Nuxt](/resources/frontend/nuxt), [SvelteKit](/resources/frontend/sveltekit), [SolidStart](/resources/frontend/solidstart), [TanStack Start](/resources/frontend/tanstack-start), [Remix](/resources/frontend/remix) | Its own dev server | Its own hot reload |
| [Static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) with a `dev` command | Your dev command | Your dev command's reload |
| [Relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database), [Redis](/resources/databases/redis), [DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb), [OpenSearch](/resources/databases/opensearch) | Docker on your machine | Data persists in `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/` |
| [Batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) | AWS, in the dev stack. They cannot be selected or skipped | Restart dev mode to rebuild their images |
| Everything else, such as queues, topics, buckets and state machines | AWS, in the dev stack | Restart dev mode after you change its config |

Lambda functions in AWS reach the databases on your machine through the dev box, a small EC2 instance in your account's dev network. See [Connecting to local databases](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#connecting-to-local-databases). Local databases listen on `127.0.0.1` only, and nothing is exposed on the internet.

A container counts as running once its port accepts connections, so a test started when dev mode reports it ready reaches the app. All local DynamoDB tables run in one DynamoDB Local, and workloads, local scripts and frontends connected to them get `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_DYNAMODB`, so unchanged AWS SDK code uses the local tables.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## What happens when it starts

When you run `stacktape dev`, these steps run in order:

1. **Load credentials and configuration**: Stacktape reads your AWS credentials and config file.
2. **Select resources**: You choose which resources to run via the interactive picker, or Stacktape uses the `--resources` and `--skip-resources` flags.
3. **Check references**: Before any AWS work, Stacktape checks every `$ResourceParam` that ends up in the dev stack, so a misspelled parameter or a [reference to a local database](#resources-the-dev-stack-needs-deployed) fails within seconds.
4. **Load AWS metadata**: Stacktape fetches stack information from AWS.
5. **Ensure secrets and SSM parameters**: Stacktape can generate supported missing database credentials. Other missing secrets and SSM parameters require user-supplied values: interactive runs prompt, while agent/noninteractive runs stop with creation instructions. Deleting a dev stage keeps the database secrets dev mode generated; delete one with `stacktape secret delete` when no stage needs it. See [secret ownership](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#aws-permissions).
6. **Prepare the dev network**: When deployed functions use local databases or join the VPC, Stacktape creates the account's [dev network](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#the-dev-network) on first use, once per account and region, and starts its dev box in the background. A new network's dev box exists after about 1 minute; the next step starts then, while CloudFormation finishes the network. A session that finds another session creating the network continues as soon as the dev box exists, too. A first start that creates the network and the dev stack takes about 5 minutes.
7. **Deploy dev stack**: Create the stack if missing, or update it when cloud configuration, cloud images or required outputs change. Otherwise reuse it.
8. **Start local resources and workloads**: Docker containers start for selected databases, dev mode connects to the dev box, then container workloads, frontends, and Lambda deploys run in parallel.
9. **Wait for new API stages**: AWS answers some requests to a new HTTP or WebSocket API stage with 403 or 404 for about half a minute after CloudFormation creates it. A function behind such an API reports running only after its stage is 45 seconds old. For a WebSocket API, dev mode also opens a few test connections, which run your `$connect` and `$disconnect` handlers. Later starts reuse the stage and do not wait.


> **Info:** Unchanged starts skip the dev stack deployment step. Stacktape still loads AWS metadata, prepares local resources, and starts or deploys the selected workloads.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Run part of the stack

`--resources` picks what runs. `--skip-resources` runs everything except the resources you name, alone or together with `--resources all`:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --skip-resources myDatabase
```

A skipped Lambda function stays in the dev stack without its triggers, so it does not run on queue messages, schedules, stream records or HTTP requests during the session.

If a name is wrong, the error shows the available resource names.

docs.title: Dev mode
headingPath: Keep deployed functions away from local databases
docs.content:
### Keep deployed functions away from local databases

Pass `--no-tunnel` to keep deployed Lambda functions away from your local databases for one session:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --no-tunnel
```

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Local database emulation

Selected emulatable databases run locally unless listed in `--remote-resources`. When local resources are active, dev mode runs an environment injection step so workloads can use Stacktape-provided `STP_*` variables with local endpoints. Code that reads these variables uses the same lookup path in both dev mode and deployed stacks.

| Config resource type | Local Docker image |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL / Aurora PostgreSQL | `postgres` |
| MySQL / Aurora MySQL | `mysql` or `mariadb` |
| Redis cache | `redis` |
| DynamoDB table | `amazon/dynamodb-local` |
| OpenSearch domain | `opensearchproject/opensearch` |

Local database data persists between dev mode sessions under `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/`, so you typically keep your data across restarts without re-seeding.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
### Start with a fresh database

Use `--fresh-db` to reset databases prepared during startup, including relay dependencies. DynamoDB Local tables share storage; see [reset scope](/local-development/local-databases#resetting-local-data).

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --fresh-db
```

docs.title: Dev mode
headingPath: Use a database in AWS instead
docs.content:
### Use a database in AWS instead

When the local copy is not enough, for example to test an engine feature the Docker image lacks, `--remote-resources` deploys that database in AWS as part of the dev stack, instead of running it locally:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --remote-resources myDatabase
```

This creates a real database for the dev stage (or reuses the one an earlier session created). It takes several minutes the first time and costs what the database costs, until you delete the dev stage. It is not another stage's database: the dev stack never connects to the database of a deployed stage such as `production`. To work against an existing database, pass its connection details yourself, for example from a secret. To make the choice permanent, set `dev.remote: true` on the resource. Functions and local containers that list a remote resource in `connectTo` get the same permissions as in a full deployment.

docs.title: Dev mode
headingPath: Resources the dev stack needs deployed
docs.content:
### Resources the dev stack needs deployed

The dev stack in AWS cannot use a database that runs on your machine, except through the dev box: deployed functions get a local database's address and credentials in their environment variables and through `connectTo`. Two cases need the deployed resource:

- **DynamoDB stream triggers.** A [stream trigger](/resources/triggers/dynamodb-streams) reads the stream of the deployed table, which DynamoDB Local cannot provide. When a deployed function has a stream trigger on a table, dev mode deploys that table in the dev stack automatically and says so when it starts. Local containers and functions then use the deployed table too.
- **Any other reference to a local resource in the dev stack**, for example `iamRoleStatements` with `$ResourceParam('mainTable', 'arn')` on a function or container. Dev mode stops before it starts anything and names the resource and the config path. Add the resource to `--remote-resources` or set `dev.remote: true` on it.

For more details on local database setup, supported engines, and troubleshooting, see [Local databases](/local-development/local-databases).

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Environment variables

Workloads connected to locally-emulated resources receive `STP_*` environment variables pointing to local endpoints instead of AWS endpoints. Dev mode uses the same variable names as deployed stacks: only the values change.

For a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) resource named `myDb` connected to a workload via [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources), the connection string, host, and port point at the local emulator. For example, a PostgreSQL database may produce variables like:

```
STP_MY_DB_CONNECTION_STRING=postgres://...@localhost:5432/postgres
STP_MY_DB_HOST=localhost
STP_MY_DB_PORT=5432
```

In most applications, reading the Stacktape-provided `STP_*` variables lets the same code path work in dev mode and deployed stacks without conditional logic or environment switching.

Local containers also get `AWS_REGION` and `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` with the stage's region, as deployed containers do, so AWS SDKs that read either one (boto3 reads only `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`) find it without a profile.

Code on your machine talks to the dev stack, and deployed functions talk to your local databases, across the distance to the stage's region. In a region far from you, every first connection takes noticeably longer (several hundred milliseconds per round trip), and a client with a short connect timeout can fail. Node.js, for example, gives up on each address after 250 ms by default; raise it with `NODE_OPTIONS=--network-family-autoselection-attempt-timeout=2000`, or run dev mode in a region close to you.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Keyboard shortcuts

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+R** | Rebuild. With several workloads, pick one by its number, `a` for all, or Esc to cancel |
| **Ctrl+A** | Rebuild all workloads |
| **Tab** | Switch between the overview and the logs |
| **Ctrl+C** | Stop dev mode |

With `--watch`, workloads rebuild by themselves when their files change. Rebuilding one workload leaves the others running.

A workload whose rebuild fails, for example because of a syntax error, shows the error and stays failed until a rebuild succeeds. A Lambda function keeps its previous code until then. A rebuild deploys code only: after a change to the configuration file, stop dev mode and start it again.

That start updates the dev stack only when the change reaches it. Changing how a local container is built or started (its `packaging`, including `startCommand`), a frontend's `dev` settings or a local script restarts only what runs on your machine. When the dev stack is updated, functions whose code did not change keep their deployed code.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Local EFS storage

Configured EFS mounts are not mounted or emulated on local containers. Use explicit local test storage and verify the deployed [EFS configuration](/resources/compute/web-service#efs-storage) in a deployed stage.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Lifecycle hooks

Dev mode registers configured `beforeDev` script hooks and displays them in the dev TUI. See [Hooks and scripts](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) for configuration details, hook types, and the full execution model.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Dev stack isolation

Dev mode creates a dedicated dev stack and refuses to reuse any stack it did not create, regardless of name or status. Use a separate stage name such as `dev`, `dev-local`, or `dev-jane`. To connect selected databases or Redis resources to deployed AWS resources, keep the dedicated dev stage and pass `--remote-resources`.


> **Warning:** Dev mode only updates a stack that `stacktape dev` created. It marks every dev stack with the stack tag `stp:dev-stack`, and refuses any other stack on the stage, whatever its name or status: use a different stage name, or delete that stack with `stacktape delete --stage <stage>` yourself. Dev mode never deletes a stack.

If the first start of a stage fails or is interrupted, CloudFormation rolls the dev stack back. The next `stacktape dev` recognizes the stack by its tag and updates it again. Only a dev stack whose very first create failed (status `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`) can't be updated; dev mode then asks you to delete it with `stacktape delete --stage <stage>`.

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Agent mode for coding agents

When started with `--agent`, Stacktape spawns a detached daemon process. The daemon starts the agent server, writes a lock file with process and connection details, and reports readiness back to the parent command, which then exits. See [Agent mode in dev](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev) for the full guide.

Start dev mode as an agent:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --resources all --agent
```

When `--agent-port` is omitted, Stacktape starts at port 7331 and searches ports 7331–7430 if the default is in use. Use `--agent-port` to request a specific port. The agent listens on `127.0.0.1` only, and every request must carry the session token stored in `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token` (see [Authentication](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev#authentication)). If Stacktape finds an already running dev agent, the command returns that agent's connection details instead of starting another one. A Lambda build or deploy failure can leave the session running with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES` and `ready: false`; fix the code and rebuild. A failure that aborts startup is reported separately. Inspect the returned session and status before starting another agent.

While the agent starts, the command prints its progress as JSONL `event` lines: the agent's port first, then the dev network, the dev box, the dev stack deployment with CloudFormation resource counts, and each workload and database. A first start that creates the dev network and the dev stack takes several minutes, and a heartbeat line every 20 seconds names the step it waits for.

Stop the agent of the current project with [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop) (`--stage` chooses between several stages, `--cwd` names another project directory):

```bash
stacktape dev stop --stage dev
```

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content:
## Flags

These are the flags you use most. [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) lists every flag, and `stacktape help dev` prints them in the terminal.

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--stage` | Stage name for the dev stack |
| `--region` | AWS region |
| `--resources` | Resources to run (`all` or comma-separated names) |
| `--skip-resources` | Resources to leave out |
| `--watch` | Rebuild on file changes |
| `--remote-resources` | Databases to use in AWS instead of a local copy |
| `--fresh-db` | Start local databases from a fresh state |
| `--no-tunnel` | Keep deployed Lambda functions away from local databases |
| `--agent` | Run in the background with an HTTP API for coding agents |
| `--agent-port` | Port for that HTTP API (default: 7331) |

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Dev mode
headingPath: How do Lambda functions connect to local databases in dev mode?
docs.content:
### How do Lambda functions connect to local databases in dev mode?

Through the dev box of your account's dev network. Functions connect to the box's private address, and the box forwards each connection to your machine over an encrypted AWS Systems Manager session that your machine opens. Nothing is published on the internet. Bulk transfers are limited to about 0.7 MB/s. See [Connecting to local databases](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#connecting-to-local-databases).

docs.title: Dev mode
headingPath: What is the difference between dev mode and deploying to a dev stage?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between dev mode and deploying to a dev stage?

Dev mode (`stacktape dev`) runs workloads on your local machine with Docker and deploys a dev stack to your AWS account when one does not already exist. [Deploying](/cli/deploy) to a dev stage (`stacktape deploy --stage dev`) provisions the full AWS infrastructure for your config and runs everything in the cloud. Use dev mode for rapid daily iteration; use a deployed dev stage for integration testing against real AWS infrastructure.

docs.title: Dev mode
headingPath: Does dev mode cost anything on AWS?
docs.content:
### Does dev mode cost anything on AWS?

Dev mode creates a minimal dev stack in AWS, so AWS charges can come from the AWS resources in that dev stack, Lambda invocations, and any deployed resources you choose to use through `--remote-resources`. The dev box costs about $0.01 per hour while a dev session runs; it stops itself 30 minutes after the last session and then costs about $0.75 per month for its disk and the SSM parameter that holds its relay. Container workloads and locally emulated databases run on your machine and don't generate AWS charges. Small development workloads may fall within AWS Lambda free-tier usage, depending on account eligibility and invocation volume.
