- [Debugging Lambda functions](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions): how deployed functions reach your machine, and what it costs.
- [Deploying stacks](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks): deploy it to a stage when it works.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content:
# Local databases

Stacktape [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) runs supported databases locally in Docker, avoiding the corresponding AWS database service. Dev-stack resources and the [dev network](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#the-dev-network) can still incur AWS charges. Data persists between sessions and workloads receive connection settings automatically. Use `dev.remote: true` to connect to the deployed database instead.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content:
## When to use local databases

Local databases are the default for day-to-day development and isolate each developer's data. Local clients connect on your machine. Lambda and Batch clients in AWS reach them through the dev network and incur a cloud-to-machine round trip. Use local databases for application logic, migrations and prototypes; test cloud-specific behavior against deployed resources.

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: When to use a deployed database
docs.content:
## When to use a deployed database

<span id="when-not-to-use-local-databases" />

Switch to a [deployed database](#using-remote-databases) when your work depends on behavior that local emulation cannot replicate: Aurora multi-AZ failover, DynamoDB Streams, OpenSearch security plugins, or engine-specific query plan differences. Also prefer remote databases when you need to test against a realistic data volume or share state across a team. Set `dev.remote: true` on the resource to connect to the deployed AWS resource instead.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content:
## Supported databases

Dev mode can run the following database resource types locally. Each runs as a Docker container, with data persisted to a host directory mounted into the container.

| Resource type | Local emulation |
|---|---|
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB) | Docker container |
| RDS Aurora (PostgreSQL, MySQL — including Serverless v2) | Mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL container |
| RDS Oracle, RDS SQL Server | Not supported — set `dev.remote: true` |
| [Redis](/resources/databases/redis) | Docker container |
| [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) | `amazon/dynamodb-local` container |
| [OpenSearch domain](/resources/databases/opensearch) | Docker container |
| [MongoDB Atlas](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas) | Not supported — third-party managed service |
| [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis) | Not supported — third-party managed service |

For [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database), local containers use the literal credentials from your config. Locally, `credentials.masterUserName` defaults to `postgres` for PostgreSQL and `root` for MySQL/MariaDB. Local databases never use the deployed database's secret: when `credentials.masterUserPassword` is not set or reads a value with a directive such as `$Secret('db', 'password')`, dev mode generates a random password for each local database and stores it in `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/<resourceName>/password`, readable only by your user. Every worktree or copy of the project on your machine gives new local data the same password for a stage, so moving the stage between worktrees does not have to update the dev stack. A Redis `defaultUserPassword` read from a directive gets a generated password the same way, and Redis without a password runs without authentication. The container, deployed dev functions and local workloads all receive the same password through the injected connection information. Properties like `instanceSize` only apply to the deployed AWS resource and are ignored locally.

Aurora engine types (Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL and Aurora Serverless v2) are mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL containers locally. Aurora-specific features (multi-AZ replication, serverless ACU scaling, reader endpoints) are not available in the local emulation. For most application-level SQL access, the local container provides the same kind of SQL endpoint and connection-string shape. Test Aurora-specific behavior against a deployed stage.


> **Info:** Dev mode needs Docker to start local database containers. If Docker is not running, dev mode cannot proceed with local databases.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content:
## How it works

When you run [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev), Stacktape identifies database resources in your config and starts Docker containers for each one.

1. **Container naming**: each container is named after the project, stage, resource and a short hash of the project directory, so multiple stages, projects and Git worktrees of one project can run in parallel without sharing or stopping each other's containers.
2. **Port allocation**: dev mode finds an available host port for each container, avoiding conflicts when several sessions run in parallel. The port is published on `127.0.0.1` only, so other machines on your network cannot reach the database. The selected port is reflected in the injected connection information.
3. **Data persistence**: dev mode mounts a local data directory into the container, so data survives dev mode restarts.
4. **Readiness checks**: Stacktape polls the container until it responds, then marks the resource ready for your workloads.
5. **Connection information**: referenceable parameters (host, port, connectionString, etc.) are resolved locally so they can be used via `$ResourceParam()`. Workloads that list the database in their `connectTo` receive the documented environment variables following the `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]` pattern described in [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources).

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content: ## Relational databases

docs.title: Local databases
Local databases
Local databases
docs.content:
### Aurora engines

All Aurora engine types (Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL, Aurora Serverless v2) are mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL containers locally. The mapping is:

| Aurora engine type | Local container |
|---|---|
| `aurora-postgresql`, `aurora-postgresql-serverless-v2` | PostgreSQL |
| `aurora-mysql`, `aurora-mysql-serverless-v2` | MySQL |

This is a pragmatic tradeoff: the SQL interface, schema behavior, and connection string format match the deployed database, which is sufficient for application development. Aurora-specific behavior (ACU scaling, multi-AZ replication, reader endpoints, pause-after-inactivity) is only available on the deployed AWS resource. Test these features against a deployed stage using `dev.remote: true`.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content:
### Oracle and SQL Server

RDS Oracle (`oracle-ee`, `oracle-se2`) and SQL Server (`sqlserver-ee`, `sqlserver-se`, `sqlserver-ex`, `sqlserver-web`) engines do not have local emulation. If your config includes an Oracle or SQL Server database, use `dev.remote: true` to connect to the deployed AWS resource during development.

docs.title: Local databases
Local databases
Local databases
docs.content:
## OpenSearch

In dev mode, Stacktape runs a local OpenSearch container as a single-node cluster. Cluster-level features (sharding across nodes, dedicated master nodes) are not available locally.

Referenceable parameters available for the local domain include `domainEndpoint` and `arn`.

docs.title: Local databases
Local databases
headingPath: When to use a remote database
docs.content:
### When to use a remote database

- **Engine features the local image lacks**, such as Aurora reader endpoints and failover, or Aurora Serverless scaling.
- **DynamoDB Streams, Global Tables, TTL and backups**, which DynamoDB Local does not have. A table with a stream trigger on a deployed function is deployed automatically.
- **State several people share.** Developers who run dev mode with the same stage name use the same remote database.

To work with data from another stage, such as a copy of production, do not use `--remote-resources`. Pass that database's connection details to your workloads yourself, for example from a [secret](/configuration/secrets), and keep in mind that your local code can then change that data.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content:
## Resetting local data

Data persists across sessions in host directories mounted into the containers. Use `--fresh-db` to reset databases that startup prepares:

```bash
stacktape dev --fresh-db
```

`--fresh-db` deletes data, schema and local password/identity files when startup prepares a database. This includes selected databases and databases prepared for deployed-workload relay connections, which can include unselected resources. Databases never prepared are untouched; this is not a stage-wide wipe. The stage password can be reused, so it does not promise a new password.

Relational databases, Redis and OpenSearch store data under `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/<resourceName>/data/`. Stop dev mode before manually removing one of these data directories.

All DynamoDB Local tables share `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/dynamodb-local/data/`. Preparing any local DynamoDB table with `--fresh-db` removes every persisted table in that storage, even tables not selected this time. For a table-specific item reset that preserves schema, use the [local reset endpoint](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev#reset-and-seed-local-databases) or MCP `reset_db` with the table's `resource` name and `confirm: true`.


> **Tip:** Add `.stacktape/` to your `.gitignore` to avoid committing local database data to version control.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content:
## Databases without local emulation

Not all Stacktape database resources support local emulation:

| Resource | Local support | Alternative |
|---|---|---|
| RDS Oracle / SQL Server | No | Set `dev.remote: true` to use the deployed RDS instance |
| [MongoDB Atlas](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas) | No | Stacktape dev mode does not provide local emulation for MongoDB Atlas. Use a deployed cluster during development. |
| [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis) | No | Stacktape dev mode does not provide local emulation for Upstash Redis. Use a deployed Upstash instance during development. |

Oracle and SQL Server engines are not mapped to a local container type. MongoDB Atlas and Upstash Redis are third-party managed services without local emulation in dev mode.

docs.title: Local databases
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: Does local database data persist when I restart dev mode?
docs.content:
### Does local database data persist when I restart dev mode?

Yes. Local data survives restarts. `--fresh-db` resets databases prepared during startup, including relay dependencies, and removes their local credential/identity files. DynamoDB Local tables share storage, so resetting it removes every persisted table there. See [reset scope](#resetting-local-data).

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: Can I run multiple stages locally at the same time?
docs.content:
### Can I run multiple stages locally at the same time?

Yes. Each stage gets its own container name and its own non-conflicting port assignment, so two developers or two stages on the same machine do not collide. You can run `stacktape dev --stage dev-alice` and `stacktape dev --stage dev-bob` in parallel. Two Git worktrees of the same project can also run the same stage in parallel: each worktree has its own data directory, containers and ports. When the stage's deployed Lambda functions use local databases, only one session can receive their connections, so the second session refuses to start unless you pass [`--take-over`](/cli/dev#--take-over).

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: Why does dev mode warn that my database keeps the password `localdevpassword`?
docs.content:
### Why does dev mode warn that my database keeps the password `localdevpassword`?

Earlier Stacktape versions gave every local database without a configured password the fixed password `localdevpassword`, and a database with a `$Secret` password got the directive text itself as its password. A database stores its password in its data, so a data directory created then keeps working with that password, and dev mode warns about it. To switch to a generated password, start dev mode once with `--fresh-db`. This deletes the database's local data.

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: How do I connect to the local database with a GUI tool?
docs.content:
### How do I connect to the local database with a GUI tool?

Use the host `localhost` and the port from the injected connection string or referenceable parameters. For PostgreSQL, the local username defaults to `postgres`; for MySQL/MariaDB it defaults to `root`. If your config sets no literal password, read the generated one from `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/<resourceName>/password`. For Redis, use the injected connection string. DynamoDB Local and OpenSearch use HTTP endpoints.

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: Does local DynamoDB support Streams and Global Tables?
docs.content:
### Does local DynamoDB support Streams and Global Tables?

No. The `amazon/dynamodb-local` image used by dev mode does not include Streams, Global Tables, Time to Live (TTL), or on-demand backups. If your application depends on these features, set `dev.remote: true` on the [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) resource to connect to the deployed AWS resource.

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: How does Stacktape handle Aurora Serverless locally?
docs.content:
### How does Stacktape handle Aurora Serverless locally?

Aurora Serverless v2 engine types are mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL containers locally. Serverless scaling (ACU-based) and automatic failover are AWS-only features. For most application-level SQL access, the local container provides the same kind of SQL endpoint and connection-string shape. Test Aurora-specific behavior against a deployed stage.

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: Can I use the local database for running migrations?
docs.content:
### Can I use the local database for running migrations?

Yes. Workloads that list the database in `connectTo` receive the connection string as an environment variable, so migration tools that read the connection string from the environment work without changes. Run migrations from your application startup code, a local migration command (e.g. `npx prisma migrate dev`), or manually via a database client connected to `localhost:<port>`. Schema changes persist across dev sessions because the data directory is mounted from the host.

docs.title: Local databases
headingPath: Where can I find the actual port a local database is using?
docs.content:
### Where can I find the actual port a local database is using?

Dev mode finds an available host port for each container, so the actual port may differ from the database's default. The assigned port is reflected in the referenceable parameters and in the connection information provided to workloads via `connectTo`, so your application code does not need to handle port differences.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
# Budgets

A budget sets a monthly spending limit for one connected AWS account. When the account's spend, or the month's forecast,
crosses a percentage of that limit, Stacktape sends an alert to the [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) you
choose. AWS bills your account directly; the Stacktape subscription fee is separate.

Budgets alert you. They never stop or throttle anything, and AWS keeps charging. To stop oversized resources before they
are deployed, use [resource limit guardrails](/guardrails/resource-limits).

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Before you start

- You need the `org:manage-budgets` permission. By default, only owners and admins have it, and the **Budgets** item in
  the Console's Alerting group is hidden from other members.
- The AWS account must be [connected](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) with deployment access. Accounts
  connected as read-only cannot be selected.
- Create at least one [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels). A budget needs a channel to send to.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Creating a budget

1. Open **Alerting → Budgets** and click **New budget**.
2. Fill in the form:

| Field | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **Name** | A label for the budget, for example "Production budget". |
| **AWS account** | The connected account whose spend the budget watches. |
| **Monthly limit** | The limit in USD for the calendar month. The minimum is $1. |
| **Alert at** | Percentages of the limit that send an alert, one per row: 80% and 100% to start with. **Add** another row, up to five, or remove one. Each is a whole number from 1 to 100 and alerts once. |
| **Also alert if AWS expects spending to reach one of these percentages this month** | Adds forecast alerts for the same percentages. On by default. |
| **Alert channels** | Where the alerts go. Choose one or more. |

3. Click **Create budget**.

Stacktape creates a monthly AWS cost budget in the selected account. It counts the account's whole spend, not only
spend from Stacktape stacks. Credits and refunds are not subtracted.

You cannot edit a budget after creating it. To change the limit, percentages, account or channels, delete the budget and
create a new one.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## When alerts arrive

AWS updates budget data a few times a day, so an alert can arrive hours after spend crosses a percentage. Do not rely
on budgets for real-time cost control.

Each percentage alerts at most once a month for actual spend and, with forecast alerts on, once for the forecast. For
example, with `80, 100` you can get up to four alerts in a month: spend reached 80%, spend reached 100%, forecast
reaches 80%, forecast reaches 100%. A new month starts again with no alerts.

AWS needs some usage history before it can forecast. On a newly created account, forecast alerts may not arrive until
AWS has enough data.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Checking budgets

The **Budgets** page lists every budget with its state this month, monthly limit, alert percentages and what it applies
to. The state is the most serious alert of the month: **Over limit**, **Forecast over**, **Reached 80%**,
**Forecast 80%**, or **No alerts this month**.

Click a budget to open its page. It shows the alert percentages, whether forecast alerts are on, the alert channels, a
link to this month's costs per stage for the account, and the alerts the budget sent.

The **Alerts sent** section on the Budgets page lists the alerts all budgets sent. The same alerts also appear in
[Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history). Deleting a budget removes its AWS budget and stops its alerts; its past
alerts stay in Sent alerts.

The **Costs this month** panel on the Projects home says **Over budget** or **Over budget forecast** when a budget is over
its limit or forecast to go over it this month, and links to it.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Budgets in Slack

When a budget sends to a [Slack app channel](/observability/alert-channels), each budget gets one card per month. The
card is updated as higher percentages are crossed and shows the spending pace and the days left in the month.

- **Show drivers** replies privately with the stacks behind the month's spend and how each changed since the previous
  month.
- **Snooze until month end** stops all alerts from that budget until the month is over. It needs the
  `org:manage-budgets` permission. The budget's page in the Console shows the snooze and has a **Resume alerts** button.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Budgets created before v4

Stacktape v3 could filter a budget by project and stage. Stacktape v4 cannot create these budgets. If an older one
still exists, its **Applies to** column shows the projects and stages instead of **Whole AWS account**. Delete it and
create a budget for the AWS account instead.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Recommended setup

- Create one budget for each AWS account that runs production stages. Set the limit to your expected monthly bill and
  keep the default 80% and 100% alerts.
- Keep forecast alerts on. They give you warning before the spend actually crosses the limit.
- To separate production and development spend, run them in separate AWS accounts and give each account its own
  budget. A budget cannot filter by project or stage.

Budgets work with the other cost tools in the Console:

- [Cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards) show the projects, stages and resources behind the spend. A budget's
  page links to them as **See what drives it**.
- [Resource limit guardrails](/guardrails/resource-limits) stop deploys that would add oversized resources.
- [Cost optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) lower your baseline spend.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: Can I set a budget for one stage, project or database?
docs.content:
### Can I set a budget for one stage, project or database?

No. A budget watches a whole AWS account. To see spend per project, stage or resource, use the
[stage cost breakdown](/managing-costs/dashboards#a-stages-costs). To alert on one stage's spend, deploy that stage to its
own AWS account and create a budget for that account.

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: How much do AWS Budgets cost?
docs.content:
### How much do AWS Budgets cost?

AWS may charge for AWS Budgets depending on your account and usage. Check the
[AWS Budgets pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/aws-cost-management/aws-budgets/pricing/) for current rates.

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: Why isn't my forecast alert arriving?
docs.content:
### Why isn't my forecast alert arriving?

Check that the budget's page says it alerts "when the forecast goes over one of them". If it does, AWS probably does
not have enough usage history for this account yet. Forecasts become available as usage data accumulates.

docs.title: Cost dashboards
docs.content:
# Cost dashboards

The Console shows your AWS spend by project, stage and resource, so you can follow the bill down to the resource that drives it. Open **Organization → Costs**, pick a month, then click a stage to see its resources. The numbers come from the cost reports of your connected AWS accounts. AWS bills them to you; the Stacktape fee is not part of them.

docs.title: Cost dashboards
docs.content:
## The Costs page

**Organization → Costs** opens on this month, for all your AWS accounts. The sidebar shows it to Owners and Admins; Developers and Viewers open it with **View costs** on the Projects home and see only the projects they can access. The filters at the top pick the **Month**, one AWS account or all of them, and one project or all of them. **Report updated** at the right says when AWS last refreshed the numbers.

The summary shows:

- **The month's total**, with where it ends at this pace and last month's total for comparison.
- **Month by month**: a chart of the months before. Click a bar to open that month.
- **Where it goes**: each project's share of the month, plus **Outside projects** for spend that belongs to no stack, such as AWS Support or resources you created by hand. AWS credits are subtracted at the bottom.
- **The Stacktape fee**: on Flexible, the fee so far this month; on Free, how close the organization is to the $200 limit. It appears for members who can see billing, and only for all accounts and all projects, because the fee is charged on the whole organization. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).


> Screenshot: The Costs page: month, AWS account and project filters, the month's AWS costs so far with the forecast and the Stacktape fee, a month-by-month chart, and each project's share under Where it goes Caption: The Costs summary for all AWS accounts and projects.


Below the summary, two tabs list the details:

- **Stages**: every stage with costs, with its project, its largest AWS charge, the month's cost and the month before. A stage without a report for the month shows **Not reported**.
- **Outside projects**: the services and resources outside your stacks, with their cost.

The month picker always offers this month and the 23 before it. Stacktape has reports only from when an account was connected, so earlier months are empty, not zero. When an account has no report for a month yet, the page names it under the total as **Not counted**.

docs.title: Cost dashboards
docs.content:
## A stage's costs

Click a stage on the Costs page, or open the stage in **Projects** and its **Costs** tab. You see the stage's total for the month, how it compares with the month before, and one row per resource with its type and cost. When you compare with a past month, the rows are sorted by the largest change first.

Use it to answer questions like these:

- **What made this stage more expensive?** Pick the month and read the change column from the top.
- **Is the database or the compute driving the cost?** Compare the rows for the month.
- **Is `staging` sized like `production`?** Open both stages for the same month.

A resource you removed from the config still shows its costs for the months it existed. Click its row to see its AWS type, CloudFormation logical ID and physical ID, which you can copy to find it in the AWS console. Costs that AWS reports for the stage but can't tie to one resource show as **Other AWS costs**.

When you know what drives the bill, set a [budget](/managing-costs/budgets) on the account, or follow the [cost optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) for that resource type.

docs.title: Cost dashboards
docs.content:
## When numbers are missing

| What you see | What it means |
|---|---|
| No costs for a stage deployed today | AWS reports costs about a day after they occur. |
| **Report updated** in yellow with "recent costs may be missing" | The current month's report hasn't been refreshed for a while, so the last days can be missing. |
| **Not reported**, or a month without data | The account has no cost report for that month, for example before it was connected. That is not the same as $0. |
| A $0 row | AWS reported the stage, and it cost nothing that month. |

docs.title: Cost dashboards
docs.content: ## Cost dashboards FAQ

docs.title: Cost dashboards
headingPath: How is this different from AWS Cost Explorer?
docs.content:
### How is this different from AWS Cost Explorer?

Cost Explorer shows every charge in the account, grouped by service or tag. The Console groups the costs it can attribute by project and stage, then by resource, which is how you think about your app. It shows everything else as **Outside projects**. Use the Console for stack costs and Cost Explorer for account-wide analysis.

docs.title: Cost dashboards
headingPath: Why is my database the most expensive resource?
docs.content:
### Why is my database the most expensive resource?

Relational databases run all the time and charge by the hour for the instance, plus storage and I/O. Unlike a Lambda function, which costs nothing while idle, a database keeps its baseline cost with no traffic. See [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) for smaller and serverless options.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
# Cost optimization tips

These are the changes that lower an AWS bill the most without making your app less reliable. Before you change anything, find where the money goes on the [Costs page](/managing-costs/dashboards). Prices below are rough figures for `us-east-1`; check the AWS pricing page of each service for your region.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Choose the right compute model

The biggest cost lever is choosing the right compute model for your workload. [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), container services, and [batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) bill in different ways: per invocation, per hour or per job run. With the wrong one you pay for idle capacity, or per request where a flat rate would be cheaper.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
### Lambda functions: pay-per-invocation

[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) cost nothing when idle — you pay only for the compute time consumed during each invocation. This makes them the cheapest option for low-traffic or bursty workloads. Beyond sustained high traffic, a container service running 24/7 is usually cheaper per-request because you avoid per-invocation overhead.

Provisioned concurrency can reduce cold starts, but it adds idle compute cost — each provisioned instance bills continuously. Use it only when latency requirements justify the tradeoff. For most internal or background endpoints, occasional cold starts are an acceptable tradeoff for zero idle cost.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
### Container services: always-on cost

A Stacktape [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) is a container running 24/7 with a public HTTPS URL, so treat it as always-on compute that bills continuously. [Private services](/resources/compute/private-service) and [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service) are also container-based resources — see their resource pages for runtime and scaling behavior. Before deploying a container service, confirm your workload genuinely needs an always-on process. If traffic is sporadic, a Lambda function with an [HTTP trigger](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) is usually cheaper.

Right-size the `resources` block. For Fargate-backed container workloads, AWS pricing is tied to requested CPU and memory, so right-sizing is the first optimization. Start at the smallest combination that keeps your application responsive and scale up only when metrics show resource pressure.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: Batch jobs: pay only for runtime
docs.content:
### Batch jobs: pay only for runtime

[Batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) run containerized tasks to completion — you pay only for the compute time used. Use batch jobs for data processing, ML training, image encoding, or any task that runs to completion rather than serving ongoing traffic. Set `timeout` on jobs with a known upper bound so an overrun attempt is killed; if `retryConfig` is set, Stacktape retries the job after failure, timeout, or Spot interruption.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Lambda function | Web service | Batch job |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing model | Per-invocation | Per-hour (24/7) | Per-job runtime |
| Best for traffic pattern | Bursty / low | Steady / high | Periodic tasks |

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Use ARM/Graviton architecture

AWS Graviton (`arm64`) instances are typically priced below comparable x86 (`x86_64`) instances across Lambda and Fargate. Where your application code supports it, choosing ARM reduces compute cost without changing behavior.

ARM works with most application code without changes — Node.js, Python, Go, Java, and .NET all run natively on `arm64`. The main exception is native compiled binaries or Lambda layers built specifically for x86. Native binaries and prebuilt artifacts need to match the target architecture.

Prefer ARM unless you have native binary compatibility constraints. See the [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), [private service](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service), and [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) pages for how to configure architecture on each resource type.


> **Tip:** Start every new project on ARM where supported. Only fall back to x86 if you hit a specific compatibility issue — that's rare for modern application stacks.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: Use spot instances for batch jobs

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Pick the right load balancing

For [web services](/resources/compute/web-service), the load balancing type directly affects monthly cost. The `loadBalancing` property accepts three types:

**`http-api-gateway` (default)** charges about $1 per million requests and has no base cost. At low traffic it is the cheapest option; the cost grows with every request.

**`application-load-balancer`** charges about $16 a month per load balancer in us-east-1 even with no traffic, plus capacity units for connections, requests and bytes. For small requests, it becomes the cheaper option somewhere around 500,000 requests a day; large responses or many long connections move that point. See [API Gateway pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/pricing/) and [Elastic Load Balancing pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/pricing/). It's required for [gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments), top-level [firewalls](/resources/security/web-application-firewall), and WebSocket support.

**`network-load-balancer`** is for non-HTTP traffic (TCP/TLS) like MQTT, game servers, or custom protocols — use it only when you need raw TCP. It does not support CDN, top-level firewall, or gradual deployments.


> **Tip:** Most teams should start with the default `http-api-gateway`. Switch to `application-load-balancer` only when you need its specific features (gradual deployments, WebSockets, firewall) or when your request volume makes its hourly cost cheaper than per-request pricing.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Right-size Lambda memory

Lambda CPU scales proportionally with memory. More memory means more CPU, which often means faster execution and lower total cost — a function that takes 3 seconds at 256 MB might finish in 800 ms at 1,024 MB, costing less overall despite the higher per-millisecond rate.

Profile your functions with real-world payloads. Increase memory in steps (512 → 1,024 → 2,048) and compare total billed duration × memory. The sweet spot is where additional memory stops reducing execution time.

Set `timeout` to the lowest value your function needs. Timeouts don't affect cost directly, but they limit how long a stuck invocation runs before being killed — preventing wasted spend from runaway functions.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Choose the right database engine

[Relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) are often the largest line item in an AWS bill. The engine choice determines both the pricing model and how well it adapts to your traffic pattern.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: Aurora Serverless v2 for variable workloads
docs.content:
### Aurora Serverless v2 for variable workloads

Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with demand, between `minCapacity` and `maxCapacity` in ACUs (about 2 GB of memory each). With `minCapacity` left out, Stacktape sets 0: the database pauses after about five minutes without connections, you pay only for storage, and the first connection after a pause waits about 15 seconds. At 0.5 ACU or more it keeps running and costs money while idle. Keep the default for dev and staging, and set `maxCapacity` to cap what a spike can cost. See [Aurora Serverless v2](/resources/databases/relational-database#aurora-serverless-v2).

It suits variable or unpredictable traffic: it handles spikes without resizing an instance, and at night it shrinks to the floor instead of running at full size.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
### Standard RDS for predictable workloads

Standard RDS uses fixed instance sizes with hourly billing. If your traffic is steady and predictable, a right-sized RDS instance can be cheaper than Aurora Serverless v2 because you avoid the per-ACU premium. Use burstable `t` family instances for databases with occasional spikes, and switch to memory-optimized `r` family only for steady, memory-intensive workloads.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
### Avoid over-provisioning high availability

Enabling `multiAz` on a standard RDS instance creates a synchronous standby replica, which roughly doubles the instance cost. Skip it for development and staging stages. For production, enable it only when your uptime requirements justify the extra cost. Aurora clusters replicate across 3 AZs automatically, so multi-AZ resilience is built in without the explicit flag.


> **Tip:** For dev/staging stages, use Aurora Serverless v2 and leave `minCapacity` out, so the database pauses when idle. For production, evaluate whether your traffic is stable enough for standard RDS (cheaper per-hour when fully utilized) or variable enough to benefit from Aurora Serverless v2 (cheaper at low or fluctuating utilization).

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Use serverless databases where possible

For key-value and document workloads, [DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb) in on-demand mode charges per read and write, so with no traffic you pay only for the data stored. This makes it ideal for applications with unpredictable or spiky access patterns. Switch to provisioned throughput only when your traffic is steady and predictable enough to forecast capacity needs.

For Redis use cases that don't require sub-millisecond latency from a dedicated cluster, consider [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis) — a serverless, pay-per-request Redis with no idle cost. [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis) bill per-hour for always-on instances regardless of utilization, so they're only cost-effective when you need consistent low-latency access under sustained load.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: Add a CDN for cacheable traffic
docs.content:
## Add a CDN for cacheable traffic

A [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) (CloudFront) caches responses at edge locations for cacheable content and can reduce origin traffic. CloudFront pricing is per request and data transfer rather than a monthly base fee.

Enable a CDN on your [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) when it returns cacheable content (static assets, public API responses, server-rendered pages). The `network-load-balancer` load balancing option is designed for non-HTTP TCP/TLS traffic and does not support CDN, top-level firewall, or gradual deployments — use `http-api-gateway` or `application-load-balancer` for HTTP workloads where CDN caching is part of the design. Skip the CDN for APIs where every response is unique and user-specific — caching won't help, and the extra hop adds slight latency.

You can restrict the CDN price class to reduce per-request cost in premium regions. Lower price classes limit which edge regions serve your content, which reduces cost but increases latency for users outside the covered regions.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Delete unused stages

Every deployed [stage](/configuration/stages-and-environments) consumes AWS resources. Old feature-branch stages, abandoned test stacks, and forgotten staging environments accumulate idle cost — especially for always-on resources like container services, databases, and Redis caches.

Review your stacks regularly in the Stacktape Console or with [`stacktape stack list`](/cli/stack-list). Delete any stage that's no longer needed:

```bash
stacktape delete --stage old-feature
```

For PR-preview workflows, see the [stacks-per-git-branch pattern](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) and make cleanup part of the workflow so old stages are deleted after branches are merged.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Avoid unnecessary NAT Gateways

A NAT Gateway is one of the most expensive networking components in AWS — it bills a flat hourly rate plus per-GB data processing fees. Avoid NAT Gateways unless you have a concrete networking requirement, such as static outbound IP allowlisting, private subnet egress for a workload that needs it, or internet access for Lambda functions inside the VPC. Most workloads don't need one. When you do need NAT, `stackConfig.nat: ec2` or `ha-ec2` runs small Stacktape-managed instances instead of gateways (about $7 instead of $32 per month per zone, no per-GB fee) at the cost of about a minute of failed outbound calls when an instance dies; see [VPC and networking](/configuration/connecting-resources#vpc-and-networking). Non-production stages with `nat: ec2` share one NAT instance by default, so five preview stages pay about $7.70 per month for NAT in total instead of five times that; see [shared network for non-production stages](/configuration/shared-network).

For details on VPC networking and private subnet configuration, see the [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), and [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) resource pages.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Use dev mode during development

Running [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) lets you iterate locally without redeploying for every code change. Use it to shorten the feedback loop during development — see the [dev mode overview](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) for exact local/cloud runtime behavior.

For databases that support running locally during development, see [local databases in dev mode](/local-development/local-databases) — running a local instance avoids the cost of a deployed database while you iterate.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Set up budget alerts

AWS costs can spike unexpectedly — a misconfigured auto-scaling policy, a traffic surge, or a forgotten stack. [Budget alerts](/managing-costs/budgets) notify you when spending exceeds a threshold, giving you time to react before the bill grows.

Create a budget for each AWS account you want to watch, with the monthly limit set to your expected bill. Keep the default alerts at 80% (early warning) and 100% (act now). A budget covers the whole account, so put stages with different spending expectations in separate AWS accounts if you need separate limits.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content:
## Cost optimization checklist

Use this checklist when reviewing a stack's cost profile:

- [ ] Use ARM/Graviton architecture where supported
- [ ] Lambda memory is profiled and right-sized (not left at default)
- [ ] Container CPU/memory matches actual utilization (check metrics)
- [ ] Auto-scaling is configured for container services with variable traffic
- [ ] Load balancing type matches traffic volume (API Gateway vs ALB)
- [ ] Database engine matches workload pattern (serverless vs fixed instance)
- [ ] Database `multiAz` is disabled for non-production stages
- [ ] Log retention is reduced for development/staging stages
- [ ] Unused stages are deleted
- [ ] Budget alerts are configured
- [ ] CDN is enabled for services with cacheable responses
- [ ] Batch jobs use spot instances where safe
- [ ] Batch jobs have `timeout` set to prevent runaway costs
- [ ] No unnecessary NAT Gateways (private subnet with NAT disabled unless needed)

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: How do I see what each resource costs?
docs.content:
### How do I see what each resource costs?

The Stacktape Console provides [per-resource cost breakdowns](/managing-costs/dashboards#a-stages-costs) that attribute AWS charges to individual resources, stages, and projects. You can also view overall AWS spend across your organization using the [cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards). AWS bills your AWS account directly — these tools help you understand the bill, but they don't add charges.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: Does Stacktape add cost on top of AWS?
docs.content:
### Does Stacktape add cost on top of AWS?

Stacktape's subscription fee is separate from your AWS bill. AWS resources are billed directly by AWS to your connected AWS account. See [billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) for plan details.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: Can a Stacktape web service scale to zero?
docs.content:
### Can a Stacktape web service scale to zero?

No. A [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) is a container running 24/7 with a public HTTPS URL, so treat it as always-on compute rather than a scale-to-zero endpoint. If your workload has periods of zero traffic, a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) is cheaper — it costs nothing when idle.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: When should I use Aurora Serverless v2 vs standard RDS?
docs.content:
### When should I use Aurora Serverless v2 vs standard RDS?

Use Aurora Serverless v2 when your database traffic is variable or has long quiet periods: it scales down to `minCapacity` when unused. Use standard RDS when traffic is steady: a fixed-size instance avoids the per-ACU premium. For dev and staging, compare Aurora at 0.5 ACU with the smallest burstable RDS instance in your region.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: How do I reduce Lambda cold start costs without provisioned concurrency?
docs.content:
### How do I reduce Lambda cold start costs without provisioned concurrency?

Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts but adds idle compute cost, since each provisioned instance bills continuously. To avoid that idle cost, right-size memory instead — more memory means more CPU, which speeds up initialization (see [Right-size Lambda memory](#right-size-lambda-memory)). For most internal or background endpoints, occasional cold starts are an acceptable tradeoff for zero idle cost.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: How does DynamoDB on-demand pricing compare to provisioned?
docs.content:
### How does DynamoDB on-demand pricing compare to provisioned?

DynamoDB on-demand mode charges per read and write operation, plus storage. Provisioned mode lets you reserve a fixed throughput (reads/writes per second) at a lower per-unit price but bills continuously even at zero traffic. On-demand is cheaper for variable or low-traffic tables. Provisioned with auto-scaling is cheaper when you have sustained, predictable throughput and can accurately forecast capacity.

docs.title: Cost optimization tips
headingPath: How do I prevent unexpected cost spikes?
docs.content:
### How do I prevent unexpected cost spikes?

Set up [budget alerts](/managing-costs/budgets) with thresholds at 80% and 100% of your expected monthly spend. Cap auto-scaling with `maxInstances` on container services and `maxCapacity` on Aurora Serverless v2 databases. Set `timeout` on batch jobs so stuck jobs are killed. Review the [per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/dashboards#a-stages-costs) weekly to catch anomalies early. Delete old [stages](/configuration/stages-and-environments) you're no longer using.

docs.title: Costs overview
docs.content:
# Costs overview

AWS bills your AWS account for everything your stacks run, as it would without Stacktape. Stacktape adds no markup to that bill. If you use the Console, its fee is a separate invoice; see [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).

This section answers four questions:

| Question | Where |
|----------|-------|
| What will this cost before I deploy? | [Estimate before you deploy](#estimate-before-you-deploy), below |
| Where does this month's money go? | [Cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards) |
| How do I find out when spend gets too high? | [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) |
| How do I spend less? | [Cost optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) |

docs.title: Costs overview
docs.content:
## Estimate before you deploy

[`stacktape init`](/cli/init) prices the setup it proposes: its Review step shows the monthly price of each resource and the total, for the region you pick. `stacktape init --headless` prints the same estimate in the terminal. Both also write a config file; in a project that already has one, init writes `stacktape.generated.yml` beside it and leaves yours alone.

Init doesn't price changes you make to your config later. For those, add up the pricing notes on the resource pages, or use the [AWS Pricing Calculator](https://calculator.aws/). For example, a [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB adds about $18 a month on x86 Fargate in us-east-1, whether or not it has work.

What makes a bill large is mostly what runs all the time:

- **Always-on resources** bill by the hour, even with no traffic: web, private and worker services, multi-container workloads, relational databases, Redis, OpenSearch, load balancers, Kafka clusters and bastion hosts. They set your baseline.
- **Pay-per-use resources** bill per request, message or GB stored: Lambda functions, HTTP API Gateways, DynamoDB on demand, SQS, SNS and S3. With little traffic they cost close to nothing, but stored data still costs money.
- **Every stage is a full copy.** A `staging` stage costs about as much as `production` with the same sizes. A pull request preview that lives for three days costs about three days of its always-on resources. Delete stages you no longer use with [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete).
- **Git deployments on your own runner** add the runner's EC2 instance while it builds and its disk while it waits. See [Build runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners).

Each resource page has a pricing note, and the [resource catalog](/resources#what-resources-cost) marks which resources cost money while idle.

docs.title: Costs overview
docs.content:
## After you deploy

The Console shows your AWS spend per project, stage and resource from the cost reports of your connected AWS accounts. Cost data needs the Console and a connected account; reports arrive about a day after the costs occur. See [Cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards).

Without the Console, use AWS Cost Explorer. Every Stacktape stack carries the tags `stp:project-name`, `stp:stage` and `stp:stack-name`, which AWS copies to the resources that support tags. [Activate them as cost allocation tags](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/activating-tags.html) to group your costs by project and stage.

To hear about spend before the invoice, create a [budget](/managing-costs/budgets) for each AWS account you deploy to. A budget alerts you; it never stops anything. To prevent expensive deploys, such as oversized instances, use [resource limit guardrails](/guardrails/resource-limits).

docs.title: Costs overview
docs.content: ## Costs FAQ

docs.title: Costs overview
headingPath: How fresh is the cost data?
docs.content:
### How fresh is the cost data?

AWS delivers cost reports a few times a day. A new stack appears about a day after its first deploy, and a newly connected account has its first numbers about a day after you connect it. The Costs page says when the report was last updated.

docs.title: Costs overview
headingPath: Can a budget watch a single project or stage?
docs.content:
### Can a budget watch a single project or stage?

No. Each budget watches one whole AWS account. To track production and development separately, deploy them to separate AWS accounts and give each one a budget. To see spend per project and stage, use the [Costs page](/managing-costs/dashboards).

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
# Alarms

An alarm watches a CloudWatch metric of one resource, such as a function's error rate or a database's free storage,
and notifies you when it crosses a threshold. You define alarms on the resource in your config, and the deploy creates
them in CloudWatch in your AWS account.

- **Without the Console**, an alarm delivers to Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, email or a webhook straight from your
  AWS account. See [Notification targets](#notification-targets).
- **With the [Console](/getting-started/add-the-console)**, an alarm can also deliver to a Console
  [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels) (`console-channel`) or the Stacktape Slack app (`slack-app`), and a
  firing alarm opens an [incident](/observability/incidents). A deploy without a Console connection refuses
  `console-channel` and `slack-app` targets.

A good start for a production stage: an error-rate alarm on each public API, function or load balancer, and CPU and
free-storage alarms on each database. Runtime exceptions are better caught by [error tracking](/observability/error-tracking),
and spend by [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets).

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
## Supported resources

Stacktape supports inline alarms on five resource types. Each resource accepts a specific set of trigger types:

| Resource | Config property | Accepted alarm triggers |
|---|---|---|
| [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) | `alarms` | `lambda-error-rate`, `lambda-duration` |
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | `alarms` | `database-cpu-utilization`, `database-connection-count`, `database-read-latency`, `database-write-latency`, `database-free-storage`, `database-free-memory` |
| [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) | `alarms` | `http-api-gateway-error-rate`, `http-api-gateway-latency` |
| [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) | `alarms` | `application-load-balancer-error-rate`, `application-load-balancer-unhealthy-targets`, `application-load-balancer-custom` |
| [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) | `alarms` | `sqs-queue-received-messages-count`, `sqs-queue-not-empty` |

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content: ## Trigger types

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### Lambda function triggers

| Trigger type | Threshold property | Unit | Default statistic | Default comparison |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lambda-error-rate` | `thresholdPercent` | % | n/a | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `lambda-duration` | `thresholdMilliseconds` | ms | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### Relational database triggers

| Trigger type | Threshold property | Unit | Default statistic | Default comparison |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `database-cpu-utilization` | `thresholdPercent` | % | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `database-connection-count` | `thresholdCount` | count | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `database-read-latency` | `thresholdSeconds` | s | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `database-write-latency` | `thresholdSeconds` | s | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `database-free-storage` | `thresholdMB` | MB | `min` | `LessThanThreshold` |
| `database-free-memory` | `thresholdMB` | MB | `avg` | `LessThanThreshold` |


> **Info:** For threshold-based triggers that expose `comparisonOperator`, the default is `GreaterThanThreshold`, except `database-free-storage` and `database-free-memory`, which default to `LessThanThreshold` — the alarm fires when the metric drops *below* the threshold.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### HTTP API Gateway triggers

| Trigger type | Threshold property | Unit | Default statistic | Default comparison |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `http-api-gateway-error-rate` | `thresholdPercent` | % | n/a | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `http-api-gateway-latency` | `thresholdMilliseconds` | ms | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### Application Load Balancer triggers

| Trigger type | Threshold property | Unit | Default statistic | Default comparison |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `application-load-balancer-error-rate` | `thresholdPercent` | % | n/a | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `application-load-balancer-unhealthy-targets` | `thresholdPercent` | % | n/a | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `application-load-balancer-custom` | `threshold` (+ `metric`) | varies | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |

The `application-load-balancer-custom` trigger lets you alarm on additional ALB CloudWatch metrics beyond the built-in error-rate and unhealthy-targets triggers. See the API reference for supported properties.

The `application-load-balancer-unhealthy-targets` trigger also accepts an optional `onlyIncludeTargets` array to scope monitoring to specific container services behind the load balancer.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### SQS queue triggers

| Trigger type | Threshold property | Unit | Default statistic | Default comparison |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sqs-queue-received-messages-count` | `thresholdCount` | count | `avg` | `GreaterThanThreshold` |
| `sqs-queue-not-empty` | *(none)* | — | — | — |

The `sqs-queue-not-empty` trigger has no configurable threshold — it fires whenever the queue has any unprocessed messages (visible, in-flight, messages received, or messages sent).

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### Customizing comparison and statistic

Most triggers accept two optional overrides:

- **`comparisonOperator`** — how the metric is compared to the threshold. Options: `GreaterThanThreshold`, `GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold`, `LessThanThreshold`, `LessThanOrEqualToThreshold`. The default varies by trigger type (see tables above).
- **`statistic`** — how metric values within each evaluation period are aggregated. Options: `avg`, `min`, `max`, `sum`, `p90`, `p95`, `p99`. Available on triggers that aggregate over time (duration, latency, counts, utilization, storage, memory). Error-rate triggers compute the ratio directly and don't expose a statistic override.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
## Defining alarms on resources

Stacktape alarms are defined inline on individual resources using the `alarms` property. Each alarm specifies a `trigger` (what to monitor and the threshold) and optionally an `evaluation` window and `notificationChannels`.

docs.title: Alarms
Alarms
Alarms
Alarms
docs.content:
## Evaluation windows

Stacktape alarm evaluation windows control how CloudWatch evaluates the metric before firing the alarm. The `evaluation` property prevents short-lived spikes from triggering false alerts while still catching sustained problems.

Three settings control the evaluation:

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `period` | `60` | Duration of one evaluation window in seconds. Must be a multiple of 60. |
| `evaluationPeriods` | `1` | How many recent periods to look at. |
| `breachedPeriods` | `1` | How many of those periods must breach the threshold to fire. Must be ≤ `evaluationPeriods`. |

**How it works:** At the end of each `period`, CloudWatch checks whether the metric breached the threshold during that period. If `breachedPeriods` out of the last `evaluationPeriods` periods are in breach, the alarm fires.

**Example:** With `period: 300`, `evaluationPeriods: 5`, `breachedPeriods: 3`, CloudWatch looks at the last 25 minutes (5 × 300s). If the threshold was breached in at least 3 of those 5 periods, the alarm fires. This pattern catches sustained issues while ignoring isolated spikes.


> **Tip:** For production error-rate alarms, start with `evaluationPeriods: 3` and `breachedPeriods: 2` at a 60-second period. This gives you a 3-minute detection window that filters out single-period noise while still alerting within minutes.

For database storage alarms, the defaults (`period: 60`, `evaluationPeriods: 1`, `breachedPeriods: 1`) are usually appropriate — you want to know immediately when storage is running low.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
## Notification targets

Stacktape alarms can send notifications to one or more targets when they fire and when they recover. Configure the `notificationChannels` array on each alarm to specify where alerts are delivered. Supported target types include MS Teams, Slack, email, Discord, and webhooks.

Inline targets (`slack`, `ms-teams`, `discord`, `email` and `webhook`) are sent by the stack's own service Lambda, from your AWS account. The Lambda reads `$Secret` and secure SSM values when it sends the notification. Tokens, webhook URLs, signing secrets and headers are never sent to Stacktape. Email goes through Amazon SES in your account from the `sender` address. Microsoft Teams, Discord and webhook receivers get the same request format as from a Console [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels). A webhook request carries the alarm's EventBridge event ID as `id`, so a receiver can drop a repeated delivery.

Each target receives one message when the alarm fires and one when it returns to OK after firing. A new alarm's first evaluation to OK sends nothing. If a target fails, the Lambda retries it without resending the targets that already received the message. Muting an incident in the Console does not silence inline targets, because the Console does not deliver them.

To reuse a named Console [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels), add a `console-channel` reference to the alarm's `notificationChannels`. The Console delivers `console-channel` and `slack-app` targets with the credentials it keeps:


Example (YAML):

```yaml
notificationChannels:
  - type: console-channel
    properties:
      channelName: production-alerts
```


A firing alarm also opens an [incident](/observability/incidents). Configure [notification rules](/observability/notifications) to route incident alerts to your team. Choose the delivery paths you need to avoid duplicate notifications.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### Alarm description

Use the optional `description` property on an alarm to include a custom message in notification messages and the AWS console. This is helpful when you have multiple alarms on the same resource — the description makes it clear what the alarm means without looking up the config.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### History tracking

The `includeInHistory` property controls whether alarm state changes should appear in monitoring history. It defaults to `true`. Set it to `false` on noisy development-stage alarms that would clutter the history view. Such an alarm is not reported to the Console, so it opens no incident. Its inline targets are still notified. `console-channel` and `slack-app` targets need history, and the deploy refuses an alarm that combines them with `includeInHistory: false`.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### What leaves your AWS account

[What leaves your AWS account](/observability/overview#what-leaves-your-aws-account) compares every feature in one table.

When an alarm with history changes state, the stack's service Lambda sends the Console the alarm event: the alarm name and trigger type, the project, stage and region, the new state and its time, the alarm's description, ARN and condition (comparison, statistic and unit), the stack name, the affected resource with its AWS console link, a link to the alarm, and the EventBridge event ID. It also sends the `console-channel` names and resolved `slack-app` channel IDs, which the Console delivers. Inline targets and their settings stay in your account.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
## Migrating legacy Console alarm rules

The Console no longer creates or edits alarm rules. Existing rules appear under **Legacy alarm rules** on the Alarms page. They keep applying to every matching resource until you exclude them on that resource or delete them.

Run [`stacktape alarm export`](/cli/alarm-export) to print those rules as config entries, including their project and stage scope. Add each entry to the `alarms` list of every resource it should monitor, and preserve stage-specific behavior with [stage-based configuration](/configuration/stages-and-environments).

On the same resources, list the rule's name in `disabledGlobalAlarms`. Without it the legacy rule still applies next to the alarm you added, and the resource gets two alarms that notify twice. Deploy each affected stage, check the alarms, and then delete the legacy rule in the Console. The [`alarm export` guide](/cli/alarm-export#moving-the-rules-into-your-configuration) shows a complete example.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content: ## Viewing alarm states

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### CLI

Use [`stacktape alarm list`](/cli/alarm-list) to inspect alarms from the CLI. See the [CLI reference](/cli/alarm-list) for flags and output details.

```bash
stacktape alarm list --stage production --region eu-west-1
```


> **Info:** `INSUFFICIENT_DATA` typically means the resource hasn't produced enough metric data yet — common right after deployment or for resources with low traffic. It does not indicate a configuration error.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
### Console

The Console's **Alarms** page shows deployed alarms and their states across projects and stages. Open an alarm to inspect its state history. Configure thresholds and evaluation windows in the stack config, then deploy to apply them.

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content:
## Alarms as event triggers

Stacktape alarm state changes can be used as event sources for [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), enabling automated remediation workflows. See [alarms as triggers](/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers) for configuration details.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |

| `description` | no | `string` | - |

docs.title: Alarms
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Alarms
headingPath: How much do CloudWatch alarms cost?
docs.content:
### How much do CloudWatch alarms cost?

AWS charges per alarm metric per month. Stacktape alarms use standard resolution, so their periods are multiples of 60
seconds. For most stacks, alarms cost a small fraction of compute and database spend. See
[CloudWatch pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/pricing/).

docs.title: Alarms
headingPath: Can I set different thresholds for production and development?
docs.content:
### Can I set different thresholds for production and development?

Yes. Use [stage-based configuration](/configuration/stages-and-environments) to pick thresholds or leave alarms out for
a stage, then deploy each affected stage.

docs.title: Alarms
headingPath: How do I test that an alarm works?
docs.content:
### How do I test that an alarm works?

Deploy it, check it with [`stacktape alarm list`](/cli/alarm-list), then set a threshold your current traffic breaches (for
example `thresholdPercent: 0` on an error-rate alarm), deploy and wait one evaluation period. Check that the alert
arrives, then restore the real threshold.

docs.title: Alarms
headingPath: Can I alarm on a custom metric my application publishes?
docs.content:
### Can I alarm on a custom metric my application publishes?

Not from the Stacktape config. Each resource type has a fixed set of triggers; only `application-load-balancer-custom`
takes any ALB metric by name. For your own metrics, create the alarm in CloudWatch or add it as raw CloudFormation in
your config's [overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches).

docs.title: Alert channels
docs.content:
# Alert channels

An alert channel is a place where the Stacktape Console delivers alerts: a Slack channel, email addresses, a Microsoft
Teams or Discord channel, or your own HTTPS endpoint. You create it once, and incidents, deploy notifications, budget
alerts and alarms can all deliver to it. Alert channels need the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console).

docs.title: Alert channels
docs.content:
## Create a channel

1. In the Console sidebar, open **Alerting → Channels** and click **New channel**.
2. Choose the kind and fill in its fields:

| Kind | Fields |
|---|---|
| **Slack** | **Connect Slack** once for the workspace, then pick the **Channel**. See [Slack](#slack). |
| **Email** | **Recipient emails**, comma-separated. |
| **Teams** | The channel's **Webhook URL**. |
| **Discord** | The channel's **Webhook URL**. |
| **Webhook** | **Webhook URL**, and an optional **Signing secret**. See [Webhook](#webhook). |

3. Give it a **Name**. Config alarms and uptime checks refer to the channel by this name.
4. Check **What it receives** and click **Add channel**. The channel's page opens.

Every new channel starts with these [notification rules](/observability/notifications), which you can change on its
page:

- incidents opened, escalated and resolved, from every stage;
- failed deploys, rollbacks and deletes, from every stage;
- successful deploys and rollbacks, from production stages;
- new security findings.

Managing channels needs the `org:manage-alert-channels` permission (Owners and Admins).

docs.title: Alert channels
docs.content:
## Slack

Slack connects through the Stacktape Slack app. Click **Connect Slack** in the New channel form and approve the app in
Slack. After that, every new Slack channel is picked from a list, and no token passes through your hands. Slack issues
the app's bot token for your workspace, and the Console keeps it in AWS Secrets Manager in Stacktape's AWS account.

Messages from the app are cards that Stacktape keeps up to date. An incident is one message that changes as it is
acknowledged and resolved, with later events in its thread. Turn on **Only pull request preview deploys** for a channel
that should receive preview deploys only, so they don't land where incidents do.

If the New channel form asks for a **Bot token** and a **Conversation ID** instead of **Connect Slack**, the Slack app
isn't available in your Console. Create a Slack app of your own with a bot token that can post to the channel, and
paste both. Such a channel gets plain messages, without the cards and buttons below. Its token is stored with the
channel and never shown again.

The app asks only for what it uses: posting and editing messages, uploading evidence images, listing channels, and
reading member names and emails to match Slack users to Console users. It never reads message history. It joins public
channels by itself; invite it to a private channel first (`/invite @Stacktape`).

docs.title: Alert channels
docs.content:
### What the cards do

- **Incidents.** One card per incident, updated as it changes. When a CloudWatch alarm caused it, the thread gets a
  graph of the alarm's metric over the last three hours with the threshold. The card names the release that was live
  and links to what changed. **Acknowledge** works for anyone in the workspace. **Mute 1 hour**, **Mute 24 hours**,
  **Resolve** and **Roll back to** the previous version run as your Console user and need the same permissions as in
  the Console (`incidents:manage`, `deployments:rollback`). Resolve and Roll back ask for confirmation in the card.
- **Deployments.** One card per deployment, with who started it and how, the commit and branch, the duration, a link
  to what changed, and the endpoints or the failure. A finished card has **Redeploy** and **Roll back to**, which need
  `deployments:deploy` or `deployments:rollback`. Pull request previews get one card per pull request, edited on every
  redeploy.
- **Security findings.** One digest per security report with the critical and high findings. **Ignore** on a finding
  needs `security:manage` and asks for an optional reason.
- **Budgets.** One card per budget and month, updated as higher thresholds are crossed, with the amounts, the forecast
  and the spending pace. **Show drivers** answers privately with the stacks behind the spend. **Snooze until month end**
  needs `org:manage-budgets`; the budget in the Console has **Resume alerts**.

The first time you click a button that runs as your Console user, Stacktape matches your Slack email to your Console
account. If they differ, you get a private link, valid for 15 minutes, that connects the two.

docs.title: Alert channels
docs.content:
### What Stacktape sends to Slack

Slack receives only what the cards show:

- **Incidents:** the incident title and state, the project and stage, one short evidence line per signal (for example the failing uptime regions and their failure reason, or an alarm's metric, value and threshold), the AI assessment summary when there is one, the release that was live and its commit, and a graph image of a firing alarm's metric.
- **Deployments:** who started the deployment and how, the commit and branch, the duration, a link to the changes, the stack's endpoints on success and the failure text on failure.
- **Security findings:** the severity, title and resource name of each new critical or high finding.
- **Budgets:** the budget amounts, the threshold crossed, the forecast and the spending pace. **Show drivers** replies privately with stack names and their cost changes.

Application logs are never posted. Error text in incident evidence comes from what error tracking already recorded, and that text was masked before it left your AWS account (see [what leaves your AWS account](/observability/error-tracking#what-leaves-your-aws-account)).

docs.title: Alert channels
docs.content:
## Teams and Discord

Create an incoming webhook for the channel in Teams or Discord and paste its URL. Messages are plain alerts. The URL
is stored with the channel and never shown again.

docs.title: Alert channels
docs.content:
## Email

Alerts go to each recipient address. Use email for people who aren't in your chat, or when you want each alert in an
inbox.

docs.title: Alert channels
Alert channels
docs.content:
## The channel page

- **What it receives**: its [notification rules](/observability/notifications), with **New rule** to add one, and
  the [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) that alert it.
- **Recent alerts**: the last alerts sent to it and whether each was accepted. Click one for the delivery details.
- **Settings**: the destination. Webhook URLs, tokens and secrets are not shown after they are saved.

**Send test** sends a test message. **Delete** removes the channel once nothing uses it; if a rule or budget still does,
the error lists them.

docs.title: Alert channels
headingPath: Use a channel from your config
docs.content:
## Use a channel from your config

[Alarms](/observability/alarms#notification-targets) and [uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) in your stack
config deliver to a Console channel by its name:

```yaml
notificationChannels:
  - type: console-channel
    properties:
      channelName: on-call-slack
```

For a channel of the connected Slack workspace, `slack-app` takes the Slack channel name or ID. The name is resolved to
the ID when you deploy, so renaming the channel in Slack later doesn't break delivery:

```yaml
notificationChannels:
  - type: slack-app
    properties:
      channel: '#alerts'
```

Alarms can also deliver straight from your AWS account to Slack, Teams, Discord, email or a webhook, without a Console
channel. Those credentials never reach Stacktape, and those alerts don't appear in [Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history).
See [alarm notification targets](/observability/alarms#notification-targets).

To check whether an alert reached a channel, open the channel's page, or **Alerting → Sent alerts** for every channel.

docs.title: Sent alerts
docs.content:
# Sent alerts

**Alerting → Sent alerts** in the Stacktape Console lists every alert the Console sent to your
[alert channels](/observability/alert-channels): incidents, deploys and other events covered by a channel's
[notification rules](/observability/notifications), [alarms](/observability/alarms#notification-targets) that deliver
through the Console, and [budget alerts](/managing-costs/budgets). Use it to check what was sent and whether it arrived.

docs.title: Sent alerts
headingPath: Find an alert that didn't arrive
docs.content:
## Find an alert that didn't arrive

1. Open **Alerting → Sent alerts** and set **Delivery** to **Failed**.
2. Open the alert. For each channel it shows whether the provider accepted it, every attempt with its time, and the
   error when it failed.
3. Follow the link to the failed channel, fix its settings, and click **Send test** on its page.

"Accepted" means the provider took the message, for example "Accepted by Slack". Stacktape doesn't see whether someone
read it. If an alert shows as accepted but never showed up, check the receiving system.

An event that no channel receives is not sent and doesn't appear here. If you expected one, open the channel under
**Alerting → Channels** and check which events and which projects and stages its rules cover.

docs.title: Sent alerts
docs.content:
## Columns

| Column | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Time** | When the alert was sent. Hover for the exact time. |
| **Alert** | What happened, for example an opened incident or a failed deploy. |
| **Project / stage** | Where it happened, or "Organization" for organization-wide alerts such as budgets and secret changes. |
| **Sent to** | The channels it went to. A channel that didn't accept it is shown in red. |
| **Delivery** | **Sent** when every channel accepted it, **Failed** when none did, **1 of 3 failed** when some didn't, and **Sending** while it is being delivered. |

docs.title: Sent alerts
docs.content:
## Filters

- **Alert**: incidents, deploys and changes, or budgets.
- **Channel**: one channel. A channel's page links here with this filter set.
- **Delivery**: **Failed** shows only alerts with a failed delivery.

An incident's page links here filtered to that incident.

docs.title: Sent alerts
docs.content:
## Other history

- An alarm's own history, opened from the alarm on **Alerting → Alarms**, shows its CloudWatch state changes.
- **Alerting → Budgets** lists each budget's alerts in its **Alerts sent** section.

Sent alerts is a Console page with no CLI command. For CloudWatch alarm states in the terminal, use
[`stacktape alarm list`](/cli/alarm-list).

docs.title: Debug commands
docs.content:
# Debug commands

These CLI commands inspect a deployed stack from your terminal. Each takes the stage and region (`--stage`,
`--region`), reads the project from your config, and runs with your AWS credentials, or through the Console when the
CLI is signed in. `status` and `stack history` read the Console's records, so they need a Console sign-in. Except for
the container and bastion sessions, the commands only read.

docs.title: Debug commands
docs.content:
## Pick a command

| You want to | Command |
|---|---|
| Read a function's or container's logs, or follow them live | [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) |
| See a metric of a function, container, database or HTTP API | [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics) |
| Check which alarms are firing | [`stacktape alarm list`](/cli/alarm-list) |
| Run a `SELECT` against a SQL database | [`stacktape query sql`](/cli/query-sql) |
| Look at items of a DynamoDB table | [`stacktape query dynamodb`](/cli/query-dynamodb) |
| Look at keys of a Redis cluster | [`stacktape query redis`](/cli/query-redis) |
| Search an OpenSearch domain | [`stacktape query opensearch`](/cli/query-opensearch) |
| Read the state of any other AWS resource | [`stacktape aws call`](/cli/aws-call) |
| See the stack's status, outputs and resources (Console sign-in) | [`stacktape status`](/cli/status) |
| Find why a recent deploy failed (Console sign-in) | [`stacktape stack history`](/cli/stack-history) |
| Run one command in a running container | [`stacktape container exec`](/cli/container-exec) |
| Open a shell in a running container | [`stacktape container shell`](/cli/container-shell) |
| Reach a VPC-only database from your machine | [`stacktape bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) |

docs.title: Debug commands
docs.content:
## Logs and metrics

```bash
stacktape logs api --stage production --region eu-west-1 --since 30m
stacktape metrics api Errors --stage production --region eu-west-1 --stat Sum --since 24h
```

[Logs](/observability/logs) covers live tail, a fixed incident window, filter patterns and Logs Insights queries.
