## What else goes in a stack

[Uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) and [synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests) are configured in the stack too, and [alarms](/observability/alarms) are set on the resource they watch. Their pages are under Observability.

docs.title: Resource catalog
docs.content:
## What resources cost

Always-on resources bill by the hour even with no traffic. These include web, private and worker services, multi-container workloads, relational databases, Redis, OpenSearch, load balancers, Kafka clusters, bastion hosts and Convex. Most other resources bill per request, per message or per GB stored. Each resource page has a pricing note, and [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview) explains how to track the bill.

docs.title: AWS CDK constructs
docs.content:
# AWS CDK constructs

An `aws-cdk-construct` adds the resources of an AWS CDK construct to your stack. You write a construct class in
TypeScript or JavaScript, and Stacktape synthesizes it and deploys its resources with the rest of the stack. Use it for
AWS services that have no Stacktape resource, such as Cognito identity pools, IoT rules or MediaConvert, when the CDK's
higher-level constructs save you work.

Check the [resource catalog](/resources/) first; GraphQL APIs, for example, have a native
[AppSync API](/resources/networking/appsync-api) resource. For one or two plain resources,
[raw CloudFormation](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources) needs no extra dependencies. To change a resource
Stacktape already creates, use [overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches).

docs.title: AWS CDK constructs
AWS CDK constructs
AWS CDK constructs
docs.content:
## Use the construct's resources

A construct can't be a `connectTo` target, and it has no [referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters).
To use one of its resources from a Stacktape resource:

1. Run `stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1` and find the resource's logical ID in `compiled-template.yaml`.
2. Reference it with [`$CfResourceParam`](/configuration/directives). For the topic in the basic example that is
   `$CfResourceParam('AlertsTopicCF7C81C9', 'TopicArn')`.
3. Grant access with `iamRoleStatements` on the workload.

The CDK keeps a logical ID stable as long as the construct's path doesn't change.

docs.title: AWS CDK constructs
docs.content:
## Limits

- Stacktape deploys the synthesized template only. It doesn't publish CDK assets, so constructs that package local
  files or Docker images, such as `lambda.Code.fromAsset()` or `BucketDeployment`, don't work. Run code with Stacktape
  [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or containers instead.
- No `overrides` and no dev mode. Change the construct's code instead.
- The construct's resources count toward CloudFormation's 500-resource limit per stack. CDK constructs often create more
  resources than you expect.

docs.title: Custom resources
docs.content:
# Custom resources

A custom resource runs your Lambda function when the stack creates, updates or deletes it. Use it to manage something
outside AWS together with the stack: a webhook in Stripe, a monitor in Datadog, a DNS record at another provider. It's
created on deploy, updated when its properties change and removed when you delete the stack.

It has two parts. A `custom-resource-definition` is the Lambda function with your code. A `custom-resource-instance`
is one managed thing: it names a definition and passes it properties. One definition can serve many instances.

For a step that just runs once per deploy, such as a migration, a [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts)
is simpler: it doesn't need the response protocol below. For an AWS resource type Stacktape doesn't have, use
[raw CloudFormation](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources).

docs.title: Custom resources
Custom resources
Custom resources
Custom resources
docs.content:
## Use the result elsewhere

Values in `Data` are attributes of the instance. Read them with
[`$CfResourceParam`](/configuration/directives) and the instance's logical ID, which is its name in PascalCase plus
`CustomResource`:

```typescript
environment: { WEBHOOK_ID: $CfResourceParam('ApiWebhookCustomResource', 'webhookId') }
```

`stacktape synth` writes the template to `compiled-template.yaml`, where you can confirm the logical ID.

docs.title: Custom resources
docs.content:
## Packaging and access

The definition takes the same packaging as a Lambda function: [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle),
[`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) or [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) with a
`handler` in `file:function` format. `runtime` is detected from the entry file unless you set it.

`connectTo` gives the function access to resources in the stack and injects their parameters, for example
`STP_CONFIG_BUCKET_NAME`. For other AWS services, add `iamRoleStatements`. See
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources).

The function runs only during deploys and deletes, so it costs a few Lambda invocations per deploy.

docs.title: Deployment scripts
docs.content:
# Deployment scripts

A `deployment-script` is a Lambda function that Stacktape runs during a deploy (`after:deploy`) or before a delete
(`before:delete`). Use it for work that must run inside AWS at that moment: database migrations, seed data, search
index mappings, cleanup before a stack is removed. With `connectTo` and `joinDefaultVpc` it can reach databases in the
stack's VPC.

Work that runs on your machine or CI runner, such as builds, belongs in [hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts). Work
longer than 15 minutes needs a [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job). The
[lifecycle guide](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts#choose-the-right-tool) compares the options for migrations.

docs.title: Deployment scripts
Deployment scripts
headingPath: When it runs and what a failure does
docs.content:
## When it runs and what a failure does

An `after:deploy` script runs on every deploy, after every other resource in the stack has been created or updated.
By then your new application code is already deployed and serving traffic, so for the length of the migration the new
code runs against the old schema.

If the script fails, the deploy fails:

- By default, the stack stays in `UPDATE_FAILED` with everything that already updated, including the new code. Fix the
  script and deploy again, or run [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/stack-recover) to return the stack to its previous
  version.
- With `deploymentConfig.autoRollback: true`, CloudFormation returns the infrastructure and the code to the previous
  version automatically.

Neither undoes what the script already wrote to the database. A rollback only means the old code runs against whatever
schema the script left behind. So:

- Make each migration work with both the old and the new code: add columns and tables, don't rename or drop them.
- Deploy the code that needs the new schema in the next release, after the migration is in.
- Drop old columns in a later release still, once no deployed code reads them.

docs.title: Deployment scripts
headingPath: When it runs and what a failure does
docs.content:
### before:delete

A `before:delete` script runs at the start of [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete), before any resource is removed. Use it
to export data or unregister webhooks. If it fails, the stack ends in `DELETE_FAILED` with the script's error. Fix the
script, or catch the errors you can live with inside it, and run the delete again.

```typescript
new DeploymentScript({
  trigger: 'before:delete',
  packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './scripts/cleanup.ts' }),
  timeout: 300
})
```

docs.title: Deployment scripts
docs.content:
## Run a script manually

```bash
stacktape deployment-script run migrate --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The command rebuilds the script from your local code, **replaces the code of the deployed script Lambda** with it,
resolves `parameters` from your local config and invokes it. So it runs the code in your working directory, not the
last deployed version, and that code stays deployed afterwards. Changes to `environment`, `connectTo`, memory, timeout
or VPC settings still need a [`deploy`](/cli/deploy). See [`deployment-script run`](/cli/deployment-script-run).

docs.title: Deployment scripts
docs.content:
## Packaging

| Type | When to use |
|------|-------------|
| [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle) | JavaScript and TypeScript. Stacktape bundles the entry file and what it imports. |
| [`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) | Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET or Rust. |
| [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) | A zip or directory you built yourself, with `handler` in `file:function` format. |

Stacktape picks the Lambda runtime from the file extension unless you set `runtime`. `memory` takes 128 to 10,240 MB
(more memory also means more CPU), and `storage` sets the `/tmp` space from 512 MB (the default) to 10,240 MB.

docs.title: Deployment scripts
docs.content:
## Connecting to resources

`connectTo` grants the script access to resources in the stack and injects their parameters as
`STP_<RESOURCE_NAME>_<PARAMETER>` variables, for example `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`. See
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for what each resource provides.

Databases and Redis run in the VPC, so the script also needs `joinDefaultVpc: true`. A Lambda function in the VPC has
no internet access unless the VPC has NAT (see `stackConfig.nat`). If the script must call an outside API too, set up
NAT or split it into two scripts. For AWS services that `connectTo` doesn't cover, add `iamRoleStatements`.

docs.title: Raw CloudFormation resources
docs.content:
# Raw CloudFormation resources

`cloudformationResources` adds plain CloudFormation resources to your stack's template. Use it for an AWS service
that has no Stacktape resource, such as a CloudWatch dashboard, a Cognito identity pool or a Glue job. Stacktape
merges them into the template as written and deploys them with the rest of the stack.

Check the [resource catalog](/resources/) first: a Stacktape resource gives you `connectTo`, alarms, dev mode and the
Console views, which raw resources don't get. To change one property of a resource Stacktape already creates, use
[overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches). For several related resources with sensible defaults, an
[AWS CDK construct](/resources/advanced/aws-cdk-constructs) saves you writing every property.

docs.title: Raw CloudFormation resources
Raw CloudFormation resources
Raw CloudFormation resources
Raw CloudFormation resources
headingPath: Check the template before you deploy
docs.content:
## Check the template before you deploy

A logical ID that matches one Stacktape generates breaks the deploy. Give your keys a distinct prefix and look at the
final template:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

`synth` writes the template to `compiled-template.yaml` without deploying. Search its `Resources` for your keys and for
the logical IDs of Stacktape's resources. Stacktape's own logical IDs are internal and can change between versions, so
reference Stacktape resources with `$ResourceParam` instead of their logical IDs.

docs.title: Raw CloudFormation resources
docs.content:
## Limits

A CloudFormation template holds at most 500 resources, raw ones included, and AWS doesn't raise this limit. One
Stacktape resource creates several CloudFormation resources, so a large stack reaches it sooner than the number of
entries in your config suggests. Stacktape warns from 470 resources and stops the deploy above 500. Error tracking
adds one log subscription per function and container; `deploymentConfig.errorTracking.enabled: false` frees them.
Beyond that, split the stack into several stacks.

CloudFormation itself is free. You pay for the AWS resources you add.

docs.title: Raw CloudFormation resources

- [Directives](/configuration/directives): `$ResourceParam`, `$CfResourceParam` and the others.

docs.content:
# AgentCore Browser

An `agentcore-browser` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser: a managed, isolated web browser your agent can drive to
read pages, fill in forms and click through sites. Use it with an [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime)
when the agent has to work with real web pages.

If the agent only calls APIs, it doesn't need a browser: call them from the agent's code, or expose them through an
[AgentCore Gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway).

docs.title: AgentCore Browser
AgentCore Browser
AgentCore Browser
docs.content:
## Cost

AgentCore bills browser sessions per second for the CPU and memory they use. Recordings add S3 storage. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

docs.title: AgentCore Code Interpreter
docs.content:
# AgentCore Code Interpreter

An `agentcore-code-interpreter` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter: a managed sandbox where your agent runs
code it writes, for example to analyze a CSV file, do exact calculations or draw a chart. Use it with an
[AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime).

An agent that only calls APIs or queries your databases doesn't need it; give the runtime access with `connectTo`
instead. Long-running jobs belong in a [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job).

docs.title: AgentCore Code Interpreter
AgentCore Code Interpreter
docs.content:
## Network and permissions

The sandbox runs in AgentCore's public network mode, so the code it runs can reach the internet. Its role allows every
`bedrock:*` and `bedrock-agentcore:*` action on all resources. Code that a model generates from user input runs with
those permissions, so treat what users can make the agent run as untrusted.

docs.title: AgentCore Code Interpreter
docs.content:
## Cost

AgentCore bills interpreter sessions per second for the CPU and memory they use. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

docs.title: AgentCore Gateway
docs.content:
# AgentCore Gateway

An `agentcore-gateway` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: one MCP endpoint that exposes your Lambda functions as
tools an agent can discover and call. Each tool declares its operations with a JSON schema, and the gateway invokes the
function behind it. Use it when an agent needs several tools, or when other MCP clients should use the same tools.

For one or two functions, an agent can invoke them directly with `connectTo` and skip the gateway. Tools behind a gateway
must be Lambda functions.

docs.title: AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Gateway
docs.content:
## Authorization

`authorizer` is required, because the gateway exposes every tool it lists:

- `type: 'jwt'` accepts only callers with a valid token from your identity provider. `discoveryUrl` points to the
  provider's `/.well-known/openid-configuration`; `allowedAudience`, `allowedClients` and `allowedScopes` narrow it
  down. For a [user auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool), the URL is
  `https://cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com/<user pool ID>/.well-known/openid-configuration`.
- `type: 'none'` lets anyone who reaches the endpoint call the tools. Use it only for tools that are safe in public.

With `jwt`, the agent must send a token with each request; `useGateway` doesn't give it one.

docs.title: AgentCore Gateway
docs.content:
## Other settings

- `instructions` tells agents in plain language what the gateway is for and when to use which tool.
- `searchType: 'SEMANTIC'` lets agents search the tools by meaning, useful with many tools.
- `supportedVersions` limits the MCP protocol versions the gateway accepts.
- `exceptionLevel: 'DEBUG'` returns detailed errors. Turn it off in production, where the details can expose internals.

docs.title: AgentCore Gateway
docs.content:
## Cost

AWS bills the gateway per tool call and per search, and the Lambda functions as usual. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

docs.title: AgentCore Memory
docs.content:
# AgentCore Memory

An `agentcore-memory` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory store. An agent saves conversation events to it and recalls
them later, also in a new session: what a user asked last week, their preferences, facts the agent extracted. Use it
with an [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime).

For your application's own data, use a [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) or a
[relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database). An agent that only needs context within one session
doesn't need a memory resource.

docs.title: AgentCore Memory
AgentCore Memory
docs.content:
## Retention

`eventRetentionDays` sets how long AgentCore keeps raw events before deleting them: 30 days by default, 7 to 365 days
allowed. Keep it short for passing conversational context; make it longer for agents that build up knowledge about a
user over months.

```typescript
new AgentCoreMemory({ eventRetentionDays: 90 })
```

docs.title: AgentCore Memory
docs.content:
## Memory strategies

Without strategies, the memory stores raw events only. A strategy makes AgentCore extract long-term records from them,
for example facts, summaries or user preferences. `memoryStrategies` is passed to AWS as written, in the CloudFormation
[`MemoryStrategies`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-resource-bedrockagentcore-memory.html)
format:

```typescript
new AgentCoreMemory({
  memoryStrategies: [
    { SemanticMemoryStrategy: { Name: 'facts', Namespaces: ['/users/{actorId}/facts'] } },
    { UserPreferenceMemoryStrategy: { Name: 'preferences', Namespaces: ['/users/{actorId}/preferences'] } }
  ]
})
```

Stacktape doesn't check the shape; AWS rejects an invalid strategy during the deploy.

docs.title: AgentCore Memory
docs.content:
## Encryption

AgentCore encrypts the memory at rest. To use your own KMS key, set `encryptionKeyArn`:

```typescript
new AgentCoreMemory({ encryptionKeyArn: 'arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:123456789012:key/your-key-id' })
```

docs.title: AgentCore Memory
docs.content:
## Cost

AgentCore Memory bills for events stored and for long-term records extracted and read. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
# AgentCore Runtime

An `agentcore-runtime` runs your AI agent as a container on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. AWS starts an isolated
session per conversation, scales them and bills for the CPU and memory a session uses. Stacktape builds the image,
creates the runtime and its endpoints, and connects the agent to AgentCore [memory](/resources/ai/agentcore-memory), a
[gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway), a [browser](/resources/ai/agentcore-browser) and a
[code interpreter](/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter).

For a service that calls a model and returns the answer, a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service) is simpler.

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
## Protocols

| `protocol` | Use when the container |
|----------|-------------|
| `HTTP` (default) | Serves `/invocations` and `/ping` as above |
| `MCP` | Is an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server |
| `A2A` | Speaks the Agent-to-Agent protocol |
| `AGUI` | Implements the AG-UI protocol |

Each protocol has its own port and paths, described in the
[AgentCore developer guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/).

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
headingPath: Tools: memory, gateway, browser and code interpreter

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
## Endpoints

An endpoint is the address callers use, passed as `--qualifier` when invoking. Without `endpoints`, Stacktape creates one
named `default`. List names, or objects with a `description` and a pinned `runtimeVersion`:

```typescript
endpoints: ['default', { name: 'beta', description: 'Preview of the next version' }]
```

The `endpointName` and `endpointArn` parameters point to the endpoint named `default`, or to the first one if none has
that name.

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
## Sessions and lifecycle

AWS keeps a session alive between requests with the same session ID. `lifecycle` limits how long:

- `idleTimeoutSeconds` ends a session after it has been idle this long. AWS's default is 15 minutes.
- `maxLifetimeSeconds` ends a session after this long even while it's active. AWS's default is 8 hours.

```typescript
lifecycle: { idleTimeoutSeconds: 300, maxLifetimeSeconds: 7200 }
```

A shorter idle timeout lowers cost for agents that answer quickly. Keep it longer when users pause mid-conversation and
the agent holds state in memory.

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
## Authentication

Without an `authorizer`, callers sign requests with AWS credentials that are allowed to invoke the runtime. To let users
call it with tokens from your identity provider, set a JWT authorizer:

```typescript
authorizer: {
  discoveryUrl: 'https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_abc123/.well-known/openid-configuration',
  allowedAudience: ['my-app-client-id'],
  allowedClients: ['trusted-client'],
  allowedScopes: ['agent:invoke']
}
```

`discoveryUrl` is required; the other three are optional filters on the token's claims.

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
## Access to other resources

The runtime's role allows every `bedrock:*`, `bedrock-agentcore:*` and `bedrock-agentcore-control:*` action on all
resources, so the agent can call Bedrock models and AgentCore tools without extra permissions. Keep that in mind when
you review what the agent's code is allowed to do.

`connectTo` gives the agent access to resources in the stack and injects their parameters, for example
`STP_CONVERSATIONS_NAME` for a DynamoDB table named `conversations`. For other AWS services, add `iamRoleStatements`.

`environment` passes other settings; put secrets there with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives).
`requestHeaders` lists request headers, such as `X-Tenant-Id`, that AgentCore forwards to the container.

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
## Packaging

AgentCore Runtime takes the [container packaging](/packaging/overview) types: `js-bundle` (`JsBundleImagePackaging`) for
one TypeScript or JavaScript entry file, `buildpack` for Python and other languages without a Dockerfile, `dockerfile`
for full control, and `prebuilt-image` for an existing arm64 image.

docs.title: AgentCore Runtime
docs.content:
## Cost

AgentCore Runtime bills per second for the CPU and memory a session actually uses, and doesn't charge CPU while the agent
waits for a model or a tool. Model calls, memory, gateway and browser are billed separately. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

docs.title: Batch job
docs.content:
# Batch job

A batch job runs a container until it finishes: a nightly export, a video transcode, an import, a model training run.
A trigger starts it (a schedule, an HTTP request, a file upload, a queue message and others), and you declare the CPU,
memory and optional GPU it needs. It runs on AWS Batch, which starts EC2 instances for queued jobs and stops them when
the queue is empty.

You pay for the EC2 instances while jobs run, including their start-up time, and nothing between jobs. Spot capacity
costs up to 90% less if the job can be interrupted. For work under 15 minutes, a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) starts faster; for a process that never ends, use a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service).

docs.title: Batch job
Batch job
Batch job
docs.content:
## Packaging

A batch job supports four container image packaging types. Start with `js-bundle` for JavaScript or TypeScript and `buildpack` for other languages, then switch only when the image needs precise runtime control.

| Type | When to use |
|------|-------------|
| [`js-bundle`](/packaging/containers/js-bundle) | A JavaScript or TypeScript job with one entry file. Stacktape bundles it into a small image. |
| [`buildpack`](/packaging/containers/buildpack) | Build from source without a Dockerfile. Detects Python, Go, Rust, Java, PHP, Ruby, .NET, Node.js and more. |
| [`dockerfile`](/packaging/containers/dockerfile) | Control the Dockerfile, build context, build args and startup command |
| [`prebuilt-image`](/packaging/containers/prebuilt-image) | Run an image that already exists in a registry and optionally override its command |

Put the job's settings in `container.environment`, secrets in [`$Secret()`](/configuration/secrets).

docs.title: Batch job
docs.content:
## Triggers

Pick the trigger by where the work comes from. Sources that retry delivery can start the same job twice, so make the
job safe to repeat.

| Trigger type | Use it for |
|--------------|------------|
| `schedule` | Recurring jobs such as reports, cleanup, imports, and periodic syncs |
| `s3` | Object-created, object-removed, restore, or replication events from a bucket |
| `sqs` | Queue-backed jobs where each message or batch represents work to process |
| `sns` | Pub/sub fanout where a topic delivery should start the job |
| `kinesis-stream` | Stream records processed in batches |
| `dynamo-db-stream` | Table change records after DynamoDB streams are enabled |
| `http-api-gateway` | HTTP request starts a job through an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) |
| `application-load-balancer` | HTTP request starts a job through an [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) rule |
| `cloudwatch-log` | Matching CloudWatch log records start the job |
| `event-bus` | EventBridge events matching a pattern start the job |

The [configuration reference](#configuration-reference) has each trigger's options, and the
[triggers overview](/resources/triggers/overview) compares them.

docs.title: Batch job
Batch job
Batch job
Batch job
Batch job
Batch job
docs.content:
## Dev mode

Batch jobs always run in AWS Batch, also in [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview): dev mode builds and
pushes their images at startup, so restart it after changing job code. `--resources` and `--skip-resources` don't apply
to them; use a dev-specific config to leave a job or its triggers out. A job reaches local databases through the
[dev network](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#the-dev-network), with its AWS costs and network round
trip.

docs.title: Convex
docs.content:
# Convex

The Convex resource runs a self-hosted [Convex](https://www.convex.dev) backend in your AWS account: the Convex server
on ECS, a PostgreSQL database on RDS, five S3 buckets for its storage, an Application Load Balancer for HTTPS and
WebSocket traffic, and the admin dashboard. After each deploy, Stacktape pushes your Convex functions to it.

It runs all the time. With the defaults, an idle deployment costs about $60 a month in us-east-1:

| Part | Default size | Per month |
|---|---|---|
| Backend | 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB on Fargate | about $18 |
| Dashboard | 0.25 vCPU, 0.5 GB on Fargate | about $9 |
| Database | `db.t4g.micro`, 20 GB | about $14 |
| Load balancer | Application Load Balancer | about $16 plus traffic |

Each container and the load balancer also pay $3.65 a month per public IPv4 address. Prices are x86 Fargate, RDS and
ELB on-demand rates for 730 hours ([Fargate pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/fargate/pricing/)).

Use it when your data must stay in your AWS account or you want Convex next to the rest of your stack. Otherwise
Convex's own cloud is cheaper to start with and runs the backend for you.

docs.content:
## Database

Convex stores its data in a PostgreSQL database that it owns: single-AZ RDS PostgreSQL 16 on `db.t4g.micro` by default,
with 20 GB of storage, one day of backups and access from the backend only. You can't point Convex at an existing
database.

`database.engine` takes the PostgreSQL engines of a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database):
RDS PostgreSQL (default), Aurora Serverless v2 or provisioned Aurora. Convex needs PostgreSQL 13 or later. The
`database` property also takes `automatedBackupRetentionDays` (default 1; raise it for production),
`preferredMaintenanceWindow` and `logging`. Leave `accessibility` as it is: only the backend needs the database.

docs.content:
## Deletion protection

`deletionProtection: true` protects the database and the five buckets. A delete then stops until you deploy with
`deletionProtection: false`. It's off by default; turn it on for production stages.

docs.content:
## Backups

The database has daily automated backups (one day by default). For a portable copy of your data, use
`npx convex export`. `storage.versioning` lets you recover overwritten or deleted files.

docs.content:
# Edge function

An edge function is a Lambda@Edge function that CloudFront runs on requests and responses of a
[CDN](/resources/networking/cdn), at locations close to your users. Use it for small decisions before or after the
origin: redirects, URL rewrites, security headers, A/B routing or a quick token check.

It can't use environment variables or reach anything in your VPC, and a viewer-side function gets at most 128 MB and
5 seconds. Lambda@Edge costs $0.60 per million requests plus run time, with no free tier
([Lambda@Edge pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/pricing/)). For rules a CDN can express without code, such as
caching or path routing, use the [CDN settings](/resources/networking/cdn); for application logic, a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function).

docs.title: Edge function
Edge function
docs.content:
## CDN attachment

A CDN's `edgeFunctions` names the function for one of four hooks: `onRequest` and `onResponse` run between the
viewer and CloudFront; `onOriginRequest` and `onOriginResponse` run between CloudFront and your origin, only on cache
misses. Route rewrites can attach their own functions. See [Edge functions on the CDN](/resources/networking/cdn#edge-functions).

Edge functions write their logs to CloudWatch in the region where CloudFront ran them, which is often not your stack's
region. Look for them in the region closest to the users who made the requests. `logging` sets retention and
forwarding.

docs.title: Lambda function
docs.content:
# Lambda function

A Lambda function runs your code on AWS Lambda each time an event arrives: an HTTP request, a queue message, a
schedule, a file upload. It scales from zero to thousands of parallel invocations, and you pay per request and per
millisecond of run time, so an idle function costs nothing. One invocation can run for at most 15 minutes.

For an always-on server or a long-running process, use a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) or a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service). For jobs longer than 15 minutes, use a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job).

docs.title: Lambda function
Lambda function
docs.content:
## Packaging

Stacktape supports three Lambda packaging types: [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle), [`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) and [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact).

| Type | Best for |
|---|---|
| **`js-bundle`** (JavaScript, TypeScript) | Point to a source file. Stacktape bundles, minifies and source-maps the code, moves code shared between functions into a shared layer, and uploads the package. |
| **`buildpack`** (Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET, Rust) | Point to a source file. Stacktape installs dependencies and compiles the code in Docker on the Lambda build image of the function's `runtime`. |
| **`custom-artifact`** | Provide a pre-built zip. Use when your CI already produces a deployment package or when you need a build step Stacktape does not support. |

`js-bundle` and `buildpack` are the better defaults: they detect the runtime from the file extension, build for the selected architecture and skip unchanged packages. Use [custom artifact](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) only when you own the build outside Stacktape.

docs.title: Lambda function
Lambda function
Lambda function
Lambda function
Lambda function
Lambda function
docs.content:
## Runtime resources

`runtime`, `architecture`, `memory`, `timeout` and `storage` set the language version, CPU, time limit and scratch
disk of each invocation.

`runtime` comes from the file extension with `js-bundle` and `buildpack` packaging. Set it to pin a version, for Rust
(`provided.al2023`) and for `custom-artifact` packaging. The accepted values are listed in the
[configuration reference](#configuration-reference).

`memory` is 128 MB unless you set it, and accepts 128 to 10,240 MB. CPU grows with memory: 1,769 MB is one vCPU. For
CPU-bound code, more memory often costs less in total, because the function finishes sooner.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const imageProcessor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/image-processor.ts' }),
    runtime: 'nodejs22.x',
    architecture: 'arm64',
    memory: 2048,
    timeout: 120,
    storage: 2048
  });

  return { resources: { imageProcessor } };
});
```


`architecture: 'arm64'` (AWS Graviton) costs about 20% less per GB-second than the default `x86_64` and usually needs no
code changes. `js-bundle` and `buildpack` build for the architecture you pick; with a custom artifact, compile native
dependencies for it yourself.

`storage` sets the size of `/tmp`, from 512 MB (default) to 10,240 MB. It's scratch space: it isn't shared between
instances and can disappear between invocations.

docs.title: Lambda function
Lambda function
docs.content:
## Networking

A function runs outside your VPC by default and can reach the internet. Set `joinDefaultVpc: true` only when it must
reach something that accepts VPC connections only: a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database)
in a VPC access mode, a [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) or an [EFS file system](/resources/storage/efs-filesystem).

A function in the VPC loses internet access. S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints, but calls to payment
providers, AI APIs or webhooks fail. To keep them working, set `stackConfig.nat`: VPC functions then run in private
subnets and go out through NAT. The `ec2` NAT is one small instance managed by Stacktape (about $7 a month, no
failover), `ha-ec2` runs one per availability zone with failover, and `gateway` uses AWS NAT Gateways (about $32 a
month per zone plus $0.045 per GB). See [VPC and networking](/configuration/connecting-resources#vpc-and-networking).
Without NAT, `stacktape deploy` warns about every VPC function that has no internet access.

docs.title: Multi-container workload
docs.content:
# Multi-container workload

A multi-container workload runs several containers as one ECS task. They start and stop together, share the task's
CPU and memory and reach each other on `localhost`, and each container can take traffic from its own load balancer or
API gateway. It runs on Fargate by default, or on EC2.

Use it when containers must run as one unit, for example an API with a metrics exporter, or a broker and its admin UI.
For a single container, a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), [private service](/resources/compute/private-service)
or [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) takes less configuration; they also run helper containers with
`sideContainers`. The task bills while it runs, shared by all its containers: 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB cost about $18 a month
on x86 Fargate in us-east-1.

docs.title: Multi-container workload
Multi-container workload
Multi-container workload
docs.content:
## Traffic

A multi-container workload creates no load balancer of its own. Each container lists `events` that point at a gateway
or load balancer defined elsewhere in the config, so different containers can take different traffic:

| Type | Traffic |
|---|---|
| `http-api-gateway` | HTTP from an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) |
| `application-load-balancer` | HTTP and WebSockets from an [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) |
| `network-load-balancer` | TCP or TLS from a [Network Load Balancer](/resources/networking/network-load-balancer) |
| `workload-internal` | Other containers of the same workload |
| `service-connect` | Other container workloads in the stack, by name |

## Private subnets and NAT

Containers run in public subnets with a public IP address by default and reach the internet directly.
`usePrivateSubnetsWithNAT: true` moves the task to private subnets and sends outbound traffic through NAT, for example
when a partner API allowlists your IP addresses.

The flag requires `stackConfig.nat`, which decides the NAT device, its cost and the outbound IP addresses: one
Stacktape-managed instance (`ec2`, about $7 a month), one per availability zone with failover (`ha-ec2`), or AWS NAT
Gateways (`gateway`, about $32 a month per zone plus $0.045 per GB). See
[VPC and networking](/configuration/connecting-resources#vpc-and-networking).

Each container's output goes to CloudWatch Logs, kept for 90 days by default. `logging` on a container changes its
retention, turns it off or sets up [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding). Read logs with
[`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs).

docs.content:
# Private service

A private service runs always-on containers that only other resources in your stack can call, such as an internal
API or a gRPC backend. It runs on ECS (Fargate by default, or EC2), has no public endpoint, and Stacktape handles
service discovery and scaling. Add a [health check](#health-checks) so ECS replaces a container that runs but stops
answering.

At least one container runs and bills all the time: 0.25 vCPU and 512 MB cost about $9 a month on x86 Fargate in
us-east-1 ([Fargate pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/fargate/pricing/)). For a container with a public URL, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service); for one nothing calls, such as a queue consumer, a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service).

docs.title: Private service
Private service
docs.content:
## Compute resources

Fargate (default) runs containers without servers to manage. EC2 runs them on instances Stacktape manages.

## Load balancing

Two modes decide who can reach the service:

| | `service-connect` (default) | `application-load-balancer` |
|---|---|---|
| Who can call it | Container workloads in the stack | Anything in the VPC, including VPC Lambda functions and a bastion |
| Cost | The stack's service discovery namespace, about $0.50 a month for all services | About $16 a month plus capacity units |

Keep `service-connect` unless something other than a container must call the service.

# Web service

A web service runs your app in a container with a public HTTPS URL: an API, a backend web app or any HTTP server
that stays running. It runs on ECS (Fargate by default, or EC2), and Stacktape adds the HTTPS endpoint, scaling and
logs.

At least one container runs and bills all the time: 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB cost about $18 a month on x86 Fargate in
us-east-1, plus $1 per million requests through the default HTTP API Gateway. For code that should cost nothing while
idle, use a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function). For a container only your other services call, use
a [private service](/resources/compute/private-service).

## CDN

`cdn` puts CloudFront in front of the service. It helps when responses are cacheable or users are far from your
region; for dynamic APIs, start without it. See [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) for caching and routing.

`useFirewall` attaches a regional [firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) to the service's Application
Load Balancer (only with `application-load-balancer`). `cdn.useFirewall` attaches a `cdn` firewall to CloudFront.

## Packaging

Start with `js-bundle` for JavaScript or TypeScript with one entry file, and `buildpack` for everything else.

| Type | Use it for |
|---|---|
| [`js-bundle`](/packaging/containers/js-bundle) | JavaScript or TypeScript with one entry file. Stacktape bundles it into a small image. |
| [`buildpack`](/packaging/containers/buildpack) | Other languages and frameworks without a Dockerfile: Python, Go, Rust, Java, PHP, Ruby, .NET, Next.js and more |
| [`dockerfile`](/packaging/containers/dockerfile) | Your own Dockerfile |
| [`prebuilt-image`](/packaging/containers/prebuilt-image) | An image another pipeline already built |

`js-bundle` images are based on Alpine. Set `requiresGlibcBinaries` when native dependencies such as `sharp`, `canvas`,
`bcrypt` or `puppeteer` need glibc. A `buildpack` service must listen on `PORT`; set `startCommand` if the detected
start command doesn't.

docs.content:
## Health checks

There are two kinds:

- **Load balancer health check** (`application-load-balancer` and `network-load-balancer`): decides whether a container
  gets traffic. Configure it under `loadBalancing.properties`. A Network Load Balancer checks TCP or HTTP;
  `healthcheckPath` applies only to HTTP.
- **`internalHealthCheck`**: ECS runs a command inside the container and replaces the container when it keeps failing.
  It catches a process that runs but is broken, for example with a dead database pool. Keep the command cheap and
  local; a check that depends on a slow external service replaces healthy containers.

The default `http-api-gateway` mode has no load balancer check. Stacktape can tell that a new container runs, not that
your app works. Add an `internalHealthCheck` and a failing release stops the deploy and rolls it back. For a Node.js
app on port 3000:
`internalHealthCheck: { healthCheckCommand: ['CMD', 'node', '-e', "fetch('http://localhost:3000/health').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"] }`.
Use a command your image has and an endpoint that succeeds only when the app is ready.

docs.title: Web service
docs.content:
## How deploys replace containers

A deploy starts the new containers next to the old ones. Once the new containers are up, the old containers stop
receiving new requests, get 30 seconds to finish the requests they are handling, and shut down: ECS
sends `SIGTERM` and, if the process is still running after `stopTimeout` (default 30 seconds), `SIGKILL`. Handle
`SIGTERM` in your app so an old container exits once its requests are done. An app that ignores the signal keeps a full
deploy waiting for the whole `stopTimeout`.

A full deployment finishes after the old containers have stopped, because CloudFormation waits for that. A
[fast deployment](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#fast-deployments), which Stacktape uses when only your code
changed, lets the old containers drain and shut down in the background. What "up" means, and when the deploy finishes,
depends on your health checks and load balancing:

- **Default `http-api-gateway`, no `internalHealthCheck`:** the deploy finishes once every new task is `RUNNING` and
  API Gateway can route to it, plus 4 seconds. Only tasks from the new deployment count; an old task still draining
  cannot satisfy this check. API Gateway sends requests to a new container within about 2 seconds of its start, even
  before your app listens. This confirms that the containers started, not that your app works: an app that stays
  running without listening, or returns errors, can still count as deployed.
- **Default `http-api-gateway` with `internalHealthCheck`:** the deploy finishes 4 seconds after every new container
  has passed its check and API Gateway can route to it. A failing check stops the deploy and rolls it back. In our
  measurements, the first request reached the new containers at most 2.2 seconds after they became routable, and ECS
  removed the old containers from Cloud Map 8 to 22 seconds after the new ones passed the check.
- **Behind an `application-load-balancer` or `network-load-balancer`:** the deploy finishes 4 seconds after the load
  balancer reports every new container healthy in each of its target groups. The load balancer starts sending
  requests a few seconds after that: 1 to 3 seconds for an application load balancer in our measurements; we have not
  measured network load balancers. Old containers keep receiving part of the requests until ECS removes them from the
  load balancer. Without an `internalHealthCheck`, that happens about 50 seconds after the deploy finishes, because ECS
  counts a new container healthy only after it has run for 40 seconds. With one, it happened 15 to 40 seconds after the
  new containers turned healthy.
- **First deploy with Stacktape v4 (`http-api-gateway`):** v4 protects old containers behind API Gateway while they
  shut down (see below). The first deployment that adds this protection still retires old containers without it. Keep
  an application shutdown delay for that one deployment, or deploy in a maintenance window.
- **With [gradual deployments](#gradual-deployments):** the deploy follows the CodeDeploy traffic-shifting strategy
  instead, and containers keep a 5-second drain and a 2-second default `stopTimeout`.

Stacktape does not check that requests already reach the new containers when a fast deployment finishes; no AWS API
shows that moment. The 4 seconds are an allowance for routing to catch up.

docs.title: Web service
docs.content:
### Old containers behind API Gateway

With the default `http-api-gateway` load balancing, API Gateway finds containers through AWS Cloud Map and has no
health check of its own. It sends requests to the containers Cloud Map returns: the healthy ones or, while none is
healthy, all of them. Without an `internalHealthCheck`, ECS registers a new container as healthy as soon as it starts.
With one, ECS registers it as unhealthy and marks it healthy once the check passes, and Cloud Map applies that change
seconds to a minute later. Once ECS removes the old containers from Cloud Map, it returns only the new ones.

API Gateway can keep routing requests to an old container after ECS removes it from Cloud Map. To cover that, Stacktape
adds a small `stp-cloudmap-drain` container to tasks behind an HTTP API:

- ECS stops this container first. It waits 35 seconds before ECS signals your application containers, so your app can
  then close its server on `SIGTERM` and use its own `stopTimeout` to finish in-flight work.
- Code-only deploys keep their completion timing: this delay runs in the background and does not add a readiness check.
  Full CloudFormation deploys, scale-in and deletion take about 36 seconds longer per stopped task; tasks stopped in
  parallel wait in parallel.
- The delay is 35 seconds. To raise it, use task definition `overrides` to change the drain container's command and
  raise its `StopTimeout` above the new delay.
- The container is non-essential. If it exits unexpectedly, your app keeps running but loses this protection.
- It uses a digest-pinned BusyBox image that Stacktape copies once into the stack's private ECR repository, for both
  amd64 and arm64, without Docker. Later deploys reuse the cached images, and task starts pull only from private ECR.
- The privileged Console connection role already allows this copy. Restricted deployer roles need
  `ecr:BatchGetImage`, `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability`, `ecr:InitiateLayerUpload`, `ecr:UploadLayerPart`,
  `ecr:CompleteLayerUpload` and `ecr:PutImage` on the stack's deployment repository, even when all application images
  are prebuilt.
- Upgrade the CLI for your whole team and on Console runners before you deploy with this helper. Older CLIs can delete
  its cached images during image retention.

## In-place code swap

`codeSwap: true` opts into [in-place code swaps](/deployment-and-lifecycle/code-swap): a code-only deploy replaces the
code inside the running containers instead of starting new ones. It supports Node.js and Python on x86 Fargate behind an
HTTP API or an Application Load Balancer, up to ten tasks. Old and new processes share memory for a moment, so a sudden
jump in memory use can fail requests. Services it doesn't support deploy a new image as usual.

docs.content:
# Worker service

A worker service runs an always-on container with no URL: a queue consumer, a polling loop or a background job
runner. It runs on ECS (Fargate by default, or EC2) in your stack's VPC and can reach your databases, queues and the
internet.

At least one container runs and bills all the time. A task with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB costs about $18 a month on x86
Fargate in us-east-1, and Graviton (`arm64`) about 20% less ([Fargate pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/fargate/pricing/)).
For work that arrives in bursts with long quiet gaps, a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) with an
[SQS trigger](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) costs nothing while idle. For a container other services call, use a
[private service](/resources/compute/private-service); for one with a public URL, a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service); for work that finishes, a [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job).

docs.title: Aurora DSQL
docs.content:
# Aurora DSQL

A `dsql-database` is an Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster: a serverless, PostgreSQL-compatible database with no instances,
passwords or network rules to configure. It scales on its own, and your code connects over TLS with a short-lived IAM
token.

You pay for the work done (distributed processing units, $8 per million) and $0.33 per GB-month of storage, with a
monthly free allowance of 100,000 units and 1 GB ([DSQL pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/aurora/dsql/pricing/)). An
idle database costs only its storage.

DSQL supports a subset of PostgreSQL. Check the
[compatibility guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aurora-dsql/latest/userguide/working-with-postgresql-compatibility-migration-guide.html)
before moving an existing app, especially one that uses extensions, uncommon data types or long-running sessions. For
full PostgreSQL, MySQL and the other engines, password sign-in or backup settings in your config, use a
[relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database).

docs.title: Aurora DSQL
Aurora DSQL
Aurora DSQL
docs.content:
## Least-privilege access

`connectTo` intentionally uses the built-in `admin` database role so a new cluster is immediately useful. That is full database access. When a platform engineer needs a narrower production boundary:

1. Connect as `admin`, create an application database role, and map it to an IAM principal using DSQL's `AWS IAM GRANT` SQL command.
2. Pass `endpoint`, `region`, and the other required values explicitly with `$ResourceParam()` or the TypeScript resource properties.
3. Grant only `dsql:DbConnect` for the cluster ARN in the workload's `iamRoleStatements`.

Do not leave the same workload connected through `connectTo`, because that would retain the `dsql:DbConnectAdmin` grant.

docs.title: Aurora DSQL
docs.content:
## Data protection

Set `deletionProtection: true` for production. Stacktape also treats DSQL as a database for the `require-deletion-protection` guardrail. When enabled, AWS rejects deletion until you redeploy with deletion protection disabled.

Deletion protection is not a backup. This v1 resource does not configure AWS Backup, point-in-time recovery, or a final snapshot, and deleting a cluster can be irreversible without a separately configured backup. Restoring an AWS Backup recovery point creates a new cluster rather than rewinding the existing one.

docs.title: Aurora DSQL
docs.content:
## Encryption

By default, DSQL uses an AWS-owned encryption key. Set `kmsKeyArn` only when you need control over the key policy and lifecycle:

```yaml
resources:
  database:
    type: dsql-database
    properties:
      deletionProtection: true
      kmsKeyArn: arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:123456789012:key/example
```

docs.title: Aurora DSQL
docs.content:
## Current boundaries

Stacktape v1 creates a single-region DSQL cluster using its public service endpoint. It does not yet configure multi-region peering, PrivateLink VPC endpoints, AWS Backup plans, adoption of an existing cluster, local emulation, or `query sql` support. A DSQL resource therefore fails the `require-vpc-databases` and `require-data-backups` guardrails closed. These boundaries are explicit so a short configuration does not silently create cross-region infrastructure or account-level backup resources.

Stacktape validates regional availability before deployment. Within Stacktape's region catalog, DSQL is supported in
US East (N. Virginia and Ohio), US West (Oregon), Hong Kong, Mumbai, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Canada
Central, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Paris, Stockholm, and São Paulo. An unsupported region fails before
CloudFormation with the valid choices in the error.

For CloudFormation properties not exposed above, use the `cluster` child through [overrides and transforms](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches).

docs.title: DynamoDB
docs.content:
# DynamoDB

A DynamoDB table is a serverless key-value and document store with single-digit millisecond reads and writes at any
scale. There are no servers or connections to manage, and in the default on-demand mode you pay per request:
$0.625 per million writes and $0.125 per million reads in us-east-1, plus $0.25 per GB-month of storage after the
first 25 GB ([DynamoDB pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/on-demand/)). An idle table costs nothing
beyond its storage.

It fits data you read by known keys: users, sessions, carts, device readings, counters. If you need joins, ad-hoc
queries or reports, use a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database); for full-text search, use
[OpenSearch](/resources/databases/opensearch).

docs.title: DynamoDB
DynamoDB
DynamoDB
docs.content:
## Capacity modes

DynamoDB offers two billing modes that control how you pay for reads and writes. The choice is a cost vs. operational tradeoff.

docs.title: DynamoDB
docs.content:
### On-demand mode

On-demand is the default when you omit `provisionedThroughput`. DynamoDB manages capacity for you and you pay per request. This is the safest default for variable or unpredictable traffic — it requires zero capacity planning. Very large or sudden traffic changes can still run into AWS service limits, but for most teams this is the right starting point.

On-demand pricing is higher per-request than provisioned mode, but you avoid paying for unused capacity. Start here and switch to provisioned only after your traffic patterns stabilize and you can predict capacity needs.

docs.title: DynamoDB
DynamoDB
docs.content:
### Auto-scaling

`readScaling` and `writeScaling` let DynamoDB adjust capacity between `minUnits` and `maxUnits`. `keepUtilizationUnder`
is required: the target utilization in percent. A lower target, such as 70, leaves more headroom before requests are
throttled.

For most provisioned-mode workloads, enable auto-scaling. Without it, a traffic spike throttles requests immediately.

| Mode | Best for | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| On-demand (default) | Variable or unpredictable traffic | Higher per-request cost, zero management |
| Provisioned | Steady, predictable traffic | Lower per-request cost, requires capacity planning |
| Provisioned + auto-scaling | Mostly predictable with occasional spikes | Balance of cost and flexibility |

# MongoDB Atlas

A MongoDB Atlas cluster is a MongoDB database that MongoDB runs for you on AWS, in the region of your stack. Stacktape
creates it through your Atlas organization, gives your workloads access to it and peers it with your stack's network.

The cluster runs in MongoDB's account and you pay MongoDB, not AWS. Dedicated clusters start at M10, about $57 a month
([Atlas pricing](https://www.mongodb.com/pricing)). For a document or key-value store that costs nothing while idle and
stays in your AWS account, use [DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb).

docs.title: MongoDB Atlas
MongoDB Atlas

docs.content:
## Cluster tiers

`clusterTier` sets the size and price of each node, from `M10` up to `M700`, with Low-CPU (`'M40 Low-CPU (R40)'`) and
NVMe (`'M40_NVME'`) variants from M40. Most teams start production on M10 or M20. Sharding needs M30 or larger.

MongoDB retired the shared `M2` and `M5` tiers in 2025. Stacktape still accepts the names, but Atlas no longer creates
new clusters on them, so pick M10 or larger. The free M0 tier and Flex clusters aren't available through Stacktape.

`version` is `'7.0'` by default; `'6.0'` and `'5.0'` are also accepted.

docs.title: OpenSearch
docs.content:
# OpenSearch

An OpenSearch domain is a managed Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster for full-text search, log analytics and
dashboards. You set the node types, counts and storage; AWS runs the cluster.

It runs all the time. The basic example below, one `t3.medium.search` node with 20 GB, costs about $56 a month in
us-east-1 ([OpenSearch pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/pricing/)). For key-value lookups, use
[DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb); for occasional simple text search, PostgreSQL full-text search in a
[relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) may be enough. In
[dev mode](#dev-mode) it runs locally in Docker at no AWS cost.

docs.title: OpenSearch
OpenSearch
OpenSearch
docs.content:
## Cluster configuration

`clusterConfig` sets the data nodes and, optionally, dedicated master and UltraWarm nodes.

docs.title: OpenSearch
docs.content:
### Data nodes

Data nodes hold the indices and answer queries. One `t3.small.search` or `t3.medium.search` node is enough for
development; production clusters usually run memory-optimized nodes such as `r6g.large.search`.

docs.title: OpenSearch
docs.content:
### Dedicated master nodes

Dedicated master nodes manage the cluster state and keep heavy queries from destabilizing it. Add three (an odd count
for quorum) once you have three or more data nodes. They hold no data, so a general-purpose type such as
`m6g.large.search` is enough.

docs.title: OpenSearch
docs.content:
### Warm storage

UltraWarm nodes store rarely read data, such as old logs, for much less than hot storage. Queries on it are slower.

docs.title: OpenSearch
OpenSearch
docs.content:
### Multi-AZ and standby

With two or more data nodes, Stacktape spreads them across availability zones so the cluster survives a zone outage.
`multiAzDisabled: true` turns that off; don't do it in production.

`standbyEnabled: true` uses three zones with one as standby, which takes over without rebalancing. It needs OpenSearch
1.3 or later, three dedicated masters, three or more data nodes and gp3 or SSD-backed instance types.

(`opensearchproject/opensearch`), and workloads get its local `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` endpoint without
authentication. Run `stacktape dev --remote-resources search` to use the deployed domain instead, for example to test
IAM access.

docs.title: Redis
docs.content:
# Redis

A `redis` resource is a managed Redis-compatible cache on Amazon ElastiCache, for caching, sessions, rate limits,
queues and pub/sub with sub-millisecond reads and writes. It runs Valkey, the open-source continuation of Redis that AWS
maintains, so Redis clients such as ioredis, node-redis, redis-py and Jedis work unchanged. The cache lives in your
stack's VPC, has no public endpoint and encrypts traffic.

The smallest cache costs about $6 a month idle (Valkey Serverless) or $9.40 a month (one `cache.t4g.micro` node). It's
not a system of record: keep the data you can't lose in a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database)
or [DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb). For Lambda functions outside a VPC, [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis)
works over HTTPS.

docs.title: Redis
docs.content:
## Choose an engine

`engine.type` decides which software runs the cache and how AWS runs it. There is no default: the choice changes cost and which command patterns work.

| | `valkey-serverless` | `valkey` | `redis` |
|---|---|---|---|
| How it runs | Serverless, scales automatically | Fixed-size nodes | Fixed-size Redis OSS nodes |
| Billing | Per GB stored + per request | Per node-hour | Per node-hour (25% more than Valkey) |
| Smallest cost | ~$6/month idle (100 MB minimum) | ~$9.40/month (`cache.t4g.micro`) | ~$11.70/month (`cache.t4g.micro`) |
| High availability | Built in, across Availability Zones | Add replicas + automatic failover | Add replicas + automatic failover |
| Cache creation | About 2 minutes | About 5 minutes | About 5 minutes |
| Multi-key commands | Keys must share a hash slot | Unrestricted | Unrestricted |
| Use for | New caches with small or spiky data | Large datasets, any client pattern | Existing caches only |

Prices are for us-east-1, running all month ([ElastiCache pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/pricing/)).

docs.title: Redis
Redis
Redis
Redis
docs.content:
### Changing engines later

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| `redis` → `valkey` | In place; brief write pause; cannot be reversed |
| `valkey` → `redis` | Not supported |
| Serverless ↔ node-based | Not allowed: AWS would replace the cache, with a new endpoint and no data |
| Version upgrade | In place |
| Version downgrade | Not supported |

To move between serverless and node-based, create a new resource with a different name, move your application to it, then remove the old one.

docs.title: Redis
docs.content:
## Versions

Without `engine.properties.version`, a new cache gets the latest version and an existing cache keeps the version it runs. A Stacktape update never upgrades a cache on its own.

- `valkey-serverless`: major versions `9`, `8`, `7`.
- `valkey`: `9.1`, `9.0`, `8.2`, `8.1`, `8.0`, `7.2`.
- `redis`: `7.1`, `7.0`, `6.2`, `6.0` (required).

docs.title: Redis
docs.content:
## Instance sizing

For `valkey` and `redis`, `engine.properties.instanceSize` determines the memory, CPU, and cost of every node (primary and replicas). You can change it after creation without data loss.

| Instance | Family | Memory | Approx. Valkey cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cache.t4g.micro` | Burstable (Graviton) | 0.5 GB | ~$0.013/hr | Dev/test, low-traffic apps |
| `cache.t4g.small` | Burstable (Graviton) | 1.37 GB | ~$0.026/hr | Small production, session stores |
| `cache.m7g.large` | General purpose (Graviton) | 6.38 GB | ~$0.12/hr | Moderate production workloads |
| `cache.r7g.large` | Memory-optimized (Graviton) | 13.07 GB | ~$0.16/hr | Large datasets, heavy caching |

- **`t` (burstable)**: cheapest, variable CPU performance. Good for development and intermittent traffic.
- **`m` (general purpose)**: consistent CPU performance for production workloads.
- **`r` (memory-optimized)**: highest memory-to-CPU ratio for large datasets.
- **Graviton suffix (`g`)**: ARM-based instances with better price-performance. Prefer `t4g`/`m7g`/`r7g`.

docs.title: Redis
docs.content:
## High availability (node-based)

Serverless caches replicate across Availability Zones automatically. Node-based caches have a single primary node by default.

docs.title: Redis
Redis
Redis
Redis
Redis
Redis
Redis
docs.content:
## Logging (node-based)

Node-based caches send slow-query logs to CloudWatch by default, retained for 30 days. View them with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs). Customize them with `engine.properties.logging` (`format`, `retentionDays`, `disabled`, and [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding)). Serverless caches have no slow-query log.

docs.title: Redis
Redis
docs.content:
## Migrating from `redis-cluster`

Stacktape v4 renamed `redis-cluster` to `redis` and moved node settings under `engine.properties`. To keep a deployed cache unchanged, set `engine.type: redis` with the version it runs (`6.2` if `engineVersion` was not set):

```yaml

docs.title: Redis
docs.content:
# Stacktape v3
cache:
  type: redis-cluster
  properties:
    defaultUserPassword: $Secret('redis', 'password')
    instanceSize: cache.t4g.micro

docs.title: Redis
docs.content:
# Stacktape v4
cache:
  type: redis
  properties:
    defaultUserPassword: $Secret('redis', 'password')
    engine:
      type: redis
      properties:
        instanceSize: cache.t4g.micro
        version: '6.2'
```

The cache keeps its endpoint and data. Switch it to Valkey afterwards by changing `engine.type` to `valkey`.

docs.title: Relational database
docs.content:
# Relational database

A relational database is a managed SQL database on Amazon RDS or Aurora. You pick the engine, and Stacktape creates the
database, its network access, its credentials and its backups in your AWS account.

Standard RDS and provisioned Aurora bill for every hour an instance runs, used or not. The smallest PostgreSQL
instance, `db.t4g.micro`, is about $12 a month in us-east-1 plus storage. Aurora Serverless v2 bills for the capacity it
uses and, by default, pauses when nobody connects. For key-value data with no idle cost, use
[DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb).

docs.title: Relational database
Relational database
docs.content:
## Engine types

| | Standard RDS | Aurora | Aurora Serverless v2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Engines | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server | PostgreSQL, MySQL | PostgreSQL, MySQL |
| Compute | One instance of a size you pick | Instances of a size you pick | Scales between `minCapacity` and `maxCapacity` |
| Idle cost | Full instance price | Full instance price | Storage only while paused |
| High availability | `multiAz` standby (doubles the instance cost) | Add a second instance | Add a reader |

Start with standard RDS when you want one fixed monthly price, or with Aurora Serverless v2 when traffic is uneven or
the database sits idle for long periods (dev and preview stages). Provisioned Aurora suits large production databases
that need fast failover and several readers.

Choose before you store data you care about. Changing `instanceSize` or `multiAz` later updates the instance in place,
with a short interruption for a size change. Changing the engine type, for example from RDS to Aurora, replaces the
database: the deploy creates an empty new one and deletes the old one with its data. Dump the data first and restore
it into the new database, and keep `deletionProtection` on so a deploy can't delete the old database by accident.

docs.title: Relational database
docs.content:
### Standard RDS

Engine types: `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `oracle-se2`, `sqlserver-ee`, `sqlserver-ex`, `sqlserver-se` and
`sqlserver-web` (classes `RdsEnginePostgres`, `RdsEngineMysql`, `RdsEngineMariadb`, `RdsEngineOracleSE2` and the
`RdsEngineSqlServer*` classes). Oracle and SQL Server run with a license included in the instance price. AWS includes
the Oracle license only for Standard Edition 2, and Stacktape has no bring-your-own-license option, so use `oracle-se2`
for Oracle.

`instanceSize` sets CPU and memory. PostgreSQL prices in us-east-1, single-AZ, on-demand
([RDS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/postgresql/pricing/)):

| Instance | vCPU | RAM | Per month (730 hours) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `db.t4g.micro` | 2 | 1 GB | about $12 |
| `db.t4g.medium` | 2 | 4 GB | about $47 |
| `db.r6g.large` | 2 | 16 GB | about $164 |

The `t` family is burstable: it earns CPU credits while idle and slows down when it runs out under sustained load. It
suits development and small production apps. The `r` family gives steady performance and more memory. Move to it when
CPU stays above about 60% for long periods.

Storage is billed separately; see [Storage](#storage).

docs.title: Relational database
Relational database
Relational database
docs.content:
## Database name, port and version

| Property | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `dbName` | `defdb` | The database created with the instance. For Oracle it's the SID (8 characters at most). SQL Server doesn't accept it. |
| `port` | 5432 PostgreSQL, 3306 MySQL and MariaDB, 1521 Oracle, 1433 SQL Server | Not configurable on Aurora Serverless v2. |
| `version` | Required | A release line (`'16'` for PostgreSQL, `'8.4'` for MySQL) or an exact version (`'16.9'`). |

With a release line, AWS runs a current minor version and applies new minor versions in the maintenance window.
Switching a deployed database from `'16.6'` to `'16'` doesn't change the running version. Oracle and SQL Server need an
exact version. Set `disableAutoMinorVersionUpgrade: true` on the engine to stop automatic minor upgrades.

docs.title: Relational database
Relational database
docs.content:
## Credentials

`masterUserPassword` is required; `masterUserName` defaults to `db_master_user`. Keep the password in a
[secret](/configuration/secrets) with `$Secret()`, as in the examples.


> **Warning:** Changing `masterUserName` after the first deploy replaces the database and deletes all its data.


Avoid these characters in the username and password: `[]{}(),;?*=!@`. Many drivers and ORMs fail to parse connection
strings that contain them.

docs.title: Relational database
Relational database
Relational database
Relational database
docs.content:
## Backups and maintenance

AWS backs up the database every day. `automatedBackupRetentionDays` sets how long backups are kept (default 1 day):

- Standard RDS accepts 0 to 35. 0 turns automated backups off.
- Aurora accepts 1 to 35. Aurora backups can't be turned off.

Raise it to 7 or more for production. With one day of backups, you can't go back past yesterday when someone finds bad
data on Monday. A restore creates a new database from a backup; you do it in the AWS console and then point your config
or workloads at the restored database.

`preferredMaintenanceWindow` sets when AWS applies patches, in UTC (for example `Sun:02:00-Sun:04:00`). By default it's
Sunday 02:00–04:00 in the region's local standard time, and the daily backup runs an hour before it. The database can be
unavailable for a short time during maintenance; `multiAz` and Aurora readers shorten it.

Deleting the stack, or removing the database from the config, deletes the database without a final snapshot.
`deletionProtection: true` prevents that for production data. While it's on, `stacktape delete` lists the protected
databases and stops before deleting anything, and a deploy can't remove or replace the database. To remove it, deploy
with `deletionProtection: false` first.

docs.title: Relational database
Relational database
Relational database
docs.content:
## Dev mode

In [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview), PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and Aurora databases run
locally in Docker with their own generated password. Oracle and SQL Server can't run locally. Set `dev.remote: true` to
use the deployed database instead. See [Local databases](/local-development/local-databases).

| `connectionString` | Fully-formed connection string that can be used to access the primary instance. For aurora databases, this is connectionString to cluster endpoint, which can be used for both reads and writes. Includes **host**, **port**, **username**, **password** and **dbName**. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "connectionString")` |

docs.title: Upstash Redis
docs.content:
# Upstash Redis

Upstash Redis is a serverless Redis database run by Upstash, outside your AWS account. Your code reaches it over HTTPS
(the REST API) or the Redis protocol, so [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) need no VPC and no
connection pool. Stacktape creates the database through your Upstash account.

You pay Upstash, per command: $0.20 per 100,000 commands, plus $0.25 per GB-month of stored data after the first GB
([Upstash pricing](https://upstash.com/pricing/redis)). An idle database costs only its storage. For high, steady
traffic from containers, a [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) in your VPC is faster and cheaper per request.

docs.title: Upstash Redis
docs.content:
## Provider configuration

Stacktape needs your Upstash account email and an Upstash API key, created in the Upstash console under
**Account → Management API**. Store the key as a [secret](/configuration/secrets):

```bash
stacktape secret set upstash-api-key
```

Then reference it in `providerConfig.upstash`, once per stack, as in the example below. You can also save the
credentials once on the **Third-party providers** page of the [Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).

docs.title: Upstash Redis
Upstash Redis
Upstash Redis
docs.content:
## Connecting from workloads

Add the database to a workload's [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources). For a database named `cache`, the
workload gets:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `STP_CACHE_REST_URL` | REST API URL |
| `STP_CACHE_REST_TOKEN` | REST token with full access |
| `STP_CACHE_READ_ONLY_REST_TOKEN` | REST token that can only read |
| `STP_CACHE_REDIS_URL` | Redis protocol URL, with the password |
| `STP_CACHE_HOST`, `STP_CACHE_PORT`, `STP_CACHE_PASSWORD` | Redis protocol parts |

Give code that only reads the read-only token.

docs.title: Astro
docs.content:
# Astro

An `astro-web` deploys an Astro app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a
Lambda function, puts static assets in S3 and serves both through a CloudFront CDN. You pay per request and for traffic.
No server runs while nobody visits; the stored assets still cost a little.

For a fully static Astro site (no `output: 'server'`), [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) with `hostingContentType: 'astro-static-website'` is simpler and has no function to pay for. To run Astro as a long-running Node server instead, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

docs.title: Astro
Astro
docs.content:
## Build and dev mode

Stacktape runs `astro build` in `appDirectory`. Set `buildCommand` when your repository builds through a script, for
example `pnpm --filter web build`.

[`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) starts `astro dev` locally. Change it with `dev.command`, and
with `dev.workingDirectory` (relative to the project root) when the command must run from another folder. Neither
changes the deployed build.

```typescript
new AstroWeb({
  appDirectory: './apps/web',
  buildCommand: 'pnpm --filter web build',
  dev: { command: 'pnpm --filter web dev' }
})
```

docs.title: Astro
docs.content:
## Server function

`serverLambda` tunes the function that renders pages:

- `memory`: 1024 MB by default, 128 to 10,240. More memory also means more CPU; 1,769 MB is one vCPU.
- `timeout`: 30 seconds by default, which is also the maximum.
- `joinDefaultVpc: true`: needed to reach a relational database or Redis. The function then has no direct internet
  access; S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints.
- `logging`: retention and forwarding of its CloudWatch logs.

docs.title: Astro
Astro
docs.content:
## Custom domain

```typescript
new AstroWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the
deploy stops with an error. Stacktape then creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.

To keep DNS at another provider, request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers both paths.

docs.title: Astro
docs.content:
## Firewall

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) in front of the CDN. The
firewall resource needs `scope: 'cdn'`.

```typescript
new AstroWeb({ appDirectory: '.', useFirewall: 'firewall' })
```

docs.title: Astro
docs.content:
## Caching

The defaults cache static assets on the CDN and send page requests to the function. To cache server-rendered pages
that change rarely, and save function runs, add rules per path:

```typescript
new AstroWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  cdn: {
    pathCachingOverrides: [{ path: '/blog/*', cachingOptions: { defaultTTL: 300 } }]
  }
})
```

Don't cache pages that depend on cookies or the signed-in user; every visitor would get the cached copy.

- `cdn.defaultCachingOptions` sets caching (`minTTL`, `defaultTTL`, `maxTTL`) for all server responses.
- `fileOptions` sets headers such as `Cache-Control` on static files matching an `includePattern`.
- Stacktape clears the CDN cache after each deploy; `cdn.disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true` turns that off.
