docs.title: Next.js
docs.content:
# Next.js

A `nextjs-web` deploys a Next.js app on AWS. Stacktape builds it with OpenNext, runs server rendering in a Lambda
function, puts static assets in S3, serves both through a CloudFront CDN, and creates what ISR and image optimization
need. Nothing runs while nobody visits: you pay per request and for traffic, plus a little storage.

For a site exported with `output: 'export'`, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) is simpler. To run
Next.js as a long-running Node server instead, use a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

docs.title: Next.js
Next.js
Next.js
docs.content:
## Server function

`serverLambda` tunes the function that renders pages:

- `memory`: 1024 MB by default, 128 to 10,240. More memory also means more CPU; 1,769 MB is one vCPU.
- `timeout`: 30 seconds by default, which is also the maximum.
- `joinDefaultVpc: true`: needed to reach a relational database or Redis. The function then has no direct internet
  access; S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints, but the ISR revalidation queue (SQS) doesn't.
  See [Connect to resources](#connect-to-resources).
- `logging`: retention and forwarding of its CloudWatch logs.

docs.title: Next.js
docs.content:
### Cold starts

`warmServerInstances` keeps that many server function instances warm with a scheduled warmer function, so the first
request after a quiet period doesn't wait for a cold start. It's 0 by default. Use it for production apps where cold
starts are visible to users; each warm instance adds a small number of invocations.

docs.title: Next.js
docs.content:
### Streaming

`streamingEnabled: true` streams server-rendered responses, so the browser gets the first bytes before the page is
finished, and responses can be larger than the 6 MB limit of a buffered Lambda response.

```typescript
new NextjsWeb({ appDirectory: '.', streamingEnabled: true, warmServerInstances: 2 })
```

docs.title: Next.js
docs.content:
### Edge rendering

`useEdgeLambda: true` renders pages in Lambda@Edge, close to each visitor. Deploys get slower, and it can't be combined
with `warmServerInstances` or `streamingEnabled`. Keep regional rendering unless measured latency for distant users
says otherwise.

docs.title: Next.js
Next.js
docs.content:
## Custom domain

```typescript
new NextjsWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once, before the first deploy that uses it. First decide where its DNS lives:

- **DNS in Route 53.** Follow [Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain). If the
  domain already serves a website or email at another DNS provider, copy those records into the new hosted zone before
  you change the name servers at your registrar, or they stop working. The command also requests the certificate the
  CDN needs in `us-east-1`. Without an issued certificate, the deploy stops with an error. After that, Stacktape
  creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.
- **DNS stays at your current provider.** Request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set
  `customCertificateArn` and `disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. See
  [External DNS](/resources/networking/custom-domains#external-dns).

docs.title: Next.js
docs.content:
## Firewall

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) in front of the CDN. The
firewall resource needs `scope: 'cdn'`.

```typescript
new NextjsWeb({ appDirectory: '.', useFirewall: 'firewall' })
```

docs.title: Next.js
docs.content:
## Caching

Next.js sets cache headers itself, and the CDN follows them: static assets are cached, dynamic pages are not, and ISR
pages are served from the cache and revalidated in the background. Stacktape clears the CDN cache after each deploy;
`cdn.disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true` turns that off.

`cdn.defaultCachingOptions`, `cdn.pathCachingOverrides` and `fileOptions` change CDN caching and static file headers,
as on the other [framework resources](/resources/frontend/astro#caching). Most Next.js apps don't need them.

docs.title: Next.js
docs.content:
## Cost

A quiet app costs little: Lambda bills per request and duration, S3 per GB stored and per request, CloudFront per GB
and per request, and the DynamoDB table that tracks ISR per GB stored (with point-in-time recovery) and per request.
Warm instances add their scheduled invocations, whether or not anyone visits. After a deploy, the
[cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards) show the real spend per stack.

docs.content:
# SolidStart

A `solidstart-web` deploys a SolidStart app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a
Lambda function, puts static assets in S3 and serves both through a CloudFront CDN. You pay per request and for traffic.
No server runs while nobody visits; the stored assets still cost a little.

For a site with no server rendering, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) is simpler and has no function to pay for. To run SolidStart as a long-running Node server instead, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

docs.title: SolidStart
SolidStart
docs.content:
## Build and dev mode

Stacktape runs `vinxi build` in `appDirectory`. Set `buildCommand` when your repository builds through a script, for
example `pnpm --filter web build`.

[`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) starts `vinxi dev` locally. Change it with `dev.command`, and
with `dev.workingDirectory` (relative to the project root) when the command must run from another folder. Neither
changes the deployed build.

```typescript
new SolidStartWeb({
  appDirectory: './apps/web',
  buildCommand: 'pnpm --filter web build',
  dev: { command: 'pnpm --filter web dev' }
})
```

docs.title: SolidStart
docs.content:
## Server function

`serverLambda` tunes the function that renders pages:

- `memory`: 1024 MB by default, 128 to 10,240. More memory also means more CPU; 1,769 MB is one vCPU.
- `timeout`: 30 seconds by default, which is also the maximum.
- `joinDefaultVpc: true`: needed to reach a relational database or Redis. The function then has no direct internet
  access; S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints.
- `logging`: retention and forwarding of its CloudWatch logs.

docs.title: SolidStart
SolidStart
docs.content:
## Custom domain

```typescript
new SolidStartWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the
deploy stops with an error. Stacktape then creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.

`disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers both paths.

docs.title: Static hosting
docs.content:
# Static hosting

A `hosting-bucket` hosts a static site: Stacktape builds it, uploads the output to S3 and serves it through a CloudFront
CDN. Use it for single-page apps (React, Vue, Angular, Vite) and for static sites and fully pre-rendered framework
output. You pay for storage, requests and traffic, which for most sites is a few dollars a month or less.

For server rendering, use the framework resource instead: [Next.js](/resources/frontend/nextjs),
[Astro](/resources/frontend/astro), [Nuxt](/resources/frontend/nuxt), [SvelteKit](/resources/frontend/sveltekit),
[SolidStart](/resources/frontend/solidstart), [TanStack Start](/resources/frontend/tanstack-start) or
[Remix](/resources/frontend/remix). For files that aren't a website, use an [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket).

docs.title: Static hosting
Static hosting
docs.content:
## Build

`build.command` runs through the shell, so `npm ci && npm run build` works. `workingDirectory` (relative to the project
root, which is the default) sets where it runs; if that folder has its own `package.json`, Stacktape installs its
dependencies first. Point `uploadDirectoryPath` at the build output, not the sources.

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './apps/site/dist',
  build: { command: 'npm run build', workingDirectory: './apps/site' },
  dev: { command: 'npm run dev', workingDirectory: './apps/site' }
})
```

Leave out `build` when another CI step already produced the files. `excludeFilesPatterns`, such as
`['**/*.map', '**/.DS_Store']`, keeps files out of the upload. Everything uploaded is public, so never put secrets in
the output folder.

docs.title: Static hosting
docs.content:
## Caching and routing presets

`hostingContentType` sets browser caching, CDN caching and routing for the kind of site you have:

| Preset | For | What it does |
|--------|-----|--------------|
| `static-website` (default) | Multi-page static sites | CDN caches files; browsers revalidate, so visitors see a new deploy right away |
| `single-page-app` | React, Vue, Angular, Vite and other client-routed apps | Serves `index.html` for client-side routes; caches hashed `.js` and `.css` forever |
| `astro-static-website` | Static Astro builds | Caches hashed `_astro/` assets forever; keeps HTML fresh |
| `sveltekit-static-website` | Static SvelteKit builds | Caches hashed `_app/` assets forever; keeps HTML fresh |
| `nuxt-static-website` | Static Nuxt builds | Caches hashed `_nuxt/` assets forever; keeps HTML fresh |
| `gatsby-static-website` | Gatsby builds | Follows Gatsby's caching recommendations |

`fileOptions` adds headers, such as `Cache-Control`, to files matching an `includePattern` when a preset is close but
not exact.

`indexDocument` (default `/index.html`) is served for `/`, and `errorDocument` for missing pages, for example
`/404.html`. URLs are normalized so `/about` serves `/about.html`; `disableUrlNormalization: true` turns that off.

docs.title: Static hosting
docs.content:
## Deploy-time values

A static site can't ask your stack for values such as the API URL. `injectEnvironment` puts them into the page: on each
deploy, Stacktape writes them into the uploaded HTML files, where your code reads `window.STP_INJECTED_ENV.API_URL`.
Your build doesn't change.

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './dist',
  build: { command: 'npm run build' },
  injectEnvironment: { API_URL: $ResourceParam('api', 'url') }
})
```

These values end up in the browser, so use them for public settings, not secrets. `writeDotenvFilesTo` also writes
them to `.env.<stage>` in the given folder after each deploy, merged with what's there, for local scripts and tools.

In dev mode, `stacktape dev` passes the `injectEnvironment` values to the `dev.command` server as environment variables.
A `$ResourceParam` of a function or container resolves to the URL dev mode runs it at. The values are also written to
`.env.local` in the dev `workingDirectory`, inside a block between `# >>> stacktape dev` and `# <<< stacktape dev <<<`
lines; your own lines in that file stay. Bundlers expose only prefixed variables to browser code, so name them
accordingly, for example `VITE_API_URL`, and read `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`.

docs.content:
## Custom domain

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './dist',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the

To keep DNS at another provider, request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set `customCertificateArn` and

covers both paths.

docs.title: Static hosting
headingPath: API routes on the same domain
docs.content:
## API routes on the same domain

`routeRewrites` sends matching paths to another origin, for example `/api/*` to an HTTP API Gateway, so the site and its
API share one domain and need no CORS. Rules are checked in order; anything unmatched goes to the bucket.

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './dist',
  hostingContentType: 'single-page-app',
  routeRewrites: [{ path: '/api/*', routeTo: { type: 'http-api-gateway', properties: { httpApiGatewayName: 'api' } } }]
})
```

The [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) page lists all origin types and caching options for rewrites.

docs.title: Static hosting
docs.content:
## Edge functions and firewall

`edgeFunctions` runs an [edge function](/resources/compute/edge-function) on each request (`onRequest`, before the
cache lookup) or response (`onResponse`), for example for redirects, basic auth or headers. Keep application logic in a
normal backend.

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) with `scope: 'cdn'` in
front of the site.

docs.title: Email sender
docs.content:
# Email sender

An `email-sender` gives your workloads a verified Amazon SES identity to send email from: a domain or one email
address. Stacktape verifies the identity, sets up DKIM and bounce handling, and grants connected workloads permission
to send from it and nothing more.

docs.title: Email sender
Email sender
docs.content:
## Verification and DNS

For a domain, Stacktape sets up 2048-bit Easy DKIM. If the domain has a public Route 53 hosted zone that the domain is
actually delegated to, Stacktape creates the three DKIM CNAME records. A hosted zone that exists but isn't delegated
doesn't count.

With DNS elsewhere, the deploy succeeds while verification is pending and prints the three CNAME names and values. Add
them at your DNS provider. For a single email address, SES sends a verification link to that mailbox instead.


> **Warning:** SES identities and the SES sandbox are per region. In the sandbox you can send only to verified recipients, with low
daily limits. Stacktape warns and links to the production access request, but doesn't block the deploy. Request
production access before you send to customers.

docs.title: Email sender
docs.content:
## Shared identity

An SES identity belongs to the AWS account and region, not to one project or stage. Stacktape creates it in a separate
shared CloudFormation stack with termination protection, one per identity. Every project and stage in that account and
region that uses `example.com` shares it; `billing@example.com` is a different identity.

Deleting a project's stack doesn't delete the shared stack, and the delete output lists it as retained. Stacktape
doesn't remove unused shared identities for you.

The shared stack also has:

- a configuration set that suppresses addresses that bounced or complained;
- an SNS topic for feedback;
- a destination that publishes `BOUNCE` and `COMPLAINT` events to that topic.

Because they're shared, a feedback subscriber sees the feedback for every send from that identity, including other
projects and stages. Make feedback processing idempotent.

docs.title: Email sender
docs.content:
## Handle bounces and complaints

Subscribe a function to the feedback topic with an [SNS event](/resources/triggers/sns-events):

```yaml
resources:
  mail:
    type: email-sender
    properties:
      identity: example.com

  processEmailFeedback:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/process-email-feedback.ts
      events:
        - type: sns
          properties:
            snsTopicArn: $ResourceParam('mail', 'feedbackTopicArn')
```

docs.title: Email sender
docs.content:
## Use an identity managed elsewhere

Set `manageIdentity: false` to use an identity that another tool created. Stacktape checks that the exact identity
exists, but never takes it over, changes it or widens it to a parent domain.

```yaml
resources:
  mail:
    type: email-sender
    properties:
      identity: billing@example.com
      manageIdentity: false
      configurationSetName: centrally-managed-mail
```

`configurationSetName` is optional. When you set it, Stacktape checks that it exists and limits the send permission to
it. External identities don't get Stacktape's feedback topic; set up feedback where the identity is managed.

docs.title: Email sender
docs.content:
## What it doesn't set up

Custom MAIL FROM domains, DMARC records, your own DKIM keys, SES templates, bulk sending, inbound email, dedicated IPs,
Virtual Deliverability Manager and multi-region identities. Add those with
[raw CloudFormation resources](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources) and `iamRoleStatements`.

docs.title: Event bus
docs.content:
# Event bus

An `event-bus` is an Amazon EventBridge event bus. Services publish events such as `OrderPlaced` to the bus, and rules
deliver each event to the consumers whose pattern matches it: [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function),
[batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) or [SQS queues](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue). The producer doesn't know
who listens, and a new consumer doesn't need a change to the producer. You pay $1.00 per million published events in US
East.

For one consumer working through jobs, an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) is simpler. When every subscriber
needs every message, an [SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic) is enough. A container can't be a rule's target:
deliver the events to an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue#deliver-eventbridge-events-to-the-queue) and let a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) poll it.

docs.title: Event bus
Event bus
Event bus
docs.content:
## Archive and replay

`archivation` stores the events published to the bus so you can replay them later, for example to debug an incident
or to fill a new consumer with past events. Replayed events go through the bus again and the current rules route them.

```typescript
new EventBus({ archivation: { enabled: true, retentionDays: 30 } })
```

Without `retentionDays`, archived events are kept forever. Archive storage and replays are billed separately. Setting
`enabled` back to `false` deletes the archive. The archive's ARN is the bus's `archiveArn` parameter.

docs.title: Event bus
docs.content:
## AWS and partner events

You don't need a bus for events from AWS services: they arrive on the account's default bus. Subscribe with
`useDefaultBus: true` on the [event bus trigger](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events).

For a SaaS provider that sends events through EventBridge (Zendesk, Auth0, Datadog and others), set `eventSourceName`
to the partner event source name the provider gave you:

```typescript
new EventBus({ eventSourceName: 'aws.partner/example.com/1234567890/my-integration' })
```

docs.title: Kafka cluster
docs.content:
# Kafka cluster

A `kafka-cluster` is an Amazon MSK Serverless cluster with IAM authentication in the stack's VPC. There are no broker
sizes, capacity units or network settings to choose; Stacktape sets secure defaults and a dedicated security group. Use
it only when you need Kafka itself, for example for existing Kafka clients or tools.


> **Warning:** An MSK Serverless cluster costs about $0.75 per cluster-hour in AWS's US East (Ohio) example, or about $558 for a
31-day month, before partition, data and storage charges. Every stage gets its own cluster. For queues and streams
without Kafka, use an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) or a [Kinesis stream](/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream).

docs.title: Kafka cluster
docs.content:
## Basic example

```yaml
resources:
  events:
    type: kafka-cluster

  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      joinDefaultVpc: true
      connectTo:
        - events
```

`connectTo` injects `ARN`, `NAME` and a comma-separated `BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS` (here `STP_EVENTS_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`). It
grants IAM Kafka connect, topic and consumer group actions on this cluster, including `CreateTopic`, but not
`AlterTopic` or `DeleteTopic`.

A Lambda function that connects as a Kafka client needs `joinDefaultVpc: true`. Containers already run in the VPC. To
consume a topic with a Lambda trigger instead, use a [Kafka topic event](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics); its poller
has its own networking and the function doesn't join the VPC.

docs.title: Kafka cluster
Kafka cluster
docs.content:
## Lambda triggers and VPC endpoints

A [Kafka topic event](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics) on a cluster in the stack makes Stacktape create Lambda and STS
interface endpoints in the VPC for Lambda's poller. They add hourly and per-GB charges in every availability zone.

docs.title: Kafka cluster
docs.content:
## Dev mode

Stacktape doesn't emulate Kafka locally, and `stacktape dev` doesn't deploy the cluster unless you ask for it:

```yaml
events:
  type: kafka-cluster
  properties:
    dev:
      remote: true
```

`--remote-resources events` does the same for one session. Either way the real cluster is deployed and billed.
Containers running on your machine can't reach the private cluster by themselves; use a deployed workload or set up
private access to the VPC.

docs.title: Kafka cluster
docs.content:
## Regions and deletion

Stacktape checks that MSK Serverless is available before deploying. Supported regions: US East (N. Virginia and Ohio),
US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Seoul, Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London and
Paris. Other regions fail with the list of valid ones.

Deleting the stage deletes the cluster and all topic data; Stacktape doesn't keep it, because a forgotten cluster costs
around $558 a month. Back up or replicate data before you delete.

Every property of an MSK Serverless cluster requires a replacement, and AWS needs a fixed cluster name, so a
replacement may delete the old cluster before creating the new one. Stacktape's change preview marks this as
destructive. To keep it from happening by accident, the resource has no capacity, network, authentication, tag or
override settings.

In a reused VPC, Stacktape picks one public subnet per supported availability zone and needs at least two. MSK doesn't
support the `use1-az3` zone, and zone names map to physical zones differently in each account. So in `us-east-1` the
cluster requires `stackConfig.vpc.reuseVpc`, and Stacktape leaves out `use1-az3` when it picks subnets. In other regions
Stacktape can create the VPC itself.

Prices: [Amazon MSK pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/msk/pricing/) and
[AWS PrivateLink pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/privatelink/pricing/).

docs.title: Kinesis stream
docs.content:
# Kinesis stream

A `kinesis-stream` is an Amazon Kinesis data stream: producers write records, and consumers read them in order per
partition key and can read them again later. Use it for high-volume, ordered data such as clickstreams, telemetry or
change events that several consumers read independently.

A stream costs money while idle. The default on-demand mode charges $0.04 per stream-hour in US East (about $29 for a
30-day month) before any data. For background jobs, an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) has no idle charge.
For events that several services react to, an [event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) is cheaper at low volume.

docs.title: Kinesis stream
Kinesis stream
Kinesis stream
docs.content:
## Capacity mode

|  | On-demand (default) | Provisioned |
|---|---|---|
| Scaling | AWS adds capacity as traffic grows | You set `shardCount` |
| Throughput | Scales with traffic | Per shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in, 2 MB/s out |
| Idle cost in US East | $0.04 per stream-hour | $0.015 per shard-hour |
| Traffic cost | Per GB written and read | Per million PUT units ($0.014) |

On-demand needs no planning and suits uneven traffic. For steady traffic, provisioned is cheaper: one shard costs about
$11 a month in US East before PUT units. See [Kinesis pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/kinesis/data-streams/pricing/).

```typescript
new KinesisStream({ capacityMode: 'PROVISIONED', shardCount: 2 })
```

docs.title: Kinesis stream
docs.content:
## Retention

Records stay for 24 hours by default. `retentionPeriodHours` keeps them up to 8,760 hours (365 days), so consumers can
reprocess after a bug fix or a new consumer can read history. Retention beyond 24 hours costs extra.

```typescript
new KinesisStream({ retentionPeriodHours: 168 })
```

docs.title: Kinesis stream
docs.content:
## Encryption

`encryption: { enabled: true }` encrypts records at rest with the AWS-managed Kinesis key, which needs no extra
permissions. Set `kmsKeyArn` to use your own KMS key. `connectTo` doesn't grant access to that key, so add
`kms:GenerateDataKey` for producers and `kms:Decrypt` for consumers with `iamRoleStatements`.

docs.title: Kinesis stream
docs.content:
## Enhanced fan-out

Consumers share each shard's 2 MB/s read throughput. When several consumers read the same stream and latency matters,
give a Lambda consumer its own throughput with `autoCreateConsumer: true` on its
[Kinesis event](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events#enhanced-fan-out). AWS charges per consumer-shard hour and per GB
read. The stream's own `enableEnhancedFanOut` property is deprecated and does nothing; setting it prints a warning.

docs.title: SNS topic
docs.content:
# SNS topic

An `sns-topic` is an Amazon SNS topic: you publish a message once and every subscriber gets its own copy. Use it when
one event needs several independent reactions, such as an order that triggers a receipt, an inventory update and
analytics. A standard topic costs $0.50 per million publishes in US East after the first million each month, and
delivery to Lambda and SQS is free.

SNS doesn't store messages. With one consumer, an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) is simpler and keeps
messages until they're processed. To route on fields inside the message, use an
[event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus).

docs.title: SNS topic
SNS topic
SNS topic
SNS topic
docs.content:
## Standard or FIFO

|  | Standard | FIFO |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Best effort | Kept within each message group |
| Duplicates | A message is sometimes delivered twice | Duplicate publishes within 5 minutes are dropped |
| Subscribers | Lambda, SQS, HTTP, email, SMS | SQS queues only |
| Throughput | Practically unlimited | Limited per topic, see the [AWS quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/sns.html) |

A standard topic bills per publish, and each 64 KB of a message counts as one. Delivery to Lambda and SQS is free;
HTTP, email and SMS deliveries are charged. A FIFO topic bills per published and delivered message and per GB of
payload, so each extra subscriber adds cost. See [SNS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/sns/pricing/).

Use a standard topic unless the order matters. `fifoEnabled: true` creates a FIFO topic. Each publish then needs a
`MessageGroupId` and a deduplication ID, or set `contentBasedDeduplication: true` to use a hash of the body.

```typescript
new SnsTopic({ fifoEnabled: true, contentBasedDeduplication: true })
```

A FIFO topic can't invoke Lambda. Subscribe FIFO queues and consume them with [SQS events](/resources/triggers/sqs-events)
to keep the order. It can also deliver to standard queues, but those don't keep the order or drop duplicates.

docs.title: SNS topic
docs.content:
## SMS sender name

`smsDisplayName` (up to 11 characters) is the sender name on SMS messages sent through the topic. SMS has its own price
per message by country, and new AWS accounts start in an SMS sandbox that only sends to verified numbers.

docs.title: SQS queue
docs.content:
# SQS queue

An `sqs-queue` is an Amazon SQS message queue. One part of your app puts a job on the queue and returns; a consumer
processes it at its own pace, and a burst of jobs waits in the queue instead of overloading the consumer. You pay per
request: the first million each month are free, then $0.40 per million for standard queues in US East.

A queue delivers each message to one consumer. When several services need the same message, publish it to an
[SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic) or an [event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) and give each consumer its
own queue.

docs.title: SQS queue
SQS queue
SQS queue
SQS queue
docs.content:
## Visibility timeout and polling

After a consumer receives a message, the queue hides it for `visibilityTimeoutSeconds` (30 by default). If the consumer
doesn't delete it in time, the message comes back and runs again. Set it above your longest processing time; for a
Lambda consumer, at least the function's `timeout`. Stacktape refuses to deploy a Lambda trigger whose function timeout
is longer than the queue's visibility timeout.

`longPollingSeconds` makes a receive call wait up to that many seconds for messages instead of returning empty at once.
Set it to 20 for container consumers: fewer empty calls, lower cost. Lambda triggers poll on their own and ignore it.

```typescript
new SqsQueue({ visibilityTimeoutSeconds: 300, longPollingSeconds: 20 })
```

docs.title: SQS queue
SQS queue
docs.content:
## Standard or FIFO

|  | Standard | FIFO |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Best effort | Kept within each message group |
| Duplicates | A message is sometimes delivered twice | Duplicate sends within 5 minutes are dropped |
| Throughput | Practically unlimited | 300 calls per second, 3,000 messages with batching |
| Price in US East | $0.40 per million requests | $0.50 per million requests |

Use a standard queue unless the order of messages matters. FIFO stops duplicate *sends*, but a consumer can still get
a message again when it fails or runs past the visibility timeout. Write consumers to be idempotent with either type.

`fifoEnabled: true` creates a FIFO queue. Each message then needs a deduplication ID, or set
`contentBasedDeduplication: true` to use a hash of the body. Every message also needs a `MessageGroupId`; messages with
the same group ID are processed in order.

```typescript
new SqsQueue({ fifoEnabled: true, contentBasedDeduplication: true })
```

`fifoHighThroughput: true` raises the FIFO limit to thousands of calls per second (up to 70,000 in the largest regions).
Order then holds only within each message group, which is already the rule for consumers.

docs.title: SQS queue
headingPath: Deliver EventBridge events to the queue

docs.title: SQS queue
docs.content:
## Other settings

- `delayMessagesSecond` (0 to 900) keeps new messages hidden for that long before consumers can receive them.
- `messageRetentionPeriodSeconds` sets how long unprocessed messages stay, from 60 seconds to 14 days. The default is
  4 days.
- `maxMessageSizeBytes` lowers the size limit below 1 MiB. For larger payloads, upload the data to an
  [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) and send the object key.
- `policyStatements` adds statements to the queue policy, for another account or an AWS service principal. Workloads in
  the stack use `connectTo` instead.

docs.title: SQS queue
docs.content:
## Alarms

Two alarm triggers watch a queue:

- `sqs-queue-not-empty` goes off when the queue has visible, in-flight, received or sent messages. Use it on a
  dead-letter queue, or on a queue that should be drained.
- `sqs-queue-received-messages-count` goes off when received messages cross `thresholdCount` (average per period by
  default), for unexpected traffic.

See [Alarms](/observability/alarms) and [Alert channels](/observability/alert-channels).

docs.title: Application Load Balancer
docs.content:
# Application Load Balancer

An Application Load Balancer (AWS ALB) receives HTTP and HTTPS traffic and routes it to container workloads and
[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) by path, host, header, query string or source IP. It keeps
WebSocket connections open to containers, takes a [firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) directly and
is required for [gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments) of containers.

It costs $0.0225 an hour (about $16 a month in us-east-1) even with no traffic, plus capacity units as traffic grows.
For Lambda APIs with modest traffic, an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) costs less; see
[the cost comparison](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway#choosing-between-http-api-gateway-and-a-load-balancer).

docs.title: Application Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
docs.content:
## Routing

Each integration has a `priority` and conditions. Rules are checked from the lowest priority up, and the first match
wins:

| Condition | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| `paths` | `['/api/*', '/health']` | URL path, with `*` and `?` wildcards, case-sensitive |
| `methods` | `['GET', 'POST']` | HTTP method |
| `hosts` | `['api.example.com', '*.myapp.com']` | `Host` header, with wildcards |
| `headers` | `[{ headerName: 'X-Tenant', values: ['acme'] }]` | Header value |
| `queryParams` | `[{ paramName: 'version', values: ['v2'] }]` | Query parameter value |
| `sourceIps` | `['10.0.0.0/8']` | Client IP range |

All conditions of one integration must match; any value in a list matches. Leave gaps between priorities (10, 20,
30) so you can add rules later. See [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) for the integration options.

docs.title: AppSync API
docs.content:
# AppSync API

An AppSync API is a GraphQL endpoint run by AWS AppSync. You write the schema and attach a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) to each field you want to resolve. Stacktape creates the API, the
resolvers, the roles that let AppSync call your functions, and the logs. It costs $4 per million queries and mutations
in us-east-1 and nothing while idle ([AppSync pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/appsync/pricing/)).

Each field has one Lambda resolver; there are no VTL or JavaScript resolvers and no pipelines.

docs.title: AppSync API
docs.content:
## Basic example

Create `schema.graphql` in the project root:

```graphql
type Query {
  user(id: ID!): User
}

type User {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
}
```

Then configure the API and field handler:

```yaml
resources:
  graphql:
    type: appsync-api
    properties:
      authentication:
        type: aws-iam

  getUser:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/get-user.ts
      events:
        - type: appsync-api
          properties:
            appsyncApiName: graphql
            field: Query.user
```

The resolver gets the standard AppSync event: `arguments`, `identity`, `source` and field information. It returns
the value of the field:

```ts
export const handler = async (event: { arguments: { id: string } }) => {
  return { id: event.arguments.id, name: 'Ada' };
};
```

Stacktape reads `schema.graphql` (or `schemaFilePath`) before deploying and stops if a configured `Type.field` isn't in
it. AppSync directives and custom scalars are allowed.

After the deploy, run a query in the AWS console under **AppSync → your API → Queries**, which signs requests with
your IAM identity:

```graphql
query {
  user(id: "1") {
    id
    name
  }
}
```

It returns `{"data":{"user":{"id":"1","name":"Ada"}}}`. From your own code, call the `url` parameter with
SigV4-signed requests.

docs.title: AppSync API
docs.content:
## Authentication

`authentication` is required and takes one mode:

- **`aws-iam`**: for calls from your AWS workloads. A workload that lists the API in `connectTo` gets permission to
  query this API's fields.
- **`user-auth-pool`**: signed-in users of a Stacktape [user auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool).
- **`api-key`**: for deliberately public or short-lived access. `expiresAt` is a fixed RFC 3339 time 1 to 365 days in
  the future; Stacktape never extends it, so the key stops working on that date until you set a new one. The key is a
  sensitive parameter and isn't printed in the deploy output.

docs.title: AppSync API
docs.content:
## Operational defaults

By default the API logs errors without request content and keeps logs for 30 days, limits queries to a depth of 10 and
1,000 resolver calls, allows introspection and leaves X-Ray off. Each setting can be changed. Verbose logging can
record headers, variables and personal data, so turn it on only while debugging.

The Infrequent Access log class works only without log forwarding, because AWS can't forward from it.

docs.title: AppSync API
docs.content:
## Custom domains

`customDomain` serves the API at your own hostname. The certificate must be in `us-east-1`, even when the API runs in
another region; `stacktape domain add` creates one there (see
[Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain)). Stacktape creates the DNS record unless
you turn that off.

docs.title: CDN
docs.content:
# CDN

A CDN puts an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of a [bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket), an
[HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway), an
[Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) or a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function). It's not a resource of its own: you turn it on with the `cdn`
property of that resource. CloudFront serves cached responses from locations near your users, routes paths to several
backends from one domain, runs [edge functions](/resources/compute/edge-function) and takes a
[firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall).

It has no monthly fee. The first 1 TB of transfer and 10 million requests each month are free, then North America costs
$0.085 per GB and $0.01 per 10,000 HTTPS requests
([CloudFront pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/pricing/pay-as-you-go/)). A CDN in front of an API whose
responses are all personalized adds cost without caching anything.

docs.title: CDN
docs.content:
## Basic example

Set `cdn.enabled: true` on the parent resource. By default CloudFront serves from all its locations, compresses
responses with Gzip and Brotli, and Stacktape clears the cache on every deploy.

docs.content:
### Route prefixes

A `routePrefix` on a rewrite prepends a path prefix before forwarding to the origin. For example, with `routePrefix: '/v2'`, a request for `/users` is forwarded to the origin as `/v2/users`.

The top-level `defaultRoutePrefix` prepends a path prefix to all requests forwarded to the default origin. This is useful for versioned APIs or when your origin serves content from a sub-path. For example, setting `defaultRoutePrefix: '/v2'` on the CDN forwards all unmatched requests with `/v2` prepended to the path.

## Document defaults

The `indexDocument` and `errorDocument` properties control which files are served for root requests and error responses. The `indexDocument` defaults to `/index.html` — requests to `/` serve this file. The `errorDocument` defaults to `/404.html` — requests for missing paths return this page. These defaults are most relevant for bucket-backed CDN distributions serving static sites and SPAs.

docs.title: Custom domains
docs.content:
# Custom domains

A custom domain serves a resource at your own address, such as `api.example.com`, instead of the hostname AWS
generates. You need a domain you already own. With its DNS in Route 53, Stacktape finds the certificate and creates the
DNS record on every deploy. You can also [keep DNS at your current provider](#external-dns).

Without a custom domain, API Gateways, CDNs and the frontends still get an HTTPS URL from AWS, which is enough for
development stages. Load balancers don't. Stacktape serves an application load balancer, or a network load balancer's
TLS listener, on a `*.stacktape-app.com` domain that the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console)
provides. Without the Console, give it a custom domain or your own certificate, or the deploy stops and asks for one. A
network load balancer's TCP listeners use the AWS hostname without TLS.

docs.title: Custom domains
docs.content:
## Set up the domain

Do this once per root domain and AWS region, before the first deploy that uses the domain.

1. Run `stacktape domain add` with the region you deploy to and enter the domain when it asks:

   ```bash
   stacktape domain add --region eu-west-1
   ```

   If the domain's DNS isn't in Route 53 yet, the command offers to create a hosted zone for the root domain and prints
   its name servers.

2. If the domain already serves traffic, copy its existing DNS records into the new hosted zone first (see the
   [AWS migration steps](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/migrate-dns-domain-in-use.html)).
   Then set the printed name servers at your registrar. Your registrar keeps the registration.
3. When the name servers have changed, run `stacktape domain add` again. It requests free ACM certificates in your
   region and in `us-east-1` (CDNs and AppSync use `us-east-1`) and adds their validation records to the zone.
4. Wait until the certificates show **Issued** in ACM, usually a few minutes after the validation records exist.

For a two-part root domain such as `example.com`, the certificates cover `example.com` and `*.example.com`. A wildcard
covers one level only, so for `api.dev.example.com` enter that full name in `stacktape domain add` to get a certificate
for it. The command still uses the `example.com` zone. For a longer root domain, such as `example.co.uk`, the command
requests no wildcard, so enter each hostname you use, such as `api.example.co.uk`. Check the names a certificate covers
in ACM before you deploy.

docs.title: Custom domains
Custom domains
docs.content:
## Supported resources

These resources take a `customDomains` list with the same three fields: `domainName`, `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation`.

| Resource | Typical hostname |
|---|---|
| [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) | `api.example.com` for Lambda APIs |
| [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway) | `realtime.example.com` |
| [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) | `app.example.com` for containers |
| [Network Load Balancer](/resources/networking/network-load-balancer) | TCP or TLS services |
| [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) | `www.example.com` in front of a bucket, a load balancer, an API or a function |

[Web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) and the SSR
frontends accept `customDomains` on the resource itself. [AppSync APIs](/resources/networking/appsync-api) and
[user auth pools](/resources/security/user-auth-pool) take a single `customDomain`.

One API Gateway hostname can't serve both a WebSocket API and an HTTP API. Use two names, such as `api.example.com` and
`realtime.example.com`; Stacktape rejects the config before deploying.

docs.title: HTTP API Gateway
docs.content:
# HTTP API Gateway

An HTTP API Gateway is a public HTTPS endpoint, run by AWS API Gateway (HTTP API), that routes requests to
[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and container workloads. It costs $1 per million requests in
us-east-1 and nothing when idle, which makes it the default entry point for APIs. [Web services](/resources/compute/web-service)
use one by default too.

An integration must answer within 30 seconds and a request or response can be at most 10 MB. For long-lived
connections use a [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway), and for TCP use a
[Network Load Balancer](/resources/networking/network-load-balancer).

docs.title: HTTP API Gateway
HTTP API Gateway
docs.content:
## Routing

A gateway serves routes from any number of functions and containers. Each integration sets a `method` (`GET`, `POST`,
`PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` or `*` for any) and a `path`:

| Pattern | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Exact | `/users` | Only `/users` |
| Parameter | `/users/{id}` | `/users/123`, with `id` in `event.pathParameters` |
| Greedy | `/api/{proxy+}` | Everything under `/api/` |

The most specific route wins, so exact paths beat greedy ones. A container integration also needs `containerPort`.
Each integration can have its own authorizer (a Cognito user pool, a Lambda function or IAM), which runs before your code. See
[HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) for integration and authorizer options.

docs.title: HTTP API Gateway
HTTP API Gateway
headingPath: Choosing between HTTP API Gateway and a load balancer
docs.content:
## Choosing between HTTP API Gateway and a load balancer

An [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) costs a fixed $0.0225 an hour (about
$16 a month) plus load balancer capacity units (LCUs, $0.008 each per hour) that grow with new connections, active
connections, traffic and rule evaluations. An HTTP API Gateway costs $1 per million requests. Monthly cost in
us-east-1 for small (2 KB) requests at a steady rate, each on a new connection
([API Gateway pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/pricing/),
[Elastic Load Balancing pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/pricing/)):

| Requests per month | HTTP API Gateway | Application Load Balancer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 million | $1 | about $17 |
| 10 million | $10 | about $17 |
| 50 million | $50 | about $21 |
| 200 million | $200 | about $34 |

The load balancer gets cheaper from about 20 million requests a month. Bursty traffic and large responses add LCUs, and
connections that clients reuse remove them. Cost isn't the only difference: a load balancer also routes by header,
query string and source IP, keeps WebSocket connections to containers and has no 30-second limit, while the gateway
has per-route authorizers and scales to zero cost.

The gateway has no firewall setting of its own. Enable `cdn` and attach a
[web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) to the CDN, or use an Application Load
Balancer with `useFirewall`.

docs.title: Network Load Balancer
docs.content:
# Network Load Balancer

A Network Load Balancer (AWS NLB) accepts TCP or TLS connections on the ports you list and passes them to container
workloads, without looking at HTTP. Use it for MQTT brokers, game servers, database proxies, gRPC with your own TLS or
any other non-HTTP protocol.

It costs $0.0225 an hour (about $16 a month in us-east-1) even with no traffic, plus $0.006 per capacity unit-hour as
connections and traffic grow ([Elastic Load Balancing pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/pricing/)).
For HTTP, an [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) routes by path and host and
takes a CDN and a firewall, which a Network Load Balancer can't.

- [Application load balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer): for HTTP routing, WebSockets or a firewall.

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
docs.content:
# WebSocket API Gateway

A WebSocket API Gateway is a `wss://` endpoint, run by AWS API Gateway, whose routes are Lambda functions: `$connect`,
`$disconnect`, `$default` and your own, such as `sendMessage`. It suits chat, live notifications, job progress and
presence without an always-on server. Stacktape creates the API, the routes, the permissions to send to connections,
and the access logs.

You pay $1 per million messages (32 KB each) and $0.25 per million connection-minutes in us-east-1, and nothing while
idle ([API Gateway pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/pricing/)). If you already run a WebSocket server such
as Socket.IO in a container, put it behind an [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer)
instead.

Clients pick a route with the `action` field of a JSON message: `{ "action": "sendMessage", "text": "hello" }` invokes
the function that owns `sendMessage`.

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
WebSocket API Gateway
docs.content:
## Route behavior

| Route | When it runs |
|---|---|
| `$connect` | During the opening handshake. Returning an error rejects the connection. |
| `$disconnect` | After a connection closes. Delivery is best-effort and is not guaranteed. |
| `$default` | When no custom route matches, including messages that cannot be selected. |
| Custom key | When the route selection expression resolves to that key. |

Only JSON messages can be selected by `$request.body.action`. Non-JSON messages and JSON without a matching action go to `$default` when that route exists.

Route handler return bodies are not sent to the client by default. Use `returnResponse: true` for a simple reply to the calling client, as described below. Use the API Gateway Management API when the application should send later, broadcast, or target a different connection.

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
headingPath: Sending a message to a connection

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
docs.content:
## Connection storage and broadcasts

Stacktape does not create a DynamoDB connection registry automatically. A direct reply needs only the `connectionId` in the current event, while broadcast, rooms, and user-to-connection lookup each need different application data. An automatic table would impose the wrong schema on many applications.

When you need lookup or broadcast:

1. Add a normal [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) for the fields your application needs.
2. Connect the `$connect`, `$disconnect`, and broadcasting workloads to that table with `connectTo`.
3. Store connection IDs with a TTL.
4. Delete stale records when a Management API send returns `GoneException`.

TTL and failed-send cleanup matter because `$disconnect` is best-effort and may not run.

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
WebSocket API Gateway
headingPath: Return a response to the calling client

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
docs.content:
## Custom domains

Add `customDomains` when clients should connect through your own hostname:

```ts
const realtime = new WebSocketApiGateway({
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'realtime.example.com' }]
});
```

[Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) with `stacktape domain add` first, so an
issued certificate for the hostname exists in the stack's region. The deploy then creates the domain mapping and the
Route 53 record. For DNS or certificates you manage elsewhere, use `disableDnsRecordCreation` or
`customCertificateArn`; see [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains#external-dns).

One API Gateway hostname can't serve both a WebSocket API and an HTTP API, so give each its own name. Stacktape rejects
the config before deploying.

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
docs.content:
## Logs

JSON access logs are enabled by default with connection ID, event type, route, status, source IP, request time, and integration error context. Payload data is not logged by default. Configure retention or forwarding through `logging`, or set `logging.disabled: true`.

API Gateway needs a CloudWatch Logs role in the account's API Gateway settings to write these logs, and new accounts
have none. Before the deploy, Stacktape checks the region's setting. If no role is set, it creates the IAM role
`stacktape-api-gateway-cloudwatch-logs` (one per account, with the AWS managed policy
`AmazonAPIGatewayPushToCloudWatchLogs`), registers it and says so. It never replaces a role that is already set; if
that role was deleted, the deploy stops and says so.

Restricted deployer roles need `apigateway:GET` on `/account` for the check (without it, Stacktape warns and deploys),
and `iam:GetRole`, `iam:CreateRole`, `iam:AttachRolePolicy`, `iam:PassRole` on the role and `apigateway:PATCH` on
`/account` to register it.

`logging.logClass: 'infrequent-access'` lowers the ingestion price for new log groups. Those logs can be read only with
Logs Insights and can't be forwarded.

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
docs.content:
## Dev mode

`stacktape dev` keeps the WebSocket gateway deployed and hot-swaps its Lambda handlers. Dev stages have no access logs. The dev UI shows the deployed `wss://` URL. Stacktape does not emulate API Gateway's connection lifecycle locally, so test clients continue to use the deployed endpoint while code changes are updated quickly.

docs.title: WebSocket API Gateway
docs.content:
## AWS limits to design around

API Gateway currently limits a connection to 2 hours with a 10-minute idle timeout. Frames are limited to 32 KB, messages to 128 KB, binary frames are unsupported, and integrations can run for at most 29 seconds. Split large payloads and design clients to reconnect.

docs.title: State machine
docs.content:
# State machine

A state machine is an AWS Step Functions workflow: steps that call your Lambda functions and other AWS services, with
branching, retries, parallel branches and loops defined in [Amazon States Language](https://states-language.net/spec.html)
(ASL) instead of code. Each execution has a visible history, and a standard workflow can run for up to a year.

Standard workflows cost $0.025 per 1,000 state transitions in us-east-1, with 4,000 free each month
([Step Functions pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/pricing/)), and nothing while idle. For one step after
another without branching or retries, a Lambda function with an [SQS trigger](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) is
simpler and cheaper.

docs.title: State machine
State machine
docs.content:
## Workflow definition

`definition` is an ASL workflow: `StartAt`, `States`, and optionally `Comment`, `Version` and `TimeoutSeconds`.

docs.title: State machine
docs.content:
### State types

Stacktape checks eight ASL state types:

| State type | Purpose | Key properties |
|---|---|---|
| **Task** | Invokes a Lambda function or another supported ASL task target | `Resource`, `Retry`, `Catch`, `TimeoutSeconds`, `HeartbeatSeconds`, `Parameters` |
| **Choice** | Branches based on input conditions | `Choices` (condition rules), `Default` (fallback state) |
| **Parallel** | Runs multiple branches concurrently, waits for all to complete | `Branches` (each a `StartAt`/`States` workflow), `Retry`, `Catch` |
| **Map** | Iterates over an array, running a sub-workflow per item | `ItemProcessor` (or the older `Iterator`), `ItemsPath`, `MaxConcurrency` |
| **Wait** | Pauses execution for a duration or until a timestamp | `Seconds`, `Timestamp`, `SecondsPath`, `TimestampPath` |
| **Pass** | Passes input to output, optionally injecting or transforming data | `Result`, `Parameters`, `ResultPath` |
| **Succeed** | Marks successful completion — terminates the workflow | — |
| **Fail** | Terminates execution with an error | `Error`, `Cause` |

Stacktape checks the state types and the fields listed above. Other ASL fields, such as `QueryLanguage`, `Arguments` or `Assign`, are passed to AWS unchanged, and a path set to `null` (for example `OutputPath: null`) is kept.

docs.title: State machine
docs.content:
### Permissions of the workflow

The workflow runs with one IAM role that Stacktape creates for all state machines in the stack. It can:

- invoke Lambda functions of this stack,
- read and write DynamoDB items, publish to SNS, send to SQS,
- run ECS tasks, submit AWS Batch jobs and run Glue jobs.

A Task that calls another service, for example S3, Bedrock or another state machine, fails at run time with an access
error. Call that service from a Lambda function task instead, and give the function the permission with
`iamRoleStatements`. This role is separate from the role of the code that starts executions; see
[Starting executions](#starting-executions).

docs.title: State machine
docs.content:
### Referencing Lambda functions

Task states use the `Resource` property to identify a Lambda function or another supported ASL task target. For a function in the same config, use the [`$ResourceParam` directive](/configuration/directives) with the function's resource name and its `arn` parameter. Stacktape resolves it to the function's ARN at deploy time.

```yaml
resources:
  scoreReceipt:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/score-receipt.ts
  approvalWorkflow:
    type: state-machine
    properties:
      definition:
        StartAt: ScoreReceipt
        States:
          ScoreReceipt:
            Type: Task
            Resource: $ResourceParam('scoreReceipt', 'arn')
            End: true
```

Use a plain string when you already have a concrete Task `Resource` value, such as the ARN of a function outside this config or an [ASL service integration](https://states-language.net/spec.html) URI. An object with a CloudFormation intrinsic function, such as `Fn::GetAtt`, also works when you need one.

docs.title: State machine
docs.content:
### Workflow timeout

A standard workflow can run for up to a year and bills every transition. Set `TimeoutSeconds` at the top of the
definition for any workflow that should finish in minutes or hours, and on Task states to bound one step.
`HeartbeatSeconds` makes a long task report progress.

docs.title: Bastion host
docs.content:
# Bastion host

A bastion host is a small EC2 instance in your stack's VPC that lets you reach private resources from your machine:
[relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database), [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis) and other
services that accept VPC connections only. You connect through AWS Systems Manager, so there are no SSH keys and no
open SSH port.

It runs all the time. In us-east-1 the default `t3.micro` costs about $7.60 a month, plus about $3.65 for its public
IPv4 address and a few cents for its disk ([EC2 pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing/on-demand/)). For a
database that's open to the internet, you don't need one.

docs.title: Bastion host
Bastion host
docs.content:
## Connecting to private resources

[`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) forwards local ports to one resource. It works with
[relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database), [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis),
[MongoDB Atlas clusters](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas),
[application load balancers](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) and
[private services](/resources/compute/private-service) behind a load balancer.

[`bastion shell`](/cli/bastion-shell) opens a shell on the instance itself:

```bash
stacktape bastion shell --stage production
```

With several bastions in one stack, pick one with `--bastion-resource`. For a one-off query, `stacktape query sql` and
`stacktape query redis` take `--bastion-resource` too and need no tunnel.

docs.title: Bastion host
docs.content:
## Scripts

Two [script](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) types use a bastion, for example to run migrations from a hook against a
private database:

- **`local-script-with-bastion-tunneling`** runs on your machine and routes its connections through the bastion. The
  `connectTo` variables it gets point at the tunnel, so the script needs no changes.
- **`bastion-script`** runs the commands on the bastion instance and streams the output to your terminal.

Both take `bastionResource` when the stack has more than one bastion.

docs.title: User authentication pool
docs.content:
# User authentication pool

A user authentication pool is an Amazon Cognito user pool: sign-up, sign-in, password reset, email or phone
verification, MFA, social and enterprise sign-in (Google, Facebook, Apple, SAML, OIDC) and OAuth 2.0. It issues JWTs
that an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) can check on every request, so your code gets only
signed-in users.

New pools use Cognito's Essentials tier: the first 10,000 monthly active users are free, then $0.015 per user in
us-east-1. Users who sign in through SAML or OIDC have a separate free allowance of 50
([Cognito pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/cognito/pricing/)).

Stacktape configures password, email or phone, MFA, social and enterprise sign-in. Passkeys and other passwordless
sign-in that Cognito offers aren't Stacktape settings; set them with [overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches)
or pick a provider such as Auth0 or Clerk. For service-to-service calls without users, IAM is simpler.

docs.title: User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
docs.content:
## Verification

Stacktape user authentication pools support four verification strategies that control how new users prove ownership of their contact information. Set `userVerificationType` to choose the strategy:

| Strategy | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `email-code` | Cognito emails a short numeric code the user enters during sign-up |
| `email-link` | Cognito emails a clickable verification link |
| `sms` | Cognito sends a verification code via SMS to the user's phone number |
| `none` | No email or phone verification is required during sign-up |

For most web apps, `email-code` is the best default: it needs nothing else and users know it. Use `email-link` for a smoother UX where users just click a link instead of copying a code. Use `sms` when phone numbers are the primary identifier (ride-sharing, delivery apps). Use `none` only for internal tools where you trust all users.

You can customize the email subject and body text for both code and link verification using `userVerificationMessageConfig`. To fully customize the email sender and message format, configure `emailConfiguration.sesAddressArn` with a verified SES identity. Without SES configuration, Cognito sends emails through its built-in sender, which works for standard verification flows but has lower daily sending limits.


> **Warning:** `requireEmailVerification` and `requirePhoneNumberVerification` have no effect yet; `userVerificationType` decides
verification.

docs.title: User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
docs.content:
## OAuth

The user pool client's OAuth configuration controls which flows, scopes, and redirect URLs are allowed. Configure these explicitly when using the Hosted UI or integrating with external identity providers:

- **`allowedOAuthFlows`**: which OAuth 2.0 flows the client can use: `code` (Authorization Code, recommended for web apps), `implicit` (legacy browser-only flow), or `client_credentials` (server-to-server with no end user). For most web applications, use `['code']`.
- **`allowedOAuthScopes`**: a string list of scopes the user pool client can request. Common values are `email`, `openid`, and `profile`. These are passed to the Cognito user pool client as `AllowedOAuthScopes`. For scopes requested from an external provider (e.g., Google Calendar access or Facebook friend list), set `authorizeScopes` on that provider's `identityProviders` entry instead.
- **`callbackURLs`**: URLs where Cognito redirects users after authentication. Must exactly match the URLs configured in your application. Include `http://localhost:3000/...` during development and your production URL for deployed environments.
- **`logoutURLs`**: URLs where Cognito redirects after sign-out. Must also be explicitly configured.
- **`generateClientSecret`**: set to `true` when your backend can safely store a client secret (server-side apps, not SPAs). Defaults to `false`.

For server-rendered web apps or backend-mediated OAuth flows, use the `code` flow with `generateClientSecret: true`. For single-page applications that call Cognito directly from the browser, use the `code` flow without a client secret (PKCE is handled automatically by the Cognito SDK).

docs.title: User authentication pool
User authentication pool
docs.content:
## Client restrictions

The pool's app client accepts every sign-in flow and can read and write every user attribute unless you limit it:

| Property | Limits |
|---|---|
| `allowedAuthFlows` | Which sign-in flows the client accepts, for example `ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH` and `ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH` only |
| `readAttributes` | Which user attributes tokens and `GetUser` return through the client |
| `writeAttributes` | Which attributes users can set through the client, for example to keep `custom:role` admin-only |

```typescript
new UserAuthPool({
  allowedAuthFlows: ['ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH', 'ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH'],
  readAttributes: ['email', 'name'],
  writeAttributes: ['name']
});
```

docs.title: User authentication pool
docs.content:
## Token lifetimes

Stacktape lets you control how long tokens issued by the user pool remain valid:

| Property | Controls | Allowed values | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `accessTokenValiditySeconds` | How long access tokens (used for API authorization) are valid | 300 to 86400 seconds | 3600 (1 hour) |
| `idTokenValiditySeconds` | How long ID tokens (containing user profile claims) are valid | 300 to 86400 seconds | 3600 (1 hour) |
| `refreshTokenValidityDays` | How long refresh tokens can obtain new access/ID tokens | 1 to 3650 days | 30 |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    accessTokenValiditySeconds: 3600,
    idTokenValiditySeconds: 3600,
    refreshTokenValidityDays: 30
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


Shorter access token lifetimes reduce the window for token theft at the cost of more frequent refresh calls. Longer refresh token lifetimes keep users signed in longer but extend the window for session hijacking. The defaults, 1 hour for access and ID tokens and 30 days for refresh tokens, are a common starting point.

Before Stacktape v4, Cognito read `accessTokenValiditySeconds` and `idTokenValiditySeconds` in hours, so only values from 1 to 24 deployed. Such a value still means that many hours, and the CLI warns you to write it in seconds instead: `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 1` becomes `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 3600`.

The client's `TokenValidityUnits` are seconds for access and ID tokens and days for refresh tokens. An `overrides` entry that sets `AccessTokenValidity` or `IdTokenValidity` on the client is read in seconds too, so a value written in hours before v4 fails to deploy. Set the unit you mean in the same override; the other units stay as they are:

```yaml
resources:
  auth:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
    overrides:
      AuthUserPoolClient:
        AccessTokenValidity: 2
        TokenValidityUnits:
          AccessToken: hours
```

docs.title: User authentication pool
User authentication pool
User authentication pool
docs.content:
## Email configuration

By default, Cognito sends emails (verification codes, password resets, admin invitations) through its built-in email service. This works for development but has low daily sending limits. For production, configure `emailConfiguration.sesAddressArn` with a verified SES identity to use your own sender address and get higher throughput:

- **`sesAddressArn`**: ARN of a verified SES email or domain. `EMAIL_OTP` MFA requires it.
- **`from`**: the sender address recipients see. It must be verified in SES.
- **`replyToEmailAddress`**: where replies go; by default the `from` address.

The `inviteMessageConfig` property customizes the email and SMS sent when an administrator creates a user account. Use `{username}` and `{####}` placeholders in the message body for the username and temporary password.

`connectTo` auto-injects `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_ID`, `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_CLIENT_ID`, and `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_ARN` as environment variables. The remaining parameters (`providerUrl`, `domain`, `clientSecret`) are accessible via [`$ResourceParam`](/configuration/referenceable-parameters).

docs.title: Web application firewall
docs.content:
# Web application firewall

A web application firewall (AWS WAF) inspects HTTP requests before they reach your app and blocks common attacks:
SQL injection, cross-site scripting, known bad inputs and floods from one IP address. You define it as its own
resource and attach it to a load balancer, a CDN, a website or a user pool.

A firewall with the two default rule groups costs about $7 a month ($5 for the firewall and $1 per rule group) plus
$0.60 per million requests ([AWS WAF pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/waf/pricing/)). Bot Control and other paid rule
groups add their own fees.

docs.title: Web application firewall
Web application firewall
docs.content:
## Rules

Three rule types: managed rule groups, rate-based rules and custom rule groups. Each rule has a `name` and a unique
`priority`; lower priorities run first. Setting `rules` replaces the defaults, so list the default groups again if you
want to keep them.

docs.title: Web application firewall
Web application firewall
Web application firewall
Web application firewall
docs.content:
## Default action

`defaultAction` decides what happens to requests no rule matched. `'Allow'` (default) makes your rules a blocklist.
`'Block'` returns 403 for everything your rules don't allow, which suits only APIs with a small, known set of allowed
requests.

docs.title: Web application firewall
Web application firewall
docs.content:
## CAPTCHA and challenge immunity

After a client solves a `'Captcha'` or `'Challenge'`, it isn't asked again for `captchaImmunityTime` or
`challengeImmunityTime` seconds (300 by default). `tokenDomains` lets several of your domains accept the same token.

docs.title: Web application firewall
docs.content:
## Metrics and request sampling

Each firewall and rule publishes CloudWatch metrics unless `disableMetrics: true`. `sampledRequestsEnabled: true`
keeps samples of matched requests to inspect in the AWS WAF console, which is how you find false positives. Both can
be set on the firewall and on each rule.

docs.title: EFS file system
docs.content:
# EFS file system

An EFS file system is shared, persistent file storage on Amazon Elastic File System. Containers and Lambda functions
mount it as a directory and read and write it with normal file calls, several at once. It grows and shrinks with the
data. Use it for apps that need a real directory: CMS uploads, model files shared between containers, state that must
survive container replacement.

In us-east-1, Standard storage costs $0.30 per GB-month, and in the default elastic throughput mode reads cost $0.03 and
writes $0.06 per GB transferred ([EFS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/efs/pricing/)). Files your code uploads and
downloads through an API belong in an [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket), which stores a GB for about $0.023.

docs.title: EFS file system
EFS file system
docs.content:
## Throughput modes

`throughputMode` decides how read and write speed scales and what you pay for it:

| Mode | Speed | You pay | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `elastic` (default) | Scales with demand | Per GB read and written | Most workloads, spiky access |
| `provisioned` | Fixed `provisionedThroughputInMibps` | Per MiB/s provisioned, used or not | Steady heavy throughput |
| `bursting` | 50 KiB/s per GiB stored, plus burst credits | Included in storage | Large file systems with light access |

docs.title: EFS file system
docs.content:
### Elastic (default)

Throughput follows your workloads up and down, and you pay for the data they move. Keep it unless you measured a need
it can't meet.

docs.title: EFS file system
EFS file system
docs.content:
### Bursting

Throughput is 50 KiB/s per GiB stored, with short bursts above that from credits. A small file system runs out of
credits quickly and slows down, so use it only for large file systems with light access.

docs.title: S3 bucket
docs.content:
# S3 bucket

A bucket is an Amazon S3 bucket for files: user uploads, images, PDFs, exports, backups, data for pipelines. S3 keeps
your files with eleven nines of durability and scales without limits.

You pay for what you store, the requests you make and the data you send out to the internet. In us-east-1, S3 Standard
costs $0.023 per GB-month, uploads $0.005 per 1,000 and downloads $0.0004 per 1,000 requests
([S3 pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/)). Many small, frequently read files cost more in requests than in
storage. For a website, use [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting); for a directory that containers
mount, an [EFS file system](/resources/storage/efs-filesystem).

docs.title: S3 bucket
S3 bucket
S3 bucket
S3 bucket
S3 bucket
S3 bucket
S3 bucket
docs.content:
### Storage classes

The `storageClass` property in transition rules determines where objects move. Cheaper classes have higher retrieval costs or latency:

| Storage class | Access pattern | Retrieval speed | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `STANDARD_IA` | Infrequent access | Instant | Backups, older data you still query occasionally |
| `ONEZONE_IA` | Infrequent, single AZ | Instant (less durable than multi-AZ) | Reproducible data like thumbnails or transcoded media |
| `INTELLIGENT_TIERING` | Unknown or changing | Instant (auto-tiered by AWS) | Data with unpredictable access patterns |
| `GLACIER` | Archive | Minutes to hours | Compliance archives, old logs |
| `DEEP_ARCHIVE` | Long-term archive | 12+ hours | Data you rarely need but must retain for years |


> **Tip:** Add an `abort-incomplete-multipart-upload` rule to every bucket. Large file uploads that fail midway leave invisible partial objects that accumulate storage charges. A 7-day cleanup rule prevents this waste.

docs.title: Alarms as triggers
docs.content:
# Alarms as triggers

A `cloudwatch-alarm` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) when one of your
[alarms](/observability/alarms) goes into the `ALARM` state. Use it when the response needs code: restart something,
open a ticket, page an on-call tool the alarm can't notify directly.

If a person only needs to see the alert, skip the function and add `notificationChannels` to the alarm. Alarms notify
Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, Discord and webhooks without code; see [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels).

docs.title: Alarms as triggers
Alarms as triggers
Alarms as triggers
docs.content:
## Alarm types

The referenced alarm can use any trigger type its resource supports:

| Resource | Alarm trigger types |
|---|---|
| [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) | `lambda-error-rate`, `lambda-duration` |
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | `database-read-latency`, `database-write-latency`, `database-cpu-utilization`, `database-free-storage`, `database-free-memory`, `database-connection-count` |
| [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) | `http-api-gateway-error-rate`, `http-api-gateway-latency` |
| [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) | `application-load-balancer-error-rate`, `application-load-balancer-unhealthy-targets`, `application-load-balancer-custom` |
| [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) | `sqs-queue-received-messages-count`, `sqs-queue-not-empty` |

Thresholds, evaluation windows and notifications are covered in [Alarms](/observability/alarms).

docs.title: Alarms as triggers
docs.content:
## Limits

- Only Lambda functions accept `cloudwatch-alarm` events.
- `alarmName` is the only property. You can't reshape the event or reference an alarm in another stack or account.
  For those, send the alarm's events to an [event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) and use an
  [event bus trigger](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events).
- Dev mode doesn't create alarms, so the trigger doesn't fire in a dev stack.

docs.title: CloudWatch Logs
docs.content:
# CloudWatch Logs

A `cloudwatch-log` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) when new records arrive in a CloudWatch log group. Use it to act on log
content: extract errors, enrich and forward records, or watch CloudTrail or VPC flow logs.

To read logs, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs). To send logs to Datadog or another service without code, use
[log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding). To react when a metric crosses a threshold, use an
[alarm trigger](/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers).

docs.title: CloudWatch Logs
CloudWatch Logs
docs.content:
## Filter patterns

`filter` uses the
[CloudWatch filter pattern syntax](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html).
Without it, every record invokes the function.

| Pattern | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `ERROR` | Lines that contain `ERROR` |
| `ERROR -DEBUG` | Lines with `ERROR` but not `DEBUG` |
| `{ $.level = "error" }` | JSON lines whose `level` is `error` |
| `{ $.statusCode >= 500 }` | JSON lines whose `statusCode` is 500 or more |

docs.title: CloudWatch Logs
docs.content:
## Limits

- A log group accepts at most two subscriptions, and each trigger uses one. Stacktape may already use one on a
  function's log group for error tracking or log forwarding. When you hit the limit, have one function forward the
  records to an SQS queue, an SNS topic or an event bus.
- Log groups with `logging.logClass: infrequent-access` don't support subscriptions. Stacktape stops the deploy if a
  trigger points at one.

docs.title: CloudWatch Logs
docs.content:
## Failures and retries

CloudWatch Logs invokes the function asynchronously. If the function throws, Lambda retries it twice. The same records
can arrive more than once, so deduplicate on each log event's `id` when it matters.
