docs.title: DynamoDB streams
docs.content:
# DynamoDB streams

A `dynamo-db-stream` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) when items in a
[DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) are created, updated or deleted. Use it to keep an audit log, update a
search index or cache, or notify another system after a write, without changing the code that writes.

The table's stream keeps changes for 24 hours and allows two readers per shard. To fan changes out to many consumers,
have one function forward them to an [event bus](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events) or a
[Kinesis stream](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events). Batch jobs accept `dynamo-db-stream` events too.

docs.title: DynamoDB streams
DynamoDB streams
docs.content:
## Batching and ordering

Lambda invokes the function when the batch is full, when the batching window ends, or when the batch reaches the 6 MB
invocation payload limit.

| Property | Default | Maximum |
|---|---|---|
| `batchSize` | 100 | 10,000 |
| `maxBatchWindowSeconds` | 0 (no wait) | 300 |
| `parallelizationFactor` | 1 | 10 |

Changes to the same item always arrive in the order they were made. With `parallelizationFactor` above 1, Lambda
processes up to 10 batches per shard at the same time. Changes to one item stay in order, but changes to different
items can be processed in any order.

Lambda reads DynamoDB streams for free. You pay for the function's invocations and run time, so a larger `batchSize` or
a batching window lowers the bill on busy tables.

docs.title: DynamoDB streams
DynamoDB streams
docs.content:
## Dev mode

In [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview), DynamoDB tables normally run locally in DynamoDB Local, which has
no stream Lambda can read. When a function has a stream trigger, `stacktape dev` deploys that table in the dev stack
instead and says so when it starts. Your local code then reads and writes the deployed table with the permissions its
`connectTo` grants.

A function left out with `--skip-resources` has no triggers in the dev stack. The table stays deployed, so skipping
the function doesn't delete the table or its data.

docs.title: Event bus events
docs.content:
# Event bus events

An `event-bus` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) when an event that matches a pattern arrives on an EventBridge
[event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus). Services publish events such as `OrderPlaced` without knowing who listens,
and each consumer picks the events it needs by their content. The default bus also carries events from AWS services.

When every consumer needs every message, an [SNS topic](/resources/triggers/sns-events) is simpler. For one consumer
with batching and retries, use an [SQS queue](/resources/triggers/sqs-events).

docs.title: Event bus events
Event bus events
docs.content:
## Pick the bus

Set exactly one of these:

| Property | Bus |
|---|---|
| `eventBusName` | An [event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) in the stack, by its key under `resources` |
| `eventBusArn` | A bus outside the stack: another stack, another account or one made by hand |
| `useDefaultBus: true` | The account's default bus, which receives events from AWS services |

The default bus lets you react to AWS itself. This function runs when an EC2 instance stops:

```typescript
new EventBusIntegration({
  useDefaultBus: true,
  eventPattern: {
    source: ['aws.ec2'],
    'detail-type': ['EC2 Instance State-change Notification'],
    detail: { state: ['stopped'] }
  }
})
```

A bus in another account must allow your account in its resource policy.

AWS charges per event published to a custom bus, $1.00 per million in US East. Events from AWS services on the default
bus are free, and rules cost nothing. See [EventBridge pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/pricing/).

docs.title: Event bus events
docs.content:
## Event patterns

`eventPattern` is required. An event matches when every field in the pattern matches; within a field, any listed value
matches. Fields you leave out match anything.

| Field | Matches | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `source` | Who sent the event | `['my-app.orders']`, `['aws.ec2']` |
| `detail-type` | The kind of event | `['OrderPlaced', 'OrderCancelled']` |
| `detail` | Fields of your payload, nested | `{ status: ['ACTIVE'] }` |
| `account`, `region` | Where the event came from | `['eu-west-1']` |
| `resources` | ARNs the event is about | `['arn:aws:ec2:…']` |

`detail` takes operators too. This matches orders above 1,000 from the US or EU:

```typescript
eventPattern: {
  'detail-type': ['OrderPlaced'],
  detail: {
    amount: [{ numeric: ['>', 1000] }],
    region: ['US', 'EU']
  }
}
```

Other operators are `prefix`, `suffix`, `anything-but` and `exists`. The
[AWS pattern reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-event-patterns.html) has the full
syntax.

docs.title: Event bus events
Event bus events
docs.content:
## Failures and retries

EventBridge invokes the function asynchronously. If the function throws, Lambda retries it twice and then drops the
event. To keep events that still fail, set
[`destinations.onFailure`](/resources/compute/lambda-function#api-ref_lambda-function-props--destinations) on the
function. Events can arrive more than once, so make the handler idempotent.

`onDeliveryFailure` covers the rarer case where EventBridge can't hand the event to Lambda at all, for example because
of a missing permission. It names an SQS queue for those events:

```typescript
new EventBusIntegration({
  eventBusName: 'orderBus',
  eventPattern: { 'detail-type': ['OrderPlaced'] },
  onDeliveryFailure: { sqsQueueName: 'undeliveredOrders' }
})
```

docs.title: HTTP triggers
docs.content:
# HTTP triggers

An HTTP trigger runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) for each request that matches a route.
There are two kinds: `http-api-gateway` routes by method and path on an
[HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway), and `application-load-balancer` routes on paths, methods,
hosts, headers, query parameters and source IPs on an
[Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer). Containers of a
[multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) and [batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job)
accept both too.

A [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) or a [private service](/resources/compute/private-service) gets its
traffic from its own properties, not from these triggers.

docs.title: HTTP triggers
docs.content:
## API Gateway or load balancer

|  | HTTP API Gateway | Application Load Balancer |
|---|---|---|
| Routes on | Method and path | Paths, methods, hosts, headers, query parameters, source IPs |
| Which route wins | The most specific path | The rule with the lowest `priority` |
| Authorizers | Cognito, Lambda, IAM | None, check auth in your code |
| Cost without traffic | Nothing | Hourly charge |

Use HTTP API Gateway for Lambda APIs: you pay per request and nothing while it's idle. Use a load balancer when you
route on headers or hosts, or when you already run one for containers and want Lambda routes behind the same address.

docs.title: HTTP triggers
HTTP triggers
docs.content:
### Routes

`path` takes three shapes. The most specific match wins.

| Path | Matches |
|---|---|
| `/users` | Only `/users` |
| `/users/{id}` | One segment, available as `event.pathParameters.id` |
| `/users/{proxy+}` | Everything under `/users/` |

`method` is `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` or `*`. To send different routes to different
functions, give each function its own integration on the same gateway.

docs.title: HTTP triggers
docs.content:
### Payload format

`payloadFormat` sets the event shape the function receives. The default is `'1.0'`; `'2.0'` is flatter and has a
`cookies` field. Frameworks with a Lambda adapter handle both, so it matters mostly for hand-written handlers. You can
set it on the gateway for all routes, and all HTTP API routes of one function must use the same format. The
[AWS comparison](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/http-api-develop-integrations-lambda.html)
shows both shapes.

docs.title: HTTP triggers
docs.content:
### Authorization

An `authorizer` checks the request before the function runs:

- `cognito` accepts tokens from a [user auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool) and rejects the rest with `401`.
- `lambda` runs your own function to decide, and rejects with `401`.
- `aws-iam` requires requests signed with AWS credentials allowed to call `execute-api:Invoke`, and rejects the rest
  with `403`. Use it for routes that other AWS workloads call.

docs.title: HTTP triggers
HTTP triggers
docs.content:
## Containers

Each container of a [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) can list `http-api-gateway`
and `application-load-balancer` events with the same properties, plus the `containerPort` that receives the traffic.
Containers also accept `network-load-balancer` events for TCP and TLS traffic, and `service-connect` and
`workload-internal` events for traffic inside the stack. The multi-container workload page shows each one.

docs.title: Kafka topic events
docs.content:
# Kafka topic events

A `kafka-topic` event makes Lambda read one Kafka topic and run a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function)
with batches of records. The simplest source is a Stacktape [Kafka cluster](/resources/messaging/kafka-cluster):
Stacktape sets up IAM access, networking and the event source mapping. Existing Amazon MSK clusters and self-managed
Kafka work too.

Kafka is expensive for plain background jobs. Use an [SQS queue](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) or a
[Kinesis stream](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events) unless you need Kafka itself.

docs.title: Kafka topic events
docs.content:
## Stacktape Kafka cluster

```yaml
resources:
  events:
    type: kafka-cluster

  consumeOrders:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/consume-orders.ts
      events:
        - type: kafka-topic
          properties:
            kafkaClusterName: events
            topicName: orders
            startFrom: latest
```

`startFrom` is required, so you choose on purpose:

- `latest` processes records that arrive after the trigger becomes active.
- `earliest` starts from the oldest retained records. Expect a large first burst of invocations.

The topic must exist before records can flow. MSK Serverless doesn't create topics automatically and CloudFormation
can't declare them; [Create topics](/resources/messaging/kafka-cluster#create-topics) shows the setup code.

The function doesn't need `joinDefaultVpc` to receive records; Lambda's poller has its own networking. For the poller,
Stacktape creates Lambda and STS interface endpoints in the stack's VPC. They're shared by the stack and charged per
hour and per GB in every availability zone.

A Stacktape cluster in a reused VPC (`stackConfig.vpc.reuseVpc`) can't feed a `kafka-topic` trigger, because the
endpoints would collide with ones another project owns. Use a Stacktape-created VPC outside `us-east-1`, or an existing
cluster with networking you provide.

Records arrive grouped by topic and partition, with keys and values base64-encoded:

```typescript
type KafkaEvent = { records: Record<string, Array<{ offset: number; key?: string; value: string }>> };

export default async (event: KafkaEvent) => {
  for (const records of Object.values(event.records)) {
    for (const record of records) {
      const order = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(record.value, 'base64').toString('utf-8'));
      console.info(record.offset, order);
    }
  }
};
```

docs.title: Kafka topic events
docs.content:
## Existing Amazon MSK cluster

Use `mskClusterArn` for a cluster in the same account and region that uses IAM authentication:

```yaml
events:
  - type: kafka-topic
    properties:
      mskClusterArn: arn:aws:kafka:eu-west-1:123456789012:cluster/events/cluster-uuid
      topicName: orders
      startFrom: earliest
```

Stacktape scopes the function's role to that cluster, topic and consumer group. The cluster's network is yours to
prepare: its subnets need NAT or Lambda and STS endpoints, because a public subnet with an internet gateway isn't enough
for the poller. MSK clusters in another account aren't supported. For SCRAM or mTLS credentials, use the self-managed
form below.

docs.title: Kafka topic events
docs.content:
## Self-managed Kafka

For Kafka outside Amazon MSK, give the brokers and an authentication secret in Secrets Manager:

```yaml
events:
  - type: kafka-topic
    properties:
      customKafkaConfiguration:
        bootstrapServers:
          - broker-1.internal.example.com:9096
          - broker-2.internal.example.com:9096
        topicName: orders
        authentication:
          type: SASL_SCRAM_512_AUTH
          properties:
            authenticationSecretArn: arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:123456789012:secret:kafka-creds
      startFrom: latest
      vpc:
        subnetIds:
          - subnet-0123456789abcdef0
          - subnet-0123456789abcdef1
        securityGroupIds:
          - sg-0123456789abcdef0
```

`vpc` places the poller, not the function. Give it subnets and security groups that can reach the brokers, ideally in
more than one availability zone. Those subnets also need NAT or Lambda and STS endpoints, plus a Secrets Manager
endpoint if the secret can't be reached through NAT.

Authentication types are `BASIC_AUTH`, `SASL_SCRAM_256_AUTH`, `SASL_SCRAM_512_AUTH` and `MTLS`. A SASL secret holds
`username` and `password`. For mTLS, set the `clientCertificate` secret and optionally `serverRootCaCertificate`.
Stacktape grants read access to the secrets. If a secret uses a customer-managed KMS key, add `kms:Decrypt` for that key
with `iamRoleStatements`.

docs.title: Kafka topic events
docs.content:
## Batching and consumer groups

`batchSize` is 100 by default and up to 10,000. Without `maxBatchWindowSeconds`, Lambda waits up to 500 ms to fill a
batch; the maximum is 300 seconds.

Leave `consumerGroupId` out and AWS gives the trigger its own group. Set it only to keep an existing group's identity.
It can't change after creation, and the group's committed offsets win over `startFrom`. Two active consumers with the
same ID split the partitions between them instead of each getting every record.

Changing the source, topic, start position or explicit group replaces the trigger. AWS can refuse to create the new one
while the old one still owns the same explicit group. Then remove the trigger in one deploy and add it back in the next.

docs.title: Kafka topic events
docs.content:
## Failures and retries

If the function throws, Lambda retries the whole batch until it succeeds or the records expire from the topic, and the
partition doesn't move on meanwhile. Records can arrive more than once, so make the handler idempotent. Functions with a
Kafka trigger can run for at most 14 minutes (`timeout: 840`).

docs.title: Kinesis events
docs.content:
# Kinesis events

A `kinesis-stream` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) with batches of records from a
[Kinesis stream](/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream). Lambda reads each shard in order and keeps the position, so the
stream works for ordered, high-volume data such as clickstreams, telemetry or change events that several consumers read
independently.

For plain background jobs, an [SQS queue](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) is cheaper and simpler: it has no hourly
charge and no ordering to manage. Batch jobs accept `kinesis-stream` events too. A container reads the stream with its
own consumer, such as the Kinesis Client Library, in a [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) with
[`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources).

docs.title: Kinesis events
Kinesis events
docs.content:
## Starting position

`startingPosition` decides where Lambda starts reading when the trigger is first created.

| Value | Reads |
|---|---|
| `TRIM_HORIZON` (default) | Every record still in the stream, oldest first |
| `LATEST` | Only records written after the trigger exists |

docs.title: Kinesis events
docs.content:
## Batching

Lambda invokes the function when the batch is full, when the batching window ends, or when the batch reaches the 6 MB
invocation payload limit.

| Property | Default | Maximum |
|---|---|---|
| `batchSize` | 100 | 10,000 |
| `maxBatchWindowSeconds` | 0 (no wait) | 300 |
| `parallelizationFactor` | 1 | 10 |

`parallelizationFactor` runs up to 10 batches from one shard at the same time. Records with the same partition key are
still processed in order; records with different keys may run in parallel.

When the function can't keep up, its `IteratorAge` metric in CloudWatch grows: records wait longer before they're
processed. Raise `batchSize` or `parallelizationFactor`, give the function more memory, or add shards to a provisioned
stream.

docs.title: Kinesis events
docs.content:
### Enhanced fan-out

By default the trigger shares each shard's read throughput (2 MB/s) with every other consumer of the stream. Set
`autoCreateConsumer: true` to give it a dedicated consumer with its own throughput and lower latency. AWS charges extra
per consumer-shard hour and per GB read. If you manage the consumer yourself, pass `consumerArn` instead; the two can't
be combined.

```typescript
new KinesisIntegration({ kinesisStreamName: 'clickStream', autoCreateConsumer: true })
```

docs.title: Kinesis events
docs.content:
## Failures and retries

If the function throws, Lambda retries the whole batch, including records it already processed. Until the batch
succeeds, Lambda doesn't move past it, so one bad record blocks its shard. By default Lambda keeps retrying until the
record expires from the stream (24 hours unless you raise `retentionPeriodHours` on the stream). Make the handler
idempotent and give the trigger a way out:

```typescript
new KinesisIntegration({
  kinesisStreamName: 'clickStream',
  maximumRetryAttempts: 3,
  bisectBatchOnFunctionError: true,
  reportBatchItemFailures: true,
  onFailure: { arn: $ResourceParam('failedClicks', 'arn'), type: 'sqs' }
})
```

- `maximumRetryAttempts` stops retrying a batch after this many attempts.
- `bisectBatchOnFunctionError` splits a failing batch in two before each retry, which narrows it down to the bad record.
- `reportBatchItemFailures` lets the handler return `{ batchItemFailures: [{ itemIdentifier }] }` with the sequence
  number of the first record it couldn't process. Lambda then retries from that record instead of the whole batch.
  A handler that returns nothing with this setting on is treated as having processed every record.
- `onFailure` names an SQS queue or SNS topic for batches that still fail.

The `onFailure` destination receives a description of the failed batch, not the records: the shard ID, the first and
last sequence number and the error. To reprocess the records, read them from the stream by sequence number before they
expire. If you need the payloads kept longer, raise the stream's retention or have the handler save failed records to
S3 or a queue itself.

docs.title: Triggers overview
docs.content:
# Triggers overview

A trigger connects an event source to your code: an HTTP request, a schedule, a queue message, a file upload or a
database change. You add triggers to the `events` list of a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job), and Stacktape creates the route, rule, subscription or event source mapping
in AWS. A Lambda function costs nothing while no trigger fires.

docs.title: Triggers overview
docs.content:
## Pick a trigger

| The work starts with | Trigger |
|---|---|
| An HTTP request | [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers): `http-api-gateway`, or a load balancer |
| A WebSocket message | [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway): `websocket-api-gateway` |
| A GraphQL query or mutation | [AppSync API](/resources/networking/appsync-api): `appsync-api` |
| A time or an interval | [Schedule](/resources/triggers/schedule-triggers): `schedule` |
| A file upload or delete | [S3 events](/resources/triggers/s3-events): `s3` |
| A job on a queue, one consumer | [SQS events](/resources/triggers/sqs-events): `sqs` |
| A message several consumers need | [SNS events](/resources/triggers/sns-events): `sns` |
| An event routed by its content | [Event bus events](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events): `event-bus` |
| A change to a DynamoDB item | [DynamoDB streams](/resources/triggers/dynamodb-streams): `dynamo-db-stream` |
| Ordered, high-volume records | [Kinesis events](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events): `kinesis-stream` |
| A Kafka topic | [Kafka topic events](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics): `kafka-topic` |
| A matching log line | [CloudWatch Logs](/resources/triggers/cloudwatch-logs): `cloudwatch-log` |
| An alarm going off | [Alarms as triggers](/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers): `cloudwatch-alarm` |

For messages between your own services, start with SQS: one queue per consumer, with retries and a dead-letter queue.
Add SNS or an event bus in front when a second consumer needs the same message.

For HTTP, an HTTP API Gateway costs nothing without traffic and is the default for Lambda APIs. A load balancer has an
hourly charge and routes on headers, hosts, query parameters and source IPs; pick it when you already run one for
containers. [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) compares them.

docs.title: Triggers overview
docs.content: ## What each resource accepts

docs.title: Triggers overview
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Lambda function | Batch job | Containers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP API Gateway | yes | yes | yes |
| Application Load Balancer | yes | yes | yes |
| Network Load Balancer | no | no | yes |
| WebSocket API Gateway | yes | no | no |
| AppSync API | yes | no | no |
| Schedule | yes | yes | no |
| S3 | yes | yes | no |
| SQS | yes | yes | no |
| SNS | yes | yes | no |
| Event bus | yes | yes | no |
| DynamoDB stream | yes | yes | no |
| Kinesis stream | yes | yes | no |
| Kafka topic | yes | no | no |
| CloudWatch Logs | yes | yes | no |
| CloudWatch alarm | yes | no | no |


Containers are always running, so they don't need a trigger to start. They only receive traffic. Each container of a
[multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) has its own `events` for HTTP API Gateway,
load balancers and the internal `service-connect` and `workload-internal` ports. A
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service) and a [private service](/resources/compute/private-service) set up their
traffic with their own properties instead. A container that should process a queue is a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) that polls SQS in its code.

A batch job receives the trigger's event in the `STP_TRIGGER_EVENT_DATA` environment variable. Each event starts one
job.

docs.title: Triggers overview
Triggers overview
docs.content:
## How events are delivered

Triggers deliver events in one of three ways. The way decides what happens when your code fails.

| Delivery | Sources | When the function fails |
|---|---|---|
| Request and response | HTTP API Gateway, load balancers, WebSocket, AppSync | The caller gets the error. Nothing is retried. |
| Pushed by the source | Schedule, S3, SNS, event bus, CloudWatch Logs, alarms | Lambda retries twice, then drops the event unless the function has `destinations.onFailure`. |
| Polled in batches | SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB streams, Kafka | The batch is retried. Each trigger page explains limits, dead-letter queues and partial failures. |

Pushed and polled sources can deliver the same event more than once. Write handlers so that running twice on the same
event does no harm, for example by using the event or message ID as an idempotency key.

To keep pushed events that still fail after the retries, set
[`destinations.onFailure`](/resources/compute/lambda-function#api-ref_lambda-function-props--destinations) on the
function to an SQS queue or SNS topic.

docs.title: Triggers overview
docs.content:
## Filtering events

Filtering at the source means the function isn't invoked for events it would ignore, and you don't pay for them.

| Trigger | Property | Filters on |
|---|---|---|
| S3 | `filterRule` | Key prefix and suffix |
| SNS | `filterPolicy` | Message attributes |
| Event bus | `eventPattern` | Any field of the event, including the body |
| CloudWatch Logs | `filter` | The log line, with CloudWatch filter syntax |

The other triggers have no filter property. Skip unwanted events in your handler.

docs.title: S3 events
docs.content:
# S3 events

An `s3` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) when objects are created, deleted or restored in an
[S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket). Use it to process files as they arrive: resize images, import CSV files,
scan uploads.

To process uploads in batches or at a controlled rate, put an [SQS queue](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) between the
bucket and the consumer.

docs.title: S3 events
S3 events
docs.content:
## Event types

`s3EventType` picks the operation. `s3:ObjectCreated:*` covers every way an object is created and is the right choice
for most uploads.

| Event type | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `s3:ObjectCreated:*` | An object is created in any way |
| `s3:ObjectCreated:Put`, `:Post`, `:Copy`, `:CompleteMultipartUpload` | An object is created in that specific way |
| `s3:ObjectRemoved:*` | An object is deleted |
| `s3:ObjectRemoved:Delete` | An object is permanently deleted |
| `s3:ObjectRemoved:DeleteMarkerCreated` | A versioned object gets a delete marker |
| `s3:ObjectRestore:*`, `:Post`, `:Completed` | A Glacier restore starts or finishes |
| `s3:Replication:*` and its four `Operation…` types | A replication event happens |
| `s3:ReducedRedundancyLostObject` | A Reduced Redundancy object is lost |

docs.title: S3 events
docs.content:
## Filter by key

`filterRule` takes a `prefix`, a `suffix` or both. With both, the key must match both:

```typescript
new S3Integration({
  bucketArn: $ResourceParam('dataBucket', 'arn'),
  s3EventType: 's3:ObjectCreated:*',
  filterRule: { prefix: 'imports/', suffix: '.csv' }
})
```

S3 filters only on the key. To skip objects by size or content type, check them at the start of the handler.

Several functions can react to the same bucket if their filters don't overlap: S3 rejects two notifications for the
same event type whose prefix and suffix can match the same key. When several consumers need every event, set
`enableEventBusNotifications: true` on the bucket and give each one an
[event bus trigger](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events) on the default bus with `source: ['aws.s3']`.

docs.title: S3 events
docs.content:
## Avoid loops

If the function writes its output to the same bucket and the trigger matches that output, every write runs the
function again. The loop can run thousands of invocations per second and costs money until you stop it.

- Write output to a different bucket. This is the safest option.
- Or read from one prefix and write to another: trigger on `uploads/`, write to `processed/`.
- Or filter on the suffix: trigger on `.jpg`, write `.webp`.

If a loop is already running, remove the trigger and deploy, or set the function's reserved concurrency to 0 in the
AWS console.

docs.title: S3 events
docs.content:
## Failures and retries

S3 invokes the function asynchronously. If the function throws, Lambda retries it twice and then drops the event. To
keep events that still fail, set
[`destinations.onFailure`](/resources/compute/lambda-function#api-ref_lambda-function-props--destinations) on the
function. S3 can deliver the same event more than once, so make the handler idempotent: processing the same file twice
should give the same result.

docs.title: Schedule triggers
docs.content:
# Schedule triggers

A `schedule` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) at fixed times or intervals: nightly cleanup, hourly syncs, weekday reports.
A scheduled function costs nothing between runs, unlike a container that runs a cron daemon all day.

The shortest interval is one minute. Schedules are AWS EventBridge rules, and cron times are in UTC.

docs.title: Schedule triggers
Schedule triggers
docs.content:
## Rate expressions

`rate(<value> <unit>)` runs at a fixed interval. The unit is `minute`, `hour` or `day`, plural for values above 1.

| Expression | Runs |
|---|---|
| `rate(1 minute)` | Every minute |
| `rate(5 minutes)` | Every 5 minutes |
| `rate(12 hours)` | Every 12 hours |
| `rate(7 days)` | Once a week |

docs.title: Schedule triggers
docs.content:
## Cron expressions

`cron(...)` runs at set times. AWS uses six fields, not the five of Unix cron, and all times are UTC:

```text
cron(minutes hours day-of-month month day-of-week year)
```

One of the two day fields must be `?`. You can't use `*` in both.

| Expression | Runs |
|---|---|
| `cron(0 9 * * ? *)` | Every day at 9:00 UTC |
| `cron(0 18 ? * MON-FRI *)` | Weekdays at 18:00 UTC |
| `cron(0 0 1 * ? *)` | The first day of each month at midnight UTC |
| `cron(0/15 * * * ? *)` | Every 15 minutes |
| `cron(0 12 ? * 2#1 *)` | The first Monday of each month at noon UTC |

Cron doesn't follow daylight saving time. A job at 9:00 New York time needs `cron(0 14 …)` in winter and `cron(0 13 …)`
in summer, or a check of the local time in your code. The
[AWS reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-scheduled-rule-pattern.html) lists every
wildcard.

docs.title: Schedule triggers
Schedule triggers
docs.content:
## Pause a schedule

Set `enabled: false` and deploy. The rule stays in the stack with its expression and payload. Setting it back to `true`
(the default) resumes it at the next scheduled time.

docs.title: Schedule triggers
docs.content:
## Failures and overlapping runs

EventBridge invokes the function asynchronously. If the function throws, Lambda retries it twice. A scheduled job that
fails quietly is easy to miss, so add a `lambda-error-rate` [alarm](/observability/alarms) to the function.

If a run is still going when the next one is due, the next one starts anyway, in parallel. Make the job safe to overlap,
or take a lock (for example a conditional write to DynamoDB) at the start.

docs.title: SNS events
docs.content:
# SNS events

An `sns` event subscribes a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) to an
[SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic). Every message published to the topic invokes the function with its own
copy. Use it to fan one event out to several independent consumers: an order is placed, and billing, inventory and email
each get the message.

SNS invokes the function once per message; the trigger has no `batchSize`. To process messages in batches, or with a
single consumer, subscribe an [SQS queue](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) to the topic instead: it adds batching and
keeps messages while the consumer is down. To route on fields inside the message body, use an
[event bus](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events). Batch jobs accept `sns` events too. Delivery to Lambda is free; the
[SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic#standard-or-fifo) page explains what publishing costs.

docs.title: SNS events
SNS events
docs.content:
## Filter messages

A `filterPolicy` makes SNS skip the function for messages that don't match. The function isn't invoked and you don't pay
for it.

```typescript
new SnsIntegration({
  snsTopicName: 'orderEvents',
  filterPolicy: {
    orderType: ['premium', 'enterprise'],
    amount: [{ numeric: ['>=', 1000] }]
  }
})
```

The policy matches **message attributes**, the key-value metadata the publisher sets when it calls `Publish`. A field
with the same name inside the JSON body doesn't match. The
[AWS filter policy reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-subscription-filter-policies.html) lists
the operators.

docs.title: SNS events
SNS events
docs.content:
## FIFO topics

A FIFO topic keeps the order of messages in a message group, but it delivers only to SQS queues, not to Lambda. For
ordered fan-out, subscribe a FIFO [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) per consumer and give each consumer an
[SQS event](/resources/triggers/sqs-events). A FIFO topic can also deliver to standard queues, but those don't keep the
order or remove duplicates.

docs.title: SQS events
docs.content:
# SQS events

An `sqs` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) with the messages that arrive in an
[SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue). Lambda polls the queue for you, passes the messages in batches and deletes
them when the function succeeds. Use it for background work: an API puts a job on the queue and the function processes
it at its own pace.

A queue message goes to one consumer. When several functions need the same message, publish it to an
[SNS topic](/resources/triggers/sns-events) or an [event bus](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events) instead. Batch jobs
accept `sqs` events too. A container that should read the queue itself is a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) that polls SQS in its code.

docs.title: SQS events
SQS events
docs.content:
## Batching

Lambda invokes the function when the batch is full, when the batching window ends, or when the batch reaches the 6 MB
invocation payload limit, whichever comes first.

| Property | Standard queue | FIFO queue |
|---|---|---|
| `batchSize` | 10 by default, up to 10,000 | 10 by default, up to 10 |
| `maxBatchWindowSeconds` | Off by default, up to 300 | Not supported |

AWS needs a batching window of at least 1 second for a `batchSize` above 10. A larger batch with a window means fewer
invocations and a lower Lambda bill, at the cost of latency:

```typescript
new SqsIntegration({ sqsQueueName: 'orderQueue', batchSize: 100, maxBatchWindowSeconds: 30 })
```

This waits up to 30 seconds to collect 100 messages. If 100 messages arrive in 5 seconds, the function runs right away.

docs.title: SQS events
docs.content:
### Limiting concurrency

`maximumConcurrency` (2 to 1000) caps how many copies of the function the queue runs at once. Use it to protect a
database or a rate-limited API. Messages wait in the queue while the cap is reached.

```typescript
new SqsIntegration({ sqsQueueName: 'orderQueue', maximumConcurrency: 5 })
```

To see that the queue is falling behind, watch `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` (backlog) and
`ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` (lag) in CloudWatch. The queue can alarm on its backlog with the
`sqs-queue-received-messages-count` or `sqs-queue-not-empty` [alarm](/observability/alarms). When the backlog keeps
growing, raise `batchSize` or remove a `maximumConcurrency` cap.

docs.title: SQS events
docs.content:
## Failures and retries

If the function throws, the whole batch goes back to the queue. It becomes visible again when the queue's visibility
timeout ends (30 seconds by default) and Lambda delivers it again. Messages also arrive more than once now and then,
even without errors, so write the handler to be idempotent: processing the same `messageId` twice must not charge a card
twice.

The function's `timeout` can't be longer than the queue's `visibilityTimeoutSeconds`, or AWS refuses the trigger.
Stacktape checks this before deploying and stops with:


> **Error:** Error in `function` `orderProcessor`: its `timeout` (60 s) is longer than the visibility timeout of its trigger queue
`orderQueue` (30 s, the default). AWS refuses such a trigger, because a message would become visible to other
consumers while the function still processes it.


Raise `visibilityTimeoutSeconds` on the queue or lower the function's `timeout`. AWS recommends a visibility timeout of
six times the function timeout.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
# Account settings

Account settings is your personal page in the Stacktape Console. Open it with **Account** in the profile menu at the top
right. It holds your name and the ways you sign in, and it shows where you are signed in. These settings belong to you,
not to an organization, so they apply in every organization you are a member of.

Rules that an organization sets for all its members, such as requiring two-factor sign-in or single sign-on, are on
[Members](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#requiring-two-factor-sign-in) and
[Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on).

docs.title: Account settings
headingPath: If you used the Console before v4
docs.content:
## If you used the Console before v4

Stacktape v4 moved Console sign-in to a new system. Your account, organizations, roles and API keys did not change. A few
things work differently:

- **Password.** The first time you sign in with your email and password, Stacktape checks the password against the old
  system and keeps it. If your password is not accepted, use **Forgot password?** on the sign-in page to set a new one.
- **Authenticator app.** If you used one before, the sign-in page asks for its code once more. The old authenticator
  does not carry over: after that sign-in, Account settings asks you to set up an
  [authenticator app](#authenticator-app-and-backup-codes) or a [passkey](#passkeys) again. Until you do, a password
  sign-in does not count as two-factor, and an organization that requires two-factor sign-in stays closed to you. SMS
  codes are no longer offered.
- **Google.** Sign in with Google as before. Your account is matched by its verified email address.
- **CLI.** `stacktape login` now asks you to approve the sign-in in the browser. See [login](/cli/login).

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Profile

- **Name** is shown to your teammates. Edit it and click **Save**.
- **Email** is the address you sign in with. It cannot be changed on this page.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Ways to sign in

You can have several ways to sign in at once. All of them except a password alone count as two-factor sign-in, which
matters when an organization requires it.

| Way to sign in | Where you set it up | Counts as two-factor |
|---|---|---|
| Password | When you sign up, or with **Forgot password?** | No |
| Password and authenticator app | [Authenticator app](#authenticator-app-and-backup-codes) on this page | Yes |
| Passkey | [Passkeys](#passkeys) on this page | Yes |
| Google or GitHub | [Google and GitHub](#google-and-github) on this page | Yes |
| Single sign-on | Your organization's [identity provider](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on) | Yes |

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content: ## Password

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
### Change your password

1. In the **Password** row, click **Change password**.
2. Enter your **Current password**, then the **New password** twice.
3. Click **Change password**.

A password must have at least 8 characters (at most 128) and must not appear in a known data breach. Stacktape checks
this with Have I Been Pwned, which receives only the beginning of the password's hash, never the password.

After the change, this browser stays signed in and every other browser and device is signed out. CLI logins
(`stacktape login`) and API keys keep working; see [Sessions](#sessions) for how to end them.

docs.title: Account settings
headingPath: Add a password or reset a forgotten one
docs.content:
### Add a password or reset a forgotten one

If you signed up with Google or GitHub, the **Password** row shows **None**. To add a password, or to replace one you
forgot:

1. Sign out, and on the sign-in page click **Forgot password?**.
2. Enter your email and click **Send reset code**.
3. Enter the **Reset code** from the email and your **New password**, then click **Change password**.

A reset signs you out of every browser and device. Sign in again with the new password.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Authenticator app and backup codes

The **Authenticator app** row appears when your account has a password. With it on, a password sign-in also asks for a
6-digit code from an app such as 1Password, Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
### Turn it on

1. In the **Authenticator app** row, click **Turn on**.
2. Enter your password and click **Continue**.
3. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app. If you cannot scan it, copy the secret shown under the code into the
   app instead.
4. Enter the 6-digit code from the app and click **Turn on**.
5. The **Save your backup codes** dialog shows 10 backup codes. Copy them to a safe place, such as your password
   manager, and click **I saved them**.


> **Warning:** The backup codes are shown only once. Each code signs you in once instead of an authenticator code. Without the
codes, a lost phone can lock you out unless you have another way to sign in, such as a passkey or Google.


The change counts from your next sign-in. If an organization requires two-factor sign-in, sign out and sign in again
with your password and a code to open it.

When you sign in, the **Two-step verification** screen asks for the code. If you do not have your phone, choose
**Use a backup code**.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
### Turn it off

Click **Turn off** and confirm with your password. Your password sign-ins stop asking for a code, so organizations that
require two-factor sign-in then need you to sign in with a passkey, Google or GitHub.

To move the authenticator to a new phone, turn it off and on again. The old entry in your authenticator app stops
working.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Passkeys

A passkey signs you in with your device's fingerprint, face recognition or PIN instead of a password. It counts as
two-factor sign-in on its own.

1. In the **Passkeys** row, click **Add passkey**.
2. Follow your browser's or password manager's prompt.

Passkeys are named `Passkey 1`, `Passkey 2` and so on, with the date each was added. To use one, click
**Sign in with a passkey** on the sign-in page.

To remove a passkey, click **Remove** next to it. Also remove it from your device's password manager, which keeps
offering it otherwise.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Google and GitHub

The **Google** and **GitHub** rows let you sign in with those accounts. Click **Connect** and approve the request at the
provider.

The provider account must have verified the same email address as your Stacktape account. Otherwise it is not
connected, and the page says which address it needs.

**Disconnect** removes the connection. You cannot disconnect your only way to sign in; add another one first.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Sessions

The **Sessions** row lists the browsers signed in to your account, with the browser and system, IP address and when
each was last active. **This browser** marks the one you are using.

- **Sign out** next to a session signs that browser out at its next request.
- **Sign out everywhere else** ends every session except this one.

A browser that is not used for 30 days is signed out. Changing your password also signs out every other session.

CLI logins are not browser sessions and do not appear here. Run [`stacktape logout`](/cli/logout) on a machine to end
its CLI login. Owners, Admins and Developers also see their CLI logins as **CLI session** on the
[API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) page and can revoke them there.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Delete your account

Account deletion is not self-service. Email [support@stacktape.com](mailto:support@stacktape.com) from the address you
sign in with.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## What organizations see

Changes on this page are recorded in the [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log) of every organization you belong
to: password changes, the authenticator app turned on or off, passkeys added or removed, Google or GitHub connected or
disconnected, and sessions ended. Sign-ins themselves are not recorded. Owners and Admins can also see on the
[Members](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) page whether you have two-factor sign-in.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
### The authenticator code is rejected

Codes change every 30 seconds. Enter the current one, and check that your phone's clock is set automatically. If codes
are still rejected, sign in with a backup code or another way, then turn the authenticator app off and on again.

docs.title: Account settings
headingPath: I lost the phone with my authenticator app
docs.content:
### I lost the phone with my authenticator app

On the **Two-step verification** screen, choose **Use a backup code**. You can also sign in with a passkey, Google or
GitHub if you added one. Then turn the authenticator app off and on again with your new phone. If you have none of
these, contact [support@stacktape.com](mailto:support@stacktape.com).

docs.title: Account settings
headingPath: "Google was not connected" or "GitHub was not connected"
docs.content:
### "Google was not connected" or "GitHub was not connected"

The provider has not verified the email address of your Stacktape account. Verify that address at the provider, or
connect a provider account that uses the same address.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
### "This organization requires two-factor sign-in"

Set up an authenticator app or a passkey on this page, then sign out and sign in again with it.

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
### "This organization requires single sign-on"

Sign out, then on the sign-in page click **Sign in with SSO** and enter your work email. See
[Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on).

docs.title: Account settings
docs.content:
## Related features

- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control): members, roles and the two-factor requirement
- [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on): sign in through your organization's identity provider
- [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys): keys and CLI sessions for the CLI and CI
- [`stacktape login`](/cli/login): sign in to the CLI

docs.title: API keys
docs.content:
# API keys

An API key signs the Stacktape CLI in to the Console where nobody can open a browser: a CI pipeline, a server or a script. Keys live on **Organization → API keys**, and there are two kinds:

| You need | Use |
|---|---|
| A pipeline or tool your team shares | An **organization key**. It belongs to the organization and keeps working when people leave. Owners and Admins create it. |
| Your own script or server | A **personal key**. It acts as you, with your role and access, and stops working if you leave the organization. |
| The CLI on your own machine | No key: run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login). |

A personal organization has only personal keys. CI that a team shares belongs in a team organization, with an organization key.

docs.title: API keys
docs.content:
## Create an organization key

1. Open **Organization → API keys** and click **New organization key**.
2. Name it after where it runs, for example `github-actions`.
3. Pick its role: **Developer** with the projects and AWS accounts the pipeline deploys, or **Admin** for everything.
4. Pick when it expires, from 30 days to a year.
5. Copy the key from the next dialog. It is shown only once.

Store it as the `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret of your CI. When the organization has more than one connected AWS account, pass `--aws-account <name>` on the CLI commands, so a pipeline never has to guess. See [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd).

The table shows each key's access, status, when it was last used, when it expires and who created it. Organization keys can't create organizations or connect AI subscriptions, which belong to people.

docs.title: API keys
docs.content:
## Create a personal key

Click **New personal key** (in a personal organization, **New API key**), give it a name and an expiry, and copy the key from the next dialog. The dialog says whose access the key uses: yours, in the organization that is open, with your role and, for a Developer, your projects and AWS accounts. Viewers have no API keys page and can't create keys.

`stacktape login` creates a key for this machine too. It is listed as a **CLI session**, and [`stacktape logout`](/cli/logout) revokes it.

docs.title: API keys
docs.content:
## What a key can reach

A key never does more than its role. A Developer key reaches only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for it; asking it for credentials in another AWS account fails with "Your access does not include the AWS account". See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for the roles.

A key is a password. Keep it in your CI's secret store, never in code, chat, issue trackers or shell history.

docs.title: API keys
docs.content:
## Rotate and revoke keys

A key can't be shown again, reactivated or extended. To replace one, create the new key, put it in your CI secret, check that a pipeline run works, then revoke the old key. [Authenticate the pipeline](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd#with-the-console) shows where each CI provider keeps the key.

**Revoke key** stops every CLI session and pipeline that uses the key at once. Expired and revoked keys stay in the list with their status.

Owners and Admins can also revoke a member's personal keys from the Members page, and [removing a member](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#removing-a-member) revokes theirs. The removal dialog warns when one of their keys was used in the last 7 days, because a pipeline may depend on it. Before you remove someone whose key runs a shared pipeline, replace it with an organization key.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
# Audit log

The **Audit log** page answers "who changed what" for your organization. It shows three kinds of rows in one table,
newest first:

- **Stacktape events**: changes made through Stacktape, such as a member invited, an API key revoked or an AWS account
  connected.
- **Stack operations**: deploys, deletes and the other CLI operations that the Activity page lists, with who ran them.
- **AWS events**: what AWS CloudTrail recorded in your connected AWS accounts, read live from those accounts.

Open it from **Audit log** in the Organization group of the sidebar. It is available on every plan.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## Who can see it

Owners and Admins. Developers and Viewers do not see the page in the sidebar, and opening its address tells them that
only Owners and Admins can see the audit log.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## What Stacktape records

Stacktape records an event for every change that affects access, credentials, integrations or settings, including:

- members invited, removed, or given another role or other projects and AWS accounts
- API keys created or revoked, deployment tokens created, and CLI logins (`stacktape login`) and logouts
- AWS accounts connected and disconnected
- projects, stages, secrets and SSM parameters created, changed or deleted (names only, never values)
- Git, Slack and AI provider connections
- runner settings and runner terminal sessions
- guardrails, budgets, alert channels and notification rules
- organization settings, such as the two-factor requirement, and single sign-on and SCIM changes
- exports of the audit log itself

Changes people make to their own sign-in appear in every organization they belong to: password changed, authenticator
app turned on or off, passkey added or removed, Google or GitHub connected or disconnected, and sessions ended.
Sign-ins themselves are not recorded.

Refused attempts to change members, API keys, AWS connections, the two-factor requirement and single sign-on are
recorded too, with the outcome **Denied**.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## Reading the table

| Column | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Time | When it happened. Hover for the exact time. |
| Source | **Stacktape** or **AWS** |
| Actor | Who did it, and how: in the Console, from the CLI, with an API key, or through Stacktape in AWS |
| Action | For example `member.removed` or an AWS API call such as `DeleteBucket` |
| Target | What it changed |
| AWS account · region | Where it happened, when it happened in AWS |
| Outcome | **Succeeded**, **Denied**, **Failed**, **In progress** or **Unknown** |

Click a row to see all its fields. For an AWS event, the panel also shows the event record as CloudTrail returned it and
links to the event in the AWS console.

The table shows 50 rows at a time. **Load more** continues further back.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## Filters

- **Time range**: from **Last 24 hours** to **Last 400 days**. The default is **Last 7 days**.
- **Source**: **All sources**, **Stacktape** or **AWS**.
- **Person**: everyone, or one member. Organization keys are listed with "(organization key)".
- **AWS account**: one connected account. It keeps that account's AWS events, the stack operations in it, and the
  Stacktape events that changed it.
- **Read-only AWS events**: off by default, so AWS rows show only changes. Turn it on to include reads, such as
  `Describe*` and `List*` calls.

The filters are part of the page address, so you can share a filtered view by copying the link.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## AWS events are read live

Stacktape does not copy your CloudTrail events into its own storage. When you open or filter the page, Stacktape reads
them from your AWS accounts through each account's connection role.

Stacktape reads:

- every connected AWS account, or the one you filtered on;
- the regions where your organization has run Stacktape operations in that account, plus `us-east-1`, where AWS records
  global services such as IAM, CloudFront and Route 53;
- management events only. Data events, such as S3 object reads or Lambda invocations, are not available here.

For an event in another region, use CloudTrail in the AWS console.

The line above the table says which accounts and regions were read and which time they cover. AWS limits how fast
CloudTrail can be read, so on a busy account the line can say "Complete back to" a time; **Load more** reads further.
When an account cannot be read, the line names it and the reason: access denied, region not enabled, throttled by AWS,
or could not be read.

The **Person** filter works on AWS events after they are read. The line above the table says so when it applies.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## Who did it in AWS

For an AWS event, the **Actor** column names the person when Stacktape can tell:

- **"through Stacktape (purpose)"**: a member caused Stacktape to act in AWS, for example by creating a budget or
  deleting a project in the Console. The purpose says what for, such as "budget" or "project delete".
- **Stacktape, "background work (purpose)"**: Stacktape's own scheduled or background work.
- **"with their own AWS credentials"**: the event used AWS access keys that a member's recorded Stacktape operation also
  used, for example when they ran `stacktape deploy` with their own AWS profile.
- Otherwise the AWS principal as AWS reports it, such as a role or an IAM user.

AWS events name only current members. Someone who has left shows as an unknown Stacktape user there. Stacktape events
keep naming the person after they leave.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
### Older AWS account connections

AWS account connections created from an older connection template need an update so that AWS records the person
behind each action everywhere. Until then, Stacktape names the person only for actions the connection role makes directly; actions made
through further roles show the AWS principal instead.

Owners and Admins see an **Update** button next to these accounts on **Configuration → AWS accounts**. It opens a
dialog with the steps and a link that updates the connection stack in AWS CloudFormation. See
[AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions#who-can-use-the-role) for how the person is recorded.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## How long events are kept

| Rows | Kept for | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Stacktape events | 400 days, also after the organization is deleted | Stacktape |
| AWS events | 90 days, CloudTrail's event history | Your AWS account |

The page shows at most the last 400 days. When a time range reaches further back than 90 days, AWS events cover only the
last 90 days and older rows are Stacktape events only; the line above the table says so. To keep AWS events longer, set
up a CloudTrail trail that delivers them to an S3 bucket in your AWS account.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## Export

Click **Export** and choose **Stacktape events as CSV** or **Stacktape events as JSON**.

- The file has the Stacktape events and stack operations of the selected time range, narrowed by the **Person** and
  **AWS account** filters. The **Source** and **Read-only AWS events** filters do not apply.
- AWS events are not exported: you already have them in your AWS account.
- One export holds at most 50,000 rows, the newest ones. When there are more, the Console says so; narrow the time range
  to export the rest.
- The columns are `time`, `type` (`event` or `stack operation`), `actor`, `actorEmail`, `action`, `targetType`,
  `target`, `awsAccountId`, `region`, `outcome`, `details` and `id`. In the CSV file, `details` is a JSON object.
- In the CSV file, a value that starts with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` gets a leading apostrophe, so a spreadsheet does not run
  it as a formula.

Each export is itself recorded in the audit log, with its format, time range and filters.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
### There are no AWS events

Check that the **Source** filter is not **Stacktape**, that the time range ends within the last 90 days, and that the
organization has a connected AWS account. Events from regions where your organization never ran a Stacktape operation
are not read, except `us-east-1`.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
### An account shows "access denied"

Stacktape could not use the account's connection role. Check the account's state on the **AWS accounts** page.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
### An account shows "throttled by AWS"

AWS limited the reads. Try again in a minute.

docs.title: Audit log
headingPath: An AWS event shows a role instead of a person
docs.content:
### An AWS event shows a role instead of a person

The action did not go through Stacktape, or it went through further roles in an account whose connection has not been
updated. See [Older AWS account connections](#older-aws-account-connections).

docs.title: Audit log
docs.content:
## Related features

- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control): members, roles and organization keys
- [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on): SSO and SCIM changes appear in the audit log
- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account): the connection role the AWS events are
  read through

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
# AWS permissions

Connecting an AWS account to the Console creates one CloudFormation stack in it. The stack holds an IAM role that the Console assumes to deploy your stacks and read their logs, metrics and costs. This page says exactly what the stack creates, who can use the role and how to limit or remove it. [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) covers the steps.

The CLI without an account doesn't use any of this: it deploys with your own AWS credentials.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
## What the connection stack creates

The stack is created in `eu-west-1`, whatever regions you deploy to. It holds:

- **The role Stacktape assumes.** Only Stacktape's AWS account can assume it, and only with an external ID unique to this connection. Sessions last at most 12 hours.
- **A cost report bucket**, `stacktape-cur-<connection ID>`. AWS writes the account's Cost and Usage Reports there, and Stacktape reads them for the [cost pages](/managing-costs/dashboards). Reports are deleted after 30 days, and the bucket blocks public access.
- **A reporting policy** that lets the role manage the cost report definition, read the bucket, list CloudFormation stacks and turn on cost allocation tags.

Connecting is free, and the role costs nothing in AWS. The cost report bucket is billed as normal S3 storage and holds at most 30 days of reports.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
## Deploy access or read-only

The role gets one of two AWS managed policies:

| Access | AWS policy | Stacktape can |
|---|---|---|
| **Can deploy** | `AdministratorAccess` | Deploy, update and delete your stacks, and read their logs, metrics and costs |
| **Read-only** | `ReadOnlyAccess` | Read logs, metrics and costs. Deploys, budgets and other writes fail. |

A connection made in the Console or with `stacktape connect` can deploy. The connection stack's `StacktapeConnectionMode` parameter decides: `PRIVILEGED` can deploy, `BASIC` is read-only. To make an account read-only:

- **New connection:** on the AWS page that **Open AWS CloudFormation** opens, change **StacktapeConnectionMode** to `BASIC` before you choose **Create stack**.
- **Existing connection:** in the AWS CloudFormation console, in `eu-west-1`, update the stack `stacktape-<connection ID>`, keep its current template and set **StacktapeConnectionMode** to `BASIC`.

The **Status** column of the AWS accounts page then shows **Read-only** next to **Connected**, and in IAM the role has `ReadOnlyAccess` and the reporting policy, nothing else. An Owner or Admin can switch it back with **Allow deploys**.

Deploy access is administrator access because a stack can contain almost any AWS service: functions, containers, databases, networking, IAM roles for your workloads and more. A policy limited to some services would fail on the next resource you add. Your workloads don't get these permissions: each one runs with its own role that allows only what its config declares.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
## Who can use the role

The role's trust policy names Stacktape's AWS account. Inside Stacktape, the Console decides who may use the account:

- Owners and Admins reach every connected account.
- Developers and Viewers reach only the AWS accounts chosen for them on the Members page. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#project-and-aws-account-access).
- Only Owners and Admins can connect, update or disconnect an account.

When a person causes an AWS call, Stacktape names them in it: the source identity `stp-<user ID>` and a role session name that starts with `stp-`. Background work uses session names that start with `stacktape-`. The Console's [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log) turns these into names. A connection created before source identities were supported shows an update link on the AWS accounts page.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
## Supported regions

The role works in every region, but Stacktape deploys only to the regions it supports. The allowed values of [`--region`](/cli/deploy#option-deploy-region) list them. An AWS service can still be missing in a supported region, and an SCP or organization guardrail can block a region.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
## Restrict what Stacktape can do

**Service control policies.** An SCP in AWS Organizations limits every role in the account, Stacktape's included, whatever its own policy allows. Use it to block regions, protect resources with a tag, or deny actions you never want. A deploy that an SCP blocks fails with `AccessDenied`; the CloudFormation event names the action.

**Separate accounts.** The usual setup is one AWS account for production with stricter SCPs and one for development and previews. Each account has its own connection and its own role, and members can get access to one without the other.

**Read-only.** Keep an account read-only when you only want logs, metrics and costs in the Console, for example an account another tool deploys.

**Guardrails.** Console [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) refuse deploys that break your rules, such as oversized instances or a region you don't use, before anything reaches AWS.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
## Revoke access

1. Open **Configuration → AWS accounts** and choose **Disconnect account** in the account's menu. The Console blocks this while [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) target the account and lists the projects to change first.
2. Delete the connection stack in the AWS CloudFormation console, in `eu-west-1`. That removes the role and the cost report bucket.

Deleting only the stack leaves the account in the Console as **No access**. Your deployed stacks are separate CloudFormation stacks and keep running either way; manage or delete them with the CLI and your own credentials.

docs.title: AWS permissions
docs.content:
## Audit Stacktape's activity

Filter AWS CloudTrail by the role's ARN to see each call Stacktape made. The `stp-` source identity and session names say which person caused it, and the Console's [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log) shows the same events with names.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
# Billing and subscription

The Stacktape CLI is open source and free, and it works without a Stacktape account; see [Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli). This page covers the plans of the Stacktape Console: Free, Flexible and Enterprise. AWS bills you for your infrastructure as before; the Stacktape fee is a separate invoice from Stacktape.

You compare and change plans on **Subscription plans**, and see the fee estimate and invoices on **Organization → Billing**. Owners and Admins can change the plan. Developers can compare plans but don't see Billing, and Viewers see neither.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
## Plans

Stacktape charges a share of the AWS costs of the stacks it manages, not per seat, deployment or request.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Free | Flexible | Enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price | $0 | 19–25% of managed AWS spend | Custom |
| Managed AWS spend | Up to $200/mo | No limit | No limit |
| Team members | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Deployments and stacks | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Single sign-on and SCIM | no | yes | yes |
| Shared Slack channel with the founders | no | yes | yes |
| Your feature requests come first | no | yes | yes |
| Single-tenant Console in your AWS account | no | no | yes |
| Support | — | Shared Slack channel | Up to 24x7 premium |

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
### Free plan

The Free plan is the whole Console except single sign-on and SCIM provisioning. It costs $0, needs no credit card and has no member limit. It covers managed AWS spend up to $200 a calendar month (UTC). When an organization passes $200, deploys keep working for 7 days the first time, then pause until it upgrades or the next month starts. See [Free plan cost limit](#free-plan-cost-limit).

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
### Flexible plan

The Flexible plan has no spend limit. Its fee is one rate applied to the whole month's managed AWS spend. The rate depends on how large that spend is:

| Monthly managed AWS spend | Rate |
|---|---|
| Up to $2,000 | 25% |
| Over $2,000, up to $5,000 | 23% |
| Over $5,000, up to $10,000 | 21% |
| Over $10,000, up to $25,000 | 20% |
| Over $25,000 | 19% |

Each band includes its upper limit: exactly $2,000 is charged 25%, $2,000.01 is charged 23%.

For example:

| Managed AWS spend in a month | Stacktape fee |
|---|---|
| $500 | $125 (25%) |
| $1,000 | $250 (25%) |
| $2,000 | $500 (25%) |
| $3,000 | $690 (23%) |
| $8,000 | $1,680 (21%) |

Managed spend is what the resources in Stacktape stacks cost, summed over all AWS accounts connected to the organization. Everything else in those accounts doesn't count. Say your two accounts cost $1,400 in a month: $1,000 for your Stacktape stacks and $400 for AWS Support and an old EC2 instance. You pay AWS $1,400 and Stacktape $250 (25% of $1,000), plus tax where it applies. The [Costs](/managing-costs/dashboards) page shows the same split: your projects, and costs outside projects.

The fee for a month is charged on the 7th of the next month (UTC), after AWS finishes the month's cost reports. The Subscription plans page shows what Flexible would cost your organization, in dollars, from its own costs.

On top of the Free plan, Flexible adds [single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on) (SAML or OIDC) with SCIM provisioning, a shared Slack channel with the founders, and priority for your feature requests. Priority means your requests are worked on first; it comes with no SLA or delivery dates.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
### Enterprise plan

The Enterprise plan runs a single-tenant Console in your own AWS account and region, for data residency. It includes single sign-on and SCIM and up to 24x7 premium support, and its price is agreed with you. Click **Schedule a meeting** on the Subscription plans page to talk to the Stacktape team.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
## Free plan cost limit

A Free organization can deploy while its managed AWS spend for the current calendar month (UTC) is $200 or less.

- **What counts.** The same managed spend the Flexible fee is based on, from the AWS billing data Stacktape reads.
- **Grace, once per organization.** The first time the organization is over the limit, Stacktape emails its Owners and Admins and starts a 7-day grace period. Deploys keep working during it, but only within the calendar month (UTC) it started in: a grace period that starts on November 29 doesn't cover December. In any later month, deploys pause as soon as the organization passes the limit, with no new grace period.
- **What pauses.** After the grace period, every new deploy: `stacktape deploy`, including code-only (fast) deploys, remote and runner deploys, deploys after a Git push and deploys started from the Console. `stacktape dev` does not start either, because it deploys a dev stack. A deploy that already started finishes normally.
- **What keeps working.** Your running infrastructure is never touched. Deleting stages, rolling back, running scripts and the rest of the Console keep working.
- **How it lifts.** Upgrading to Flexible lifts it immediately. Without an upgrade, deploys resume when the next calendar month starts.
- **Missing cost data.** AWS delivers billing data a few times a day, and a new connection has none at first. Until Stacktape has this month's costs, deploys are not limited.

The Console shows where you are. The sidebar shows this month's managed spend against the limit, and from $150 on it adds what Flexible would cost this month. During the grace period every page has a banner, for example "Day 3 of 7 over the Free limit. Flexible would cost about $53 this month." While deploys are paused, every page opens with an upgrade notice, which you can close to keep reading. Members who can't change the plan see which Owners and Admins can.

The CLI tells you too. From $150 on, and during the grace period, a successful deploy prints one line with the month's spend or the days left and what Flexible would cost. A refused deploy or dev session stops before it changes anything in AWS. [`deploy`](/cli/deploy#free-plan-cost-limit) shows both messages.

The limit applies to the Console only. The open-source CLI without an account has no limit.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
## Change your plan

1. Open **Subscription plans**. From Billing, click **Compare plans**. The card of your plan says **Current plan**.
2. Click **Upgrade to Flexible**. Paddle's checkout opens; enter your payment details there.
3. When Paddle accepts the payment, the page shows **Confirming your Flexible plan** until Paddle confirms it to Stacktape, usually within seconds. Don't start the checkout again. If the confirmation takes more than a minute, the page shows **Not confirmed yet** with a **Check again** button.

To go back, click **Downgrade to Free** on the Free card. If this month's managed spend is already above $200, the [Free plan cost limit](#free-plan-cost-limit) applies right after the downgrade. An Enterprise plan is changed through your agreement.

The buttons are disabled, with the reason, for members who can't change the plan.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content:
## Billing page

**Organization → Billing** shows:

- **Next charge, estimated**: the Flexible fee so far for this month, or for last month until it is charged on the 7th, with the managed spend it is based on. A fee is estimated only when your AWS cost reports are in US dollars, because the rates are set on dollar amounts. On Free, this tile shows this month's spend against the $200 limit instead.
- **Plan and payment**: the plan, who is billed, the invoice email and currency, and the Paddle subscription ID to quote when you contact support. Paddle stores the card, address and tax ID. **Update payment details** opens Paddle.
- **Invoices**: one row per charged month with the fee, tax and total, and **View invoice**.

The estimate uses the cost reports Stacktape has so far, and AWS keeps finishing a month's reports for a few days after it ends. The invoice charges the final amount.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
docs.content: ## Billing FAQ

docs.title: Billing and subscription
headingPath: Why is my plan still Free after paying?
docs.content:
### Why is my plan still Free after paying?

Paddle confirms the payment to Stacktape separately, usually within seconds. While it does, Subscription plans shows **Confirming your Flexible plan**. If it says **Not confirmed yet**, click **Check again**, and contact support if it stays that way.

docs.title: Billing and subscription
headingPath: Can I calculate the fee before connecting anything?
docs.content:
### Can I calculate the fee before connecting anything?

Yes, from the table above and your expected AWS bill for the stacks Stacktape would manage. For a stack you haven't deployed yet, [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) shows a monthly AWS estimate before the first deploy. See [Costs overview](/managing-costs/overview) for what drives an AWS bill.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
# Connecting your AWS account

The Stacktape Console works with your AWS accounts through a connection: an IAM role in your account that Stacktape
assumes with short-lived credentials, so you never create or rotate access keys for Stacktape. With it, the Console
runs Git deployments, shows logs, metrics and costs, and runs deploys for the CLI when it is signed in. You connect each
AWS account once.

The open-source CLI doesn't need a connection. Without a Stacktape account, it deploys with your own AWS credentials.
See [Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli).

There are two ways to connect an account:

- **From the terminal**, if you already deploy with the CLI: [`stacktape connect`](/getting-started/add-the-console#connect-from-the-terminal)
  signs you in, creates the connection with your local AWS credentials and adds the Stacktape stacks already in the
  account as projects and stages. Nothing is redeployed.
- **In the Console**, on the **AWS accounts** page, as described below.

Connecting costs nothing by itself. The Console is free while the AWS spend it manages for your organization stays at
or under $200 a month; see [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription). AWS bills your
account for the resources.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
headingPath: Connect an account in the Console
docs.content:
## Connect an account in the Console

You need to be an Owner or Admin of the organization.

1. Open **AWS accounts**. With no account connected yet, the page shows **Connect an AWS account**. To add another
   account later, click **Connect AWS account**.
2. Fill in **Account name**, a name your team recognizes, such as `production`. You use it in the CLI as
   `--aws-account production`.
3. Click **Open AWS CloudFormation**. AWS opens in a new tab with everything filled in.
4. At the bottom of the AWS page, check the box that lets CloudFormation create IAM resources, then choose **Create
   stack**.
5. Come back to the Console. Setup takes about a minute after you choose **Create stack**. The page shows
   **Connected** when it's done.

The role has administrator access, so Stacktape can create and update everything your configurations declare. See
[AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions) for what it can do and how to restrict it.

The connection stack is always created in `eu-west-1`. That doesn't limit where you deploy: your projects can deploy
to any region Stacktape supports.

To bring in stacks that were deployed before the account was connected, open the account's menu and choose **Find
existing stacks**.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
## Account status

The **Status** column on the AWS accounts page says what Stacktape can do with each account:

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| **Connected**, Can deploy | Stacktape deploys your projects here and shows their logs, metrics and costs. | Nothing. |
| **Connected**, Read-only | Stacktape shows logs, metrics and costs but can't deploy. | An Owner or Admin can click **Allow deploys**. |
| **Connecting** | The role is being created in AWS. | Wait; the page updates by itself. |
| **Setup not finished** | Someone started connecting, and AWS hasn't confirmed it. | Click **Finish setup** to see what to check. |
| **Could not connect** | The CloudFormation stack in AWS failed. | Click **Finish setup** to see what to do. |
| **No access** | The role was deleted in AWS, or Stacktape can't reach the account. | Disconnect the account, then connect it again. |

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content: ## Common tasks

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
### Connecting multiple AWS accounts

Organizations commonly connect separate AWS accounts for different purposes, such as a production account with stricter controls and a development account for experimentation. Click **Connect AWS account** and repeat the steps for each additional account.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
headingPath: Choosing the account for a CLI command
docs.content:
### Choosing the account for a CLI command

CLI commands that work with a deployed stack, such as `deploy`, `delete` and `rollback`, run in one connected account. The CLI picks it in this order:

1. `--aws-account <name>`, the account's name in the Console.
2. The account your local AWS credentials belong to: `--profile`, then `AWS_PROFILE`, then `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in the environment. The CLI reads the account ID from the profile's `sso_account_id` or `role_arn` when it can, and otherwise asks AWS STS.
3. The default saved with [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-set).
4. Your organization's only connected account.
