If the local credentials belong to an account that is not connected, the command stops before it changes anything and lists the connected accounts. It also stops when their account cannot be determined, for example when an SSO session has expired, and when a profile and environment keys point to different accounts. To deploy anyway, pass `--aws-account`, unset the profile, or connect the account.

`--aws-account` takes precedence over a profile; the CLI prints a line saying the profile is ignored. AWS credentials in environment variables are still used for the deployment when they are set, so they must belong to the selected account.

Each of these commands prints the account it uses, for example `AWS credentials loaded via Stacktape for account production (222222222222)`.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
### Revoking access

Revoking stops Console deploys to the account. Your deployed stacks keep running. You can revoke access in two ways:

- **Disconnect the account in the Stacktape Console**: open the account's menu on the AWS accounts page and choose **Disconnect account**. This removes the connection from Stacktape's side.
- **Delete the CloudFormation connection stack in the AWS Console**: this removes the IAM role from your AWS account. The Console then shows the account as **No access**.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
### Updating an older connection

A connection made from an older template shows an **Update** button next to it. It opens a dialog with the steps and a
link that updates the connection stack in AWS CloudFormation, so the [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log) can name the
person behind each AWS action.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
headingPath: Checking which regions an account uses
docs.content:
### Checking which regions an account uses

The **Regions** column of the AWS accounts page shows the regions each account has deployments in. Stacktape checks them once the account is connected.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
headingPath: Account stuck in Connecting or Setup not finished
docs.content:
### Account stuck in Connecting or Setup not finished

1. Click **Finish setup**. If you closed AWS before creating the stack, choose **Open AWS again**. If AWS reports a stack creation failure, the Console shows why.
2. Check that the stack is created in the **eu-west-1** region. The link the Console opens targets it automatically.
3. If you can't complete the AWS side, an Owner or Admin can remove the account from its menu and start a new connection.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
### Cannot disconnect an AWS account

<span id="cannot-delete-a-connected-aws-account" />

**Disconnect account** fails while Git deployments of a project target the account, and the error lists those projects. In each one, open the **Project settings** menu (the cog on the project page), choose **Configure Git deployments** and remove the rules that deploy to this account. Then disconnect again. Right after that, the Console may still be removing the account's [build runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners); try again a few minutes later.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
### Account shows No access

The connection is no longer usable: someone deleted Stacktape's role in AWS, or Stacktape can't reach the account. Deploys to it fail and its logs can't be shown. Disconnect the account, then connect it again.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
headingPath: "You do not have permission to manage AWS accounts"
docs.content:
### "You do not have permission to manage AWS accounts"

Connecting and disconnecting accounts is for Owners and Admins. Ask one of them, or ask for that role. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for details.

docs.title: Connecting your AWS account
docs.content:
## Related features

- [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions) — details on what the cross-account role can do
- [Organizations, projects, and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) — how connected accounts relate to your project structure
- [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) — deploy to connected accounts on push
- [Add the Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) — connect the Console to stacks you deployed with the CLI

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
# Console overview

The Stacktape Console is the web app for the stacks you deploy with Stacktape. It shows your projects and stages with their deployments, logs, metrics, errors, incidents and AWS costs. It also manages team access, Git deployments, alert channels, budgets, secrets and AWS account connections.

The Console is optional. The [CLI](/cli) is open source and deploys without it; see [Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli) for what needs the Console and why. The Console is free while your organization's managed AWS spend is up to $200 a month. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).

docs.title: Console overview
headingPath: Get your stacks into the Console
docs.content:
## Get your stacks into the Console

- **You already deploy with the CLI.** Run [`stacktape connect`](/cli/connect). It signs you in and connects the AWS account of your current AWS credentials. The stacks already in that account appear as projects and stages, without a redeploy.
- **You start in the Console.** Sign in, open **AWS accounts** in the Configuration group and click **Connect AWS account**. [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) walks through it. Then deploy with [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy), or connect a repository for [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

docs.title: Console overview
headingPath: Find your stack and its logs
docs.content:
## Find your stack and its logs

1. Open **Projects** at the top of the sidebar and select your project. A project is usually one repository, with stages such as `production` and `dev`. [Organizations, projects and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) explains how they relate.
2. Select the stage in the row of stages in the project header. Its page has the tabs **Overview**, **Activity**, **Costs**, **Configuration**, **Diagram** and **Danger zone**. Overview lists the stage's endpoints and resources.
3. Click a resource. Its tabs depend on its type. A web service has **Overview**, **Tasks**, **Logs**, **Metrics**, **Environment**, **Shell**, **Settings**, **Outputs** and **AWS** (the AWS resources behind it), plus **CDN** when it has one. A function has **Invoke** in place of Tasks and Shell, and a database adds **Backups** and **Queries**.


> Screenshot: A web service in a stage of the Console: its tabs, including Logs and Metrics, its running tasks, request, error rate, latency and CPU charts, and its latest log lines with an Open logs link Caption: A resource of the storefront production stage, with its latest logs.


The **Logs** page in the Observability group searches the logs of the whole organization. From the terminal, [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) reads the same logs. See [Logs](/observability/logs).

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
## The Projects home

**Projects** opens after you sign in. Before your first deploy, it shows how to make one and a search for stacks that are already in your connected AWS accounts. After that, **Your app** shows the stage you deployed most recently with its URL, its state and its recent deploys. The home also lists recent deployments of other projects, **Costs this month** with any budget that is over its limit, and the deploys of the last 30 days.

docs.title: Console overview
headingPath: What you can do in the Console
docs.content:
## What you can do in the Console

- Review deployments and AWS costs across projects and stages
- Respond to [incidents](/observability/incidents), which group signals such as a failing uptime check, a firing alarm or a new error in a production stage
- Read [logs](/observability/logs), [metrics](/observability/metrics) and [traces](/observability/tracing), and see the state of [uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) and [synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests)
- Triage runtime errors on the [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) page
- Review [security findings and vulnerable packages](/stacktape-console/security-scanning) from each deployment, and set [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) that every deployment must pass
- Create [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels), [notification rules](/observability/notifications) and [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets), and check delivery in [Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history)
- Manage secrets in AWS Secrets Manager and values in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
- Connect [AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account), [Git repositories](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) and [custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
- Manage [members and roles](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control), sign in through your identity provider with [single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on), and review the [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log)

Alarms, uptime checks and synthetic tests are defined in the Stacktape configuration and go live when the stack is deployed. The Console shows their state.

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
## Console navigation

The sidebar starts with **Projects** and **Incidents**, followed by five groups. Some items appear only when your role has the required permission; see [Permission-gated navigation](#permission-gated-navigation). Incidents, Error tracking, Security Overview and Alarms show a count when there is something to look at.

- **Organization**: Activity (the CLI operations of every project), [Costs](/managing-costs/dashboards), [Members](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control), [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys), [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log), [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on) and [Billing](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).
- **Observability**: [Logs](/observability/logs), [Metrics](/observability/metrics), [Traces](/observability/tracing), [Uptime](/observability/uptime-checks), [Synthetics](/observability/synthetic-tests) and [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).
- **Security**: [Overview](/stacktape-console/security-scanning) (findings and scores), Exposure (what the internet can reach), [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) and Settings.
- **Alerting**: [Channels](/observability/alert-channels) with their [notification rules](/observability/notifications), [Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history), [Alarms](/observability/alarms) and [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets).
- **Configuration**: [Secrets](/configuration/secrets), SSM parameters, [AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account), [Git connections](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console), [Runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners), Third-party providers and [Domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains).

The account menu in the header has **Account** (your [account settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings)) and **Sign out**. **Subscription plans** opens from Billing.

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content: ## Common tasks

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Viewing deployment activity

Open **Activity** in the Organization group. The page lists Stacktape CLI operations across your organization, so you can see who ran deploys, deletes, scripts, bucket syncs and other recorded commands. The **Activity** tab of a stage lists the operations of that stage.

For each recorded operation, the CLI sends the command, the project, stage, region and AWS account, the Git branch, commit and repository URL, the Stacktape version, timing and the result. It also sends the flags that name the target and change how the command runs, such as `--stage`, `--region`, `--config`, `--full`, `--auto-rollback`, `--no-cache`, `--target-version`, `--script-name`, `--resource-name` and `--bucket-id`. Flags whose value is free-form input are never sent: `--docker-args`, script `--env` values, commands, SDK inputs, secret values and API keys stay on your machine or CI runner.

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Managing secrets

Open **Secrets** in the Configuration group to manage sensitive values stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Secrets created here can be referenced in your Stacktape configuration. The page requires the `secrets:view` permission. See [Secrets](/configuration/secrets).

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Managing SSM parameters

Open **SSM parameters** in the Configuration group to manage values stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use parameters for non-sensitive configuration your workloads need at runtime, such as feature flags or endpoint URLs. Click **New parameter** to add one. The page requires the `ssm-params:view` permission.

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Setting up alarms

Alarms are defined in the Stacktape configuration, in the `alarms` list of a resource, and are created when the stack is deployed. The **Alarms** page in the Alerting group shows the current state of the CloudWatch alarms in your connected AWS accounts. See [Alarms](/observability/alarms).

Alarm rules created in the Console earlier are legacy. They are listed under **Legacy alarm rules** on the Alarms page and keep applying to matching deployments until the stack's configuration defines its alarms. Run `stacktape alarm export` to move them into your configuration.

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Tracking runtime errors

The **Error tracking** page in the Observability group is an error inbox for your deployed workloads. Stacktape reads runtime errors from your logs and groups repeated occurrences into one entry per distinct error and resource. Error tracking is on for every stage by default; a stack turns it off or limits it to some stages with `deploymentConfig.errorTracking`. The page requires the `issues:view` permission. See [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Inviting members

Open **Members** in the Organization group and click **Invite members**. Each member has a role that determines what they can view and change. The page requires the `members:view` permission. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Setting budgets

Open **Budgets** in the Alerting group and click **New budget**. Each budget monitors one connected AWS account for the calendar month. Stacktape creates the AWS budget when you save it and removes it when you delete the budget. The **Alerts sent** section on the same page lists the budget alerts that were sent. See [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets).

docs.title: Console overview
headingPath: Configuring alert channels and notification rules
docs.content:
### Configuring alert channels and notification rules

Channels are the destinations where alerts are delivered, such as a Slack channel, an email address or a webhook. Open **Channels** in the Alerting group and click **New channel**. The new channel's page opens; click **New rule** there to choose which events (for example a failed deployment, an opened incident or a changed secret) it receives. Adding rules requires the `org:manage-notifications` permission. **Sent alerts** lists every alert that was sent and its delivery status per channel.

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
## Permission-gated navigation

The Console uses role-based access control. Sidebar items are hidden when your role lacks the required permission:

| Navigation item | Required permission |
|---|---|
| Incidents | `incidents:view` |
| Members | `members:view` |
| API keys | `api-keys:manage-own` (not Viewers) |
| Audit log | `audit-log:view` (Owners and Admins) |
| Single sign-on | `sso:manage` (Owners only) |
| Costs, Billing | `org:view-billing` (Owners and Admins) |
| Error tracking | `issues:view` |
| Security group | `security:view` |
| Alarms | `org:manage-alarms` |
| Budgets | `org:manage-budgets` |
| Secrets | `secrets:view` |
| SSM parameters, Third-party providers | `ssm-params:view` |
| Git connections | Not Viewers |
| Domains | `domains:manage` |

Projects, Activity, Logs, Metrics, Traces, Uptime, Synthetics, Channels, Sent alerts, AWS accounts and Runners are shown to every role. Every role that sees the Security group can read Guardrails; only owners and admins (`org:manage-guardrails`) can change them.

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Cost data is not appearing

Cost reports are generated daily from AWS Cost and Usage Reports and may take up to a day to appear. If the Costs page shows no data, check that you have a connected [AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) and allow up to 24 hours for data to arrive.

docs.title: Console overview
headingPath: An alarm does not exist in AWS
docs.content:
### An alarm does not exist in AWS

Alarms are created when the stack is deployed. After you add an alarm to a resource's `alarms` list, run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) for the target stage. Legacy Console alarm rules also take effect only on the next deployment of each matching stage.

docs.title: Console overview
headingPath: The Error tracking page is empty despite errors in logs
docs.content:
### The Error tracking page is empty despite errors in logs

A stack reports errors only after it has been deployed with Stacktape v4 while signed in to the Console, because the log subscriptions are added during that deployment. Stacks you deployed without an account and brought in with `stacktape connect` need one signed-in deploy. Click **Settings** on the Error tracking page to open **Error tracking settings**: it shows whether error tracking is on for the organization and lists each deployed stack with whether its last deployment wired error tracking. Also check that the stack's `deploymentConfig.errorTracking` does not turn it off for that stage, and that the resource does not use `logging.logClass: infrequent-access`. See [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
### Sidebar items are missing

Some sidebar items need a permission your role may not have, for example Costs or Alarms. The [permission table](#permission-gated-navigation) lists them. An Owner or Admin of your organization can change your role; see [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#roles).

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content:
## Related pages

- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account): what the Console's access to your account is, and how to revoke it
- [Organizations, projects, and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages): how the Console organizes your work
- [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys): authenticate from the CLI and CI/CD
- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control): invite members and manage roles
- [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on): sign in through your identity provider and provision members with SCIM
- [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log): who changed what in your organization and its AWS accounts
- [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription): subscription details
- [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console): deploy on push
- [Observability overview](/observability/overview): incidents, alarms, error tracking and notifications in depth

docs.title: Console overview
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Console overview
headingPath: Does Stacktape deploy into my own AWS account?
docs.content:
### Does Stacktape deploy into my own AWS account?

Yes. Stacktape uses a cross-account IAM role to manage resources in your AWS account, so you never hand over long-lived AWS credentials. Connect more accounts from **AWS accounts** in the Configuration group. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for the required role.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
# Organizations, projects and stages

The Console organizes your work in three levels. An **organization** holds members, connected AWS accounts and projects. A **project** is one application, usually one Git repository. A **stage** is one deployment of that project, such as `production`, `staging` or `dev-alice`, with its own copy of every resource.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
## Organizations

Everything in the Console belongs to the organization you have open: projects, costs, alarms, members and billing. Switch organizations in the header.

Most teams need one organization. Create another for a separate boundary, such as each client of an agency, a business unit, or work that must not share members and AWS accounts. Each organization has its own plan and bill. Your personal organization has only you; to work with others, create a team organization. From the CLI, use [`stacktape org create`](/cli/org-create) and [`stacktape org list`](/cli/org-list).

An organization is not an AWS account. You connect one or more AWS accounts to it, and its stages deploy into them. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account).

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
## Projects

A project appears in the Console with its first deploy, from the CLI or from a Git push. There's no separate setup: [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) writes a config with `projectName`, and a signed-in deploy creates the project. Stacks you deployed before you had an account appear as projects when you run [`stacktape connect`](/cli/connect). **New project** in the Console shows the commands to run, and [`stacktape project create`](/cli/project-create) creates an empty project.

Projects are listed on the **Projects** home, the most recently deployed first.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
## Stages

A stage is one deployment of the project: its own CloudFormation stack, with its own databases, functions and URLs. Non-production stages in an AWS account and region usually share one VPC; [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments#are-stages-fully-isolated-from-each-other) explains what that means. Most teams deploy the same config to every stage and change sizes per stage in the config.

Each stage costs money for its always-on resources. Delete stages you no longer use.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
### Find a stage

Open a project. Its stages are a row of buttons in the project header, each with a dot for its state, so you see every stage's health on every page of the project. `production` and `staging` come first. Past five stages, the rest are in the menu at the end of the row, which has a **Find a stage** search and lists pull request previews under **Pull-request previews**. The AWS account and region of the open stage are at the right of the row.

Click a stage to open its overview: what is deployed, the resources and their URLs, recent deploys, logs, metrics and costs.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
### Create a stage

From the CLI, deploy with a new stage name:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage staging
```

In the Console, click **New stage** in the project header. Name the stage and pick the AWS account and region. A project with a connected Git repository also asks for the branch, commit and config, and **Deploy** starts the deploy on your runner. Without a repository, the page shows the CLI command to run. The new stage gets its own copy of every resource, and existing stages don't change.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
headingPath: Redeploy, roll back or delete a stage
docs.content:
### Redeploy, roll back or delete a stage

- **Redeploy** a stage from its overview. The Console asks you to confirm the commit, then shows the deploy's logs.
- **Roll back** with **Roll back to previous** on the stage's latest deploy, **Roll back to this** on an earlier deploy in its activity, or [`stacktape rollback`](/cli/rollback).
- **Delete** a deployed stage with [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete). It deletes the stack and its data. A Developer can delete only stages that are not production.

A failed first deploy shows as a failed stage until you deploy it again or dismiss it. Dismissing removes its deploy history from the Console; it doesn't touch AWS.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
### Project settings

The gear icon next to the project name opens the settings, for members with the `projects:update-settings` permission:

| Setting | Shown when | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Configure Git deployments** | A repository is connected | Opens [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) for the project |
| **Configure Runner** | Always | Sets the project's [build runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) |
| **Configure GitHub Actions runner** | A repository is connected | Sets up a [self-hosted GitHub Actions runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners) |
| **Delete project** | You also have `projects:delete` | Removes the project from the Console |

A project created by a CLI deploy has no repository until you click **Connect** on its page, or accept the CLI's offer to deploy on push after a deploy.

Deleting a project in the Console removes it from the Console only. Its deployed stages keep running in AWS, so delete them first with `stacktape delete`. [`stacktape project delete`](/cli/project-delete) refuses while stages exist and prints the commands to delete them.

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content:
## Who can do what

Owners and Admins can do everything here. Developers deploy, roll back and delete non-production stages in the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them. Viewers see their projects, deploys, logs and metrics. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
docs.content: ## Organizations, projects and stages FAQ

docs.title: Organizations, projects and stages
headingPath: Why does a new stage show $0?
docs.content:
### Why does a new stage show $0?

AWS reports costs about a day after they occur, so a stage deployed today shows its costs tomorrow. See [Cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards#when-numbers-are-missing).

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
# Security scanning

Every deploy checks the stack for risky settings and records which packages it uses. The **Security** section of the
Stacktape Console then shows, for each deployed stack, what should change, which packages have known vulnerabilities
and what the internet can reach.

Scanning only reports. It never stops a deploy, even for a critical finding. To block deploys that break a rule, use
[guardrails](/guardrails/overview). An owner or admin can turn on a finding's matching guardrail from the finding's
page (see [Blocking deploys with a guardrail](#blocking-deploys-with-a-guardrail)).

Scanning is on by default. It adds no AWS resources to your stack.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## What is checked

Each AWS account runs two kinds of checks, both on unless an organization owner or admin turns them off.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
### Configuration checks

While you deploy, the Stacktape CLI evaluates the stack's resolved configuration against the rules below. It adds no
noticeable time to the deploy.

| Finding | Severity | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Database reachable from the internet | High; low outside production | Guardrail: **Keep SQL and OpenSearch private** |
| Production database without deletion protection | Medium | Production only. Guardrail: **Protect databases from deletion** |
| Production data store without backups | Medium | Production only. Guardrail: **Require recoverable data stores** |
| Public load balancer without a web application firewall | Medium; low outside production | Guardrail: **Require WAF on application load balancers** |
| Bucket readable or writable by anyone | Medium | |
| IAM statement allows every action | High | |
| IAM statement grants a whole service on every resource | Medium | For example `s3:*` on `*` |
| Production stack without termination protection | Low | Production only. Guardrail: **Protect stacks from deletion** |
| Production container service runs a single instance | Low | Production only. Guardrail: **Require two container instances** |
| Queue without a dead-letter queue | Low; info outside production | Guardrail: **Require dead-letter queue** |
| Secret stored as a plain environment variable | Critical | A value in `environment` that looks like a credential |

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
### Dependency checks

The CLI also lists the packages the deployment uses: the packages in your lockfiles and the operating-system and
language packages inside every container image the deploy rebuilt. Images that were not rebuilt keep the packages from
the previous list. The CLI uses the Trivy scanner for this, which it downloads once (about 50 MB).

The list is a CycloneDX file stored in the stack's deployment bucket in your AWS account. After the deploy, the Console
reads it through your AWS account connection, checks every package against the [OSV.dev](https://osv.dev)
vulnerability database, and keeps only the vulnerabilities it finds. It checks every stack's latest list again every
night, so a vulnerability published after your deploy shows up without a new deploy.

Dependency checks run only when configuration checks run.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## The Security pages

The sidebar's **Security** group has four pages: **Overview**, **Exposure**, **Guardrails** and **Settings**.

**Overview** is where you start. Its summary counts the open findings to **Fix now** (critical and high) and to **Fix
when you can** (medium and lower), and how many of your stacks were scanned. Below it, the list of findings has the
severity, what to fix, the stack, when it was last seen and its status, and you can search it. It holds both kinds of
finding: configuration findings, including secrets found in environment variables, and vulnerable packages, with the
versions in use and the version that fixes them (**Fixed in**) or **No fix yet**.

Each stack also has a **Score**: it starts at 100 and loses 25 points for each open critical finding, 10 for each high,
3 for each medium and 1 for each low. Ignored findings don't count. A stack that was deployed but never reported shows
**Not scanned**, so a quiet row is not mistaken for a clean one. Click a stack's counts to see only its findings.

**Exposure** lists what the internet can reach in each stack: public endpoints and whether a web application firewall
protects them, how databases can be reached, and buckets that anyone can read or write. Being reachable is not a
finding by itself; the findings on Overview say what should change.

Click a finding to open its page. It shows **What was found** and **How to fix it**. A configuration finding also
explains **Why it matters**, and a vulnerability shows its **Advisory**: the advisory ID with a link to OSV.dev, other
IDs such as the CVE, the affected and fixed versions, the CVSS rating and references.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## When results appear

The CLI prints a one-line summary and the most severe findings in the output of `stacktape deploy` and
`stacktape validate`. `validate` also lists the findings that only apply to production.

The Console receives the findings after the deploy succeeds:

- **Configuration findings** appear right after the deploy.
- **Vulnerabilities** appear a few minutes later, once the Console has checked the package list. Until then the
  Overview shows **Checking…**. If the check fails, it shows **Check failed**; hover it for the reason. A failed check
  is retried automatically.

A stack is scanned only when it is deployed with Stacktape 4 or newer. Run `stacktape upgrade`, then deploy.

docs.title: Security scanning
headingPath: How a finding changes over time
docs.content:
### How a finding changes over time

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Open | The last deploy (or, for a vulnerability, the last check) found the problem. |
| Resolved | A later deploy or check no longer found it. It reopens on its own if the problem returns. |
| Ignored | Someone accepted the risk. It no longer counts as open, also after later deploys, until someone reopens it. |

An ignored finding reopens on its own when it comes back after being resolved, or when its severity rises to high or
critical, for example because the stage became a production stage. The earlier decision to ignore it does not carry
over.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## Production and non-production stages

Some rules matter only once real users depend on the stack, so their findings are reported for production stages only.
Others are reported at a lower severity outside production: a password-protected database that the internet can reach
is a reasonable default for a dev or preview stage, but a real exposure in production. The table in
[Configuration checks](#configuration-checks) shows both.

A stage counts as production when:

1. its `stackConfig.stageType` is `production`; otherwise,
2. it was created as a production stage in the Stacktape Console; otherwise,
3. its name is `prod`, `production`, `prd` or `live`, also with a number such as `prod2`.

The deploy output says which of these decided, for example ``stage `dev` is non-production by its name``. When a
non-production deploy skips production-only findings, it says how many there are; `stacktape validate` lists them.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content: ## Choosing what is scanned

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
### For an AWS account

Click **Settings** on the Security overview to open **Security settings**. The **AWS accounts** section has two
switches per connected account:

- **Configuration** turns the configuration checks on or off. Off means the account's stacks are not scanned at all.
- **Dependencies** turns the dependency checks on or off. It can be on only while **Configuration** is on.

A newly connected account runs both checks. Only organization owners and admins can change the switches. A change
to the configuration checks applies from each stack's next deploy. Turning **Dependencies** off also stops the
vulnerability checks of packages already listed, including the nightly re-check, and turning it back on resumes them
within about an hour, without a deploy. Findings already reported stay visible.

docs.title: Security scanning
headingPath: For a stack or some stages
docs.content:
### For a stack or some stages

Use `deploymentConfig.securityScanning` in the stack's configuration:

```yaml
deploymentConfig:
  securityScanning:
    enabled: true        # default; false turns scanning off for this stack
    stages: [production] # omitted or empty means every stage; names must match exactly
```

```ts
export default defineConfig(() => ({
  deploymentConfig: { securityScanning: { stages: ['production'] } },
  resources: { /* ... */ }
}));
```

When scanning is off for a stack or stage, nothing is evaluated, recorded or sent for it.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
### Which setting wins

The AWS account's setting in the Console wins over the configuration:

1. If the account has **Configuration** off, the stack is not scanned, whatever its configuration says.
2. Otherwise, `enabled: false` turns scanning off for the stack.
3. Otherwise, a stage that is missing from `stages` is not scanned.
4. Otherwise, the stack is scanned. Its dependencies are checked unless the account has **Dependencies** off.

The deploy output names the reason, for example
``Security scanning: off (turned off for AWS account `Production` in the Stacktape Console).``

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## Ignoring and reopening a finding

Open the finding and click **Ignore**. You can add a reason, which everyone in the organization sees on the finding.
Click **Reopen** on an ignored finding to count it as open again in the lists, the score and the sidebar badge.
Ignoring and reopening need the `security:manage` permission.

A finding resolves on its own when you fix the problem; you do not need to mark it.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## Fixing a finding

- **Configuration findings:** **How to fix it** lists the steps and the configuration change, in TypeScript or YAML
  (it starts with the format the stack was last deployed from). Change your configuration and deploy. The finding
  resolves after the next deploy that no longer has the problem.
- **Secrets in environment variables:** store the value with `stacktape secret set`, reference it with
  `$Secret('...')`, and rotate the credential. The old value stays in your Git history and in earlier deployments, and
  it stays valid until you revoke it. See [Secrets](/configuration/secrets).
- **Vulnerabilities:** upgrade the package to a version listed under **Fixed in**, in your lockfile or in the container
  image, and deploy. The vulnerability resolves after the next check that no longer finds it.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
### Blocking deploys with a guardrail

When a finding's rule has a matching guardrail, its page has a **Guardrail** section. It lists the stacks that the
guardrail would block, because they have the same finding open or ignored. An organization owner or admin can click
**Enforce as guardrail** to turn it on for the whole organization.

Once the guardrail is on, the next deploy of a stack that breaks the rule is blocked until the problem is fixed.
Ignoring the finding does not lift the block. Guardrails apply to every stage, including the non-production stages
where a production-only finding is not reported. See [Security and data protection
guardrails](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection).

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## Notifications

To hear about new findings, add a rule with the event **New critical or high security findings** to an
[alert channel](/observability/alert-channels). A new Slack (Stacktape app) channel has this rule by default. A channel
receives one message per deploy or nightly check that opens new critical or high findings in a stack. It lists the
first ten and links to the Console. The **When something is found** section of Security settings lists the channels
that receive these messages.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## Permissions

| Action | Permission | Roles |
|---|---|---|
| See the Security pages | `security:view` | Owner, Admin, Developer, Viewer |
| Ignore and reopen findings | `security:manage` | Owner, Admin, Developer |
| Change an AWS account's checks, enforce a finding as a guardrail | `org:manage-guardrails` | Owner, Admin |

Members limited to some projects see only the stacks of those projects. See
[Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## What leaves your AWS account

The CLI sends one report per deploy to the Stacktape Console. It contains:

- **Each configuration finding:** the rule ID, severity, title, message, fix description, resource name and type, an
  identifier that keeps the finding stable across deploys, and a few details: the database's accessibility mode, the
  index and actions of an IAM statement, or, for a secret, the kind of credential it looks like, the variable name and
  where it is set. **The value of a secret is never sent.**
- **Each exposure entry:** the resource name and type, how it can be reached, and whether a firewall protects it.
- **The package list's location:** the bucket, object key, SHA-256 hash, size, format and package count, the scanner
  name and version, and for each workload its name, how its packages were read, its package count and its image digest.
- **About the report:** the deployment it belongs to, the rule catalog version and the Stacktape version.

The package list itself stays in your deployment bucket. To check it, the Console reads the file through your AWS
account connection, keeps it in memory only, and sends each package's identifier (name and version) to OSV.dev. It
stores only the vulnerabilities it finds: the package, the versions in use, the workloads that run them, and the
advisory's IDs, summary, affected and fixed versions, rating and references.

docs.title: Security scanning
docs.content:
## Related pages

- [Guardrails overview](/guardrails/overview): rules that block deploys
- [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments): `stackConfig.stageType`
- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account)

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
# Single sign-on

Single sign-on lets your team sign in to Stacktape through your company's identity provider: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID,
Google Workspace, or any SAML 2.0 or OIDC provider. With SCIM, your directory also adds and removes members, so
disabling someone in the directory removes them from your Stacktape organization.

An organization Owner sets it up on the **Single sign-on** page in the Organization group of the sidebar. The page has
five steps, in this order: email domains, identity provider, test sign-in, access, and SCIM.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## Before you start

- **Plan.** Single sign-on and SCIM are part of the Flexible and Enterprise plans. On the Free plan the page shows an
  upgrade prompt. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).
- **Role.** Only Owners can see and change the page. Admins do not see it.
- **Access you need.** You must be able to add a DNS record for your company's email domain, and to create an
  application in your identity provider.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## What your members will see

After setup, people sign in like this:

1. On the Stacktape sign-in page, they click **Sign in with SSO** and enter their work email.
2. Stacktape sends them to your identity provider, and they sign in there.
3. They return to the Console, signed in.

Starting from the identity provider also works, for example from a Stacktape tile in the Okta dashboard.

The first SSO sign-in links the person to the Stacktape account with the same email address, or creates one. If they
are not a member of your organization yet, they join it with the [role for new people](#role-of-new-people). Existing members keep
their role.

An SSO sign-in counts as two-factor sign-in, because your provider enforces its own factors. `stacktape login` works
with SSO too: the CLI opens a browser page where the person signs in with SSO and approves the login.


> **Warning:** Anyone with an address in a verified domain whom your identity provider lets sign in to the Stacktape application
joins your organization. If you remove a
member on the Members page, they join again at their next SSO sign-in. To remove someone for good, remove them from the
Stacktape application in your identity provider, and remove them on the Members page or let [SCIM](#5-scim-provisioning)
do it.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## 1. Verify your email domains

People can sign in through your provider only with an address in a verified domain. You prove that your organization
owns a domain with a DNS record.

1. Under **1. Email domains**, enter the part after @ in your team's addresses, such as `acme.com`, and click
   **Add domain**.
2. The domain appears as **Not verified**, with a TXT record to create. Copy its **Name** and **Value** and add the
   record at your DNS provider. The name has the form `_stacktape-verification.acme.com`.
3. Click **Verify**. DNS changes can take up to an hour to appear. If Stacktape does not find the record yet, try again
   later.

The domain then shows **Verified**.

Keep the TXT record in place. Stacktape checks it daily. If the record is missing, the domain shows **Record missing**
with the date sign-ins will stop. After 7 days without the record, the domain is no longer verified, and people with
addresses in it can no longer sign in through your provider.

A few rules apply to domains:

- Public email providers, such as gmail.com or outlook.com, are refused.
- A subdomain is a separate domain. Add `eu.acme.com` on its own if your team uses it.
- A verified domain belongs to one Stacktape organization. An organization can claim at most 20 domains.

Removing a verified domain stops sign-ins through your provider for addresses in it, and SCIM can no longer add them.
Their Stacktape accounts and memberships stay.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## 2. Connect your identity provider

An organization has one connection. Under **2. Identity provider**, choose the **Protocol**: **SAML 2.0** suits Okta,
Entra ID and Google Workspace; **OIDC** suits providers that offer it.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### SAML 2.0

1. In your identity provider, create a SAML application for Stacktape.
2. Copy these values from the Stacktape page into the application:
   - **ACS URL**, also called the single sign-on URL or reply URL.
   - **Entity ID**, also called the audience URI or identifier.

   If your provider can import service provider metadata, click **Download metadata** instead.
3. Configure the application to send the person's email address as the Name ID, in the `emailAddress` format. The
   attributes `email`, `givenName`, `surname` and `groups` are optional. Microsoft Entra ID's default claims also work.
4. Make sure the provider signs its assertions with SHA-256 or stronger, and that it does not require signed
   authentication requests. Stacktape does not sign its requests.
5. Back in Stacktape, enter the application's **Metadata URL**, or paste the downloaded file into **Metadata XML** when
   the provider has no metadata URL.
6. Click **Save connection**.

Stacktape downloads a metadata URL once, when you save. When your provider changes its signing certificate, save the
connection again.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### OIDC

1. In your identity provider, create an OIDC web application for Stacktape. Set its redirect URI to the
   **Redirect URI** shown on the Stacktape page.
2. Allow client-secret authentication for the application (`client_secret_basic` or `client_secret_post`).
3. In Stacktape, enter the provider's **Issuer URL**, such as `https://acme.okta.com`, and the application's
   **Client ID** and **Client secret**.
4. Click **Save connection**.

Stacktape stores the client secret encrypted and never shows it again. When you edit the connection later, leave
**Client secret** empty to keep the saved one.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### Change or delete the connection

Saving a changed connection asks for a new successful test sign-in before you can turn enforcement on again. If
enforcement is already on, it stays on.

**Delete connection** stops all sign-ins through your provider and turns enforcement off. People keep their Stacktape
accounts and memberships and sign in another way.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## 3. Test the sign-in

**Test sign-in** checks the connection without signing anyone in. It needs a saved connection and at least one verified
domain.

1. Under **3. Test sign-in**, click **Test sign-in**.
2. Sign in at your identity provider as any person from a verified domain. Finish within 10 minutes.
3. You return to the Single sign-on page, still signed in as yourself.

**Last test** shows **Succeeded** or **Failed**. It shows what the provider sent (name, email, groups and attribute
names) or the exact error. You cannot require single sign-on until a test has succeeded.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content: ## 4. Access

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### Role of new people

**Role of new people** is the role a person gets when they first sign in through your provider or your directory adds
them: **Viewer** (the default), **Developer** or **Admin**. Owners and Admins can change anyone's role later on the
Members page.


> **Info:** A Developer or Viewer who joins through SSO or SCIM starts without projects or AWS accounts. An Owner or Admin gives
them access with **Edit access** on the [Members](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#project-and-aws-account-access)
page. An Admin reaches everything from the start.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### Require single sign-on

**Require single sign-on** makes your provider the only way into the organization for members whose address is in a
verified domain. It is off until you turn it on, and it needs a successful test sign-in first. Turn it on and confirm
with **Require SSO**.

While it is on:

- Members in your verified domains who signed in another way (password, passkey, Google or GitHub) see a
  **Sign in with SSO** screen instead of the organization. Their other organizations keep working.
- The password form refuses their address and tells them to use SSO.
- `stacktape login` for this organization works only when the login is approved from an SSO sign-in.
- API keys and CLI logins created before you turned it on keep working until they expire or are revoked.
- Members whose address is outside your verified domains, such as contractors, are not affected.


> **Tip:** Owners are exempt from the requirement, so a broken identity provider cannot lock the organization out. An Owner can
still sign in another way and fix or delete the connection.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## 5. SCIM provisioning

SCIM is optional. It lets your directory add and remove members, so that leaving the company also removes Stacktape
access.

1. Under **5. SCIM provisioning (optional)**, copy the **SCIM base URL** into your directory's provisioning settings.
2. Click **Create SCIM token**. Copy the token from the **Your SCIM token** dialog into your directory as the bearer
   token or secret token, then click **Done**. Stacktape keeps only a digest of the token and cannot show it again.
3. Assign people to the Stacktape application in your directory.

What the directory's changes do:

- **Assigning a person** adds them as a member with the [role for new people](#role-of-new-people). Only addresses in
  verified domains are accepted. If Stacktape already has an account with that address, the directory uses it and does
  not change its name or address.
- **Unassigning, deactivating or deleting a person** removes their membership, exactly as an Owner removing them on the
  Members page. Their CLI logins and personal API keys for the organization stop working. Stacks they deployed keep
  running. When no directory keeps them active any more, they are also signed out of every Console session.
- **Groups** are stored and shown in the test result, but they do not change roles yet.

The last Owner of an organization is never removed this way; the directory gets an error instead.

The **Bearer token** row shows when the token was created and last used.

- **Rotate token** creates a new token that replaces the old one at once. Update your directory immediately, or its
  next changes fail.
- **Revoke** stops your directory from adding or removing people. Everyone it added stays a member.

docs.title: Single sign-on
headingPath: If the organization moves to the Free plan
docs.content:
## If the organization moves to the Free plan

The connection keeps working, so nobody is locked out. You cannot change it until you upgrade again, but you can still
remove domains, delete the connection, revoke the SCIM token and turn enforcement off.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## Audit log

Every change on this page is recorded in the [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log), including refused attempts.
Members that SSO or SCIM add or remove appear as `member.provisioned` and `member.deprovisioned`, with Stacktape as the
actor and SSO or SCIM as the source.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Single sign-on
headingPath: Verify says no TXT record holds the value
docs.content:
### Verify says no TXT record holds the value

The record is not visible yet, or its name or value differs. DNS changes can take up to an hour. Some DNS providers add
your domain to the name automatically: then enter only `_stacktape-verification` as the name.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### "is verified by another Stacktape organization"

Another Stacktape organization verified the domain first. A domain belongs to one organization. Use that organization,
or ask its Owner to remove the domain.

docs.title: Single sign-on
headingPath: The test sign-in fails with "is not a verified domain"
docs.content:
### The test sign-in fails with "is not a verified domain"

The provider sent an address outside your verified domains. Check which address it sent in **Last test**. With
Microsoft Entra ID, make sure the address is the person's email address and not a sign-in name from another domain.
Otherwise, add and verify that domain.

docs.title: Single sign-on
headingPath: The test sign-in fails at the provider
docs.content:
### The test sign-in fails at the provider

Check the error under **Last test**. Common causes are unsigned assertions, SHA-1 signatures, a provider that requires
signed authentication requests, or an ACS URL or entity ID copied incorrectly.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### A member sees "requires single sign-on"

They signed in another way. They sign out, click **Sign in with SSO** on the sign-in page and enter their work email.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
### A removed member is back

Your identity provider still lets them sign in to the Stacktape application. Remove them there.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.content:
## Related features

- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control): roles, project and AWS account access
- [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log): who changed what in your organization
- [Account settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings): each person's own ways to sign in
- [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription): plans that include single sign-on

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
# Team and access control

The **Members** page in the Organization group of the Stacktape Console controls who can use your organization and
what they reach. Invite people, choose their role, projects and AWS accounts, require two-factor sign-in, and see what
stops working before you remove someone. Keys for CI are on the [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) page.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Overview

The page has up to three parts:

- **Sign-in rules** (Owners and Admins): whether members who sign in with a password must also use an authenticator
  app.
- **People**: everyone who has joined, with their role, what a Developer or Viewer reaches, two-factor status, when
  they were last active and when they joined. Search by name or email, filter by role, or show only members without
  two-factor or inactive for 30 days or more.
- **Pending invitations**: invitations that have not been accepted yet, who sent them, and when they expire.

Click a member's name to open their page. Owners and Admins can open anyone's page; Developers and Viewers can open
their own.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Roles

| Role | Can do | Reaches |
|------|--------|---------|
| Owner | Everything, including deleting the organization, billing and appointing other Owners | Every project and every connected AWS account |
| Admin | Everything except deleting the organization, setting up single sign-on and changing Owners | Every project and every connected AWS account |
| Developer | Deploy, delete non-production stages, manage secrets and parameters | Only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them |
| Viewer | Read projects, deployments, logs, incidents and members | Only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them |

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Project and AWS account access

A Developer or Viewer has two lists, set when you invite them and changed with **Edit access**:

- **Projects** decide which projects they see in the Console and which projects the CLI lets them deploy.
- **AWS accounts** decide where Stacktape gives them AWS access: CLI credentials for deploys, scripts and stack
  commands, deployments started from the Console, and the Console pages that read AWS directly (logs, metrics,
  secrets, parameters, debug sessions, redeploys and rollbacks, Investigate and Fix with AI).


> **Warning:** AWS access always covers the whole account. A Developer given the account `production` for the project `shop` can,
with the credentials the CLI receives, also reach other projects' stacks in `production`. Give a person an account
only if they may act in all of it. Agencies with one AWS account per client get a clean boundary by giving each
person only their clients' accounts.


A Developer with no AWS accounts can still see their projects in the Console, but the CLI refuses to deploy, and the
pages that read AWS say that their access does not include the account. Owners and Admins always reach every account.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Inviting members

1. Open **Members** and click **Invite members**.
2. Enter one or more email addresses, separated by commas or new lines (up to 20 at once).
3. Choose a role. For a Developer or Viewer, choose their projects and AWS accounts.
4. Click **Send invitations**.

Someone who already has a Stacktape account becomes a member at once. Anyone else gets an email and appears under
**Pending invitations** until they sign up. An address that is already a member, or that could not be invited, stays in the
field with the reason, so the rest are not lost.

An invitation works for 14 days after its email last went out. **Resend invitation** sends it again and starts the
14 days again; an expired invitation can be resent the same way. **Copy invite link** copies the sign-up link to
share another way; it only works for the invited address. **Cancel invitation** stops the link from working.

Personal organizations have exactly one member. To work with others, create a team organization; team organizations
have no member limit.

With [single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on), people from your company's email domains can also join
without an invitation, by signing in through your identity provider or being added by your directory.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Organization keys for CI

A personal API key acts as the person who created it and stops working when they leave the organization, so CI that
uses one breaks when that person is removed. Give CI an organization key instead: it belongs to the organization and
has a role of its own. Owners and Admins create it on **Organization → API keys**; see
[Create an organization key](/stacktape-console/api-keys#create-an-organization-key).

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Requiring two-factor sign-in

Owners and Admins can require two-factor sign-in with **Require** in **Sign-in rules**. Members must then sign
in with a passkey, Google, GitHub, single sign-on, or a password with an authenticator app; a password alone is not
enough. The confirmation lists the members who sign in with a password only. After that, those members see only a
screen that sends them to [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings) to add an authenticator app or a
passkey; the rest of the organization opens again as soon as they sign in that way. API keys, including the CLI and CI,
keep working.

You need two-factor sign-in on your own account before you can require it.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Removing a member

Open the member's row menu, or their page, and choose **Remove**. The dialog lists what stops working with them:

- their personal API keys, with when each was last used,
- their own AI subscriptions for incident runs,
- their Slack link.

If one of their keys was used in the last 7 days, the dialog says so, because CI may depend on it, and offers to
create an organization key first. Stacks they deployed keep running, their deployments stay in the history, and
organization keys keep working, including ones they created.

**Revoke API keys** in the row menu revokes a member's personal keys without removing them.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Last active

The Last active column shows the most recent of three times, listed separately when you hover it and on the member's
page:

- **Console**: their last visit, recorded at most once an hour.
- **CLI**: the last request with one of their personal API keys.
- **Last deploy**: the last deploy they started.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Team and access control
headingPath: "Your access does not include the AWS account"
docs.content:
### "Your access does not include the AWS account"

The member is a Developer or Viewer and the account is not in their AWS accounts. An Owner or Admin adds it with
**Edit access** on the Members page. The CLI shows the same reason, and `stacktape` lists only the accounts the member
can use.

docs.title: Team and access control
headingPath: The CLI stopped deploying for a Developer after an upgrade
docs.content:
### The CLI stopped deploying for a Developer after an upgrade

Developers and Viewers reach only the AWS accounts chosen for them. When this was introduced, each of them was given
the accounts their projects had deployed to; an account their projects never used must be added with **Edit access**.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
### Invite members is disabled

Either your role cannot invite (only Owners and Admins can), or this is a personal organization.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
### An invitation shows Expired

Its 14 days passed. Choose **Resend invitation**; the person can sign up for 14 more days.

docs.title: Team and access control
docs.content:
## Related features

- [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings): password and two-factor authentication
- [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on): sign-in through your identity provider, and SCIM
- [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log): member, key and access changes, and AWS events
- [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys): organization keys for CI and personal keys
- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account): what Stacktape can do in an account
- [Organizations, Projects, and Stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages)

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
# Agent mode in dev

`stacktape dev --agent` runs [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) as a background session with a local HTTP API. A coding agent, or any HTTP client, uses it to check workload status, rebuild workloads, read logs, query local databases and call read-only AWS operations, so it can edit, test and fix code in a loop. This page calls that session agent mode. On other commands, `--agent` only switches the output to JSONL and turns off prompts.

Agent mode is in preview: `GET /` on the running agent lists the endpoints it has.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
## When to use

Agent mode is designed for workflows where an AI coding assistant drives the edit-test-fix loop. Enable it when:

- **AI-driven development** — You're using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, or another AI coding assistant to build your application. The assistant starts `stacktape dev --agent` as a shell command, then uses the HTTP API to check status, rebuild workloads, read the log file path, query local databases, call AWS SDK commands, and stop dev mode.
- **Automated test harnesses** — You want a script to verify application behavior during development by hitting the status, env, or database endpoints.
- **Database inspection without client tools** — You need to run SQL queries, check Redis keys, scan DynamoDB items, or search OpenSearch indices against local dev databases without installing separate database clients.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
## When not to use

- **Manual development** — If you're editing code yourself and checking results in a browser, standard [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) without `--agent` is simpler. The TUI output is optimized for human reading.
- **Production observability** — Agent mode runs locally. For deployed stacks, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs), [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics), or the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).
- **CI/CD pipelines** — Use [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) directly in your pipeline. Agent mode is a development-time feature.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
## Starting agent mode

Add the `--agent` flag to the [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) command to start the HTTP API server alongside your workloads. Agent mode is dev mode, so it changes your AWS account the same way: the first start deploys the stage's dev stack, and the account's dev network when deployed functions need it. Lambda functions run in AWS; containers and databases run on your machine. [Dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) explains what runs where and what it costs.

```bash
stacktape dev --agent --agent-port 9900 --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

| Flag            | Description                                                                              |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--agent`       | Enables the agent HTTP API server alongside dev mode                                     |
| `--agent-port`   | Port for the agent HTTP server                                                           |
| `--stage`       | Stage used for dev mode and the `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` directory                 |
| `--region`      | Session AWS region; `/aws/sdk` rejects any different region   |
| `--resources`   | Which workloads to run (`all` or comma-separated names)                                  |
| `--fresh-db`     | Reset local database data on startup                                                     |
| `--yes`         | Confirms creating a project that does not exist yet. `--agent` never confirms it; without `--yes` the start fails with `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` |

Once ready, Stacktape prints the agent URL and a summary of available endpoints. Local database data persists in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` between runs — see [reset scope](/local-development/local-databases#resetting-local-data) before using `--fresh-db`. It resets prepared databases, including relay dependencies, and DynamoDB Local tables share storage.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
### Startup progress

A first start creates the account's dev network and the stage's dev stack and takes several minutes; a warm start takes seconds. While the agent starts, the command prints one JSONL `event` line per step with `"phase": "DEV_STARTUP"`, so an assistant can tell a long start from a hung one:

| `eventType`    | Reports                                                                                         |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEV_SESSION`  | The agent's port and token file first (`detail.kind: "dev-agent"`), the project, stage, region and config file the session resolved (`detail.kind: "dev-target"`), a heartbeat every 20 s, and "Dev session ready" |
| `DEV_NETWORK`  | Creating, updating or reusing the dev network                                                   |
| `DEV_BOX`      | Starting the dev box and connecting to it                                                       |
| `DEV_STACK`    | Creating or updating the dev stack; CloudFormation `UPDATE_STACK` events carry resource counts  |
| `DEV_WORKLOAD` | Each workload starting and running, or its error (`instanceId` is the workload name)            |
| `DEV_DATABASE` | Each local database starting and running, or its error                                          |

If the start fails, the final `result` line carries the failure's own code and hints, for example `CLI_DEV_STACK_CONFLICT` with how to resolve it. Dev mode never updates or deletes a stack it did not create. A dev stack in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` requires explicit deletion before another start; `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` permits another start. A stack still rolling back or in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` must finish or recover before an update can proceed. A Lambda build/deploy failure may leave the agent running with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES` and `ready: false`; inspect status and rebuild it.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
## Authentication

The agent listens on `127.0.0.1` only and accepts a request only when it carries the session's token. Each `stacktape dev --agent` run creates a new random token and stores it in `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token` in your home directory (`%USERPROFILE%\.stacktape\dev-agent-tokens\{port}.token` on Windows). Because the file is named after the agent's port, any of your tools can find it from any directory. Only your user can read the file. Stacktape deletes it when the agent stops, and an agent that starts later removes the files of agents that were killed. The startup message and the `AGENT_READY` result print the file path, never the token.

Every request must send the token in an `Authorization: Bearer` header. POST requests must also send `content-type: application/json`. The examples on this page use these shell variables:

```bash
AGENT=http://127.0.0.1:9900
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/9900.token)"
JSON='content-type: application/json'

curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/status
```

The agent refuses requests that a web page or another machine could send:

| Request                                                              | Response                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| No token or a wrong token                                            | `401 UNAUTHORIZED`           |
| A `Host` header other than `127.0.0.1:{port}` or `localhost:{port}`  | `403 FORBIDDEN`              |
| Any request with an `Origin` header (sent by browsers)               | `403 FORBIDDEN`              |
| A POST without `content-type: application/json`                      | `415 UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` |

The 401 response names the token file, so a coding assistant that forgot the header can recover on its own. [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop) and the [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) read the token file themselves. `dev stop` stops the agent of the project in the current directory; pass `--cwd <directory>` for another project directory and `--stage <stage>` when several stages run.


> **Tip:** AI coding assistants can call `GET /` on the agent server to receive a full endpoint listing dynamically. Use `GET /?compact=true` for a shorter LLM-oriented response — it includes the current phase, workload names, available local resources with their primary query/schema endpoints, core action templates (rebuild, logs, env, aws, stop), and a pointer to `GET /` for full docs.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
## Response format

Every agent endpoint wraps its result in a consistent JSON envelope so clients can handle success and error uniformly.

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "message": "OK",
  "data": {}
}
```

| Field     | Description                                                                          |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `v`       | Envelope version (currently `"1.0"`)                                                 |
| `ok`      | `true` on success, `false` on error                                                  |
| `code`    | Machine-readable status. Common values include `OK`, `NOT_FOUND`, `VALIDATION_ERROR`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`, `ALREADY_EXISTS`, `AUTH_ERROR`, and `READ_ONLY_VIOLATION` |
| `message` | Human-readable description (optional — most responses include it, but not all)       |
| `data`    | Endpoint-specific payload (optional — present when the endpoint returns structured data) |

Many not-found and validation errors include contextual hints in `data`, such as an `available` array of valid resource names or a `hint` string describing expected input. For example, referencing a non-existent workload returns the list of available workloads in `data.available` and a usage hint in `data.hint`. This makes it easy for AI agents to self-correct without extra calls.

Agent endpoints return a JSON envelope with `v`, `ok`, and `code` on every response; most successful responses also include `message` and endpoint-specific `data`. Response examples throughout this page may omit envelope fields like `v` for brevity.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content: ## Core endpoints

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
### Status

The `/status` endpoint reports the current agent phase and a map of workload names to their local URLs (if running) or status strings. AI agents should poll this endpoint after starting dev mode and wait for `"ready"` before testing workload URLs.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/status
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "phase": "ready",
    "ready": true,
    "failedWorkloads": [],
    "workloads": {
      "api": "http://localhost:3000",
      "worker": "running"
    },
    "sessionId": "0b6c…",
    "projectDirectory": "/home/me/my-app",
    "projectName": "my-app",
    "stage": "dev",
    "region": "eu-west-1",
    "pid": 12345
  }
}
```

`sessionId`, `projectDirectory`, `projectName`, `stage` and `region` identify the session; `dev stop` and the MCP server use them to find the agent of a project.

The `phase` value is one of `starting`, `ready`, `rebuilding`, `stopping`, or `stopped`. Phase becomes `ready` once dev mode has started every selected workload and local resource, and `/stop` moves it to `stopping`. The `ready` field is `true` only when the phase is `ready`, every workload is `running`, and the configuration file still matches the one the session started with. A container workload with a port is `running` once that port accepts connections, after a start and after a rebuild; one that does not within 120 seconds gets the status `error`. A workload that failed, crashed or failed to rebuild makes `ready` false and appears in `failedWorkloads` with its error, so an assistant waiting for `ready` never tests against a workload that is down or runs outdated code. When the configuration file changed, `ready` is false and `restartRequired` explains that dev mode has to restart (see [Rebuild](#rebuild)). A frontend whose running dev server printed an error, such as a request that failed in the app's code with its cause, stays `running` and keeps the session ready, because its server still serves: the error is in `requestErrors` (and the workload's `requestError` in verbose mode) until the next successful request, compile or code update.

If a workload fails while `stacktape dev --agent` is starting, the command stops the session, prints each failed workload with its error and the log file path, and exits with a non-zero code.

For detailed information including uptime, per-workload type/port/error data, local resource status, and the log file path, use verbose mode.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" "$AGENT/status?verbose=true"
```

The verbose response replaces the workload string map with an array of objects containing `name`, `type`, `status`, `url`, `port`, and `error` fields, plus a `localResources` array, `uptime` in seconds, and the `logFile` path. Workload `status` is one of `pending`, `starting`, `running`, `error`, or `stopped`. Local resource status uses the same values.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
### Logs

The `/logs` endpoint returns the path to the JSONL log file on disk. Logs are **not** streamed through the HTTP response — AI agents should read the file directly using standard tools like `tail`, `grep`, or `jq`.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/logs
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "logFile": ".stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt",
    "format": "jsonl",
    "hint": "Use standard tools: tail -n 50 <logFile> | jq ."
  }
}
```

Each line in the log file is a JSON object with these fields:

| Field    | Example                      | Description                           |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `ts`     | `"2025-03-15T14:30:15Z"`    | When the line was produced. For a deployed function, the CloudWatch event time, not the time it was fetched |
| `source` | `"api"`, `"dev"`             | Workload or database that produced the line, or `dev` for dev mode itself |
| `level`  | `"info"`, `"warn"`, `"error"` | Severity level                      |
| `msg`    | `"Server started on :3000"`  | Log message content, without terminal colors |

Lines with `"source":"dev"` record dev mode's own lifecycle: startup steps, file changes, rebuilds started, finished or failed with the error, dev stack updates and dev box state. Grep them to see what dev mode did, for example whether a rebuild failed:

```bash
grep '"source":"dev"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

A restart keeps the previous session's lines. Each session appends to the file and starts with a `"msg":"Dev session started"` line whose `session` field names its session ID, project directory and stage. A file over 10 MB moves to `<file>.1` when the next session starts.

Deployed dev functions keep their source maps and run with `--enable-source-maps`, so stack traces in the log point at your source files rather than the bundle.

View the last 50 lines:

```bash
tail -n 50 .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter for errors only:

```bash
grep '"level":"error"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter by a specific workload:

```bash
grep '"source":"api"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

This file-based approach is intentional — AI coding assistants already have file-reading tools, and `tail -f` provides real-time streaming without polling overhead.

docs.title: Agent mode in dev
docs.content:
### Environment variables

The `/env/{workload}` endpoint returns the environment variables available to a specific workload. For Lambda functions, variables are fetched from the deployed AWS function configuration. A function that uses a local database shows that database's `STP_*` variables with the address of the [dev box](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#connecting-to-local-databases), through which the function reaches it.
